en: The First Chapter:
Now, therefore, the qualification [for action]. 1.
Actions accompanied by fruits. 2.
Because there is no distinction among all [beings] (3);
or rather, it refers to humans because of their capacity for undertaking [the ritual] (4);
excluding those who lack limbs, those ignorant of the Vedas, eunuchs, and Śūdras (5).
[The eligibility for Vedic study belongs] to Brāhmaṇas, Rājanyas, and Vaiśyas, because of the Śruti;
and the woman [is also eligible], because there is no distinction [in the texts]; and because it is seen [in the scriptures].
Regarding the kindling of the sacred fires by a chariot-maker,
[the fire] is obligatory;
Vātsya says it is not so, because of the absence [of the qualification].
The Niṣāda-sthapati is authorized for the Gāvedhuka sacrifice; or, for one who has broken his vow of chastity (avakīrṇin), there is the sacrifice with a donkey,
which is performed in the common fire.

The cooking of the animal sacrificial cake (paśupuroḍāśa) takes place on the ground; the offering of the cut-off portions (avadāna) takes place in the waters; the cutting off of the portion for the Prāśitra is from the penis.
In the Vaitānika rites, everything [is used] because they serve all purposes (sūtra 18);
and because it is so seen (sūtra 19);
and because there is no scriptural mention of the Āvasathya fire (sūtra 20).
21. There is a prohibition against meat in the vessel used for placing [the oblation] on the fire.
1. We shall explain the sacrifice (yajña). 2. [The sacrifice consists of] the substance, the deity, and the renunciation (tyāga).
The other [acts] are subsidiary to that [principal act] by virtue of being mentioned together and by context (3).
And those sacrifices (*yajati*) which are not connected with a fruit are subsidiary to that [principal act] (4).
What is the distinction between *yajati* and *juhoti*? (5)
The *yajatis* are those sacrifices performed while standing, characterized by the offering with the *vaṣaṭ*-call, and accompanied by both the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses.
(6) The *juhotis* are those sacrifices performed while sitting, characterized by the offering with the *svāhā*-call.
(7) The Brahmins are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), because the consumption [of the sacrificial food] is prohibited for the other two [classes]. (8)
And because [the texts] show that one may act according to one's desire at the commencement of rites associated with specific results, since there is a desire for those results;
for there is no restrictive cause for engaging in the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, the Dākṣāyaṇa, the Āgrayaṇa, or animal sacrifices.
Some say [it is so] because of the scriptural mention of the four-faced one (Caturmukha) in the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, and because of its fixed recitation together [with that].
And because it is seen [in scripture],
and because of its connection with non-abandonment,
it should be like the case of the thirty [days].
The production of the fruit occurs even when there is a deficiency [in the ritual], due to the distinction between the auxiliary and the principal elements (18),
because of the prescription of expiatory rites (19),
and because it is observed to be so (20).
Not so, because it is based on scriptural injunction;
the expiation is to be performed at that time;
its extent is determined by what is observed.

The *ṛc*s, *yajus* formulas, *sāman* chants, *nigadas*, and *mantras*— their syntactical unit (vākya) is that which is independent of further expectancy (nirākāṅkṣa) and mutually connected (mithaḥ saṃbaddha).

In the commencement of those [rites], the arrangement is according to their purpose, because they are so designated; 4. the beginning of the rite is to be performed with the ends of the mantras, because of the expression of the connection;
5. Vātsya maintains there is no fixed rule.
The teachers [state that] "ādi" (beginning) refers to the first; they are thus called "ādya" (initial); by means of the "para-ādi" (subsequent-beginning), the prior limit is established.
The performance is in a low voice, according to the Śruti;
there are no formal calls (sampraiṣas);
the sacrificial grass is made of Kuśa.
13. The measurement follows from the sense.
14. The sacrificial grass bundles have an uneven number of stalks.
15. He arranges the sacrificial grass with its tips pointing eastward in front of the bundles that have their tips pointing northward.
16. He places the fuel-stick with its tip pointing eastward upon the grass that has its tips pointing upward. 17. He hides the knots [of the grass] toward the west.
18. The fuel consists of eighteen sticks made from trees suitable for sacrificial enclosures.
Or twenty-one (19); then some [say] there are enclosing-sticks (20);
the water to be carried forward is immeasurable, minus three (21).
Having inspected the clarified butter, the sacrificer makes the *veda* (sacrificial grass-bundle) with the formula,
"Thou art the Veda" (22)— consisting of a handful of *kuśa* grass, twisted to the left, reaching to the calf's knee, and having three strands or being made of *mūta* grass (23).
Those desiring cattle, spiritual luster, or food should do so respectively (24).
The word "āmuṣmāt" (from that) is used in ritual acts;
furthermore, it is used in the sense of "limitation"; and there is the extraction of each individual act when there is no [general] application.
One whose ritual duties have ceased is a worldly person because of his connection with material objects.

(28) An injunction not arising within a specific context is a general statement (*anārabhyavāda*); it applies to all qualities because it lacks a specific basis. (29) And because there is no distinction within the context. (30)
And because it is so seen [in scripture]:
31. the vessels are made of *vaikaṅkata* wood; 32. the *sruva* ladle is made of *khadira* wood. 33.
The wooden sword (sphya) [is made of khadira wood], the juhū ladle is made of palāśa wood, and the upabhṛt ladle is made of aśvattha wood.
The *vāraṇa* ladles are joined with handles;
they are one cubit (*bāhu*) in length, with bowls one span (*pāṇi*) wide, hollowed out like a skin, with pouring-spouts shaped like the beaks of swans, and having roots for their handles.
(37–38) The *sruva* spoon is one *aratni* in length, with a bowl as round as the joint of a thumb. (39)
The *sphya* is shaped like a sword; the *prāśitraharaṇa* is shaped like a mirror or like a *camasa* cup.
The path of movement is between the *cātvāla* pit and the *utkara* heap.
In the *iṣṭi* sacrifices, it is between the *praṇītā* water-vessel and the *utkara*.
1. In the absence of an injunction, there is no undertaking [of a substitute], because that [undertaking] is established by that [injunction].
2. In the case of a fixed [substance], there may be a substitute in general. 3. From the undertaking [of the substitute], there is a restriction.
And there would be a fault if [the sacrifice] were not completed, because of its similarity;
and because it is seen [in scripture]; the observation is for another purpose, not for the sake of re-grasping.
The repetition [of the word "vow"] is for the sake of another purpose; there is no application [of the term] to a religious observance (*vrata*) because of the word "restriction" (*niyama*);
there is no disagreement regarding the word.
[The *soma* sacrifice is used] because of the absence of [the word for] species;
[it is used] in the case of clarified butter (*ājya*) because it is not seen [therein]; and in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), because of the wording of the mantra.
And because of the scriptural injunction, [the substitute] is employed as an alternative; since it is a different ritual act, [it applies] in the case of a substitute during its own time;
when there is a conflict between the purpose and the substance, the commonality of the purpose prevails, because the ritual is directed toward that.

Between a quality (*guṇa*) and a substance (*dravya*), the substance [is predominant] because of its connection with the primary [element]; (17) not because of equality; (18) and because of the subservience of the qualities. (19)
The sequence of ritual acts is not due to their simultaneous occurrence (1),
nor because of the accomplishment of the purpose (2);
rather, there may indeed be a rule of sequence based on the order of the Vedic revelation and the order of the purpose (3).
And the archetypal [rule] applies to the modified form;
4. in case of conflict, the meaning prevails because it is directed toward that specific purpose;
5. direct Vedic statement (śruti) prevails over order because it is inferential (ānumānika).
In the case of the impelling of a mantra, there is the power of the mantra because it is employed [as such];
(7) not because of equality; (8) but rather because of the abundance of qualities. (9)
In the case of equal simultaneous occurrence, the general rule takes precedence due to its connection with the established sequence;
(10) because there is no connection with a single action; (11) but in the cases of taking up, placing down, cutting off, and offering, it is so because of a specific scriptural injunction. (12)
Vātsya [holds that] there is no [difference in the result] because of the connection with the quality despite the difference in substance; 13.
[The rule applies] invariably when [the rite] has commenced, due to a specific defect; 14.
But in the case of the *ṣoḍaśin* [cup], because of the greater number of the sequence. 15.
There is no fixed rule regarding those [rites] connected with specific results (16).

The sequence is for the purpose of an injunction, because it is impossible [to establish such a sequence] in the case of the ritual action itself (17). When the portion cut off is lost, another [portion] should be used, because it favors the subordinate qualities (guṇa) (1).
Not so, because it is not a remnant of what preceded (2), because it is not enjoined [as such] (3),
and because it is connected with a sequence of order like the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering (4).
But in the case of the loss of a quality, [the rite continues] because of the existence of the remainder; (Sūtra 5).
The deity, fire, word, and action are not [abandoned], because they exist for the sake of another; (Sūtra 6).
One may [invoke] the deity at will; (Sūtra 7).
That which is prohibited [is not to be performed] because it entails sin (pratyavāya). 8.
The owner [of the material] [is the performer] because of his connection with the fruit. 9.
There is a substitute for secondary elements (guṇa), because they exist for the sake of another. 10.
But in the case of sacrificial sessions (*satra*), [the sacrificer is the officiant] because of the scriptural statement;
he possesses those duties because of his connection with the ritual act;
and sacrificial sessions belong to Brāhmaṇas because of the scriptural mention of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
14. Because there is no deficiency in the single ritual acts;
15. because it is not for the sake of another;
16. [the office of] the Gārhapatya belongs to the Vaiśya and the Rājanya.
[The thousand-year lifespan] cannot exist because it is impossible for non-human beings [to live that long];
(17) it could [only] exist [if the body were eternal], but the body is impermanent; (18) and because that [body] is something produced. (19)
20. Not so, because of impossibility;
21. Because of the possibility [of such a rule] according to Bhāradvāja;
22. Not so, because it is not observed.
Kārṣṇājini says it is a family-sacrifice (kula-satra); Laugākṣi says it is a simultaneous rising [of all members];
or rather, because of the impossibility [of such a duration] within a single day.
Because of the force of the scriptural statement (26),
and because of the favoring of the original context (27),
the simultaneous occurrence of the ritual acts constitutes a *tantra* (a single performance). 1.

[The difference between rites is established] from the scriptures concerning their being produced by human effort that is capable [of accomplishment], and concerning their inherence in a single object;
[and it is established] when there is a difference in the fruit, the action, the place, the time, the substance, the deity, and the quality, there is a difference [in the rite]. 2–4.
5. Place and time [are not restricted] in case of conflict, because there is an instruction for the whole.
6. In a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*), there is an indication of all [days] regarding the *subrahmaṇyā* formula, as in the archetype (*prakṛti*).
7. In that [case], the time and the ritual act [apply] daily, because there is no specific injunction for each individual day.
When there is a repetition of an action involving a single substance, the mantra is recited only once, because it has already been performed [once].
However, this is not the case for the acts of taking up [the vessel], cutting [the grass], spreading [the strew], and taking up the clarified butter (ājya).
Regarding the taking up of the clarified butter, however, it is recited [repeatedly] because of a specific scriptural injunction.
And in the case of the best [quality] fist, [the penance is] eleven [units].

But in the cases of dreaming, crossing a river, being rained upon, seeing impurity, and setting out on a journey, [the penance is] performed only once, because the time, the substance, and the purpose are one;
it is not [repeated] due to a difference in the occasion.
The time for the secondary [acts] is not fixed because they do not occur simultaneously;
the sacrificial post (yūpa) and the wooden chip (svaru) [are used] because of the mention of the ritual conclusion (saṃsthā). 14, 15, 16.
And because it is through that [nature] that activity occurs, the master is the primary agent among men, due to his connection with the fruit.

Because of the capacity for the abandonment of both human agency and the consecration of mantras; (20) because of a specific scriptural statement, there is something else; (21) the remainder belongs to the others according to their respective names. (22)
Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (upavītin), facing either east or north; at the ends of the circumambulations, one should proceed clockwise (pradakṣiṇa).

But when [the sacrifice] is reversed, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is given once for each of those [substances] belonging to the father; 26. When there is the attainment of the status of being the primary substance, there is a repetition of the rite together with its subsidiaries because of that injunction; 27.
For there is an injunction for the undertaking of all [subsidiaries], since the qualities have a single purpose. 1.
Because it is already accomplished,
because it is not to be undertaken,
and because it is observed.
If it is argued that the Vedic scripture would be rendered purposeless,
[we reply] that it would be purposeful at another time;
in the case of mere dharmas, there is a combination when there is no contradiction.
8. [The rule applies] to the *hotṛ* and the *adhvaryu*.
9. Not so, because of the contradiction regarding the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses.
10. And because of the observation [of this fact].
Because of the destruction of the fault through expiations (11),
because it is not heard [in scripture] otherwise (12), and because of direct perception (13).
Or rather, it may be so because of the observation [of usage] (sūtra 14); no, because it serves another purpose (sūtra 15);
and in a mantra, the application of accents is according to the traditional recitation, as there is no distinction [stated to the contrary] (sūtra 16).
Either the *bhāṣika* accent applies because of the instruction regarding the mantra as it occurs [in common speech],
or the *tāna* [monotone] applies because of its permanence;
there is monotony (*ekaśruti*) when addressing someone from a distance, except for the *subrahmaṇyā*, *sāman*, *japa*, *nyūṅkha*, and the duties of the sacrificer during sacrificial rites.
The conceptualization of number [is not established] because it is connected with the act of giving (20).

There is a combination of *ūvadhyas* (omentum), *vasā* (fat), *adhyūdhnī* (the upper part of the belly), and *vaniṣṭhu* (testicles) based on the substance, its preparation, and their differentiation (21).
And this applies to the subordinate qualities (*guṇa*) in injunctions (*codanā*) due to the connection with the established ritual procedure (22).
One should not pass between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires. Turning away or turning back is another way of proceeding. Departing after having passed [between them] is also [permitted].
The sacrifice proceeds from the north (26);
the seats for the Brahman and the sacrificer are to the south (27); the sacrificer stands behind, touching the altar (28).
The Adhvaryu [is so called] because of his application to the ritual acts (veda-yoga) in the rites (29).
He is distinct from others due to both scriptural injunctions and contradictions [in function] (30).
Among the priests who own the sacrificial vessels (haviṣ-pātra), each preceding one has priority over the succeeding one (31).
And for the officiating priests, as before (32);
or rather not, because it is not enjoined (33);
the consecrations take place at the Gārhapatya fire (34).

Or the cooking [of the grain] takes place on the Āhavanīya fire. (35) Ghee is used for the clarified butter (ājya), because of the indicative mark (liṅga). (36) Its offering (homa) occurs when there is no specific instruction. (37)
The earth from the *cātvāla* pit [is used for the altar]; the oblations are performed on the *āhavanīya* fire; [the portions] of the *dhruvā* ladle [are used];
and some [teachers] say that the *iḍā*, the *prāśitra*, and the *āghāra* libations [are also used].

The two libations (āghāra) are directed eastward; some say they are in the intermediate directions; the offerings are in the Āhavanīya fire, according to both direct scriptural statement and designation.
Because there is no mention of the *juhū* ladle [in this context],
because the purpose is accomplished by what is taken once,
and because of the absence of the *vaṣaṭ* call.
1. From the sacrificial oblation of rice or barley, he cuts two portions; 2.
three portions for the Jamadagnis.
The third [portion] is from the rear;
or rather, it is from all [parts], because both types are prescribed.
The portion to be cut off (avadāna) is the size of a thumb-joint, taken from the middle and the fore-part, without joining them together.
7. Curd and milk should be added in equal proportions.
8. Clarified butter is used at the beginning and at the end.
9. There is a single expiation for the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.
There are two pourings of clarified butter [over the oblation];
after cutting off the portions, there is a second pouring until the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering;
the cake on one potsherd is offered in its entirety.
The command for recitation is "Recite for such-and-such deity"; 13. and likewise in the command for the *āśrāvaṇa*, it is "Sacrifice to such-and-such. 14–15.
In the recitation of the *praisha* formulas, one should omit the sixth [formula], namely "for the omentum, for the parched grains, for the Soma-pressings" (vapāyai dhānāsoma-bhyaḥ).
(16) In the case of the removal [of the victim], [the formula] is "O so-and-so" (asau). (17) At the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ* call, while standing to the south, facing north-east, [he offers]. (18)

Because of the mention of both [types of] sacrificial butter from the oblation (ājyaṃ haviṣaḥ) [at sūtra 20], or because of the simultaneous [mention] (saha) [at sūtra 21], because of the description of what is currently occurring, because of the injunctive word (codanā-śabda), because of the absence of the literal meaning [of the word "butter"], because of the statement "for that purpose" (tadarthe), and because of the specific direction (nirdeśa), it is an injunction for the ritual action (karma-codaka). 1.

1. Or rather, it is the mantra [that determines the order], because of its being uttered together [with the action]. 2. The preparation of the materials is according to the enumeration of the purposes. 3. The skins are with the hair on the upper side and with the necks facing forward.

The response spoken while facing downwards is over the oblation; when there is a single substance, it is clarified butter, and its grasping is done with the Veda-bundle; otherwise, it is with the wooden sword (sphya).
With *kuśa* grass,
while the [sacrificial vessels] are not yet present, one should grasp the *juhū* with both hands and place it upon the *upabhṛt* at the time of taking them up, without making a clinking sound;
among the fruits mentioned in the Veda, heaven [is the result] by implication.
11. Regarding a single ritual act, there is a distinction in the result based on a distinction in the quality [of the materials].
12. In the cases of giving, recitation, touching for support, choosing a bridegroom, choosing a boon, vows, and measurements, one should understand the sacrificer [to be the agent].
13. Because the performance of the *yajus* formulas is impossible in the case of what is dug, cut, plucked, threshed, ground, milked, and burnt.
Having recited a mantra that is fierce, pertaining to Rākṣasas, Asuras, or malevolent magic, O Father, having touched himself [with water], he should touch water; he should touch water.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Kātyāyana Śrautasūtra.
He should fast on either the preceding full moon day or the subsequent one.
The Adhvaryu or the sacrificer performs the adding of fuel to the fire (agnyanvādhāna).

[He recites: "O Agni, may splendor be mine in the invocations; may we, kindling thee, nourish our bodies. May the four quarters bow down to me; with thee as our overseer, may we conquer the hostile armies. With this verse, he places a piece of wood on the Āhavanīya fire.
A second piece is placed silently.
In the same way for the other two [fires];
or with the Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛti) directed toward the east;
or silently, as before.
During the day, one should avoid meat and sexual intercourse;
or one may shave the hair and beard, except for the tuft of hair on the crown. In the afternoon, they eat the food for undertaking the vow, well-satiated with clarified butter.

Having gone between the two fires and standing to the east of the Āhavanīya fire while looking at the fire and touching water, he enters upon the vow, either with the formula "O Agni, lord of vows, here do I [take the vow]," or by simply speaking the truth. Speaking the truth is a constituent part of the ritual action in the subsequent [vows].
Or he may eat [fruits] from trees, wild plants, or medicinal herbs;
or he may sleep below the Āhavanīya fire or below the Gārhapatya fire;
or he may eat immediately or in the morning.

Having performed the Agnihotra, [he chooses] the Brahman priest who is most devoted to sacred knowledge, saying: "O Lord of the earth, O Lord of the world, O Lord of the great being, we choose you as our Brahman. 17.

Being chosen, he mutters: "I am the lord of the earth; I am the lord of the world; I am the lord of the great being. Bhūr, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ! O God Savitṛ, they choose thee, Bṛhaspati, as the Brahman priest. That I announce to the mind; the mind to the Gāyatrī; the Gāyatrī to the Triṣṭubh; the Triṣṭubh to the Jagatī; the Jagatī to the Anuṣṭubh; the Anuṣṭubh to Prajāpati; Prajāpati to the All-gods; Bṛhaspati is the Brahman of the gods; I am [the Brahman] of men. (18) "O Lord of Speech, protect the sacrifice," he says.
(19) He steps across to the south behind the Āhavanīya fire. (20)
"O son of a remarried woman, go away! Stand aside and sit in the dwelling of another who is more innocent than we!"—with these words he gazes at the Brahman’s seat.
(21) He throws away a blade of grass from the Brahman’s seat, saying: "Casted out is evil along with him whom we hate.

(22) "Here I sit in the seat of Bṛhaspati, impelled by the god Savitṛ; this I announce to Agni, this to Vāyu, this to the Earth"—with these words he sits down in the Brahman’s seat facing the Āhavanīya fire. (1)
He remains restrained in speech until the impulse for the after-offerings (anuyāja),
or until the setting aside of the portions, or according to the ritual procedure (āvṛt) until the vaṣaṭ-calls.
Or, in this case, there is the undertaking of the vow (vratopāyana); having uttered the *vyāhṛtis*, he should mutter the Vaiṣṇava mantra;
and the Adhvaryu likewise.

"Lead forward the sacrifice; O deity, cause it to prosper. May the sacrificer be upon the back of the firmament. Place this sacrificer where the world of the seven seers who have performed good deeds is—Oṃ, lead forward! With these words, he impels the *praṇītā* waters. (8) Thus addressed, he sprinkles the sacrifice with the syllable *Oṃ*, as well as the oblation, the fuel, and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

(9) "O Bṛhaspati, encompass the altar. May the gods be easy of access to their seats. May the sacrificial grass spread out well upon this [altar]. May the divine Earth be free from harm. [He says this] to one who is encompassing the altar. (10)
"O Prajāpati, recite for the sacrifice," [he says] to one who is about to recite the *sāmidhenī* verses.
"Do thou cause the deities to prosper," he adds to this everywhere.
"I gaze upon thee with the eye of Mitra," [with these words] he gazes at the *prāśitra* portion.
He receives it with the formula, "Thee for the god" (devasya tvā). He places it down with the formula, "Thee for the earth" (pṛthivyās tvā), having pushed aside the sacrificial grass (barhis).

Having taken it up again, he eats it with his ring finger and thumb using the formula, "Thee for the god," and with the formula, "Thee for Agni," without touching it with his teeth, provided that [the food] is there.
He places [the vessel] on the shoulder-region.

Having washed the vessel, he touches his navel with the formula: "Those deities who are within the waters, may they appease this; O Indra, go to the belly consecrated by *svāhā*; do not mix with my food; sit above my navel; I seat you in the belly of Indra.
Being addressed with the verse "This one for thee," he gives the impulse for the kindling wood.
Or he may say, "Pratiṣṭhā.

At the conclusion of the ritual act, he places a fuel-stick on the fire, or offers an oblation, or performs a prayer of adoration (*upasthāna*), saying: "Homage to the completed rite, homage to the uncompleted rite! Jātavedas has sacrificed the sacrifice; having sat down as the innermost and foremost one within this [sacrifice], grant us gain, grant us wealth, release us well with a good release! Bestow upon us riches, O Jātavedas, Svāhā! Having returned by the same way he came, this constitutes his role as Brahman for the *iṣṭi* and animal sacrifices. To the north of the Gārhapatya fire, having set down a water-pot, he touches [the victim] while saying: "Being, I shall make you become."
"O Brahman, I shall lead forward the waters; O sacrificer, restrain your speech," he says.
Having received permission, he places [the vessel] to the north of the Āhavanīya fire. "Who [will fill] thee?
[he asks]. Those desiring sorcery, spiritual luster, or stability should use vessels made of bronze, wood, or clay, respectively, according to their order.
Having strewn grass around the fires, he first arranges the vessels in pairs to the east—
either the sacrificer or [the Adhvaryu]— namely: the winnowing basket,
the Agnihotra-ladle, the wooden sword (sphya), the potsherds, the yoke-pin (śamyā), the black antelope skin, the mortar and pestle, the large and small grinding stones, and whatever else is required.

To the west or to the north of the cooking fire, having taken up the winnowing basket and the *agnihotra* ladle with the formula, "For the sake of the ritual, you two," he restrains his speech. He heats them [with the formula], "Heated!
or "Burnt away! or "Scorched! (10–11).
12. "He goes through the wide mid-air," [saying this] while standing behind the cooking fire-vessel. 13.
"Thou art the yoke-pole," [saying this] while touching the yoke-pole.
14. "Of the gods... [saying this] while standing behind the prop of the pole.
15. With the words "Viṣṇus tvā," he ascends. 16. He looks at the sacrificial foods with the verse "uru vātāya.
17. With the words "apahatam," he throws away the other [portion].
If [the animal] is not present, he should touch it;
with the words "May they yield," he seizes it;
with the words "Of the god thee," he takes four handfuls of the portion for Agni.
Thus [is performed] the offering to Agni and Soma (21);
other [offerings] are according to their respective deities (22); "For the being, thee!"—with these words, the touching of the remnants (23).
He looks toward the east with "Svaḥ! (24);
he descends with "May they be firm! (25);
he goes forth with "The wide mid-air" (26).
He places it down behind the cooking vessel with the formula, "Of the earth thee" (VS 1.27). Or he places it in a vessel that has been touched by the wooden sword (sphya).
He mutters the formulas for mounting the pole and the shaft over the rim of the vessel.

With the words "May they be firm," he cuts two blades of *kuśa* grass that are unbroken at the tips, without internal nodes, using other *kuśa* blades, with the formula "You are purifiers" (pavitre sthaḥ);
or he may cut three.
Having placed water into the *havirgrahaṇī* ladle, he purifies [the butter] with those two [ladles] using the mantra, "By the impulse of Savitṛ... (32).
He places them in their respective positions (33).
Having taken them in his left hand, he points them out with his right hand (34).
"Ye are sprinkled," with these words he sprinkles them; 35.
And the oblation [is sprinkled] with "For Agni thee! For Agni-Soma thee! 36.
Other [oblations are sprinkled] according to their respective deities. 37.
With the mantra "For the gods are the vessels" (VS 1.12),
he places the *prokṣaṇī* waters in a place free from traffic; with the mantra "Thou art a refuge" (VS 1.13), he takes up the black antelope skin.
Having moved away from the vessels, he shakes [the mortar] twice;
he spreads [the skin] with its neck facing westward, saying, "The skin of Aditi";
he places the *savyā* on the empty space, saying either, "Thou art the mortar," or "Thou art the pressing-stone."
With "Prati tvā" for both [offerings],
he releases his speech with the formula, "Thou art the body of Agni, the lord of the oblation."
And the sacrificer [is the one who calls out], or the preparer of the oblation (haviṣkṛt);
[this applies] to the last among various seeds because of the force of the context.
With the words, "O Bṛhadgrāvan," he takes up the pestle;
with "He [is] this," he places it down;
with "O preparer of the oblation, come! he calls out three times.

Therefore, the wife or another person husks; one calls out while the other husks. With the formula, "Thou art a cock," he strikes the mortar and pestle three times with the yoke-pin—twice the mortar and once the pestle.
With the formula, "Thou art increased by rain," he takes up the winnowing basket.
With "pratitva," he pours out the oblation;
with "parāpūtam," he winnows it;
with "apahatam," he casts away the husks.
"Vāyur vaḥ" (Vāyu is yours)—with these words he winnows [the husks].
"Devo vaḥ" (The god is yours)—with these words he consecrates the vessel for the Āpyas.
He threshes [the grain] three times, saying, "Be purified for the gods; be purified for the gods," though some say [he does so only once].
Having husked [the grain], he sets aside the chaff. 23.
The grinding-stones and the supporting-slab are placed down simultaneously. 24.
Having taken up the fire-brick (upaveṣa) with the formula, "Thou art the bold one," he pushes the embers eastward with the formula, "Away from Agni... 25.
Having brought a coal with the formula, "Come to the sacrifice to the gods," he covers it with a potsherd, saying, "Thou art firm.
[He uses] "of so-and-so" when performing sorcery against an enemy;
this applies elsewhere as well.
With his right forefinger, he places a charcoal on the empty spot with the mantra "O Agni, thou art Brahman" (29);
behind it with "thou art Dharuṇa" (30); and in front with "thou art Dhartṛ" (31).
With the verse "viśvābhyaḥ," he places [the bricks] on the south;
having divided them equally, two are on the south, and likewise on the north with the formula "citasthaḥ. Or, he may do so silently.
Thus there are eleven [stokes] for the Agniṣomīya; 35.
An additional one on the south; 36.
With the formula "Of the Bhṛgus," he covers it with embers. 37.
He places the secondary vessels on the fire.
He takes a black antelope skin;
upon it he places the grinding stone with the formula, "Thou art Dhiṣaṇā."
Then he pushes the wedge upward with the formula, "The northward [direction] of heaven" (VS 1.24).
He places the lower millstone upon the grinding-slab with the formula, "Thou art Dhiṣaṇā" (VS 1.25).
Having poured the rice grains with the formula, "Thou art grain" (VS 1.26), he grinds them while reciting each mantra: "For out-breath, thee! (VS 1.27), and so forth.
He wipes it with the formula, "Long [is the life]";
he looks at it with the formula, "For the eye thee";
while the grains are being ground, another pours out the clarified butter with the verse, "Of the great ones... (RV 10.75.5).
O worthy one! Into the vessel provided with a strainer, he pours the flour-grains with the mantra "devasya tvā" (VS 1.30).
He sits behind the cooking-fire, or within the sacrificial altar. Another person brings the secondary water-vessels.
He receives [the flour] with two strainers, saying, "The waters have come together.
He mixes it, saying, "For generation.
Having divided it equally, and not yet collecting it, he touches it, saying, "This for Agni; this for Agni-Soma."
The other [substances] are according to their respective deities (16).
Another [priest] places the clarified butter over the fire with the formula, "For strength, thee!
(17). For one who does not have a wife, that [butter] is placed on the Āhavanīya fire by one who maintains it (18).
With the formula, "Thou art heat," he places the two sacrificial cakes simultaneously (19).
With the formula, "Widely extend," he spreads them out as large as the potsherds, but not excessively wide (20).
With the formula, "May Agni [protect] thee," he touches them with water once or thrice (21).

He carries fire around [the animal] with the mantra, "The *rakṣas* is excluded; the enemies are excluded," together with the clarified butter (22). He cooks it with the mantra, "May the god [Agni] cook thee" (23).
He touches it with the mantra, "Do not fear" (24).
Saying, "It is offered," he covers the cooked food with ashes using either the Veda-grass mat or the *upaveṣa* stick.

He pours out the water used for washing the hands and fingers for the worthy guests. Having heated it, he pours it out toward the west so that it does not flow back, reciting for each the mantra, "For Trita thee.
He places the *anvāhārya* mess of rice on the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire.
Or here [is] the undertaking of the vow (vratopāyana). 28.

To the west of the Āhavanīya fire, he digs the altar (vedi), three finger-breadths deep, one fathom wide at the back, three cubits long from west to east, or of unlimited length; it should slope toward the east or the north, be gathered together in the middle, and have its corners on both sides [extended] up to the very roots of the plants. 2.
[This applies] from the cutting down of the plants at their roots.
He should tell [the assistant] to uproot the roots of the plants.
(3) For one desiring cattle, [he should prepare] an altar whose soil has been carried away.
(4) Having swept around the altar, at one-third [of its distance] from the north side, the Āgnīdhra makes the rubbish-heap. (5)

Having taken up the wooden sword (*sphya*) with the formula "Thee, for the God," and having placed it with its blade upward and covered with grass in his left hand, he touches it with his right hand while reciting, "The arm of Indra.

He should not touch the earth or himself with it when he is about to carry away the *stambayajus*. He places a blade of grass on the altar (*vedi*) toward the north with the formula, "Thou art the armor of the earth."
"O Earth, worthy of sacrifice!"—with these words, he strikes while the grass is held beneath.

"Go to the fold!"—with this, he takes up the loose earth. "May it rain for thee"—with this, he looks at the altar. "Bind it!"—with this, he places it on the rubbish-heap (*utkara*). Or rather, it is the remainder of the striking, because there is no specific instruction [to the contrary].
"Without leaving a gap"—this refers to the second striking and so forth.
The Agnīdh throws down the mound with the verse, "O non-malignant one, [I place] thee upon heaven";
the third time with "dra psas te";
the fourth time silently, including the grass.
First, he takes possession [of the site] from the east, then from the south, west, and north, with the wooden sword (sphya), reciting a mantra for each: "With the Gāyatra... (18).
Having drawn three lines on the altar (vedi), he says, "Bring it; three times" (19).
Having brought it, he touches the lines of the fires (20).

Because they are seen there in the case of the Pitṛyajña and the Agnicayana [rites], the construction of the altar is performed here as previously described. He performs the northern enclosure with each mantra: "O subtle one," and "Thou art full of vigor. (Sūtras 21–23)
With the verse "purā krūrasya" (VS 1.28), he performs the anupramārjana.
24. He holds the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling waters over the altar (*vedi*). 25.

Then another [priest], having raised the wooden sword (*sphya*), says: "Place the *prokṣaṇī* waters; set down the fuel (*idhma*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); cleanse the offering-ladles (*sruk*); gird the wife; bring the clarified butter (*ājya*)!"—if he so desires. 26.
As one who has been sent forth, another [may perform the action],
or he himself may do so because there is no contradiction,
and because of the statement regarding the formal commission (sampraśa).
One should not touch the altar before its strewing (30); nor should one touch the cooked oblations before they have been offered (31).
Some teachers say that one should cut off portions using the thumb and finger together with the flesh (32).

He should sweep away what has fallen [on the altar] with the formula, "The slaying of my enemies. (33) He hurls the wooden sword (sphyam) toward the north with the formula, "The slaying of my enemies.
(34) Having washed his hands, he places the wooden sword behind the *praṇītā* water-vessel. (35)
The sacrificial fuel and the sacrificial grass; first the fuel (is placed);
having brought the *praṇītā* water from the south or from the east.

Having heated the *sruva* as before, he wipes its interior from front to back with the tips of the *veda*-grass, saying "aniśitaḥ"; then, having turned it over and wiped it with the roots of the *barhis*-grass, he steps forward toward the east, heats it again and again, and hands it over, saying "aniśitaḥ" for the *sruk*s. 39–41.
He silently discards the *prāśitraharaṇa* vessel, the portion of cooked meat, and the *pātrī* pan (42).
He throws away the wiping-cloths (43).
Some [teachers] say that their disposal is in the *āhavanīya* fire (44).
He girds the wife, who is seated facing west to the south of the Gārhapatya fire, with a triple-stranded girdle of Muñja grass, saying: "Thou art the girdle of Aditi.
Having fastened the southern loop over the northern one, he draws it upward, saying: "The stride of Viṣṇu.
He does not tie a knot.
Having removed the clarified butter with the formula, "For strength, thee," he causes the wife to look at it with the formula, "With the undeceivable [eye].
He prepares another portion on the altar for the *prokṣaṇī* waters,
or having prepared it over the *āhavanīya* fire, those who desire that [result] do so.
With the formula "Of Savitṛ thee," he purifies the clarified butter and the sprinkling waters as before (7).
The sacrificer or [the priest] gazes at the clarified butter with the formula "Thou art luster" (8).
The taking of the clarified butter with the sruva-spoon into the juhū-ladle is done once with the mantra "Dhāma nāma" (9).
There are eight [spoonfuls] in the upabhṛt; if there are fewer after-offerings (anuyāja), there are four elsewhere than from the distribution [of the butter],
because they are not seen in the animal sacrifice or the ātithya.
Not so, because of the teaching of the whole; because of the specific mention of the animal and the guest-offering;
and because it is in the *dhruvā* as in the case of the *juhū*.

He sprinkles the fuel, loosens the altar and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and having placed it upon the altar with its knot toward the east, he addresses it with each mantra: "Thou art black" (VS 1.16).
He pours the remainder over the roots with the formula: "The moistening for Aditi" (VS 1.17).
Having placed the two strainers (*pavitra*) in the *praṇītā* waters, he loosens the sacrificial grass and takes up the *prastara* bundle from the front with the formula: "Of Viṣṇu" (VS 1.18).

Having offered the girdle to the Brahman priest, having loosened it, and having placed it on the southern corner of the altar, he covers it with other [grass] and then strews the altar with threefold [layers],
using the formula "O soft as wool," or he may spread it more thickly according to the requirements,
keeping the roots underneath.
The removal [of the fires] takes place afterwards, either with the *apavarga* formula or with the *prabṛha* formula;
here, the *udvāsana* (removal) belongs to one who maintains the *āhavanīya* fire.
Having taken a fuel-stick from the faggot, he prepares the Āhavanīya fire while holding the *prastara* grass-bundle directly above it.
If there are after-offerings (*anuyāja*s), he throws up two fire-brands (*ulmuka*).

He lays around the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), which should be fresh, from a single tree, arm-length in size, made of *pālāśa*, *vaikaṅkata*, *kārṣmarya*, or *bilva* wood; if these are unavailable, he uses *khadira* or *udumbara* wood for the middle, southern, and northern ones respectively, laying them down with the respective mantras beginning with "Gandharva."
Having touched the first enclosing stick with the fuel-stick, he places it [on the fire] with the mantra beginning "Vītihotra" (2).
Without touching, he places the second with "Samid asi" (3).
Looking at the Āhavanīya fire, he mutters "Sūryaḥ svā" (4), because that is the prescribed procedure for that act.
Having covered the altar with sacrificial grass, he places two blades of grass across it while reciting "Savituḥ" (5).
Or rather, [he does so] because of the connection with another [verse] (6).
[This usage of the word] also occurs elsewhere in the sense of praising (7).
And clarified butter is used for the anointing of the sacrificial post (yūpa). 8.
And if he so desires, [he uses it] for the placing of the cake (puroḍāśa) and the curd-mixture (payasyā). 9.
Upon those two, he spreads the grass-bundle (prastara) with the formula: "Soft as wool. 10.
He places [the *juhū*] down with the verse, "O Vasus, come to you.
(11) Having taken up the *juhū* with his left hand, he sets it down on its empty space with the verse, "The butter-dripping one.

(12) In the same way, he places the other two spoons—the *upabhṛt* and the *dhruvā*—on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with the following two verses respectively. When the [sacrificial cakes] have been drawn out, he pours clarified butter over the two *puroḍāśas*, removes them, places them upon the spread-out [butter], and anoints them with the formula: "O Soma, that breath of yours which has entered into the animals, which has extended through the various stations of the gods—becoming possessed of self and carrying the clarified butter, go to Agni; find the heavenly world for the sacrificer. (14)

He anoints the other [vessels] according to their respective deities (15). He anoints the potsherds with the verse: "Those potsherds which the wise ones place upon the cauldron—may Indra and Vāyu release them at Pūṣan’s rite" (16);
or he does so silently (17).
He causes [the fires] to be set aside by number:
"With a dear abode," having placed the oblations on the altar; "The steadfast ones have sat down," with this he touches all of them;
"Protect me," with this he touches himself.
"Either here or there is the undertaking of the vow; either here or there is the undertaking of the vow. Thus ends the second chapter in the Kāṭīya Śrautasūtra.
Having prepared the Hotṛ’s seat, and having taken a fuel-stick from the faggot either to the west or to the north of the rear corner of the altar, he says: "Recite for the fire being kindled! (1)
Some say "hotar" [is used] with the first designation before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; with the middle [designation], up to the *iḍā*.
"Recite the remainder for me as if continuing with the best [verse]," says the sacrificer.
With both thumbs he presses down on the two feet of the Veda, saying: "I press down so-and-so, my enemy."
Or, in its absence, [he recites] "the hating rival" (dviṣantam bhrātṛvyam). 8.
As many Sāmidhenī verses as there are, so many times he says "with this much-folded thunderbolt" (tāvatithena vajreṇa). 9. At each *praṇava*, the fire is established. 10.
If there are after-offerings (*anuyāja*s), he proceeds with the formula "Kindled... (*samiddhaḥ*) while holding all the fuel-sticks (*idhma*) except for one.

(11) At the end of the recitation, having fanned the Āhavanīya fire three times with the Veda-grass-bundle and having poured the first libation (*āghāra*) with the *sruva*-ladle, he says: "O Agnīdh, cleanse the fires!

(12) He cleanses around each enclosing stick (*paridhi*) with the cord used for binding the fuel-sticks, using the formula "O Agni, winner of booty" (*agne vājajit*), three times for each circuit. (13)
Silently above [the fire], he makes the añjali gesture toward another Āhavanīya fire from the south with the formula, "Homage to the gods; svadhā to the ancestors," extending his hands palm-upward.

Having touched water, he takes up the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles with the formula, "O well-guided one," holding the *juhū* over the other; having stepped across to the south with his foot, he says, "For Viṣṇu."
The movement of one about to offer the oblation is focused on the enclosing sticks (paridhi):
from here with the left hand, and from there with the right hand; having stood thus, [he recites] "O Earth, rich in wealth" (vasumatī).
With the words, "Hither, O Indra," he offers the second libation of clarified butter (*uttarāghāra*).
Having poured the libation and approached without letting the two ladles touch each other, he anoints the *dhruvā* with the *juhū* while reciting, "Unite the lights.
Having set down the implements and taken up the cord for binding the fuel, he says, "Oṣrāvaya! (Cause [the Āgnīdhra] to call out).
"Let it be; *śrauṣaṭ*," [the Agnīdh replies].

4. Having cut off a blade of grass from the sacrificial grass on the altar, or a chip of fuel-wood, some [do this]—5. In this same manner [it is done] everywhere in cases where there is a call and a response. 6.

Then he chooses [the Hotṛ]: "May Agni, the divine, the divine Hotṛ, sacrifice to the gods, he who knows, like Manu, like Bharata—like so-and-so, like so-and-so"—thus he pronounces the ancestral lineages (*ārṣeya*) of the sacrificer, three from the most recent back to the most ancient (7). Or as many as there are composers of mantras (8).
Or [the initiation may be performed] according to the *ṛṣi* lineage of the family priest (10);
and for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, it is always so (11); or for all [classes], it may be according to Manu (12).

"May he speak with sacred knowledge; may the Brahmins be the protectors of this sacrifice—such-and-such is the human [sacrificer]," thus is the name of the Hotṛ recited, either loudly or in a whisper.
Having been wiped down, the two sit down.
"O Agni, Hotṛ! is the formula for taking up the offering-ladle (*srugādāpana*) among the *prayāja* offerings because of its proximity [to them].

When [the Adhvaryu] says "The two ladles full of ghee," he takes up the two ladles, steps across, and having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, says "Sacrifice to the *samidhs*"; thus he performs the five *prayājas* beginning with the *samidhs*.
For the remainder, he says "Sacrifice! Sacrifice! (16–18).
Standing firm,
he pours from the *upabhṛt* into the *juhū*, either taking [the ladle] further forward each time or moving it back to its previous position; he does not touch the fourth [portion].
When they have increased in this manner,
during the *anuyāja* offerings,
he lifts up the northern *juhū* ladle, brings it forward toward the east, and makes the offering.
Thus in all cases. 25.
Holding [the breath] at the region of the navel is one;
the consecration of the fore-offerings (*prayāja*) is another: "May he who hates us and whom we hate be subject to me. 2.
Thus, with couples in their respective order:
"Nothing belongs to him" in the fifth [verse];
and "radiant, honored, glorious, possessing the splendor of sacred knowledge, and an eater of food."
For the guest [oblations], [the offering] is made from the fourth and fifth positions (6),
or from the first and fourth according to their respective gender-markers (7),
or all [of them] because they are offered by means of the highest [position] (8).
Having approached, he performs the offering and the pouring over of the *dhruvā* ladle, the oblation, and the *upabhṛt* ladle (9).
He proceeds with the two *ājyabhāga* portions for Agni and Soma (10).
In the offerings accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ*-call, there is a fourfold cutting (11).

Having set it down and having cut portions from each, he bastes the *dhruvā* with ghee, saying: "May the *dhruvā* swell with the oblation for the sake of the sacrifice toward the gods; [may she be] the udder of Sūryā, the lap of Aditi, the wide-streaming Earth in this sacrifice.
(12) Having said, "Recite the invitatory verse," the *hotṛ* should not speak out until the *āśrāvaṇa* call.
(13) Once the *āśrāvaṇa* has been made, [he should not speak] until the *agnīdh* responds with the *pratyāśravaṇa*. (14)
When the response has been given, the Adhvaryu acts until the Hotṛ's command (15);
the Hotṛ acts until the *vaṣaṭ*-call (16); and in the Soma sacrifice, having taken up the cup, he acts until the introductory formula (*upākaraṇa*) (17).
Once the animal has been offered, the Udgātṛ [recites] until the Hotṛ’s call;
the Hotṛ [recites] until the *vaṣaṭ*-call. The portion for Agni is in the north-eastern quarter, and that for Soma is in the south-eastern quarter.
Or, when [the fire] is most kindled (21),
and between the two oblations (22) and the two sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa), Agni and Soma [receive] the clarified butter in a low voice (upāṃśu) (23).
Viṣṇu [is the deity] on the new moon day because of the mention of the Hotṛ priests; 24. as much of the oblation as is taken from the northern half for the Sviṣṭakṛt; 25.
from that very portion the offering is made. 26.
Not from what remains of the clarified butter (27);
not with oblations that have been mixed together (28);
having set it down (29).

Having sprinkled water along the path of movement (*sañcara*), he cuts off the *prāśitra* portion— either the size of a barley grain or a *pippala* fruit— from either side of the clarified butter or from both sides of the portion belonging to Agni.

Having given the portions to the Brahman by way of the Adhvaryu’s path of movement, some say that after touching water to the east, he [cuts] the five-fold divided *iḍā* from the southern side and from the middle, as much as there is of the oblation, with clarified butter like that for the *sviṣṭakṛt*.
Having torn off a long portion from the eastern half for the sacrificer's share, he places it in front of the *dhruvā* ladle (4).
Having given the *iḍā* to the *hotṛ*, and releasing his hold, he steps across to the south (5).
Having received the *iḍā*, he anoints the joints of the *hotṛ*'s fingers (6).
He offers the intermediate *iḍā* as before (7);
[he offers] the *iḍā* (8);
everyone touches him from behind (9).

When the words "Invoked by Iḍā" are being recited, he places the portion for Agni upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), saying: "O radiant one, swell! Grant me long life; grant me progeny; grant me cattle; grant me spiritual power (*brahman*); grant me sovereign power (*kṣatra*); grant me the subjects (*viś*). May you swell with progeny and cattle him who hates us and whom we hate. Having divided that [portion] into four parts, he assigns it to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) upon the sacrificial grass.
Alternatively, he may assign both [the portions] without distinction.
At this point, the sacrificer mutters, "O Fathers! (13). Having released [the breath], he says, "They have rejoiced" (14). He brings each one [of the portions] forward (15).
At the invitation of Heaven and Earth, the Āgnīdhra eats the sixfold portion (ṣaḍavatta) with the formula,
"The earth is invited" (17).
The sacrificer mutters, "May this [merit] accrue to me" (18).
He eats the portion that has been invoked; the sacrificer and [the priests] eat [their portions].
Behind the altar, they purify themselves with the two strainers, saying, "May we be in the favor of the gracious ones... and so forth.
With the formula, "Protect the out-breath and in-breath of the sacrificer," he places [the two blades] upon the prastara;
or he does so silently.
At this point, the Brahman priest consumes [the portion].
He sets aside a portion for him (the guest), and [sets aside] the sacrificer’s portion when he has not gone abroad.

Having sprinkled the *anvāhārya* rice with clarified butter, having removed it from the fire, and having carried it between the Brahman and the sacrificer, he places it on the altar and touches it, saying: "Thou art the portion of Prajāpati; full of vigor, full of milk. Protect my out-breath and in-breath; protect my common breath and diffused breath; protect my upward breath and diffused breath. Thou art vigor; bestow vigor upon me. Thou art imperishable; mayest thou not perish for me, both in that world and in this. (25–27)
That is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
28 He carries away the oblation toward the north.
29 Having taken a fuel-stick from the combined embers, he says: "O Brahman, I shall set forth; having placed the fuel-stick on the fire, O Agnīdh, cleanse the fire. 1.
"This is for you," the Hotṛ recites as a consecratory formula (anumantraṇa).
The sacrificer remains unaware [of this].
He cleanses [the ladle] as before, without moving around, once for each [ladle], with the formula: "For him who has flowed together."
Permitted by Brahmā, having brought together the butter from the *aupabhṛta* ladle, he performs three after-offerings (*anuyāja*s).
Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to the gods!
For the two subsequent offerings, he says, "Sacrifice! Sacrifice! (Yaja yaja).
8. Or rather, "the gods" [is used] everywhere because of the restrictive term;
9. and because a modification is observed;
10. he offers toward the west.
And in the *upasads*,
the *dhruva* ladle is the twelfth;
having brought together the fourth [portion], it is directed eastward.

When performing a malevolent rite (*abhicāra*), one recites the *anumantraṇa* for the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) as follows: "O thunderbolt, slay so-and-so! O hail-storm, slay so-and-so! O uprooter, slay so-and-so!
(14). Thus, having increased [the number], he should divide it equally (15), because it is to be offered at its own place by means of the final [verse] (16).

Having approached, he separates the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles with the formula, "Of Agni and Soma... He places the *juhū* facing eastward on the south side with its bowl turned upward, saying "Agni and Soma have reached him..."; with the other [formula], he places the other [ladle] facing westward on the north side with its bowl turned downward.

(17) The others are according to their respective deities. (18) Or the Adhvaryu may raise them, saying, "May this sacrificer conquer... with the formula "of the strength... for the two eastern ones; and for the two northern ones, "whom this sacrificer hates and whoever hates him. (19)
Having sprinkled [the ghee] with the *juhu* ladle, he anoints the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) as before, reciting for each the mantra beginning with "To the Vasus" (VS 2.17).

Having taken hold of the first enclosing stick and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "The divine Hotṛs have not been urged; the human [Hotṛ] has been sent forth for the auspicious speech, for the *sūktavāka*; recite the hymns. (VS 2.18)
At the animal sacrifice, [the Adhvaryu] says, "Prompt! (3).
With the words, "Be of one mind," he takes up the prastara-bunch (4).
Having placed it in the position of the two separating-blades (vidhṛtī), he anoints it with the words, "May the birds eat it" (5).
He places the tip [of the blade] in the *juhu*, the middle in the *upabhṛt*, and the base in the other [the *dhruvā*].
Having carried it low with the formula "Of the Maruts," he takes a blade of grass and throws it after [the offering]. He performs this with his hand.
And [he should consume] the sacrificer's portion when [the sacrificer] is away;
this applies constantly for both Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.
"I am yours, you are mine; this is my source, I am your source. In heaven among the gods, I am indeed your son, O Father Jātavedas, world-maker! Svāhā! (11).
At the end of the *sūktavāka*, [the Adhvaryu] says, "O Agnīdh, throw [the grass] after! (12).
Having thrown a blade of grass [into the fire], he touches himself with the formula, "Protector of the eye... (13–14).

"Converse; has he come? Agnīdh, has he come? Make it heard! Śrauṣaṭ! Well-being to the divine Hotṛs; prosperity to the human ones; pronounce the words for peace and well-being!"—with these [words] they converse. "Has he come? Śrauṣaṭ!"—thus the Agnīdh [responds], and the other [the Adhvaryu] says the remainder, alternating [the responses]. (15) He throws the enclosing sticks (paridhis) into the fire with the formula, "The first enclosing stick... and so on, and the two others simultaneously with "O Agni, the beloved...
(16) He holds up the two offering-spoons (sruc) with "Partakers of the remnants... and offers the remnants (saṃsravas). (17)
He places [the vessel] on the pole with the words, "O Ghṛtācī"; if it is to be taken onto the cart, he does so with the *sphya* as the support.
If it is in a vessel, [he does so] with the *sphya*. With the words, "O Sacrifice, homage to thee," he touches the altar.
The Hotṛ takes the Veda, the Adhvaryu the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and the Agnīdh the butter-pot;
they go toward the Gārhapatya fire for the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings.

The Adhvaryu approaches the Gārhapatya from the south-east, while [the others] pass it to the east, to the west, or between [the two fires], according to some authorities, in order to avoid the wife's fire.
Having sat down and raised his right knee—
this applies in all cases of seated oblations—
they perform [the rites] in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
At the word "caraṇa," he sacrifices to all the deities elsewhere;
[specifically] to Soma, Tvaṣṭṛ, the wives of the gods, and Agni Gṛhapati.
On the third occasion, there is concealment from the front.
The wife takes hold of the Adhvaryu. It ends with the *śaṃyu* formula, or it ends with the *iḍā*.
At the conclusion of the *śaṃyu*, having taken a blade of grass from the *veda*, he anoints the *sruk* and *sruva* spoons as well as the vessel, just like the *prastara* bundle.
The *agnīdh* says, "Throw [the grass] after! (12).
Having thrown the grass and so forth as before, (13) at the conclusion of the *śaṃyu*-formula, he takes hold [of the fire] with the words, "O Agni, of unimpaired life-force... (14).
Turning to the left, he offers oblations in the Dakṣiṇāgni with the formulas, "To Agni" and "To Sarasvatī. 15.

With the formula, "Whatever has adhered to the mortar, the pestle, and the winnowing basket; whatever [has fallen] on the grinding stone or in the potsherds—the droplets and the scattered drops—I offer them all together; may the desires of the sacrificer come true, Svāhā!"—he offers the remnants of the flour. 16.
The wife releases the Veda-bundle with the formula, "Thou art the Veda," and the yoke-tie.

"I release myself from the noose of Varuṇa, with which Savitṛ, the very gracious one, has bound me. In the womb of Cosmic Order (ṛta), in the world of good deeds, may he establish me unharmed together with my husband. Thus [he says].
He spreads [the grass] up to the altar.
He offers the *sam-iṣṭayajus* oblation from the *dhruvā* ladle with the verse: "O gods who know the way... (RV X.14.5).
"Barhis, well-spread!"— with these words,
he pours out the *praṇītā* water on the altar, having gone around it with the formula "Who [has poured] for thee?
He throws away the husks with the potsherd used for the sacrificial cake, saying, "The black antelope skin is below for the sake of the Rakṣases."
Having gone around, he pours out the full vessel; the sacrificer receives it continuously with his joined palms, saying, "With splendor.
He wipes his face [with the formula], "With splendor.
He takes the steps of Viṣṇu, stepping with each mantra: "Viṣṇu in heaven," "On earth," and so on, or he rises up from here.
11. "From this food," he looks at his portion. 12. "For this support," [he looks] at the earth.
13. "We have gone to heaven," [he says] facing eastward.
With "Possessing light," he addresses the Āhavanīya fire;
with "Self-existent," the sun; and with "Bestower of luster," whichever desire he may wish for.
The phrase "of the sun" (sūryasya) is repeated as he circumambulates to the right; this also applies during eclipses of the planets and at the *pratigara* oblations.
He worships the *gārhapatya* fire, saying "O householder," or he may say "a hundred winters."
"Of the sun," he says, and he moves clockwise twenty times.
He goes forward with the words, "O Viṣṇu, stand erect!

(21). Then he takes the name of his son, saying: "Thou art the thread; extend thyself after me in this sacrifice, in this good deed, in this world; may my son continue this work of mine and this heroic power. (22)
With the formula, "For the self, for the unshaken thread; for thee, for light," or silently, he worships the Āhavanīya fire.
He releases his vow with the same [formula] with which he undertook it.
"The lord of the sacrifice invokes [the portion] together; he eats the portion" (26).
"One should say, 'A Brāhmaṇa is to be gratified,' for by this one gratifies the sacrifice itself," according to the Śruti (27).
Thus ends the third chapter of the Kātyāyana Śrautasūtra. 3.
In the afternoon, on the new moon day when the moon is not visible, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is performed.
(1) Cooking and offering [the oblation] take place in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire.
(2) Having strewn [grass around the fire], one sets out the vessels one by one as previously described. (3)
Having silently taken a pot of rice-gruel or a spoonful from another vessel near the *gārhapatya* fire, he stands and threshes it to the north of the *dakṣiṇāgni*. He husks it once (4).

Having cooked the rice with its grains intact until it is full, having poured clarified butter over it and removed it from the fire, he offers it with a stirring-spoon, saying "To Agni" and "To Soma" (5–6).
Having thrown it [the bone], he scratches the ground to the south with the mantra "apahatāḥ," or to the west; 7.
He places a firebrand at the far end with the mantra "ye rūpāṇi"; 8.

He causes [the relatives] to wash themselves with a water-pot, either keeping the sacred thread over the right shoulder (aprasavya) or over the left, according to the requirement of the rite of removal (uddharaṇa). 9.

Saying, "Wash yourself," he places three blades of grass with their tips cut off near the roots upon the line for the sacrificer’s ancestors starting from the father; then, as they were washed, he offers the rice-balls with the formula,
"This is for you," and some also add, "And those who follow you."
Having said, "O Fathers," he remains facing north until the sun sets (13).
Having turned back, he mutters, "They have rejoiced" (14).
Having sprinkled water and loosened his girdle as before, he makes the añjali gesture with the words, "Homage to you" (15).
With the words "This indeed," he fastens threads to each individual [clay ball],
or wool, or a fringe;
when weaving further, he uses the hair of the sacrificer.
With the words "Strength," he pours water down. 19. Having placed [the vessel] there, the sacrificer smells it. 20. He throws the firebrand and the *sakṛdācchinna* grass into the fire. 21.
Saying "ādhatta" (bestow), the wife who desires a son eats the middle ball of rice;
he gives [the remaining balls] to the ancestors even if his father is living, and even if [the father] has passed away but is not yet buried.
For one whose father is living, the rite ends with the oblation.
Or rather, there is no undertaking [of the rite] (anārambhaḥ).
25 Jātūkarṇya says it is not [performed] when [the father] has passed away. 26 For there is a Vedic text stating: "One does not give [the inheritance] while he is still living. 27
28. Or rather, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is a subsidiary (aṅga) because it is mentioned first.

29. It is not a subsidiary because of the favoring of the context, the time, the indicative mark, the direct statement, and the scriptural injunction regarding one who has not established the sacred fires (anāhitāgni).
30. Or rather, it is a subsidiary because of its being mentioned in close conjunction (samabhivyāhāra).
The preparation of the *sānnāyya* at the *darśeṣṭi*:

If it is thought that the moon will not rise tomorrow, or if it is not seen, he cuts a branch of the *parṇa* tree or a branch of the *śamī* tree with the formula "For food thee" (*iṣe tvā*) or "For strength thee" (*ūrje tvā*), or with "I cut [thee]" (*chinadmi*), because both [formulas] are syntactically expectant of one another. (Sūtras 1–2)
Or as it has been said: "I am restraining myself," or [he says this] at the response; [he takes] a branch with abundant leaves, its tip not dried out, facing east-north or any other direction;
he undertakes the vow.
Or as it has been stated:
having brought the calves together with their mothers, he touches a calf with a branch, saying, "O winds! (Vāyavas stha);
and some say, "O you who approach" (Upāyavas stha).
Having explained one of the mother-verses beginning with "devo vaḥ," [he recites] verse 9, which belongs either to Indra or Mahendra;
he then leans a branch against either the front of the sacrificial shed or the sacrificer's cattle-pen. 11.

He makes the *upaveṣa* from the root; it is called *upaveṣa* because it serves as a means of entry (*veṣa*) for him. "O Agni, you who are well-favored, crush the necks of the enemies here; may they be successful in their work, never failing.

(12) [The term *upaveṣa* applies] to both [the fire-stirring stick and the *upaveṣa*] because of its connection with the *sānnāyya* offering in the case of the branch, or because of its being placed upon [the altar]. (13–14)
With the formula, "The purifier of wealth," he ties two *kuśa* blades, either threefold or as a single strand, as a purifier upon this [strainer].
For one who maintains the *sannayya* offering, the *agnihotra* oblation is performed with barley-gruel for that night.
"Let him announce that [the oblation] has been offered and attended," so it is said. 18.
When it has been announced, he takes up the pot with the words, "Thou art heaven. 19. With the words, "Of Mātariśvan," he places it over the fire. 20.
With the verse, "The purifier of wealth," he makes a strainer for her, either toward the north or east; while she remains silent, he causes her to milk through one who is not a Śūdra.
While the vessel is being held [by the student], he mutters the mantra, "May the god [pour] thee," as it is being poured in.
"Kāmadhukṣa" is the question (24); when it is uttered, she says, "I am Viśvāyu" (25). In this manner, the others [respond] with the subsequent answers, mantra by mantra (26).
27. The subsequent speech is released when there is no physical contact.
28. This continues as long as one's own office lasts. 29. Or rather, it is three [verses], because of their obligatory nature.

By the force of the initial [words] (30) and because of the observation (31), he brings the washing water with the mantra: "Unite, O immortal waters, most honey-sweet with your wave; mingling milk with honey, you are pleasant for the winning of wealth" (32).
Having lifted it up, he anoints it with the remainder of the ghee from the east, saying, "For Indra thee. He covers it with water using a non-clay vessel, saying, "O Viṣṇu, the oblation.
Having set it down, the driving away of the calves is performed as before.

In the morning, for one who does not perform the *sānnāyya* offering, there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Agni and another for Indra-Agni (36). Having poured out clarified butter from the morning milking into another vessel (37),

and having performed the rites up to the washing [of the vessels], he brings the evening milking, cooks the morning milk, pours clarified butter over it, removes it from the fire, and anoints the two [spoons] (38).
"One cuts off from the cooked [portion] first," according to the Śruti; 39. the wiping is performed together; 40.
the spreading apart is performed with the mantra "indrāgnyoḥ"; 41.
The *prastara* is thrown into the fire together with its branch (42).

He offers the *upaveṣa* along with the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), saying: "I offer you, O fortunate one, for the sake of good fortune, you who are most abundant, O much-invoked one, for the sake of glory" (43).
Everything else is as at the Full Moon sacrifice (44).
One who has performed the Soma sacrifice should offer the Sānnāyya; others may do so optionally. One should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices for thirty years.
Fifteen [are] the Dākṣāyaṇa-Śaṅkhīs; 48.
Or one should simply offer the Agnihotra; 42.
The term "action" (*karman*) refers to the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) conjoined with the substance and the deity. 1.
The ritual details of the New and Full Moon sacrifices apply to the *iṣṭi* and animal sacrifices by virtue of their functional capacity and because they are so observed;
the ritual details of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice apply to the Cāturmāsya sacrifices both by virtue of a scriptural injunction and through the application of the rules.
5. And because of the prohibition of Sāmans at the Avabhṛtha bath following the Soma sacrifice;
6. as in the case of the Kaṇvarathantara, there is no mantra instruction regarding the animal sacrifice;
7. in a matter of doubt, the worldly [practice] is not applicable because it is improper.
A specific injunction regarding the ritual action [arises] from the commonality of the number one or two, the measure, the substance, the deity, and the quality.
(8) There is a restriction when there is a conflict between the substance and the deity, because of the inherent connection of the substance.
(9) In the case of the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture), both [the substance and the deity] apply, because it is produced from both. (10)
11. Because there is no single injunction;
12. because curd is a composite substance;
13. because milk possesses that [composite] nature.

That [offering] belongs to the animal sacrifice and the *sānnāyya* offering, as it has been stated; and because of the scriptural injunction regarding expiation (14); and because of the milk, the immediate sequence of time, and the favoring of the ritual properties (15–16).
17. [The view is] that you are immediately Kāśakṛtsni.
18. Vātsya and Bādari hold that there is a transfer from the preceding.
19. By virtue of its taking the place [of the former], the acquisition of properties in substances is not prohibited.
Modification according to the actual purpose applies when there is an injunction (20);
it does not apply to the archetype because of its originality (21);
and it does not apply due to scriptural statement, loss of purpose, or contradiction (22).
Because it arises for the sake of another, there is an absence [of that purpose] when that [other] is absent (23); or rather, there is its existence because it is enjoined (24);
actions would not occur in the case of the counter-example because of the syntactical connection (25).
Description of the Dākṣāyaṇa Sacrifice:
The Dākṣāyaṇa sacrifice is for one desiring progeny, cattle, food, and fame.
It is a distinct ritual because of the connection with its specific name, fruit, and quality.
Or rather, it is an injunction of qualities, because of the statements regarding proximity and abundance [of materials]:
"The animal for Agni-Soma is on the full moon day; the one for Indra-Agni is on the new moon day";
"In the morning, like the *sānnāyya*."
On the new moon day, there is a curd-mixture for Mitra and Varuṇa (payasyā maitrāvaruṇī).
At that very time, he pours sour milk into the heated milk to produce *drohaṇa*.
Having poured out the whey (*vājina*), he places it on the rubbish-heap (*utkara*).

Or, having struck [the earth] with a blade of grass that has not been smeared with clarified butter, he proceeds with it; or, having released the two offering-ladles, he takes [the butter] while sprinkling the sacrificial grass (barhis), for the Śruti declares:
"In each of the bulls he places seed."
He causes the verses for the *vājins* to be recited.

Having offered oblations at each *vaṣaṭ*-call, he supports the quarters with the remnants of the *vājina* offering, using the formula "The quarters... for each mantra, moving clockwise, beginning first from the east.
With the two final mantras, he does so in the middle and in the eastern half.

The utterance of *svāhā* applies everywhere because of the state of expectancy. Having been invited with the formula "O remnant, invite [us] to partake," and having been invited again, he partakes when prompted by the word "invited. Or [he may partake] with names that are appropriate.
Or, by implication, [he may consume it] with the common formulas, or with the formula: "I consume the strength of the strengths of the seasons."
"May I, as a steed, partake of the steed that has been invited," or "I, being invited, partake [of it]";
or "May I become a steed among steeds.
The Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, the Brahman, the Āgnīdhra, and the Sacrificer [partake].
Or, alternatively, the sacrificer may perform both [the first and the second] at once; 24.
or the sacrificial fee is a Dākṣāyaṇa; 25.
or he may sacrifice for a year. 26.
One should avoid meat, liquor, falsehood, urine, and garments made of hair.
(27) The deity for the *upāṃśu* [offering] is Kāmya;
in the *āgrayaṇa*, it is Vaiśvadeva. (28)
The cakes on one potsherd are not dedicated to Varuṇa;
the one is dedicated to Prajāpati, and the one is dedicated to Savitṛ in the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
The Vaiśvadevī [offering] (6), the Vāyavya [offering] (7), and the Tanūhavis offerings (8).
The deities of the Dīkṣaṇīyā, Prāyaṇīyā, and Ātithyā offerings; 9. the Devasū and Devikā oblations; 10. the offering to Vāyu in the fire. 11.
And [the cup] for Mitra and Varuṇa (12);
the one for Indra (13), which is the first in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice;
and that of Vāyodhas (14).
One should perform the Āgneya sacrifice for one who desires rain;
alternatively, for the sake of rain, one should say, "I am desirous of rain," regarding the original rite (prakṛti).
One should tell the Adhvaryu, "Meditate mentally upon the east wind and the lightning."
The clouds for the Āgnīdhra (18);
"all these" for the Brahman (19).

At the commencement of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, there is the Anvārambhaṇīyā offering: a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Viṣṇu, a pap for Sarasvatī, and a cake on twelve potsherds for Sarasvant (20–21).
A four-year-old cow is the sacrificial fee, or alternatively, a pair [of animals]. 22.
An eleven-potherd cake for Indra Vimṛdh follows the full-moon sacrifice. 23.
This is an alternative option from the beginning. 24.
The *āditya* oblation of cooked rice is performed on the new moon day. 25.
The description of the *āgrayaṇeṣṭi*:
the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice for the first-fruits belongs to Indra and Agni. 1.
The *caru* for the Viśvedevas is made of rice and barley (2), or it may be prepared in milk (3–4).
There is a cake on one potsherd for Dyāvāpṛthivī (Heaven and Earth). Having removed it from the fire, he should cover its edges with clarified butter; or he may sacrifice with clarified butter alone.
Or a sacrificial porridge (caru) of old grains; 8. a first-born cow is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); 9. and [this applies] to the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice as well. 10.

One who has not performed the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices should feed Brāhmaṇas with food cooked on the Dakṣiṇāgni fire—sufficient for four persons—and give them something as a gift. For one who maintains the Agnihotra, the evening and morning Agnihotra oblations are performed with new grain;
or they may be performed with milk from which [the sacrificer] has eaten.
And there is the vow of the consecrated; 14.
during the Upasad days, one should perform the two Rauhiṇa offerings; 15. during the Soma-pressing days, the Savanīya offerings. 16.

A gentle offering of wild *śyāmāka* grain porridge; in summer, a bamboo staff; a chariot consecrated again is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); linen cloth for the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), or a garment worn during the rainy season.
The description of the establishment of the sacred fires: the laying of the fires (agnyādheya) may take place on the new moon day,
or under the asterisms of Kṛttikā, Mṛgaśiras, or Phalgunī.
Hasta is for one desiring gain; Citrā is for a Kṣatriya;
and Vasantā is for a Brāhmaṇa or for one desiring spiritual luster.
The summer season is for those desiring the glory of the Kṣatriya status;
the rainy season is for those desiring offspring and cattle, as well as for Vaiśyas and chariot-makers.
They perform [the rite] in the fire-hall.
Or it may have its rafters pointing upwards;
the door is in the south-east;
the sowing of seeds is as at the Full Moon sacrifice.
The wife wears two unwashed linen garments.
When the Adhvaryu has completed his task, [the garments] are to be given away.
He churns fire and places it on the Gārhapatya hearth.
He eats either from the kitchen of a Vaiśya family or from an *ambarīṣa* (public cooking vessel) [15]; by day or by night [16].

"The gods are the ancestors, the ancestors are the gods; who I am, as such I sacrifice. Him whom I am, I do not exclude. My own is the offering, my own the toil, my own the well-poured oblation" [17].
The sacrificer enters by the eastern door and the wife by the southern door (18).
They sit down to the west of the fire, with the wife to the south (19).
He hands over the two kindling sticks, consisting of *aśvattha* wood with a *śamī* tree within it (20).

In the absence of a *garbha* (embryo), he says, "Restrain your speech until the final oblation is offered"; [this applies] at sunset, at night, or at sunrise, because that is the primary time. He binds a goat in the Gārhapatya chamber, or if one is not available, he should give it to the Āgnīdhra at sunset in the morning.
On the hide of a red bull, he measures out four vessels for the oblation; he cooks that [mixture] which is to be consumed by four.
