Having removed it from the fire and placed a vessel for pouring in the center, he pours clarified butter over it and lays on three fuel-sticks of *aśvattha* wood anointed with ghee, verse by verse, with the hymn beginning "With fuel, O Agni.
He mutters the verse beginning "Approach, O Agni."
Or the Adhvaryu [eats] the second [portion]; four officiating priests eat [the portions]. "The Brahma-rice is ready," he says.
He grants a boon.

Or, he may perform [the rite] for one year beforehand; thereafter, he should establish all the fires. If the *gārhapatya* fire has gone out, he should fetch a fire from the village, cook the *cātuṣprāśya* porridge, and then divide [the fires].
One should maintain the vigil throughout the night;
or [one may do so] with pieces [of wood]. When dawn has broken, having extinguished [the fire], one should either collect the embers if it is the Anvāhāryapacana fire, or [dispose of them otherwise].

Having marked out the place and sprinkled it with water, while [the sacrificer] maintains contact, he places gold [on the ground] and pours out earth from the pit for the post-holes; at the ends, he places pebbles.
According to some, he places gold on top.
The same procedure applies to the other two [holes].
To the east of the Āhavanīya fire, at eight, eleven, or twelve steps— or according to one's judgment—
at the third part of the distance to the south,
the churning of the fire takes place; some say it should be done before the fire has been moved.
When [the sun] has risen, however, there is the lifting up (20).
To the west of the Gārhapatya hearth (21), he should say, "Bring the horse! (22).
When the horse has stood before him (23),
the granting of a boon occurs (24);
some say it is done mentally (25).
"His exhalation has placed the breath in immortality," [he says]. "The inhalation has taken up the immortal breath," [he says].

He kindles [the fire] with pieces of wood while it is burning, over the sacrificial materials, with the words: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ! O Lord of Vows, I have established you by means of this vow for such-and-such a person. 1.
With the formula "Of Varuṇa thee," [he addresses] a Kṣatriya; with "Of Indra thee," a Rājanya;
with "Of Manu, the village-leader thee," a Vaiśya; and with "Of the Ṛbhus thee," a chariot-maker.
He gives the command: "Sing the Rathantara! 4.
The singing belongs to the Adhvaryu;
or rather, to the Brahman because of his connection with the Veda, and because the Adhvaryu is already occupied [with other duties].
Having taken up the fuel for the lifting, he should do so in such a way that the smoke reaches it; then he gives the command: "The Vāmadevya! 8–10.
A young horse is placed in front; in its absence, one that is not young; in the absence of a horse, a draft-ox.
Having caused the ritual materials to be placed upon it, he leads it eastward with its right fore-foot, turns it around, and establishes it there.
He gives the command: "Recite the Bṛhat! 11–13.

Having touched the footprint twice with fire, he places it down with the third [verse], or with the second, or with the first, as before, saying "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. Having circumambulated from the east and taken the front half of the fuel-stick, he says, "Like the sky in abundance. And he worships it with the Sārparājñī verses, saying, "This bull... and so forth.
He establishes the Dakṣiṇāgni fire; and having churned out the Sabhya fire,
he says, "Play for the cow!"
Therefore, the establishment of the *dhāraṇā* [is performed];
he commands regarding the *śyaita*, *vāravantīya*, and *yajñāyajñiya* [chants].
Having gone around the fires by the right, he releases them toward the north.

One should not perform the rites concerning the seasons, the constellations, the collection of materials, the simultaneous sowing, the eating of the four-fold portion, the vigil, the kindling wood, the first half [of the sacrifice], the taking hold [from behind], or the *sārparājñī* verses; or rather, one may perform them. However, the *agnihotra* should be performed silently at the end of the *pūrṇāhuti*, according to the sacred tradition. Having poured out the clarified butter and placed it over the *gārhapatya* fire, having cleansed the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, having taken it down, purified it, inspected it, and drawn the portion, while the sacrificer maintains contact [from behind], he should offer it everywhere with the word "svāhā."
The utterance of the words "I grant a boon" constitutes the formal bestowal of the boon.
At the end of twelve days, he offers the *tanū* oblations; [he may offer them] in the second month, the third month, after six months, or after a year, or immediately, or not at all.
The first [oblation] is for Agni Pavamāna.
The second [offering] is for Agni Pāvaka and for Agni Śuci;
the third is a caru-oblation for Aditi;
or rather, there may be an offering to Agni alone before that of Aditi.
Having divided the six sacrificial gifts, he gives twelve, twenty-four,
or more, according to his faith;
a cow is for Āditya.
One should avoid falsehood, neglecting hospitality, eating putrid food, meat from a slaughtered animal, food cooked by a pregnant woman, and food cooked with too much water.

(15) A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) who maintains the perpetual fire, having offered milk-oblations into that fire, should sleep near it for twelve nights, six nights, or at least three nights. (16) [Then follows] the re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punarādheya*).
The re-establishment of the sacred fires (punarādheya) is for one who has not previously vowed to establish them,
or for one desiring sovereignty and fame,
provided that he has not neglected the fires for less than three nights.
Or immediately [after the full moon] on the two Punarvasu days,
or at midday during the rainy season.
The establishment of the fires (ādhāna) is performed with *kuśa* grass.

He places a rice-cake (*vrīhyapūpa*) cooked on *arka* and *palāśa* wood in the place of the *gārhapatya* fire; likewise for the *āhavanīya* fire, provided it is done immediately. The offering to Agni (*āgneya*) is on five potsherds and is performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) until the final after-offering (*anuyāja*).
Or, excluding that [verse],
one may recite "agnīn" (the fires) during the first *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings;
the second *ājyabhāga* is for Agni Pavamāna or for Agni Indumat.
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is gold or a draft-ox, according to the Śruti, if one desires the rites pertaining to the establishment of the fires (agnyādheya). 13.
Everything else is like the establishment of the fires; it is performed immediately. 14.

In the afternoon, after the cow dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa has been immolated before sunset, and having completed the ritual up to the iḍā-portion of the cake-offering, they proceed with the morning rite using the meat cooked overnight; therein occurs the establishment of the fires. 15.
The examination of the ritual attendance:
when the self-offering has been made, the sacrificer attends upon the two fires with the *vātsapra* hymn,
or he does not.
Approaching it with the three [verses] beginning "tisras tisraḥ" and "asya pratnām," and with "pari te citrāvaso";
having sat down with "santvam," he goes toward a cow with "andhasva."
He sacrifices with the formula, "The Saṃhitā.
Having gone to the Gārhapatya fire, he worships it with the verse, "Approach thee.
He goes toward the cow with the call, "O Iḍā, come hither!"
One performs these optional rites in this manner.
(9) With the mantra "To Soma," one partakes of waterless food as prescribed for the commencement of a vow.
(10) The mention of the son's name is performed as at the Full Moon sacrifice. (11)
With "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," both [the teacher and the student] [depart];
when about to go on a journey, [the student] recites "sarvān aryā" for each mantra;
he goes with mindfulness, [this being] the release of speech.

One who is traveling abroad should perform the sacrifice at the proper time, because it is a purification for oneself, because it is merely a religious duty (*dharma*), and because of the scriptural injunction.
(15) Having returned, he should observe silence with his mind focused.
(16) With fuel-sticks in hand, having approached, he worships the Āhavanīya, Gārhapatya, and Dakṣiṇā fires, saying: "We have come. (17)
Having sat down, [he performs] the smoothing and sweeping of the embers; 18.
or he may perform the silent worship as before; 19. and having approached, 20. [he performs the remaining rites].
"O houses, do not fear," with these words he approaches the house; "For your security," with these words he enters.
He should not harm the members of the household, though he may do so at will on the following day.
Regarding the description of the Agnihotra:
at the evening and morning Agnihotra, the sacrificer should say, "Lift [the fire]," for the lifting of the Āhavanīya fire from the Gārhapatya fire occurs before sunset and before sunrise.
Or, facing west, he should place it in the evening; some perform the morning and evening oblations in that fire.
The southern fire (dakṣiṇāgni) is perpetual. All [these fires] belong to those who have attained prosperity.
Or always fetching [the materials]; according to some, on the day of fasting;
or when nine [days] have elapsed.
In that [fire], they should cook meatless food. 9. If there is no such food to be cooked, he should say, "Let cow's milk be placed on the fire. 10.
He should say, "Let that be made for the Brāhmaṇa to drink. 11.
Having gone between the two fires, the sacrificer sits down to the south, having circumambulated the Āhavanīya fire from right to left;
the wife does so as before.
To the west of the Āhavanīya, he places a bundle of Kuśa grass or simply some Kuśa blades.
He performs the strewing for all [fires] with grass-blades pointing eastward and northward; he makes them with their tips pointing northward and southward, according to the Śruti.
Having sprinkled water around the Āhavanīya fire, he pours out a continuous stream from it as far as the Gārhapatya fire.
And that [stream] too.

Then he milks the Agnihotra cow— provided she has a male calf and is not of Śūdra descent— into a vessel made by an Ārya with its lid facing upward, to the south of the Dakṣiṇāgni fire; [he milks] eastward or northward, omitting the continuous stream once the oblation has been offered.

Having brought [the material] from the east to the Āhavanīya fire, some place it over the Gārhapatya; having moved the embers out to the north, one proceeds in this same manner elsewhere for the bringing of materials intended for an oblation.
To the south [is the place] for the vegetable offerings.

Having illuminated [the vessel] with a blade of grass and poured water into it, having again illuminated it and set it down, he removes it from the fire three times toward the north. After sunset, he offers the oblation.
Having heated the Vaikaṅkata *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, he cleanses them with his hand.
He says, "I shall lift it up again after heating it. 8.
Standing, the sacrificer says, "Oṃ, lift it up! 9. He pours out four ladlefuls. 10.
He leaves a remnant in the pot; a Brāhmaṇa should drink that.
Holding a wooden fuel-stick above, he carries it from the Gārhapatya fire toward the Āhavanīya fire, holding it at the level of his mouth.

Holding it in the middle and concealing it, he sits down and places the fuel-stick with the mantra: "I place thee, who art the light of Agni, accompanied by Vāyu, leading to heaven, for the sake of heaven—the radiant one."
He makes an oblation into the blazing fire with the mantra "Agni is light" (RV 8.44.16) or with "Sajūs" (VS 2.2).
For one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), he uses "Agni is splendor" (VS 2.3).
Having placed [the fuel] on the grass-bundle, he gazes at the *gārhapatya* fire while about to offer.
Silently, he places more [fuel] on the northern side; having shaken the ladle twice, he sets it down most firmly.
Having wiped the *sruva* ladle, he wipes it on the grass-bundle (*kūrca*) with the formula, "Homage to the gods; *svadhā* to the ancestors," while holding it palm-upward toward the south.

(20) Having touched water, (21) one who desires prosperity [should offer] from the other two [fires] using the *sruva* from the pot: "May the Lord of Prosperity bestow prosperity here; may Prajāpati cause offspring to delight here. To Agni Gṛhapati, the possessor of wealth, the lord of prosperity, *svāhā*!"—thus at the Gārhapatya fire. (22)
A second [oblation] silently. 23.
"To Agni, the eater of food, the lord of food, svāhā!"—thus [he offers] in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire. 24.
A second [oblation] silently. 25.
He tastes it twice with the ring finger (26).
Having moved away and licked [the finger], he sprinkles [water] for the teacher, saying: "Gladden the gods; gladden the ancestors. He sprinkles a third time, saying: "Gladden the seven seers" (27).
He sprinkles the fourth time three times in the place of the grass-bundle, saying: "To Agni, who dwells on earth, svāhā! I offer the nectar of the earth, svāhā! (28).
Having heated the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles over the *āhavanīya* fire, he sets them down.
(29) He places fuel sticks upon [the fires] in all cases, according to the manner of the sprinkling: "Thou art fuel; as fuel, O Agni, shine for me; may I shine, O Agni, through thee being kindled.
(30) Remaining silent from the time of milking until the oblation, provided that he is the milk-offerer. (31)
In the morning, he offers the oblation before sunrise.
Having gone between the two fires, or having gone around the Gārhapatya fire to the south, keeping it to his right, the sacrificer sits down;
and the wife also sits in her proper place.
Then he sips water, saying: "You are rain; cut away my evil. Through truth I enter the vow. O Waters, truth is my vow.

(4) Having released his speech, he sips water again, saying: "You are lightning; cut away my evil. Strike away the waters; I enter the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha). Truth is in me; my vow is with the cows.
(5) "I draw it up," he says in the morning. (6)
The sprinkling with fuel-sticks is directed eastward, as is the stream [of water], or both may be done in either direction.
When the word "Agni" occurs, one should substitute "Sūrya.
Or one may use the formula: "O Night, with the Dawn! (rātrī yuṣasāha).
Or he may offer in the morning with the mantra "The light is the sun" (jyotiḥ sūryaḥ).

For one desiring heaven, he should offer at the first setting and at the rising of the sun. He should offer in the evening when darkness has fallen, and in the morning while the sky is still visible, for one desiring long life.
If the animal is already inside, it is for one desiring cattle; in the evening and morning, for one desiring prosperity while [the victim] is lying down;
in the morning, when the first [victim] has been prepared and is being fumigated, for one who would suddenly devour food as if having struck down his offspring.

As if suddenly grasping a blazing torch with its flames most intense, he who desires prosperity and fame would consume food with a friendly mind even when it results in the destruction of those very flames.
When the coals are glowing, [he should offer] for one desiring Brahman-splendor (19);
with milk, for one desiring heaven or cattle (20);
with barley-gruel, for one desiring a village (21).
One desiring strength [should offer] with rice grains (22);
one desiring the senses [should offer] with curd (23);
and there is no placing on the fire, according to both scripture and logical capacity (24).
One desiring splendor should offer oblations with clarified butter for one year; [he may do so] with each one of these [substances] when conjoined with a specific desire;
[the offering may be performed] either in the evening or in the morning.
In the Agnihotra sacrifices, entry is by the southern door (28).
For the evening and morning attendance at the Āhavanīya fire, one sits facing it (29).
Or, for sleeping or sitting, one does so facing the Gārhapatya fire (30).
31. Walking along while recollecting the *dakṣiṇāgni* in his mind; 32.
Without having eaten, during the morning *muhūrta*, he should approach the seat of the *sabhya* fire; 33. He should approach the fire after the ashes have been removed.
Or he may offer the oblation himself. 34. On the day of preparation (upavasatha), there is a restrictive rule (niyama).
35. Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Kātyāyana Śrautasūtra. 4.
The procedure for the Cāturmāsya sacrifices: on the full moon day of Phālguna, one who desires [specific results] should offer oblations to Vaiśvānara and Pārjanya;
the offering to Vaiśvānara consists of a cake on twelve potsherds, and the subsequent offering is a caru-oblation.

In the Vaiśvadeva section, there is an oblation for Agni, a *caru* for Soma, a *puroḍāśa* on twelve or eight potsherds for Savitṛ, a *caru* for Sarasvatī, and a *caru* of finely ground flour for Pūṣan;
[the latter] is also [offered] as a dual-deity offering because of the force of the restrictive rule.
Alternatively, it may be half-ground, due to the force of both [rules].
And because of the mention of Soma and Pūṣan;
or rather, it is not an offering-cake because of the difference in deities;
[it is so] because of a specific scriptural statement regarding the offering to Soma and Pūṣan.
In all these cases,
there is an offering on seven potsherds for the Maruts who possess their own wealth (svatavadbhyo marudbhyaḥ),
or [an offering] for the Maruts themselves.
The curdled milk (payasyā) belongs to the Viśvedevas;
the cake on one potsherd belongs to Heaven and Earth.
This is the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
On ground sloping toward the east (16), the sacrificer wears unwashed garments and so does his wife (17); these same rules apply also for the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings (18).
Having bound the sacrificial grass (barhis) in three parts, he binds it again as one;
19. the prastara-bunch of kuśa shoots is tied on; 20. having placed [the implements] near the fire, [he prepares] the fire-drilling apparatus (agnimanthana). 21.
Having taken a wooden chip with the formula, "The birthplace of Agni," he silently places it on the altar (22).
With the formula, "The two testicles," he places two young *kuśa* blades upon it (23).
With the formula, "Thou art Urvaśī," he places the lower fire-drill (*adharāraṇi*) between those two (24).
Having touched the vessel of clarified butter with the verse, "Thou art life" (RV 10.59.6), he places the fire-drill with the verse, "Purūravas... (RV 10.95.1).
With that [verse], he causes [the sacrificer] to recite after him while the fire is being churned for Agni.
He churns three times clockwise, reciting a mantra for each turn, beginning with, "With the Gāyatra [meter]... (VS 5.34).
"Born for the born," (he says) three times;
"for him who is being cast forth," while casting [the oblation];
"may there be for you," he casts it.
He offers with the ladle from the pot, saying, "Agni in Agni.
There are nine fore-offerings and nine after-offerings.
These are the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings and the Mahāhavis.
He offers three *samiṣṭayajus* oblations with the formulas: "O gods who know the way," "O sacrifice, [lead] the sacrifice," and "This is for thee.
(9) And [he does so] at the animal sacrifice.
(10) Or, at the animal sacrifice, [he uses the formula]: "Whom thou didst bring hither... (11).
Or one [offering] at the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice (12).
At the Pavamāna sacrifices, there is either shaving prior to the final one (13).
To the west of the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, he shaves the hair on the right side of the head with the mantra: "Impelled by Savitṛ, may the divine waters moisten your body for long life and splendor" (14).
Having smoothed [the hair] with a porcupine quill, he places three young *kuśa* blades in between, saying, "O herb... (15).
The sacrificer mutters, "The triple life-span...
(16). Taking a metal razor, saying, "Thou art named Śiva," he shaves, saying, "I turn back [the hair]" (17).

In the same way, [the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is performed] in eighteen houses to the west and to the north; likewise, if the full-moon oblation has been offered on both the kindled fire and the fire produced by friction, it is also for one desiring offspring. The Vaiśvadeva [is performed].
At this stage, some [teachers] maintain that he should sleep facing downward and toward the east, eat honey, and approach his wife during her season.
(21) He should avoid meat, falsehoods, and entering water until the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath).
(22) [This applies to] the Varuṇapraghāsa festival.

On the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, they perform the rite with the thought, "This is the womb. Having ascended the fires and moved away from the sacrificial ground, they churn out the fire for the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings.
On the previous day, they prepare the *karambha* vessels from dehusked, unthreshed barley in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire;
there should be as many vessels as there are members of the sacrificer's household plus one.
Or, for one who has heard [the sacred texts], it may be performed upon the birth of offspring;
or three [offerings] because of their permanence;
and also a pair of rams.
One should wash non-sheep wool and apply it to those two;
or, in its absence, use kusha-grass wool.
To the east of the Āhavanīya fire, one prepares the altar.
The space between [the two posts] is one span or wider; the northern [post] is the measure of a chariot.
Or, it is four cubits at the back, seven cubits long toward the east, or six, or three, at the front.
In their midst, he places a wooden pin (śaṅku) measuring thirteen units or of unlimited length, and performs the smoothing with the wooden sword (sphya) and other tools.
There is a single rubbish-heap for both [the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ].
To the west of the altar is the path of the Pratiprasthātṛ. He pours out the earth for the northern high-altar on the northern side.
Taking up the *śamyā* (wooden yoke-pin), he measures out the *cātvāla* pit to the east, leaving a passage free from the *utkara* heap. He places the *śamyā* pointing north in front [of the pit],
then one pointing south to the right, and one pointing north to the left.
He scratches inside with the wooden sword (sphya), saying for each mantra, "The path of the heated one" (taptāyanī). 22.
He throws [the earth] into the pit (cātvāla) with the wooden sword while [the sacrificer] maintains contact with him, saying, "May Agni bestow [it]" (vidade 'gniḥ). 23.
He carries away the loose soil (purīṣa) with his hand, saying, "In front, O Aṅgiras" (agre aṅgiraḥ). 24.
With the formula "yo 'syām," he scatters [the earth] together with a peg in the eastern half;

25. it is brought silently like the *utkara* by the *agnīdh*; 26. in this same way twice more; the distinction is that [the formulas are] "dvitīyasyām" and "tṛtīyasyām" for the second and third [scatterings]. 27.
Having recited the fourth verse, *anutva*, according to its meaning, he brings [the earth] and spreads out the *uttaravedi* with the formula, "Thou art a lioness" (*siṃhyasi*).

It is [measured] at the distance of a *śamyā*, or one-third less than that, or unlimited, or the length of a yoke, or ten paces for the sacrificer; or rather, in the case of the Soma sacrifice, it is on the northern side, because of the scriptural injunction regarding the spreading apart and because of the impossibility [of the other measurements].

In the center, he makes a navel one span in size and four-cornered (31). He sprinkles the high altar and scatters sand over it with each respective mantra, saying, "Thou art a lioness" (32). It remains covered. 1.
In the morning, having taken the fivefold-drawn [oblation], he leads forward the two fires, supporting them with two fuel-sticks;
or rather, he distributes it all, because that is the archetypal rule;
the leading forward [of the fires] is mentioned because it pertains to the Soma sacrifice.
Or rather, because the *prakṛti* (archetype) is nameless, there is no mention [of it];
the mention is for the sake of the qualities, since the fire is prescribed on the *uttaravedi*.

Having lifted the *ājya* and the *prokṣaṇī* waters and having addressed the two fires, he says: "Recite for the two fires as they are being carried forward; follow with the single wooden sword (*ekasphya*)."
When [the *sāmidhenī* verses] have been recited three times, the carrying [of the earth] takes place according to the altar. 8.
The Pratiprasthātṛ draws lines with the wooden sword (*sphya*) from the corner of the altar toward the *uttaravedi*, or up to the *uttaravedi* itself. 9.

Standing between the two altars, he sprinkles the *uttaravedi* facing north, in each direction with the respective mantra, "O Indra, may Ghoṣa [protect] thee," and so on, according to the indicative mark (*liṅga*). 10.
He pours out the remainder outside the altar along with the right shoulder, [saying], "This, O heated water, I [pour] against so-and-so," if he is practicing sorcery (11).
He offers the five-fold portion across the right shoulder, the hip, the hip, the shoulder, and the middle, while looking at gold with each mantra, "Thou art a lioness" (12).
He lifts up the ladle [with the words], "For the beings, thee" (13).
He encloses the navel with pieces of *paitudārava* wood, as before, reciting the formulas "Thou art firm" for each.

He pours down the soil of the fire-altar (*purīṣa*)—namely *guggulu*, *sugandhitejana*, and the hair-tufts (*stukā*) from the tail of a bull; if these are unavailable, other [hair] may be used instead. Upon these he places the fire.
Having sprinkled [the ground] while looking upwards, he pours down the *upayamani* [water-vessels] to the south (17). He pours them out starting from the *praṇītā* vessel (18–19).

If the formal undertaking of the vow (*vratopāyana*) has not been performed, [then] in addition to the obligatory offerings, there are an offering to Indra and Agni, a curd-offering (*payasyā*), a curd-offering to Varuṇa, a curd-offering to the Maruts, and a cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) for Ka.
(20–21) The pouring out of the clarified butter is done separately for each. (22)
The southern [portion] belongs to the Pratiprasthātṛ. 23.

In front of the *dhruvā* [ladle], there is the *pṛṣadājya*—clarified butter mixed with curds—taken five times, [accompanied by the formula] "Thou art light" (*jyotir asi*) ending with the word *samit*. 24.
This is for the sake of the *anuyāja* offerings everywhere. 25.
The placing of the *aupabhṛta* [ladle] occurs [before the *ājyabhāgas*],
because of the instruction without qualification [in the rule] "with the dear abode" (priyeṇa dhāmnā); or rather,
it occurs later, because of the reference to a subsequent time.
And the Pratiprasthātṛ [performs these acts]— or rather, he does not;

the Pratiprasthātṛ does not perform the carrying forward of the *praṇītā* waters, the girding of the wives, the churning of the fire, the *āśrāvaṇa*, *pratyāśrāvaṇa*, the *praiṣas*, the addressing of the sacrificer, the choosing of the Hotṛ’s seat, the tasting of the *prāśitra*, the anointing of the finger-joints, the intermediate portion of the *iḍā*, or the final bath at the secondary fire-altar.

He imitates what has been done elsewhere, except in the case of the southern [fire]. Having poured the *vājina* [mixture] into both [fires], he scatters *karīra* fruits mixed with *śamī* leaves and a pair of rams.
He places the ram for the Maruts on the northern altar, and all the other oblations; the Pratiprasthātṛ places the offering for the Maruts, together with the clarified butter, on the southern altar.
When the call has been given for the cleansing and it has been cleansed, the Pratiprasthātṛ, intending to lead the wife [to the Sadas], says: "With whom do you walk?"
He speaks of those with whom he has become intimate;
or he gathers up blades of grass at every encounter,
for it is stated in the Śruti that one should not disclose what is harmful to his kinsmen.
When [the wife] has been led forward, he makes her recite the verse beginning with "praghāsinaḥ" (VS 3.48).

He offers the *karambha* vessels with a winnowing basket, having placed them upon his head; having brought them by the southern fire while facing westward, the husband and wife offer them by way of the *tīrtha*, either to the east or to the west of the altar, with the verse beginning "yad grāme" (VS 3.49).
The sacrificer mutters the verse beginning "mo ṣū ṇaḥ" (VS 3.50).
He makes her recite, "This is my unblemished deed," as he leads her back.
(12) When she has arrived, [the rites] beginning with the sweeping up and ending with the two Ājyabhāga offerings take place. (13) The Pratiprasthātṛ stands by with the *sruk* ladle in his hand. (14)
He proceeds with the oblations (havirbhiḥ).
At the time of performing the offering of the curd-mixture (payasyā), they exchange the two rams. With one of the portions (avadāna), he [offers] the ram.
Having taken the two offering-spoons with his left hand, he causes the Pratiprasthātṛ to recite the invitatory formula for the Maruts with his right hand.
(18) The portioning of the oblation is like that of Varuṇa.
(19) Both perform the ritual with the sacrificial offerings, beginning from the Sviṣṭakṛt offering. (20)
Having taken a portion of the *iḍā*, [he gives it] to the *pratiprasthātṛ* (21).
Thereupon, the *pratiprasthātṛ* [takes a portion] of the offering to the Maruts (22).
The two *adhvaryus* separate their two *sruva*-ladles (23).
Having poured [the remainder] together, there is the consumption of the whey (vājina); 24.
The Pratiprasthātṛ partakes [of the whey] because he is a modification of the Adhvaryu; 25.
And the Maitrāvaruṇa [partakes] because he is a modification of both the Hotṛ and the Adhvaryu. 26.
The *samiṣṭayajus* offerings are performed silently on the southern side.
(27) The *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) is performed with the scrapings of the *vāruṇī* vessel.
(28) Having approached and entered the water silently, he immerses himself, saying, "O *avabhṛtha*! (29)
The husband and wife, having bathed but not immersed themselves,
run over each other's backs;
he then puts on two other garments.

First, he should give [the remainder] to those authorized, to whomever he may wish (33). Having returned by the same way he came, he places a fuel-stick on the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "Thou art the kindler of the gods" (34).
And the wife silently places one on the Gārhapatya fire (35).
A cow is the sacrificial fee, or a horse, or six, or ten. 36.
The Sākamedha section [takes place] on the full moon day of Kārttika; the Sākamedhas last for two days. 1.
On the preceding day, in the forenoon, there is a cake (puroḍāśa) for Agni Anīkavant;
at midday, an oblation of cooked rice (caru) for the Sāntapana Maruts;
it concludes with the Samiṣṭayajus offering.
Or, omitting the throwing of the *barhis* grass,
one places a piece of wood as a *paridhi* in the place of the fuel-wood and prepares a pap (*caru*) in milk for the Maruts, the Gṛhamedhins, in the evening;
it is performed like the *sānnāyya* offering.
Or silently;
8 because there is a single injunction;
9 having cooked it, sprinkled it with clarified butter, and removed it from the fire, he draws it out into two shallow dishes or into two vessels. 10
Having placed [the vessel] in the middle for pouring, he pours clarified butter into it for the sake of the *ājya* offering (11).
From this point onward, it is as has been stated (12).
Having touched the altar with the *staraṇa-yajus* formula, or silently—since it has already been performed—the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) follows (13).
Having placed the wood-shavings, he sets down the oblations after lifting them up with his mind;
he cleanses the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, either by removing them from their place or while leaving them as they are.
He performs the ritual with the two *ājyabhāga* portions: the one for Agni from the south and the one for Soma from the north.
In the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of the householder, the two portions are equal, like the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*),
and there is no second sprinkling of clarified butter;
or rather, without taking them out separately, he places the combined clarified butter over the fire.
Having taken it out, he places both [portions] down;
there is no *prāśitra* and it ends with the *iḍā*;
having invoked [the gods], the first cleansing takes place.

Those who are engaged eat [the remains]: the members of the sacrificer's household, the officiating priests who are entitled to the remnants of the oblation, and other Brahmins, if there are many. He sets down the vessel so that it is not empty.
Having completed the Sāntapanīyā offering,
either in the morning— because of the remaining [substances]—
or having allowed the calves to join their mothers, he binds a calf with the *nivānyā* (the cow that has recently calved).
The Agnihotra oblation is performed with barley-gruel (yavāgū).
Having offered it in the morning, whether he has already sacrificed or not, he takes [the gruel] from the pot with the ladle, saying, "The ladle is full.
He should say, "Let the bull be called."
He offers oblations on the path;
thirty-two times he does not utter [a word], and the Brahman priest says, "Offer! (33). He says, "Give to me," and then he offers (34).
A bull is the sacrificial fee (35). To the Maruts, the Playful Ones, an offering on seven potsherds (1).
A pap for Aditi (also elsewhere) (2).
Or rather, the two [sacrifices] share the same sacrificial grass because the ritual action and the time are one;
having moved away from the Mahāhavis,
one should churn [the fire] on the previous day.
In the Āgnīdhra fire, there is an oblation for Indra and Agni; a pap for Mahendra; and a cake on one potsherd for Viśvakarman.
(6) The carrying forward of the fire to the northern altar, the churning, and the speckled butter are as in the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifice. (7) A bull is the sacrificial fee. (8)
The Pitryeṣṭi is the Pitṛyajña; it is performed in a low voice (upāṃśu),
with the ritual procedure performed from the front (purastādupacāra).
And [the rule] regarding the Brahman and the sacrificer is as before, or [as in the case of] one who is without a wife.
The Dakṣiṇāgni is like the Āhavanīya. 6.
He carries the Praṇītā waters around to the east of the Āhavanīya. 7.
And this is for a specific purpose. 8.
A cake on six potsherds for the Soma-possessing ancestors (9);
or for Soma accompanied by the ancestors (10);
parched grains for the ancestors seated on the sacrificial grass (barhis) (11).
The stirred drink (mantha) is for the Agniṣvātta ancestors; 12.
the drawing [of the portions] is fourfold; 13.
the threshing and grinding take place to the east of the Gārhapatya fire. 14.
The placing of the potsherds is in the southern half [of the fire-altar] (15).
The roasting of the grains is performed in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire (16). Even when there is a reversal in the order of cooking, the ritual rules still apply (17).
Having touched [the grains], one grinds half of them; [the mixture] is churned once in the milk of a cow that has recently calved; this is the *mantha* with a single stirring-stick (18).
There is no taking up of the *mantha*, because of the Vedic text: "Then they grind half of them" (19).
Or rather, there is a taking up, because it is so enjoined (20).

To the south of the southern fire (dakṣiṇāgni), which is enclosed and has its door facing north, he prepares an altar in its center, with corners directed toward the intermediate directions and reaching to the edge [of the enclosure].
He places the southern fire in the middle of this [altar].
The Brahman and the sacrificer follow the carrying away of the *praṇītā* water.
He performs the rites beginning with the taking of the wooden sword (sphyā). 24.
Wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), he takes the clarified butter (ājya) twice into the upabhṛt ladle. 25–26.
Or [he takes it] twice into the upabhṛt. 26.
Having loosened the knot at the front of the sacrificial grass (barhis) and grasped the young end first, he goes around the fire three times while spreading it;
leaving only as much as a prastara-bunch, he returns that far.
He spreads that [grass] without a separating bar (avidhṛti),
with its ends directed toward the east, for the placing of the oblation.
From the *sāmidhenī* summons onwards until the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, all [the priests] wear the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītin*).
The Brahman and the sacrificer sit behind; the Āgnīdhra sits in front.
Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he should simply say, "Sit down, O Hotṛ!
The *prayājas* and *anuyājas* are performed without the *barhis* grass.

Or rather, there is no bringing together [of the portions], because of the connection with the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). 36. He offers after having gone back toward the west. 1. While performing the oblations, they proceed in reverse order. 2.
He cuts portions from all [the vessels] as before; for those [deities] associated with Soma, he places [the portions] together once each from the middle [of the cake].
There are two pourings of clarified butter and no overstepping [of the fire].
Or [he offers] to Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs.

Thus, to the north of those seated on the sacrificial grass (barhiṣad), [he offers] the parched grains, the stirred drink, and the sacrificial cakes; to the south of those whose food is the fire (agniṣvātta), [he offers] the stirred drink, the sacrificial cakes, and the parched grains;
to the east, to Agni Kavyavāhana, as before, that is the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.
"Oṃ svadhā," or "Let there be svadhā"—these are the responses to the *āśruta* and *pratyāśruta*; "svadhā namaḥ" is the *vaṣaṭ*-call.
(9) Having invited [the gods] to the *mantha*, the Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, Brahman, and Agnīdh smell it and set it aside.
(10) Having taken a portion for the *prāśitra*, or [taking] the *iḍā*, they all eat. (11)
The Adhvaryu, or the sacrificer himself, sprinkles water three times around the altar with the water-pot.
Having sprinkled the water for the washing of the ancestors at the corners as before— first at the north-western corner—
he takes portions from all [the offerings] together in his left hand and gives the rice-balls according to the order in which they were washed, saying, "O [Name], this is for you."

In the northeast, he wipes his hands with the formula, "Here the fathers [have been satisfied]. (15) All, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder, go out toward the north and worship the Āhavanīya fire with the verse, "They have eaten, they have rejoiced. (16) With the three verses beginning, "We summon the mind hither," they worship the Gārhapatya fire. (17)
Having entered wearing the *prācīnāvīta* cord, the giver mutters, "They have rejoiced" (*amīmadanta*).
18. Having sprinkled water as before, he circumambulates to the right.
19. Having loosened the knot of his lower garment, he makes a gesture of reverence with joined palms, saying "Homage to you" (*namo vaḥ*), or performs six salutations. 20.
And [the mantra] "O fathers, give us houses" (21).
The rites beginning with the invitation of Brahmā up until the spreading out of the *sruc* ladle are performed like the *prayāja* offerings (22).
There is a reversal of the *yajñopavīta* (sacred thread) position (23).
He does not take up the prastara-bunch (24). When told, "Throw [the fuel] into the fire," he does not throw anything into it (25). He silently touches himself (26).
Having touched [water], he does not throw the enclosing-sticks (paridhi) into the fire (27).
It concludes with the *śaṃyu* formula (28).
He throws the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), and the fire into the fire (29), as well as the remnants of the oblation (30).
Having consumed [the portion] in water, 31. [There is] the Traiyambaka sacrifice;
he offers the Traiyambaka oblations, [prepared on] single potsherds, dedicated to Rudra, as many as there are members of the sacrificer's household, plus one. 1.
Or four times, facing north, [he recites] all [the mantras] and the regions.
The oblations are offered without the *vaṣaṭ* call, or they are smeared with clarified butter (*akta*).
Having prepared the vessel, and taking a firebrand from the *dakṣiṇa* fire, the offering is made at a crossroads using the middle leaf of a *palāśa* branch.
The portions of all [the victims] are offered one by one, excluding the extra portion; 8.
there is mixing when they are moistened; 9.
he offers with the formula, "This for thee"; 10.
He scatters the excess [earth] from the mole-hill [around the mound], saying, "This for thee.
Having returned, they mutter, "Come hither, O Rudra, let us worship thee.
They circumambulate the fire three times, keeping their left thighs uncovered and striking them, while reciting the *Tryambaka* hymn.

And like the [offering] to the gods, they beat their right thighs with this very [formula]. (14) And young girls, desiring a husband or desiring fortune, [beat their thighs] on both sides toward the north.
(15) The sacrificer, having offered [the oblation] to Rudra with his joined palms, [performs] the bringing [of the meat] until it reaches the cow. (16)

He accepts these [vessels], though it is impossible for him to perform the ritual rinsing (upasparśana). Having made two bags from bamboo, he fastens them to a bamboo pole and attaches them to one of the following: a stump, a tree, a bamboo stalk, or an anthill, as if they were to be lifted up; this is "this" (etattat).
He is "clad in a skin" (kṛttivāsas). 17–19.
Having approached without looking back, they touch water;
thereafter, [they perform] the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice whenever they wish.
The ritual rules of the Full Moon sacrifice apply, with the exception of the *barhis* grass; these are in addition to the obligatory rites.
For the *Śunāsīrīya* sacrifice, there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra accompanied by Śunāsīra, or for Śunāsīra alone, and milk for Vāyu.
It is worldly,
because of the mention of fresh milk;
no, because there is no contradiction.
And because of the observation of the original form (prakṛti), [the rule applies]; or rather, it is gruel (yavāgū);
[in the case of] the offering to Sūrya, there is a cake on one potsherd (ekakapāla).
A plough with six yokes and twelve dakṣiṇās,
or two oxen;
for the Saura [offering], a white horse.

In the absence [of a cow], there is a cow for one desiring [the fruit] after a year; having sacrificed with the Śunāsīrīya on the full moon day of Phālguna, he should sacrifice with Soma or with an animal sacrifice.
For one who has not sacrificed, there is a repetition [of the rite].
On the fast-day of Phālguna, the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice is performed; in the morning, the Vaiśvadeva.

(18) Among the sacrifices involving animals, the ritual procedure for the animal sacrifice (*paśutantra*) takes precedence because of its primary importance. (19) On the previous day, the animal-related rites are performed at the Vaiśvadeva. (20)
Or [the sacrifice may be] immediate; 21.
the animal victim is for the Viśve Devas; 22.
he offers the oblations following the animal cake (paśupuroḍāśa). 23.
Because the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering for them is more frequent [than for others],
it is as stated [in the rule] without contradiction;
the shaving of the hair occurs at the end of the heart-spike rite.
In the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings, there is one for Varuṇa (27); in the Mahāhavis offering, one for Mahendra (28);
and the fourth is for Śanāsīra (29).
Either before each full-moon festival or at the end of each festival,
there is the Mitravinda sacrifice; Mitravindā is for one who desires prosperity, a kingdom, friends, and long life.

The *Daśahavis* sacrifice consists of ten oblations: 2. an offering to Agni; a pap (*caru*) to Soma; a pap or a cake on ten potsherds (*daśakapāla*) to Varuṇa; a pap to Yava; a pap to Mitra; a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra; a pap to Bṛhaspati; a cake on twelve potsherds or eight potsherds to Savitṛ; a pap to Pūṣan; a pap to Sarasvatī; and a cake on ten potsherds to Tvaṣṭṛ—this constitutes a single offering. 3. There is a combined recitation of the invitatory verses (*anu-vācana*). 4. [End.]

The calls "Sacrifice! (yajeti) and the subsequent directions (praiṣas), as well as the subsequent recitations (nigamas), may be used according to one's preference, because of the scriptural injunction regarding the choice [of formulae].
Or rather, they follow the regular order because of the quality of the exhortation;

there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses. The two *ājyabhāga* offerings contain words for prosperity: "May he obtain wealth through Agni, even nourishment day by day—glorious and most full of heroes" (RV 6.16.34);
and "O Soma, be a good friend to us—increasing our household, driving away disease, finding wealth, and augmenting prosperity" (RV 1.91.7).

The invitatory verses (*anuvākyās*) for the oblation are: "Agni, Soma, Varuṇa, Mitra, Indra, Bṛhaspati, Savitṛ who possesses a thousandfold [power], Pūṣan with his protection for our cattle, Sarasvatī, and Tvaṣṭṛ—may they adorn us with forms through sacrifices.

(11) The offering verse (*yājyā*) is: "May Tvaṣṭṛ grant forms, Sarasvatī grant them, Pūṣan, Savitṛ, and Bhaga grant me [fortune]. May Bṛhaspati grant it, Indra grant me strength, Mitra [grant] dominion, Varuṇa, Soma, and Agni. (12)

Having offered [the oblation] from the pot with the *sruva* ladle, he makes additional offerings: "Agni, the eater of food, the lord of food, may he bestow upon me the enjoyment of food in this sacrifice—Svāhā! Soma the King, the lord of kings, may he bestow upon me sovereignty in this sacrifice—Svāhā! Varuṇa the Sovereign, the lord of sovereigns, may he bestow upon me imperial power in this sacrifice—Svāhā! Mitra, the ruling power, the lord of the ruling power, may he bestow upon me the ruling power in this sacrifice—Svāhā! Indra, strength, the lord of strength, may he bestow upon me spiritual splendor in this sacrifice—Svāhā!"

May Bṛhaspati, the Brahman and lord of the Brahman, bestow upon me at this sacrifice the splendor of the Brahman; *svāhā*. May Savitṛ, the lord of the kingdom, bestow upon me at this sacrifice the kingdom; *svāhā*. May Pūṣan, the lord of fortune, bestow upon me at this sacrifice fortune; *svāhā*. May Sarasvatī, the mistress of nourishment, bestow upon me at this sacrifice nourishment; *svāhā*. May Tvaṣṭṛ, the maker of forms and lord of forms, bestow upon me at this sacrifice cattle with their forms; *svāhā*. The two *virāj* verses are the *saṃyājyās*.

"Grant us wealth consisting of thousands, wealth consisting of offspring, and nourishing riches, O Agni—splendid, full of heroic power, most excellent, and undecaying. Therefore, O Brahman, you who are most invoked by the gods, protect us in our hymns; shine auspiciously for us, O Agni, strengthened by the Maruts.
(The Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, Fifth Adhyāya, states: "Ten cows as a sacrificial fee, or a thousand, or indeed a thousand.")
The animal sacrifice is performed in the year during the rainy season (1),
or at the two beginnings of the [rainy] retreat (2), or in the house (3).
He offers the oblation for the sacrificial post (yūpāhuti) with four ladlings (caturgṛhīta) using the dipping-spoon (sruva), [reciting] "O wide one, for Viṣṇu" (uru viṣṇave).
Having taken the remainder of the clarified butter, the carpenter goes toward the sacrificial post.
He touches it [with the formula] "Beyond others" (atyanyān).
Standing facing the east, he consecrates [the staff] with a mantra, or [simply] holds it.
It should be made of *pālāśa* wood, having many leaves, with its tip unwithered, its branches pointing upward, its top bent toward the middle, and free from blemishes.
In the absence of such, it may be made of *khadira*, *bilva*, or *rauhītaka* wood.
In the absence of *khadira* wood, he touches the other [materials] with the *sruva* ladle, saying, "For Viṣṇu, thee! (10).
Having covered a young *kuśa* blade with the words, "O herb," (11), he strikes it with an axe, saying, "O well-edged one. (12)
He places down the first chip.
He cuts [a branch] that is not stunted and has grown from a single shoot.
It is one-born.
He consecrates the falling [bird] with the mantra, "Do not scratch the sky" (16). It should not fly toward the south (17).
The purification is performed with the mantra, "For this indeed is yours" (18).
Or rather, it is the remainder of the consecration (abhimantraṇa), because of the instruction without qualification;
therefore, one offers [the oblation] with "thou art this" during the cutting [of the wood].
Or rather, [it is offered] on the sacrificial post (yūpa), because that constitutes its consecration.
And because of the scriptural statement regarding Sthāṇu; 22.
[The post] should be stripped [of its bark] but not cut; 23. It should be three or four cubits long; 24.
Some [make it] starting from one cubit [in length]. 25.
He makes it eight-sided, except for the upper part. 26.
And from the front [he makes] the caṣāla, one span in width, eight-sided, and held in the middle. 27.
The hole for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) should extend two or three finger-breadths beyond [the ground].
For the *soma* sacrifice, the post shall be five *aratnis* in length up to fifteen, excluding ten, seven, and fourteen; or it may be of unlimited length.
For the *vājapeya*, it shall be seventeen [finger-breadths].
There are twenty-one [stomas] in the Aśvamedha sacrifice.

Intending to construct the altar (vedi) according to the size of the body, he mentally recites the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ formula with five portions taken up and offers either one oblation or five: "O Lord of Speech, with unimpaired speech, with an unimpaired ladle, they have sent forth the strengthening Hotṛ-offering to the gods in heaven—Svāhā! (TS 7.5.11.1–2). 33.

He prepares the altar (1). As at the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifice, [he proceeds] with the wooden sword and so forth up to the placing of the fire (2). He leads forward the fire with a single fuel-stick (3).

One should perform the taking of the vow (*vratopāyana*), the *praṇītā* water, the portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), the portions for the sacrificial offerings (*avadāna*), the full-vessel rite (*pūrṇapātra*), and the *Viṣṇukrama* steps according to the procedure of the *Haviryajña*.

Having performed the strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*), the setting out of the vessels (*pātrasaṃsādana*), the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), the pouring out of the clarified butter (*ājyanirvapaṇa*), and the placing on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*), one proceeds from the second tracing of the altar (*uttaraparigraha*) up to the placing of the clarified butter (*ājyāsādana*).
The taking of the clarified butter includes the *pṛṣadājya* (clotted butter).
He spreads Plakṣa branches upon the sacrificial grass (barhis).

Having taken up the spade with the formula "In the impulse of the god... (*devasya tvā*), he traces around the hole for the sacrificial post (*yūpāvaṭa*) with the formula "Here I... (*idam aham...*), [marking] half [the space] within the altar to the east of the Āhavanīya fire.
He digs it to the depth of the lower part of the post (*upara*).
He scatters eastern dust;
he places it in front of the sacrificial post (yūpa) facing east; he places a handful of kuśa grass upon it.
He places the first splinter with [the formula] "and the first splinter" (13), and the top-ring to the north with "and the top-ring to the north" (14).

Having thrown barley-grains into the water with "Thou art barley" (TS 1.2.1.1), he sprinkles the tip, the middle, and the root with the respective mantras: "To the sky thee! (TS 1.2.1.1) and so forth (15).
"I sprinkle," [he says] everywhere, because of the expectancy [of the action].
(16) He pours the remainder into the pit with the formula, "May they be purified.
(17) He throws [the grass] onto the sacrificial grass, both eastward and northward, with the formula, "Thou art the seat of the ancestors. (18)
He offers the first chip into the pit with the *sruva* ladle while reciting "Thou art the leader," and then silently (19).
Having circumambulated from the east, either the Adhvaryu or the sacrificer, sitting down facing north, anoints the sacrificial post (21).

He causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory formula for the sacrificial post while it is being anointed; he anoints it with the words "May the god [anoint] thee," and he anoints the top-ring on both sides.
He fastens it with the formula, "For those with good fruit.
4. Having descended from that place near the fire, the Adhvaryu should touch all around the place for the girding, and he should not let go of it until the girding is completed. 5.
He causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse for the post as it is being raised. 6.
With "dyāmagreṇa," he raises it;
with "yā te," he fixes it at the Agniṣṭhā pillar, directly facing the Āhavanīya fire;
with "brahmavani tvā," he covers it all around with dust.
With the formula "O Brahman, make firm," he thrice sprinkles around [the post] on all sides with the staff of the Maitrāvaruṇa.
Having leveled the ground and sprinkled it with water, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite "The deeds of Viṣṇu" while [the sacrificer] holds onto the sacrificial post.
And [he causes him to recite] "That of Viṣṇu" while [the sacrificer] looks at the top-ring.

While the girdle is being wound around [the sacrificial post], he recites the formula: "Thou art the girdle. It is a triple-stranded girdle made of Kuśa grass, three *vyāmas* in length; with it, he winds it three times around the post at the height of the navel, saying, "Thou art the girdler" (13).
Having joined [the ends] together, he causes one end to enter the other (14).
He hides a splinter of the sacrificial post into this [girdle] to the north of the *agniṣṭhā* (the part of the post facing the fire), saying, "Thou art the son of heaven" (15).
In the case of many [animals], he acts according to each one [individually].
Having taken a blade of grass with the mantra, "Thou art the subordinate," he touches the animal with it, saying, "Approach the gods.
Because the mantra is recited [in the scripture] as "the goat" (chāga), [it applies specifically to] the goat.
The mantra has seventeen constituent parts (19). [The mantra] is used for sprinkling according to its specific wording (20),
because it is not enjoined otherwise (21).
He churns the fire until the oblation is offered (22),

or at the time of the introductory rite and the churning (23). Having made a noose with a double-stranded cord of Kuśa grass two cubits long, he binds it between the right horns with the formula, "Thee for Ṛta" (24).
With the formula "For thee, O god... [he touches] the sacrificial post (yūpa). 25.
[The animal may be] dedicated to Indra-Agni, to Sūrya, or to Prajāpati, whichever one might desire.
26. With the formula "For the waters thee... he sprinkles the animal with the sprinkling-vessels (prokṣaṇī). 27.
With the verse "The drinker of the waters," he takes hold [of the vessel]. With the verse "O divine waters," he sprinkles [the fuel] from below.
He performs the rites beginning with the command for the fuel-sticks (idhma-praiṣa) up until the fore-offerings (prayāja).

Having poured the second libation (uttarāghāra), he anoints the animal first on the forehead, then on the shoulders, and then on the hips, with each mantra: "Be [united]," etc. (1). Having proceeded and caused the Hotṛ to utter the *āśrāvaṇa* call, he says: "Agni is the leader of the divine clans; this sacrificer is the leader of men, pressing the Soma. At the Soma-pressing, he says: "May their household-fire shine without fail for a hundred winters; may the two, uniting their wealth yet not uniting their bodies, bestow gifts" (2). He hands over the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa with the formula: "By the command of Mitra and Varuṇa, the directors, I give thee," a staff made of Udumbara wood, reaching up to the mouth of the sacrificer (3–4).
The staff of the initiated [is used] at the Soma sacrifice, either when [the Soma] has been purchased or not; there are eleven fore-offerings (prayāja) and after-offerings (anuyāja).
"O Hotṛ, give the call for the one belonging to Mitra and Varuṇa," he says at the place where the offering is made.

Having performed ten fore-offerings (prayāja), he says, "Bring the sacrificial knife. Taking the *svaru* and anointing both it and the tip of the *juhū* ladle with ghee, he touches the forehead of the animal with them, saying, "Anointed with ghee."
Having concealed the *svaru* and handing over the sword, he says: "May this be your well-known edge.
Having set down the two ladles, he draws a line to the north of the *catvāla* for the *śāmitra* fire.
He causes the recitation for the carrying of fire around [the victim].

Having taken up the firebrand from the Āhavanīya, the Agnīdh walks three times around it in all directions, [passing] by the animal, the clarified butter, the place of the Śāmitra, the sacrificial post, the Cātvāla pit, and the Āhavanīya— either including the clarified butter, the animal, and the Śāmitra, or excluding them; having thrown back the firebrand, he follows it as it is carried back.
Taking it up again, he proceeds toward the north;
the animal follows behind him.
The Pratiprasthātṛ takes hold of him from behind with two omentum-roasting spits made of *kārṣmarya* wood—one forked and one un-forked.
The Adhvaryu, the sacrificer, and the Adhvaryu [take their respective positions].
Having taken the Veda-grass, the Adhvaryu, after calling for the *āśrāvaṇa*, says: "O Hotṛ, give the impulse; [offer] the oblations to the gods.
He causes the sacrificer to recite: "O wealthy one! 10.
One should not pass beyond the *śāmitra* fire-pit. 11 He places the fire upon the *śāmitra*. 12 Some [place] the fire produced by friction (*nirmanthya*). 13.
Afterwards, he spreads grass [saying], "May the rain be more abundant. Upon that, they kill him with his head toward the west and feet toward the north, or with his head toward the east.
Having grasped it by the mouth, they cause it to subside so that it does not hiss;
or [they do so] with a cord.
Having approached and circumambulated the Āhavanīya fire, they sit down.
One should say, "Do you cause it to be known; follow after. 20.
He offers with the words, "Svāhā to the gods! 21.
When it is announced, "The animal has been immolated," he says, "Let it lie for a moment, O Soma! 22.
He offers with the formula, "Svāhā to the gods! (23).
Or rather, he should not offer these at all (24).
With the two omentum-spits, he throws the tethering-rope into the Cātvāla pit with the formula, "Do not be a hindrance! (25).
"O Pratiprasthātṛ, bring the wife here," he says; [the Neṣṭṛ] brings her in the Soma sacrifice. 26.
Having water for washing in her hand, he makes her recite, "Lead me forward, O Ātāna. 1. He purifies the breaths of the animal; the wife [does so]. 2.
Having touched together the mouth, the two nostrils, the two eyes, the two ears, the navel, the penis, the anus, and the feet, [the Adhvaryu] says for each formula, "I purify your speech. 3.
With the remainder [of the water], both the sacrificer and [the Adhvaryu] sprinkle [himself] beginning from the head, saying "The mind" over the head; 4.
saying "That which is cruel of yours" over the limbs. 5.
With the words, "Peace to the days," they sprinkle [the animal] from behind.
(6) Having turned the animal on its back, he places a blade of grass in front of the navel with the words, "O herb.

(7) Having placed it with the well-known formula, "O axe," and having cut it, he holds the tip in his left hand and anoints both ends with blood from the root with his right hand, saying, "With the blood of the Rākṣasas. (8)
9. Saying "It is cast away," he discards it;
saying "This am I," the sacrificer steps upon it. 10.
Having extracted the omentum, he covers the two omentum-roasting spits with the formula: "With ghee, O Heaven and Earth. 11.
Having removed the entrails and poured water on them at the *cātvāla* pit, he heats them over the *śāmitra* fire (12).
The *āgnīdhra* throws a portion of the *śāmitra* fire into the *āhavanīya* fire (13), and the *adhvaryu* throws a blade of grass into it with the formula, "O Vāyu, do thou carry [it] away" (14).
Standing to the north, having heated the omentum and brought it between the sacrificial post and the fire, the Pratiprasthātṛ cooks it on the south side;
having gone around, he bastes the omentum with the dipping-spoon, saying, "Agni [is the lord] of the clarified butter.
He causes the Hotṛ to recite the invitatory verse for the drops.
"When it has been boiled, 'Bring the boiled [portion],' says the Pratiprasthātṛ;
he gives the command for the *svāhākṛti* offerings.
Having offered [the oblation], he bastes the omentum with clotted butter (*pṛṣadājya*), and first [bastes] the *dhruvā* [ladle] and the two *ājyabhāga* portions."

21. Here, while performing the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāgau), when about to proceed with the omentum (vapā), having spread an underlayer of ghee and placed gold within it, while cutting off the omentum, he says: "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra and Agni for the omentum and fat of the goat.
22. Having placed gold [within], there is a double pouring of ghee over it in the case of the Soma sacrifice. 23.
Having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "O Hotṛ, give the command for Indra and Agni [to consume] the omentum and fat of the goat.

(24) And when the Soma has been pressed, he says: "It has been set forth. (25) Having offered the oblation, he throws the two omentum-spits into the fire—the one with the forked end eastward and the other westward—with the words: "Svāhā! (26)
They perform the purification at the *cātvāla* pit together with their wives, [using the mantra] "O Waters, carry this away. Another [priest] dissects the animal;
one of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) does so because no other [specific person] has been appointed for the *śāmitra* fire.
And because of the mention of "Upagā" [in the context of] non-seeing; 3.
But the seller is different because of association with Śūdras; 4. He cuts off the limbs without breaking them. 5.

The heart, the tongue, the breast, the left thigh and the front part of the left leg, the two sides, the liver and the kidneys, the middle of the rectum, and the right hip—these are the portions for the *juhū* ladle (6).
The right thigh and the front part of the right leg, the third part of the rectum, and the left hip—these are the portions for the *upabhṛt* ladle (7).
The largest portion is for the *upayaj* offerings (8).
At the time of the portioning,
he cuts off the *vaniṣṭhu* and the *jāghanī* (9); and if he so desires, he also cuts off the *kloman*, the *plīhā*, the *adhyūdhnī*, and the *purītat* (10–11).
If [the victim] is emaciated, he throws the remaining abdominal fat into the anus. 12. Having placed the undigested food (ūvadhyam) in a pit, he pours blood into it, saying, "For the Rākṣasas.
13. Having pierced the heart on a spit, he cooks it at the Śāmitra fire. 14.
The animal victim is placed in the cooking pot (ukhā). 15. There is a cake on eleven potsherds for the deity of the animal sacrifice. 16.
Or it belongs to Agni-Soma, because of the specific instruction. 17.

In this very context, there is the invocation of the *haviṣkṛt* because of the unity of the sacrifice. (18) While cutting the portion, he says: "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra and Agni regarding the *puroḍāśa*.
(19) And he cuts the portion into the *upabhṛt* ladle, as in the case of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. (20)
He issues the command: "To Indra and Agni, the sacrificial cake!
(21) Having offered it and having brought [the portions] together, he gives them to Agni. (22) In the place where there is a quality, there is no quality. (23)
24. Because all modifications are one; or 25. as it is traditionally taught, because of the difference in wording; 26.
he cuts off the *iḍā* portion, because the non-performance of the other has the same purpose.
Nor [is there a difference in the ritual] because of a difference in the injunction (codanā), nor because of a difference in time or quality;
the sacrificial fee is a cow, or the bridegroom's gift is a cow, when it has been wiped clean. 27–29.

He instructs the *śamitṛ*: "Let him move [the victim] three times; having moved it three times, let him make the heart the uppermost. When they ask you, 'Is the oblation cooked, O *śamitṛ*?'—you must say, 'It is cooked. [If they say], 'Sir, it is not cooked; it is not cooked,' [he replies].
Having moved it three times, he extracts the heart and makes it the uppermost. (ŚB 6.2.2.1–2)
Having placed the spit on the ground and taken some of the speckled butter with the *juhū* ladle, he goes out and asks three times while stepping forward: "O slaughterer, is the oblation cooked? (4)
When [the formula] "That of the gods... has been recited, he says it in a whisper. 5.
Having sprinkled the heart with clarified butter while reciting "Be peaceful, O mind," 6.
and having cut off the entire [heart] like a fatty portion (vapā), the Pratiprasthātṛ cuts portions from the Plakṣa branches on the southern side of the altar. 7.

He spreads an underlayer of ghee in the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt*, as well as in the vessel for the fat-oblation (*vasāhomahavanī*) and the vessel for the *manotā*. When it is said, "Recite for the oblation being cut off for the *manotā*," he cuts portions from the two ladles twice each, as previously stated.
(8) In the case of the third part of the intestine (*guda*), there is no remainder.
(9) It is also like the omentum (*vapā*). (10)
Having taken the fat with the formula "reḍasi," and having sprinkled it twice over [the meat], he mixes it with the side-flesh with the formula "prayutam," or [he does so] with a sword.
Having poured the remainder into the *iḍā*-vessel, he throws in the breast and the boneless parts, excluding the two hips.
Having set aside the tail and the rectum, he says: "Recite the invitatory verse for Indra and Agni for the oblation of the goat."
Having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Prompt [the Hotṛ] regarding the oblation of the goat for Indra and Agni";
and when [the offering] has been set forth, he gives the impulse.
During the interval between the half-verses of the *yājyā*, he offers a portion of the omentum with the mantra, "The ghee, O purifier of ghee... (VS 20.20).
Having offered to the deity and circumambulated to the right, while stirring the speckled butter with the *juhu* ladle, he says: "Recite the invitatory verse for Vanaspati.
(17) Having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "Prompt the offering for Vanaspati.
(18) Having made the offering and having brought together the *sauviṣṭakṛta* portion. (19)
Having returned, he sprinkles the quarters with the remainder of the fat, as in the case of the whey;
he offers it all.
He touches the animal, saying, "The breath belongs to Indra."
Having cut off the *iḍā* before the offering, he places it down; when the *iḍā* has been invoked, he gives the *vaniṣṭhu* to the *agnīdh*.
He gives the *adhyūdhnī* to the Hotṛ, or the *avāntareḍā*.

When [the Hotṛ] has performed the purification (*mārjana*), he issues the command: "O Āgnīdh, bring the embers for the after-offerings; O Upayaṣṭṛ, sit down; O Brahman, I shall set forth; having placed the fuel-stick, O Āgnīdh, cleanse the fire."
Having taken embers from the *śāmitra* fire, he scatters them on the western corner of the altar;
or, in the case of a *soma* sacrifice, from the *āgnīdhrīya* fire onto the *hotṛ-dhiṣṇya*.
The *pratiprasthātṛ* performs the secondary offerings (*upayaj*) with the third portion of the rectum, reciting for each a mantra beginning with "Go to the ocean."
Having offered at each *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, he touches his mouth with the formula, "May my mind [be satisfied].
(11) At the end of the after-offerings (*anuyāja*), he offers the *svaru* splinter with the formula, "To heaven, thy smoke.
(12) The spreading out of the offering-ladle (*sruc*) is performed for the animal deity and for Vanaspati. (13)
The Patnīsaṃyāja offerings are made with the tail.
(14) He cuts portions for the wives of the gods from the upturned [tail]. (15) And [he cuts] the iḍā-portion. (16)
Having turned [the portions] over, [they are offered] to Agni Gṛhapati and to the Āgnīdhra (17). With clarified butter, the first two [are offered] (18);
or rather, all [portions] with the tail (jāghanī), because there is no distinction (19).
Having offered the *barhis*, they go toward the water, taking the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*).
Or, having approached the *Āhavanīya* fire, if there are other vows (*vrata*) and so forth;

then, having descended [into the water], he hides the heart-spike at the junction of dry and wet ground, saying: "Thou art pain; burn him who hates us and whom we hate; do not harm the waters nor the plants. And [he says] the same as before.

Fainting, he pours out a vessel of water and hides the sacrificial post with the eastern part as previously described (Sūtra 4). "From every abode, may we be well-favored"—with these words, they touch the water (Sūtra 5).
Or rather, the former [rite] is the remainder of the hiding (Sūtra 6).
Or [the consecration] is performed with the subsequent [mantra].
(7) In the Soma sacrifice, [the ritual] is performed excluding the *anūbandhyā* animal sacrifice.
(8) The placing of the fuel-sticks (*samid-ādhāna*) is as in the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifice. (9)
Having released the vow, one should offer four portions of clarified butter into the other fires as in the case of the *yūpa-āhuti* (the oblation for the sacrificial post).
From this point on, that is the ritual procedure;
or [it may be performed] with the fire either rekindled from the embers or produced by friction.
One should give according to one's enthusiasm in this [rite].

(13) Having carried forward the fire, and having taken up the Sadas, the Havirdhāna, the Āgnīdhra, and the Hotṛ-hearths as prescribed, there is the carrying forward of the clarified butter (ājya) to the Āgnīdhra shed because of the observation of the Agniṣomīya [offering]. (14) It is not for the sake of the Soma [pressing], because it is not intended for that purpose. (15)
As a corollary, the [method of] observation: 16.
The *darvihoma* oblations follow the ritual rules of the *paurṇamāsa*, because there is no specific distinction made regarding the act of offering;
17. and also because of the observation of the *juhū* ladle.
They remain silent, their purposes not being frustrated;
they maintain the single fire;
they are without *prayāja* offerings, without *anuyāja* offerings, and without *sāmidhenī* verses.
The offerings are not recited [with the *anigada* formula] (22); they are performed with the *pratinigada* (23),
and the oblations are presented with the utterance of *svāhā* (24).
The origins of the dependent [rites] consist merely of the *juhoti* offerings (25).
In the *pākayajñas*, there is no offering of the entire portion that has been cut off (26).
Having offered, one consumes the remainder (27).
Regarding the Agnihotra, it is because of the Vedic scripture stating, "In that case, it is like a *pākayajña* for him" (28);
[the offering] is from the Agniṣomīya among the animal sacrifices (29);
and there is the tying of the branch (30).
Having offered the omentum, he cuts off three, five, or all [the portions].
(31) In the absence of all [these], he offers from the remainder for the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice. (32) The offering is made together with the *sthālīpāka*. (33)
"A full vessel is the sacrificial fee, or a boon; or a boon [is the fee]. Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Kāṭhaka Śrauta Sūtra.
According to the Vedic revelation (Śruti), "Having sacrificed with the New and Full Moon offerings, one should sacrifice with another [rite]. 1.
Or rather, one who has already prepared the Soma [should perform the installation],
because the installation of the fires has the Soma as its primary purpose;
it is not so, because there is no specific distinction made.
In the spring, the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is performed.
Having sacrificed an Aindrāgna bull that has been released again, those who have not drunk Soma for two generations [are eligible].

He chooses sixteen priests: the Brahman, Udgātṛ, Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, Prastotṛ, Maitrāvaruṇa, Pratiprasthātṛ, Potṛ, Pratihartṛ, Acchāvāka, Neṣṭṛ, Agnīdh, Subrahmaṇya, Grāvastut, and Unnetṛ.
Either the first four [of these] are *tatpuruṣa* compounds, while the others are according to the specific Veda; [the offices are] the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the Agnīdh, the Potṛ, and the Brahman.
They choose a sacrificial ground for the gods.
It should be highest in the middle, level, and without a depression, extending on all sides an area sufficient for the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), except for the front portion;
it should slope toward the east or toward the north, as much as the learned priests (*anūcāna-ṛtvij*) may determine.
At the other end, at the root of the *uddhata* plant, they construct a measured hall (14),
the *prāgvaṃśa* (15),
which is high in the front (16).
Either facing each of the cardinal directions (17), or excluding the north (18),
or [building] a hall (19).
And when the Uttarāphalgunī and Aparā (Śatabhiṣaj) constellations have revolved,
he should begin the pressing on the fifth or seventh day of the bright fortnight starting from the initiation;
for if there is a lapse of time, the prescribed rite must be performed because the proper time has arrived.
Not [so], because of equality. 23.
There are twelve initiations (dīkṣā) or an unlimited number. 24.
Initiation, the purchase [of Soma], the pressing, and the rising [from the ritual seat] should take place on an auspicious day. 25.
In the case of a conflict regarding the rising for the procession,
[the view is] "not so," because it is not enjoined;

for during the initiations, the cutting of the sacrificial post and the offering on the post must be performed after first making the *yūpāhuti* offering, or else fire is churned at the end of the post, since there is a scriptural prohibition against the initiated person performing the *agnihotra*.
At the time of raising [the sacrificial post], both [the fire and the post] are [prepared]; in the event of an interruption in the oblation, [the fire is taken from] the vicinity.
Having consigned the fires into the kindling woods (araṇis), and having grasped the eastern half of the pillar of the hall, with the araṇis in his hands, he says: "We have gone to this [world].
If the King Soma has already been brought, he places him within the hall.

Before the purchase [of the Soma], they bring him food fit for sacrifice, excluding meat. Having spread the fires at a distance of seven steps and half a fathom, that is the site for the piling of the fire-altar.
In the afternoon he eats, whether food has been obtained through sacrifice or not.
Having indicated that which is for the sake of the sacrifice, [the sacrificer] enters the enclosure from the north; there is a water-pot [there], and the consecration takes place in the waters.
The barber stands to the north; he trims the nails, beginning with those of the right hand, the thumb first.
Having parted the hair at the "cow-tail" (godāna) on the right side, he moistens it with the formula, "These are the waters."
Having placed a young kuśa blade near [the hair] like a sacrificial post (yūpa), and having cut it with a razor,
he throws it into a water-pot.
Thus he remains silent for the subsequent [rite] (11).
He hands the razor to the barber (12),
and with it the barber shaves his hair and beard (13).

Having bathed with the mantra "The waters [have cleansed] us," he steps out toward the northeast with the mantra "Up from the waters. He puts on a linen garment; if it is unwashed, he should tell someone to beat it, or if it is already washed, he should sprinkle it with water.
Or he may wear a garment worn during bathing, or one washed with urine, having his hair combed and the fringe spread out, with the mantra "For the consecration and austerity."
He does not tie the knot; 17 in this same manner, the Pratiprasthātṛ [acts] silently upon the other enclosure with the wife; 18 or there is the shaving of the hair. 19
One should not eat the meat of a cow or a bull; or rather, this is a duty for men because [the meat] is unavailable;
or else, it refers to eating meat from a powerful animal.
Having led [the sacrificer] forward, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu (23),
or a pap to the Ādityas (24);
he performs this before the *samiṣṭayajus* offering (25).
Or, excluding the *samiṣṭayajus* [offering],

they perform the rites in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) prior to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice; or they perform the *dīkṣaṇīyā* with the final [verse] in a low voice, while the others are performed in a progressively lower voice.
The Upasad rites are performed in a low voice.

Standing to the east of the hall, he anoints himself with fresh butter on the *kuśa* grass, from the top of his head downwards following the direction of the hair, including his feet, with the formula: "Thou art the milk of the great ones.
With the formula "Of Vṛtra," he anoints his two eyes with collyrium from Mount Trikakud.
In the absence [of a specific rule], it is otherwise (32).
Twice to the south, thrice to the north, and facing away (33).
The mantra is recited once each time (34).

With the tip of a blade of *śareṣīkā* grass, he purifies [the sacrificer] with seven *kuśa*-strainers, each held by the Lord of the Earth (the Adhvaryu), using seven mantras for each, saying "with an unbroken [strainer]" at every step. Having wiped upwards above the navel twice, he wipes downwards once clockwise with one, three, or seven [mantras].
Or, at the Rājasūya sacrifice, he makes [the sacrificer] recite "O gods, come to us" with one hundred and one [verses];
saying "Svāhā to the sacrifice," he anoints his fingers separately on both hands.
In this manner, he performs the remainder for each mantra (6).
Having formed a fist with the thumb and having uttered "svāhā," remaining silent,
he releases both thumbs together with that [fist] (7–8).

He causes him, with speech restrained, to enter between the Āhavanīya and Gārhapatya fires; this is his path of movement until the impulsion [of the Soma]. In the same manner, the Pratiprasthātṛ silently performs the anointing of the wife and the subsequent rites.
Or he causes it to enter by means of another [vessel].
12 He offers the Audgrabhaṇa oblations from the pot with the dipping-spoon (sruva), reciting "With intention... and so forth for each mantra. 13 He merely mutters the third [mantra]. 14
Having poured the fifth portion from the *dhruvā* into the *juhū*, he fills the *sruva* twice from the vessel and a third time with the *sruva* itself, using the verse "viśvo devasya... (VS 2.1).
Or rather, he may offer this very same full ladle.
To the south of the *āhavanīya* fire, he places the black antelope skin—provided with flesh, its edges sewn, and having holes for threading—so that it hangs behind him.
If there is one [verse], it is double the number of the latter;
he sits behind these two with his right knee bent;
he touches the junction of the light and dark [fortnights] with the words, "Of the Ṛg and the Sāman."
He mounts [the seat] with his right knee, saying, "Thou art a refuge," and sits upon it at the rear edge.
He ties a triple-stranded girdle made of hemp and *muñja* grass mixed together between the two garments, saying, "Thou art vigor. He makes a knot, saying, "The knot of Soma."
