He covers his head with [the fringe] saying, "Of Viṣṇu, a refuge" (VS 1.19). 24. He ties the black antelope horn—having three or five ridges—with its tip turned upward, to the fringe of his garment. 25.
With it, he scratches himself. 26.
He touches [the earth] with this [verse]: "The womb of Indra," over the right eyebrow. 27.
And he draws a line on the ground with [the verse]: "May there be good crops. 28.
He hands over a staff made of Udumbara wood, reaching up to his mouth. 1.
With the words, "Rise up! he raises it;
he places it to the south;
at this point, indeed, there is the closing of the fist and the restraining of speech.
In this manner, the Pratiprasthātṛ silently places the girdle and so forth, or the cord, or the net, three times around the head of the wife simultaneously.
A sacrificial wooden peg with a broad head is used for scratching;
if it scrapes the girdle and other parts,
[it is used] up to the black antelope skin and so forth, ending with the staff.
"Another says loudly three times, 'This Brāhmaṇa is initiated,'" for the Vedic revelation (śruti) states "Brāhmaṇa" even when referring to a Vaiśya or a Rājanya.
He restrains his speech until sunset.
When the sun has set, he says three times: "O initiated one, release your speech; O wife, release your speech.
Having turned toward the fire and spoken the release of speech three times with the words, "Perform the vow," and once with "Agni is Brahman," or else with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ."
Thereafter, until the release of the handfuls [of grain], while the sun has neither set nor risen, he says three times: "O initiated one, restrain your speech; O wife, restrain your speech.
(17) The release [of speech] is as previously stated. (18) He causes the two cows that yield the vow-milk to be milked. (19)
Therefore, you two shall observe the milk-vow (kṣīra-vrata).
20. In the first vow, one sows either rice or barley, or both. 21. That vow [is observed] until milking ceases. 22.
Some say that all medicinal herbs and all fragrant substances [should be used].
23. The cooking for the initiated person takes place on the Gārhapatya fire; for the wife, it takes place on the Dakṣiṇāgni.
24. For a Kṣatriya, there is gruel (yavāgū); for a Vaiśya, there is curd-mixture (āmikṣā). 25.
He gives the vow to one who is not arrogant during the latter part of the night; the evening milking in the afternoon, and the morning milking in the forenoon.
(26) With the verse, "Divine insight," he performs the ritual rinsing for the vow while seated on his own seat.
(27) With the verse, "Those gods," he consumes the vow-food in a vessel that is not made of clay. (28)
The wife [takes] two iron [objects]. 29.
With the words, "May they be auspicious and bright," she touches her navel.
30. When about to eat, he takes a clod of earth or something else with his black antelope horn, saying, "This is for thee. 31.
Saying, "I release the waters," he urinates (32).
Saying, "Arise from the earth," he deposits what has been taken up (33).
Having said, "O Agni, you... he sleeps facing eastward on his right side, lying on the ground (34).

He makes him recite "Punarmanaḥ" over the fire that has been turned toward him and has awakened, when he is about to sleep again. He says "Tvamagne," having become angry or having uttered something unrighteous.
Having touched what has been obtained, he makes him recite "Rāsveyat."
If it is impossible [to avoid him], one should recite a mantra over him.

(3) One should avoid entering into contact with a Śūdra, conversing with him, rising for him, saluting him, drinking water from his vessel, and being rained upon by him until the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).
(4) He speaks with a nasalized tone (*parihvāla*). (5)
He should speak words that are clear and pleasant;
he should not sit on a couch nor sleep during the two junctions of day and night; and he should remain on the sacrificial altar during the Soma-pressings.
There is no expiation for an offense in this case;
or rather, they may seek mutual invitation regarding one another.
Regarding the wife, there is a single initiation.
At the end of the initiation (dīkṣā), he offers the Prāyaṇīya oblation, a pap (caru) for Aditi.

Having offered the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), he sacrifices with clarified butter to four deities: Pathyā Svasti, Agni, Soma, and Savitṛ. He sets aside the pap, the stirring-spoon, and the sacrificial grass (barhis) for the Udayanīya offering.
He washes the ointment, the sacrificial porridge, and the wiped-out stirring-ladle;
or he washes the porridge;
he throws the other items into the fire.
Those very same persons are the officiating priests; even others may serve when they have passed away.
The ritual concludes with the *śaṃyu* formula.
Since the [rule] regarding the end would apply first, [the answer is:
because of the hearing of no distinction (21);
or rather, the latter [is correct], because of the favoring of the archetype and the prohibition of the after-offerings (22–23).
Because of the mention [of the word], there is no application;
24. because of the lack of hearing [the word] *santva*; 25. the prohibition of the *anuyāja* offerings is a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*). 26.
At the place of the *uparava* holes, the Pratiprasthātṛ pours out the Soma upon the hide of a red bull;
a member of the Kautsa clan or a Śūdra sifts it, while a Brāhmaṇa sits nearby attending to it.
And a water-pot is placed in front;
having closed the doors of the hall, he takes four portions of the *dhruva* butter into the *juhū* ladle.
Having tied a blade of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with gold, he places it [into the *dhruva*] with the words, "This is for thee."
He offers with the words, "Thou art aged" (7). Having taken up a piece of gold with the words, "Thou art bright" (8), he places a blade of grass on the altar;
he then ties the gold with a thread (9).
Having taken four portions [of butter], he says, "O sacrificer, hold on!
(10). They both go out through the door that has been opened (11).

To the south of the door stands the Soma-purchase cow—unmarked, without physical defects, not impregnated, not tied with a rope, brownish-red; in the absence of a brownish-red one, a tawny one; in the absence of a tawny one, a reddish-brown one; and in the absence of a reddish-brown one, a red-eyed one. (12)
He addresses her with the mantra, "Thou art consciousness" (13).
He follows her as she is being led toward the north (14).
Having passed six steps, they sit down around her at the seventh step (15).
Having placed gold within it, he makes an offering over it with the formula, "May it be thine, O Aditi" (16).
With the wooden sword (sphya), he traces around the footprint three times with the formula, "Rejoice in us" (17).
Having dug up the footprint, he pours it into the pot with the formula, "In us is thy kinship" (18).

Having poured water into its place, he gives the footprint to the sacrificer with the words, "In thee be wealth" (tve rāyaḥ). 19. The sacrificer accepts the footprint with the words, "May there be wealth for me" (me rāyaḥ). 20. With the words, "May we not [be separated]" (mā vayam), the Adhvaryu touches himself. 21.
Having taken [the earth], he gives a footprint to his wife. 22.
He makes her recite, "O Neṣṭṛ, lead her forward," and so on. 23.
And while she is looking at the Soma-purchase cow, he makes her recite, "I have looked upon her. 24.
Having washed his hands, he ties a piece of gold on his ring finger. 25.
And [he does so] during the Āpyāyana, the Abhiṣava, and the Aṃśu and Adābhya rites.
26. And he issues the directions: "Bring the Soma-wrapping cloth! Bring the Soma-covering cloth! Bring the turban! 1.
In this case, the pouring [of the grains] is auspicious;
the Soma-wrapping cloth is beautiful.

In the absence of a turban, one cuts off two finger-breadths from the Soma-binding cloth to serve as the turban. Either the Adhvaryu or the sacrificer carries the Soma-wrapping cloth; the others carry the rest.
"They go to Soma; 'This is for you,' he causes [the sacrificer] to recite.
(6) Having sat down facing east, he touches the Soma with the formula, "Thou art ours. (7) He does not sort it out; some say that from this point on, grass and wood are to be removed. (8)
He spreads out the Soma-wrapper, doubled or quadrupled, with its fringe pointing eastward or northward;
upon it he measures out the Soma ten times with the verse beginning "abhityam. He measures it for the first time using all [the verses].
And [the sequence] starting from the thumb is a single emission (12);
twice with the little finger (13); and an increase by one (14).
The tenth [verse] with joined palms, or another according to the scriptural injunction for insertion;
having gathered the ends together, he binds them with the turban, [reciting]: "For the sake of offspring, thee."
He opens [the knot] in the middle with his finger, saying, "May the subjects follow you; may the vital breaths follow you.
(18) He hands it over to the seller. (19) He bargains for the Soma five times. (1)
He says, "O Soma-seller, is King Soma for sale? 2.
"He is for sale," says the Soma-seller. 3.
"Then I shall buy him from you. 4.
"Buy! said the Soma-seller.
"I will buy from you for a sixteenth part," he said.
"King Soma is worth more than that," said the Soma-seller.

"Furthermore, King Soma deserves even more than this; indeed, great is the greatness of the cow," says the Adhvaryu. "For the cow there is the fresh milk (*pratidhuk*); from that, the boiled milk (*śṛta*); from that, the whey (*śara*); from that, the cream (*mastu*); from that, the curdling agent (*ātañcana*); from that, the butter (*navanīta*); from that, the clarified butter (*ghṛta*); from that, the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*); from that, the whey-liquid (*vājina*). (8) From this point onward, he repeats [the formula] four times. (9) At the end, he barters for it step by step: for a hoof, for a foot, for half a cow, and for a whole cow. (10)
"I buy them," [he says] at the end; "ask [the price]," [he says] at the end of the question;
"King Soma has been bought," [he says] at the end; "announce the birds," says the Soma-seller.

He says: "The moon is yours; the garment is yours; the goat is yours; the cow is yours; the pair of cattle is yours; the other three are yours. 14. Having touched the gold with the words, "The bright one is yours," he causes [the sacrificer] to recite. 15.
With the words, "In the assembly for you," he causes the seller of Soma to tremble by means of the gold. 16.
With the words "asme te," he places it together with the sacrificer. 17. The Soma-seller takes this [cup]. 18.
Having touched a goat facing westward, he makes him recite: "The body of austerity. 19.
Giving the goat with his left hand while saying "With Mitra... and taking the Soma with his right hand, he either stands up as it is brought or rises;
having pushed aside the garment on the initiated one's right thigh, he places it down with the words "On the thigh of Indra.
Looking at the Soma-seller, he mutters "Thou art the son of Svāna, the brother... 20-22.
The initiated one uncovers his head (23),
and so does the wife (24).
Having suddenly snatched away gold, he strikes it with a spotted leather thong, or he may strike it otherwise (25).
When the Soma has been taken up, he makes [the sacrificer] recite "O Agni, protect me around" (RV 10.87.21) and so forth;
and also the subsequent verses.
With the verse "Up with life-force" (RV 10.59.5), he rises, placing the Soma upon his head and interposing his hand between it and his head.

Saying "O you who go against the path," he approaches from the north while standing on the south; he spreads a black antelope skin—covered, even-jointed, and washed—upon the raised plank at the front of the cart, saying, "The skin of Aditi.
Upon that, he places the Soma, saying, "The seat of Aditi."

Having touched the Soma with the words, "He has propped up the sky," he makes [the sacrificer] recite. With the words, "In the forests, the atmosphere," having covered [the Soma] with the Soma-wrapper, he fastens the black antelope skin in front with the words, "The eye of the sun.
If there is only one [skin], he cuts out the necks.

He yokes the two oxen simultaneously with the formula, "Yoke these two oxen," because that is what the text says; 10. there is a repetition of the mantra in the case of a division, because it is directly connected to the action; 11.
standing on the ground between the poles, the Subrahmaṇya priest drives [the oxen] with a Palāśa branch. 12.

Having gone around behind and taken hold of the support, he causes [the Adhvaryu] to recite for the purchased Soma as it is being carried around, or [for it] while being carried around. The initiated sacrificer also touches [it] from behind. When [the verse] has been recited three times, they go forward to the east, turn to the right, and proceed to the hall.
He causes [the sacrificer] to recite, "May I be auspicious.
16. He invokes the Subrahmaṇyā formula, saying "Subrahmaṇyā! Oṃ Subrahmaṇyā! Oṃ Subrahmaṇyā! three times, and then recites the Nigada once for as long as the Soma-pressing lasts. 17.
To the east of the hall, the Pratiprasthātṛ stands holding the animal for Agni and Soma—a black-spotted one fit for sacrifice; in its absence, a red-spotted one. 18.

Having touched it with the mantra "namo mitrasya," he causes [the sacrificer] to recite it. 19. While the animal sacrifice is proceeding, the recitation alone [takes place]. 20. Some [teachers say that one should] bring a firebrand from the Āhavanīya fire. 21.
Having placed it nearby, he supports it with a prop, saying, "The prop of Varuṇa.
He then pulls out the two pins, saying, "You two are the releasers of the support of Varuṇa.
Four men bring a stool made of Udumbara wood, reaching to the navel, one cubit in height, and forming part of the structure.
He touches her with the formula: "Thou art the seat of Varuṇa’s Truth. (25) He spreads a black antelope skin over her with the formula: "Thou art the seat of Varuṇa’s Truth.
(26) Upon that he places the Soma with the formula: "Sit upon the seat of Varuṇa’s Truth. (27)
They lead him into the hall by the path used for the initiated (dīkṣita).
He causes him to recite, "That which is yours...
They place him to the south of the Āhavanīya fire.
Some pour out a vessel of water [at this point].
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the Kātyāyana Śrautasūtra.
He offers the guest-offering (ātithya), a cake on nine potsherds for Viṣṇu. 1.
With his wife touching him, he should quickly offer [the oblations] five times with the formulas "The bodies of Agni," etc., one for each.
(2) There is an exclusion of the Sāvitra offering because of both scriptural contradiction and logical inconsistency.

(3) The rites beginning with the adding of fuel to the fires, the undertaking of the vow, eating forest-food, giving gifts, and the choosing of the Brahman priest are omitted in the Soma sacrifice from the Dīkṣaṇīyā until the Udavasānīyā, because they have already been performed there. (4)
And the binding of the wife’s girdle is performed with the sacrificial cord;
and the sacrificer’s portion [is not eaten] because of the prohibition against eating it,
for it is not a subordinate element of the ritual action.

He should place the subsidiary waters and the boiling waters upon the fire according to the rule for the *vrata* water (Sūtra 8). From that point until the release of the handfuls, the purpose is for water (Sūtra 9).

The enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are made of *kārṣmarya* wood; the grass-bundle (*prastara*) is of horse-tail hair; and the two separating blades (*vidhṛti*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) are made of *ikṣu* reeds (Sūtra 10).

This same fourfold procedure applies also to the Agniṣomīya and the Upasad offerings. Having placed [the materials], he performs the churning of the fire until the oblation is offered. It concludes with the Iḍā.
He takes the *dhrauva* [offering] with the formula, "For the lord of the waters" (Āpataye), during the presentation of the vows (14).
And twice from the pot with the *sruva*-ladle, for Tanūnapāt, with the words "To the Śākvara," "To the most powerful of the Śakvan-songs" (15).
He says "I take" in every instance, because the formula is syntactically expectant (16).
Or rather, the latter two are remnants of the former;
for there is a scriptural injunction: "They take the portions of clarified butter, grasping them one by one.
This is the *tānūnaptra* rite.

Having placed [the vessel] on the southern corner of the altar, the officiating priests and the sacrificer touch it, saying, "Unassailable" (anādhṛṣṭam). For there is a Vedic revelation: "No one shall harm the hands of the Tanūnaptra-offerer; no one shall harm him.
Having covered it with something other than earthenware, he sets it down upon the stool.
In the afternoon, he gives to the initiated one the mixture for the vow (vratamiśra). He gives [the remainder] to the householder (gṛhapati).
Having taken a fuel-stick on the Āhavanīya fire with the verse, "O Agni, guardian of vows," and having touched the boiling water, he makes his fist and the girdle even tighter.

And the wife, having silently touched the *madantī* waters at the *gārhapatya* fire, together with the sacrificer as the sixth person, causes the *soma* to swell, saying, "Each stalk (*aṃśu*), each stalk.
Having touched the clarified butter (*ājya*), he should touch water; likewise, one who is about to touch the *soma* should do so by reversing the order.
Having returned, they make the secret invocation over the *prastara* with their hands turned upwards—the right hand being turned upwards—saying, "May we find wealth.
Some perform the spreading apart [of the grass] and the anointing of the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*).
Having torn off a portion of the *prastara*, anointed it, and taken up the enclosing-sticks, he says, "O Agnīdh, the waters are rejoicing."
"The Agnīdh says, 'They are boiling.
Saying, 'Come with them,' he carries [the water] over the Āhavanīya fire, sprinkles it, and hands it to the Agnīdh for the purpose of setting it down. He also gives the command for the Subrahmaṇyā."
14. [The ritual] includes both the *pravargya* and the *upasad*.
15. Or rather, it is like the *upasad* when there is no *pravargya*.
16. The *upasad* begins with the *praṇītā* water.
Having summoned the preparer of the oblation, there should be no threshing for the purpose of grinding, because the purpose is sharpness;
or rather, there should be [threshing], because it is merely a ritual duty,
and because of the Vedic injunction.

Having performed the strewing of the grass, the placing of the vessels, the sprinkling, the pouring out of the clarified butter, and the placing [of the oblation] upon the fire, he takes up the wooden sword (sphya) and other implements; 20.
he carries away a cutting from the sacrificial grass (barhis); 21. or he gives the command, "O carriers of the boiling water! (madantīḥ). 22.
The fuel and the sacrificial grass are of the proper measure (23). He wipes the offering-spoons, the *sruva* being the third among them (24).
He takes eight portions into the *juhū* and four into the *upabhṛt* (25).
Or according to the original nature [of the materials] (26);
the spreading of one layer (27);
the vessel for clarified butter is for the purpose of the *dhruvā* ladle (28).
Having poured the *sruva*-libation, having wiped [the ladle] and caused [the Āgnīdhra] to call for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he should simply say, "Sit down, O Hotṛ!
(29). Being impelled, as he steps across, he causes [the Hotṛ] to recite for Agni (30). Having offered half [of the oblation], he pours together [the remainder] for Soma and Viṣṇu (31).
Having set down the two *sruva*-ladles, [the procedure] continues from the swelling of the Soma until the *Subrahmaṇyā* call.
Having anointed the *prastara* grass-bundle, he offers the *upasad* oblation with the *sruva*-ladle using the verse "yā te" while the sacrificer maintains contact with him at the iron bed.
He performs the rite twice with the same formula.
It should be well-conducted in the evening and well-conducted in the forenoon;
likewise, the others [should be performed] daily, including the *rajaḥśayā* and *hariśayā* rites.
It consists of one day and includes the *upasad* ceremonies.
Or there are twelve [cows]. 38.
He causes the first cow to be milked from three udders; 1. he causes the other two to be milked with a reduction of one [udder] each. 2.
Or, having reversed [the order] in the absence of the piling of the fire-altar (anagni-citi),
one should divide it equally when it has thus increased; there is an increase according to its own place.
On the day before the Aupavasathya, having performed the morning rites, he measures out the altar (vedi). 6.
To the east of the front pillar, at a distance of three prakramas, he drives in a peg; that is the antaḥpātya. 7. From that, to the east, at thirty-six [prakramas], 8. [he drives another peg].
And the southern and northern [lines] are at fifteen and fifteen [units], or nine and seventeen and a half [units] respectively;
and from the eastern end, they are at twelve and twelve [units].
Having stretched the *pṛṣṭhyā* line, he performs the rites beginning with the *sphya*, using a post made of *khadira* wood until the covering [of the altar].
(12) He carries away the *stambayajus* from the location of the *uparava* holes.
(13) The *cātvāla* pit is one and a half steps to the west of the northern shoulder of the altar. (14)
Or as it has been stated:
having combined the two morning *upasad* rites, after performing the forenoon ritual, he bestows the half-vow (*ardhavratam*);
or he offers everything into the fire.
When he has performed both [the Pravargya rites], he discards the Pravargya; if he should perform it as previously described, he does so.

He leads forward the fire (praṇayati) up to the pouring down of the ashes (upavapana), and having done so, he places it in the two Havirdhāna sheds. Having washed two Pṛṣṭhyā poles, each two aratnis apart, and having turned them eastward on both sides of the hall, he places the southern one closer to the shed.
Upon these two, he lays the roof-covering (chadiḥ).
In the absence of a wall,
he fixes a blade of *eṣīkā* grass on the forehead-strap in front, even elsewhere.
Having enclosed [the fire] with two upright [posts],
he offers four portions of ghee from the *śālā* (hall) toward the west over the roof, with the verse beginning "yuñjate" (RV 10.13.1).
From that point, this becomes the *gārhapatya* fire.
Furthermore, having placed gold on the southern path of the southern cart, he makes an offering over it with the verse, "This [is] Viṣṇu" (RV 1.22.17).

The wife, brought in through the southern door, takes the remainder in both hands and anoints the two axle-ends with the formula, "Parāk devaśrute" (VS 5.34), since that expression applies to both simultaneously.
If there is a separation, the formula is repeated, because the action is performed for each individually.
Having taken up the *sruk* and *sthālī*, the Pratiprasthātṛ [anoints] the northern [post] with "O Erāvatī," as before (30).
And the wife, having gone around the fires by the west, anoints the northern [post] as before (31).
He causes [the Adhvaryu] to recite after the two *havirdhāna* carts as they are being moved forward (1).
When [the verse] has been recited three times, he makes them turn as if lifting them up; he causes them to recite, "Go forward toward the east," and they low, "To our own stall."
Then, having measured three steps from the northern altar (uttaravedi) toward the center, he consecrates the two [posts] standing in the middle with the formula, "May you two take delight here.
Having circumambulated to the north, he supports the southern post with the formula, "Of Viṣṇu indeed...
He drives a post into the ground to the south with the formula, "For Viṣṇu, thee."
The Pratiprasthātṛ knows the higher [space] of heaven; 8.
he [fixes] a pillar to the north as before; 9.
or both [pillars] to the south. 10.
From here and there [he sprinkles]. 11.
And because of the Vedic revelation, "And he who is human... 12.
Having touched the middle roof-panel, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite, "Pratadviṣṇu... 13.
And on the north [side],
with "O Viṣṇu, the forehead," he places the forehead-stone; with "O Viṣṇu, you two are the ear-protectors," he erects the two ear-stones.
The roof-shingles have their tips pointing upward;
afterwards, he sews around the door-posts with a cord that has been smoothed by a *laspūjana* stone, with the formula: "Thou art the suture of Viṣṇu.
He makes a knot with the formula: "Thou art the firm foundation of Viṣṇu."
When the commencement has begun, he releases [the animal] at the *prāgvamśa* and the *havirdhāna*.
Having completed [the rites], he touches it with the formula: "Thou art belonging to Viṣṇu."
During this meal, they should not eat while looking through a non-doorway into the *sadas* or the *havirdhāna*; one should say to such a person, "Do not look!
The two doorways for the *pṛṣṭhyā* line are on both sides.
He digs the *uparavas* beneath the southern pole of the cart.
He prepares them with a wooden shovel (*abhri*) and so forth, like a pit, up until the tracing of the lines; there are four of them.
Like the sprinkling [of water] diagonally;
or the northernmost and westernmost first;
or correctly.
The last one is in the northeast; he digs them, each measuring a span, at intervals of a span between them,
digging according to the tracing with the formula, "Thou art great."
He scatters this [earth] as it was dug, with a mantra for each action:
"I scatter [the earth] from the excavation," he says for all [the pits] except the last one.
They are arm-length deep.
One should break [the clod] diagonally; if unable to do so, then straight across.
With the mantra "Svarāj," he touches it according to the manner in which it was dug, reciting a mantra for each action.
The Adhvaryu and the Sacrificer touch it together: the Adhvaryu at the south-eastern part, and the Sacrificer at the north-western part.
The Adhvaryu asks, "O Sacrificer, what is here? (14) He replies, "Auspicious.
(15) The Adhvaryu says in a whisper, "May that be for us both. (16)

Again, [the Adhvaryu stands] in the south-west, the sacrificer in the north-east. The sacrificer asks, "Adhvaryu, what is here? When [the Adhvaryu] has replied, "Auspicious," the sacrificer says, "May that be mine. (17) He sprinkles them with the mantra, "O slayers of Rakṣas... (18).
There is a repetition of the mantra for each individual part, because it is a *sānnipātika* [rite]. (19)
With the formula "O Rakṣohaṇ, O Rakṣohaṇ," he performs the pouring down and the spreading out as in the case of the pit (20).

Having placed Kuśa grass beneath them, he sets down the two pressing-boards, which are washed, two finger-breadths apart, facing east, and either one cubit long or perforated; he also sprinkles around them with the formula "O Rakṣohaṇ, O Rakṣohaṇ" (21).
Upon those two, he places the skin for pressing, which has been cut out and is entirely red, with the formula "Thou art belonging to Viṣṇu" (22).
On that [spot], he says, "The five pressing-stones belong to Viṣṇu.
(23) He makes the mound (khara) from the heap [of earth], raised and sprinkled with water, square, and strewn with sand.
(24) Having gone six steps eastward from the *antaḥpātya* line, he goes southward seven steps for the large [mound]. (25)
Therein, he erects a sacrificial post made of Udumbara wood, reaching up to the height of the sacrificer (26).
It lies like a sacrificial post (27).
He performs the rites beginning with the wooden sword (abhri) up until the spreading of the grass (28).
With the words "To the sky," he raises it;
with "The radiant one," he fixes it.

Having performed the rites from the surrounding-piling up to the pouring of water, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite "Thou art firm" while touching the Audumbara post with the words "May I abound in progeny" or "with cattle."

He offers with the *sruva* ladle upon the two prongs [of the *viśākha* wood] with the mantra, "To Heaven and Earth, with ghee... When it reaches the ground, he utters *svāhā*. In all cases involving mantras, he performs the oblation because of the direct instruction (32), and also because there is no prohibition against what has not been specifically prescribed (33).
The *sadas* hall is not to be at the height of the navel (1).
Or, according to one's judgment:
(2) the north beam (udagvaṃśa) should be eighteen, twenty-one, or twenty-four cubits (aratni) long. (4)
The length of the nine [rafters] is half that of the transverse [rafter]; some place the Audumbarī [rafter] in the middle on the spine;
having placed the middle roof-plate with the mantra "Indrasya chadiḥ," one places the two [roof-plates] in the west and east.
The two triple-sets [of stakes] are to the north.
Having surrounded [the Havirdhāna] with the mantra "pari tvā" (VS 5.34), he performs the sewing, tying the knot, and touching with the Aindra mantras.
To the north of the rear end of the Havirdhāna, he places [the Āgnīdhra shed] either half-way between the Āgnīdhra and the door of the fire-hall, or further out, or covering the whole distance.
Having completed the Vaiśvadeva offering with the formula "Thou art the Vaiśvadeva," he seizes the victim.

11 He pours out the earth for the Dhiṣṇya hearths; on a spot that has been dug up and sprinkled, he pours out the loose soil while holding on to the wooden sword (sphya), sitting down facing north, reciting the formulas one by one beginning with "Thou art abundant. 12 The Āgnīdhrīya hearth comes first. 13
And sand [is placed] on top; 14. [The word] "with the Raudra" applies everywhere; 15. six [verses] in the assembly hall. 16.
Facing west, he places [the seat] to the rear of the Hotṛ’s [seat]. (17) To the southeast of the Audumbarī pillar is that of the Maitrāvaruṇa.
(18) To the north of the Hotṛ’s dhiṣṇya are four [seats] at equal intervals for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Acchāvāka. (19)

Facing south, standing at the edge of the altar opposite the Āgnīdhra fire and to the south, he points out the Mārjālīya fire—which always has its door to the east—beginning from the east, with the formulas "Thou art the sovereign," one for each: the Āhavanīya, the place for the Bahiṣpavamāna, the Cātvāla pit, the Śāmitra fire, the Udumbarī post, the seat of the Brahman, the Śālādvārya fire, and the Prājahita fire.
Having swept up the Utkara heap, he addresses it with: "Thou art the all-knowing; thou art the support of what is deficient and what is redundant."

Having performed the strewing of grass, the arranging of the vessels, the sprinkling, and the pouring out of the clarified butter, he performs the rites beginning with the northern enclosure (uttaraparigraha), including the inner path (antaḥpātya) [23–24]. He gives the command ending with the sacrificial grass (barhis). Therein, he places everything in its proper position [25].

Right here, the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is prescribed. 26. Having placed the fuel (idhma), the spreading of the altar (vedi) for the Agniṣomīya sacrifice and the non-taking of the prastara-bunch [are performed]; in the afternoon, when the half-vow (ardhavratam) has been administered, having entered, the placing of the fire to be led forward (praṇayanīya) takes place. 28.

Having performed the placing of the clarified butter on the fire, the wiping of the *sruk* ladles, the taking down [of the butter], and the inspection, the sacrificer sits to the west of the *śālādvārya* fire, having placed the Soma on his lap. He scatters [the dust] around the footprint of the Soma-purchase cow to the west of the *śālādvārya* fire. Some divide it into four parts: for the *upayamanī* ashes of the Āhavanīya, for the *agnīdhrīya* fire, and for the rubbing of the axle.

Having purified the clarified butter and the sprinkling water in the *antarpātya* region, the taking of the animal’s and the clarified butter’s portions occurs (32). They hold the clarified butters steady (33),
and those observing the vow touch the sacrificer from behind (34).
He covers them with a cloth (35).
He should not pay heed to them while they are moving (36).
He makes an offering over the blazing fuel with the *pracaraṇī* ladle, saying, "O Soma, you... (1).
He causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the second verse, "juṣāṇo aptuḥ," while the fire is being carried forward;
or rather, [he recites it] with the words, "for Soma, as he is being led forth."

Taking the pressing-stones, the *droṇakalaśa*, the Soma-vessels, the fourfold *idhma* (fuel), the two bound *vapāśrapaṇī* (omentum-roasting spits), the two cords, the *śakala* (wood-chip), the *vṛṣaṇa* (two stones for crushing Soma), and the two *araṇī* (fire-drills), they go toward the *āhavanīya* fire.
While reciting "O Agni, lead us," he causes [the sacrificer] to recite.
Having carried it north of the *sadas*, he places the fire in the *āgnīdhra*.
The pressing stones, the wooden trough (*droṇakalaśa*), and the Soma vessels [are placed];
he offers with the verse "ayāṅg" in this [fire] (9).
Having circumambulated by the north, he places [the implements] to the north of the Āhavanīya fire, with the exception of the other clarified butter and the Soma (10).
There must be no interruption for the Adhvaryu regarding the *dhiṣṇya* hearths.
(11) He performs the sprinkling of the fuel-sticks (*idhma*) and other rites.
(12) On the northern half of the *khara* mound, he spreads a single layer of grass, either behind or on the northern altar (*uttaravedi*). (13)
Having performed the inspection of the Āhavanīya fire with the verse "uru viṣṇo vikramasva" (VS 5.17), he offers an oblation;
for it is stated in the Śruti: "Or rather, having first laid two fuel-sticks.
Having set down the clarified butter, he spreads a black antelope skin on the southern cart and places the Soma upon it with the verse "deva savitaḥ" (VS 6.11).
Having released [the vessel] with the words "This art thou," he stands near [the fire].
(17) Having stepped out with "Svāhā! Out!", and having placed a fuel-stick on the Āhavanīya fire with "O Agni, guardian of vows," he touches the boiling water and releases his fingers.
(18) And the wife, having silently touched the boiling water at the Gārhapatya fire, [does the same]. (19)
Having prepared the boiling waters in the *cātvāla* pit (20),
they perform the meal consisting of the mention of his name from this point forward (21);
this is the cessation of the vow (22).
The consumption of the remnants of the oblation; 23.
From this point on, the animal sacrifice is dedicated to Agni and Soma; 24.
The sacrificial cake for the animal (paśupuroḍāśa) belongs to those same deities; 25.
He performs [the rites] with the spade and so forth;
he carries the animal-portion from the south of the *havirdhāna* shed,
as well as the third part of the rectum.
Having brought the tail-end (jāghanī) back along the south of the Mārjālīya fire, or [along the north] so as not to create an interval between it and the Soma-Āhavanīya fire;
if there is a series of eleven sacrificial posts (yūpaikādaśinī), the intervals between them should be the measure of a chariot axle.
Either dividing the eastern half equally (7),
or measuring it according to the sacrificial post (pakṣa) in the fire (8);
the offerings for the sacrificial posts, the taking up of the spades, and the sowing of barley are performed once (9).
The other [altar] is different because it is constructed by division;
having marked out the middle one, he marks out the northern or southern one, and the others in reverse order,
performing [the rites] up to the oblation in the pit (avaṭahoma).
Having performed the anointing and other rites for each one individually by means of the collyrium and so forth,
on the following day, because of the impossibility of touching them all at once, [the rite] for those on the right and left ends concludes with the covering over;
having encircled the middle one, it concludes with the covering over.
Having wound ropes around the stakes standing near the fire-altars, he leaves them there;
he performs the rites beginning with the anointing; and he raises them according to the marks made when they were dug.
The southern [post] is the tallest, and the others follow in order of decreasing height (19).
The post at the Agniṣṭha is for a Tīvrasutya sacrifice, and the altar is extended toward the east (20).
The expansion of the altar follows the [placement of the] sacrificial posts (21).
He places the twelfth [brick], the *vitaṣṭa*, to the south of the largest one, with the formula "This is for thee.
(22) He performs [the rites] from the sprinkling until the covering, as they are not omitted in their purpose. (23) Or, he does so without raising the northern [brick]. (24)

As prescribed, he immolates the Savanīya animals after having dedicated them with a single blade of grass: those for Agni, Sarasvatī, Soma, Pūṣan, Bṛhaspati, Viśve Devas, Indra, the Maruts, Indra-Agni, Savitṛ, and Varuṇa.
(25) In the case of a set of eleven animals at a single sacrificial post, having bound the one for Agni, he binds the others to each respective post facing north.
(26) The animal for Agni goes first, followed by the others in successive order as they touch him. (27)
They strike this [victim] on the right side and the others on the left.

(28) The procedure from the *upapreṣya* call down to the *paripaśyatī* is the same. [The items are: the command to slaughter (*saṃjñapaya*), the following, the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*), the fire-brand (*ulmuka*), the butcher (*śāmitra*), the intermediate covering (*antarddhāna*), the cutting (*praccheda*), the instruction regarding the drops (*tokasaṃpraiṣa*), the butcher’s instruction (*śāmitrānuśāsana*), the dialogue (*saṃvāda*), the offering to Vanaspati, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, the *iḍā* portion, and so forth; the support of the [heart-]spike (*vyādhāraṇa*) is performed by pouring together [the juices], because of their abundance.
(29) [This applies to] the cauldron (*ukhā*), the spit (*śūla*), and the two omentum-roasting spits (*vapāśrapaṇī*). (30)
Not so, because of the absence of doubt;
and because of the observation of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice;
and because there is no contradiction.

Due to the irregularity of the cooking, [the Manotā and Vasā offerings] in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice are performed separately because of the difference in time. (34) In the case of the eleven sacrificial posts (yūpaikādaśinī), having performed the rites up to the wiping of the omentum of the barren cow (vaśā), the raising of the wife’s post (patnīyūpa) of the measure of a navel should be done at the entrance of the hall. (35–36)

Having performed the strewing of grass, the placing of the vessels, the sprinkling, the pouring out of the clarified butter, and the placing [of the oblation] upon the fire, he proceeds with the wooden sword (sphya) and the other implements.
They release the goat dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ after it has been encircled by fire, for the Śruti states: "They conclude the rite with clarified butter."
And because of the carrying of fire around the animal (paryagnikaraṇa);
or rather, it ends with that [point], because of the name of the ritual action;
and because of the observation of the sacrifice to Tvaṣṭṛ and Vanaspati among the fore-offerings (prayāja).

The drawing of the Vasatīvarī waters for the Agniṣomīya sacrifice takes place at the end of the cleansing of the omentum, from waters flowing [toward the river] before sunset; if it has already set, then from the water used for washing the cart-pole (nināhya) if one has previously sacrificed;
if one has not previously sacrificed, then from the water of anyone else who has settled nearby and has previously sacrificed.
In the absence of both, holding either a firebrand or gold above [the head], he places it behind the door of the hall with the verse "The ladles full of oblation... and "Of Agni... (RV 3.27.5–6).
He also causes the Subrahmaṇyā formula to be recited, that which pertains to the lineage of father and son.

If the *āditya* oblation has not been offered at sunset, he completes the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice up to the end of the *dakṣiṇāgni* offering after the sun has set; then [the Adhvaryu] says three times, "Step out!
[The sacrificer] stands behind the door of the hall, the wife behind the *uttaravedi*, and the sacrificer, having placed Soma on his lap.
Behind the door of the hall, he carries the Vasatīvarī waters around;
having brought them out by the south, he places them on the southern corner of the northern altar-altar with the formula, "Of Indra and Agni.
Having brought them back, he places them in their proper place.
The wife touches the water-pot (kalaśa).
Having circumambulated to the north, she [touches it] on the northern side as before;
or with the formula, "Of Mitra and Varuṇa."

With the formula "Of all the gods," [he places the Soma] in the Āgnīdhra fire-hall; 21. And he places the Soma on the throne-seat; 22. And the consecrated sacrificer guards it there for that night. 23.
And he gives the *subrahmaṇyā* call. 24.
The milking for the *parivāpyā* [offering]. 25.
Rubbing the body, ornamentation, and cleaning the teeth belong to the *adhvaryu* who has not yet been initiated; [these belong] to the *adhvaryu* who has not yet been initiated. 26.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Kātyāyana Śrautasūtra.
1. During the latter part of the night, they awaken the officiating priests (ṛtvij).

Having touched water, and having performed the strewing of grass around the fire at the door of the hall, the placing of the vessels, the sprinkling, the pouring out of the clarified butter, the placing on the fire, the wiping of the *sruk* ladles, the taking down [of the butter], and the inspection, the Āgnīdhra priest, having purified the butter, performs the taking of the animal-offering butter (*paśvājyagrahaṇa*). 2. [The procedure continues: Having performed the strewing of grass around the fire at the door of the hall, the placing of the vessels, the sprinkling, the pouring out of the clarified butter, the placing on the fire, the wiping of the *sruk* ladles, the taking down [of the butter], and the inspection, the Āgnīdhra priest, having purified [the butter], performs the taking of the animal-offering butter.
Having taken the clarified butter and the Soma as required, he performs the sprinkling of the fuel-sticks and other rites at the Āhavanīya fire (sūtra 3).
The spreading of the sacrificial grass is performed as in the Agniṣomīya sacrifice (sūtra 4).

Having completed the rites up to the placing of the clarified butter, he places the two pressing-stones facing each other between the two halves of the Soma upon the wooden pressing-boards, with the formula "For the heart, thee" (sūtra 5).
Having released [the Soma] with the verse "viśvāstvām," he worships it.
(6) By this [verse], the fetching of the Soma for the pressing is performed. (7) There is no lifting up [of the Soma] from there, because it would otherwise be placed outside [the ritual space]. (8)
And because the pressing of the Soma has already been performed, there is no carrying [of the remains].
Before the utterance of speech, he performs the commencement of the Prātaranuvāka while placing a fuel-stick on the fire, saying: "Recite for the gods who come in the morning!
Some say [he says] "for the gods. 9–11.
And he sends forth the Subrahmaṇyā call.
12 The Adhvaryu should remain awake for the Prātaranuvāka, or he may sleep. 13–14.
He offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Indra; parched grains for the two bay horses (Haris) to Pūṣan; a gruel of groats (karambha) to Sarasvatī; curdled milk (dadhi) to Mitra and Varuṇa;
and clotted milk (payasyā) to Indra accompanied by the two bay horses, Pūṣan, Sarasvatī, and Mitra-Varuṇa—these parched grains and the other offerings respectively.
This is the preparation of the vessels for the Unnetṛ.
On the northern half of the western part [of the altar] are the cups for the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma;
behind those, toward the west, are the cups for the dual-deity offerings; the cup for Indra and Vāyu is shaped like a girth-rope.
The goat for Mitra and Varuṇa is from the female goat; the one for the Aśvins is from the female camel;
in the southeastern quarter are those for Śukra and Manthin.
The southern [cup] belongs to Śukra (9);
the Āgrayaṇa vessel is in the middle (10);
the southern Ukthya vessel, together with its cup, [is placed there] (11).

Likewise, the Āditya vessel is placed to the north (12). The two Ṛtu cups are made of *kārṣmarya* wood or *aśvattha* wood, shaped like the bowl of a ladle (*sruk*), with openings on both sides (13). The other vessels are turned upwards, measuring one span (*prādeśa*) in length, and are constricted in the middle (14).

From the Āgrayaṇa vessel, he carries the *pariplu* ladle with its bowl downward along the axle toward the west, and having passed over the *droṇakalaśa*, he places the filter above the axle upon it. [The filter] is white and made of sheep’s wool; it has fringes on both ends for the *pariplu* ladle.
To the east is the support; immediately to the north is the *dhruva* vessel;
on the pole to the east is the *pracaraṇī* ladle; and above the axle to the east is the *pūtabhṛt* vessel.
To the west [of the central post] is the *adhavanīya* jar (21).
To the east of the axle are ten *camasa* cups, joined together at the bottom (22).
To the west are the *ekadhanas*, an odd number, beginning with three and ending with fifteen, used for drawing water (23).
When it is said, "The dawn has become bright with cattle," he offers four ladlefuls with the *pracaraṇī* spoon, saying, "May Agni hear.
Having taken another portion, while walking northward, he says, "O Hotṛ, seek the waters."

And he sends forth [the calls]: "O Camasādhvaryu of the Maitrāvaruṇa, come! O Neṣṭṛ, lead up the wives! O Ekadhanins, come! O Agnīdh, you shall stand near the Cātvāla pit with the Vasatīvarī waters, and with the Hotṛ’s cup! 3.
Having gone to the waters, he offers an oblation into the water with the formula, "O divine waters... 4.
With the formula, "Thou art a furrow," he pushes away the clarified butter with the cup of the Maitrāvaruṇa. 5.
With the verse "samudrasya tvā," he draws [the water];
they draw up the *ekadhana* pitchers,
and the wives draw up the *pānnejana* pitchers two by two.
Having returned, he causes the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup and the Vasatīvarī waters to touch over the Cātvāla pit with the formula, "The waters together.
According to some, they pour them into each other, first into the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup.
Having placed the Vasatīvarī waters into the Hotṛ’s cup, he hands the Nigrābhya waters to the sacrificer.
Questioned by the Hotṛ, he replies, "As it were, they have bowed down" (RV 8.75.12).
In the Agniṣṭoma, he offers the residue of the *pracaraṇī* ladle; in its absence, he offers four spoonfuls with the verse, "O Agni, whom... (RV 6.16.40).
In the Ukthya sacrifice, he touches the first enclosing-stick.
He enters [the Sadas] otherwise;
or rather, there is the touching of the forehead-staff in the Ṣoḍaśin sacrifice;
and the roof-panels in the Atirātra.

Having passed by the Hotṛ to the south, he pours the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup into the Ādhavanīya vessel, along with a third portion of the Vasatīvarī water, [reciting]: "May Agni Vaiśvānara, who brings benefit to all, protect us at the morning pressing by his greatness. May he, the purifier, bestow wealth upon us; may we be long-lived, sharing in the draught. (18) And likewise for the Ekadhana waters. (19) Having placed the remnants of both in the place of the Ekadhana waters, (20)
They sit around the two pressing-boards:
(1) the Adhvaryu and the Sacrificer to the north; (2) the Adhvaryu to the east; (3) the other three, having gone around by the west.
Having taken up the pressing-stone with the formula, "Thee for the god," he restrains his speech until the *hiṅ* sound.
That [stone] is the *upāṃśusavana*.
He makes him recite over the *nigrābhya* waters while holding them against his chest with the formula, "O *nigrābhya*s!"

At the Upāṃśusavana, he measures out the Soma with the formula "O Indra, [I measure] thee who art accompanied by the Vasus and the Rudras," five times, reciting a mantra for each measurement (7). With the verse beginning "yat te" (8), he touches the measured portions. The Pratiprasthātṛ takes six stalks (aṃśu) and places two between each of his fingers (9).
With the words, "Be refreshing," he pours out the *nigrābhya* waters. When about to strike, he should mentally contemplate his enemy, saying, "I strike this one, not you, O Soma.
In the absence [of an enemy], [he should strike] a blade of grass.
"Do not fear," he says, and strikes [the stone].
13. Thus he presses three times, pouring out the *nigrābhya* waters. 14.
Eight times, eleven times, or twelve times. 15.

All five groups [of verses] are for one desiring cattle; eight groups are for one desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa). He causes [the sacrificer] to recite the *nigrābha* formula after each group, having placed small stalks of barley into the Hotṛ’s cup with the words "prāg apāk" (forward and backward), etc. With the verse beginning "adriṇā," he performs the fourth [drawing].
Or silently;
he draws the *upāṃśu* cup with [the formula], "For Vācaspati, O god, [draw] the honeyed [juices] for the gods. The Pratiprasthātṛ holds the vessel underneath.
And he hides two of his own [breaths] within each [of the others], because of the difference in grasping (22),
and because of the indicative mark of the mantra (23); or rather, there are six [to be hidden], because of the force of the scriptural statement (24).
Having taken [the cup] with "yat te," he places it upon the Soma-pressing board (25).

Having wiped it around, he sets it down for the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups (26). One practicing exorcism should set it down without releasing [his breath], saying, "I set thee down as the out-breath of so-and-so"; for the Antaryāma, he says, "as the up-breath" (27).
He covers it with his hand, saying, "I cover the breath of so-and-so.
Having said, "Svāhā to the out-breath, to the Antaryāma cup," he steps out, saying, "To the wide atmosphere.
He takes hold of another [cup] after handing over the Hotṛ’s cup.
Having chosen a boon, he gives it. Having offered with the formula "svāṅkṛta," he wipes the vessel.
On the first enclosing-stick, he wipes his hand upwards from east to west while it is turned face up, with the words "To the gods thee! (devebhyas tvā).
One should offer the *aṃśu* stalk, which is clung to the arms of Vāyu, while reciting the verse beginning with "The gods, the portions" (RV 10.123.1).
34. Having poured a portion of the remnant from the *āgrayaṇa* vessel into it, one throws the *aṃśu* stalk into it for the third pressing.
35. With the formula "For breath, thee," the vessels are set down. 36.
Having wiped the *upāṃśusavana* stone with his hand, he touches it while pointing it upwards, saying, "For the out-breath (*vyāna*), thee!
(37). While two [priests] are seated, four [others] press the juice, because of their capacity for sitting around [the mortar].
(1) The pressing consists of three rounds, ending with the swelling [of the soma]. (2)
The pouring of the *nigrābhya* water takes place during the third repetition of the *mantra*,
or at the beginning of the sequence, because of its abundance.
At the end of the *nigrābha*, having placed the stalks of *saras* grass into the *dhavanīya* vessel, he shakes them out and pours [the water] in;
in this same manner a second time, and a third time.
The *nigrābhyā* waters are as before.
Or rather, having first drawn the Upāṃśu cup, [the subsequent acts] are performed because the filling and gathering have already been accomplished;
the sitting around [the pressing stones] is merely a ritual duty (dharma).

Or else, there is a reversal of the order of the pressing, because the stalks have been touched and removed, because of the connection with the sequence of the Nigrābhya waters, and because of the capacity for mental concentration regarding that which has not yet been taken up.
And because of its state as *ṛjīṣa*,
having removed it from the *droṇakalaśa* vessel, he places it upon the mouths of the pressing-stones; the pressers spread out the filter and pour water.
Or, if they do not perform it themselves, the Unnetṛ pours [the water] from the Ādhavanīya vessel into the Nigrābhya waters; the sacrificer [places them] upon the strainers;
then follows the drawing of the cups, beginning with five first from the Āghāra-vessel at the midday pressing.

The *śukra* [cup] is from the *droṇakalaśa* (18); others [are taken] from there unless otherwise specified (19); those [cups] exhausted by the *sāvitra*, *pātnīvata*, and *hāriyojana* [rites] are taken from the *āgrayaṇa* vessel (20).
The cups for the *pūtabhṛt* vessel [are filled] at the third pressing; the *vaiśvadeva* cup [is drawn] there,
because of the scriptural injunction regarding the drawing [of soma] here even when it has not been specifically prescribed.
Having wiped [the cup] repeatedly with the fringe of the *daśāpavitra*, the placing of the cup is performed with the formula, "This indeed is your womb" (TS 3.2.5.2).
(24) This does not apply to cups that lack a womb.
(25) Vātsya, however, says it applies to all [cups], because the instruction is given without qualification. (26)
And because of the prohibition of the Sāvitra and the seasonal cups [at this point].
Having offered at each *vaṣaṭ*-call, the taking of the portion for the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ* occurs;
the cup-bowls are taken according to their respective owners.
Or rather, [the offering] belongs to the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer first, because of the force of the scriptural statement (30);
the *unnetṛ* draws it up because of the designation (31);
the drawing of the *antaryāma* cup occurs after sunrise, as indicated by the formula "grasped with a support" (*upayāmagṛhīta*). (1)
He performs [the rites] with a low-voiced recitation, excluding the selection of the remaining [portion] that has not been mentioned and excluding the pouring of water;
he wipes [the vessel] here;
and in the first [instance], he does so with his hand turned downwards toward the west.

The setting down of the vessels for that which has been touched by the *upāṃśusavana* stone is performed with the formula, "For out-breathing, thee! (5). He draws the cup for Indra and Vāyu with the verse, "Come, O Vāyu... (6).
Having drawn it, he covers it again with the formula, "Indra and Vāyu... (7).
"O you two, consisting of Mitra and Varuṇa...
(with these words) he mixes it with milk, having placed *kuśa* grass in between, [saying] "May we [be united] with wealth...
(RV 5.62.7). Thus it is in all cases of mixing.
He should offer the *śukra* with the verse "Or him with the wood-apple," or with "As of old";
some say [he should offer] the *manthin* with "This Vena. 11–13.
He mixes it with groats with the verse, "They whose mind is like the sea" (RV 9.11.8).
He pours the Āgrayaṇa cup from two streams with the verse, "Those gods who...
(RV 9.62.23). Having caught the Āgrayaṇa with the *daśāpavitra* filter, he utters the *hiṃ* sound three times; then, for the remainder, he says once, "Soma purifies himself" (RV 9.107.1).
In the morning pressing, the rites are performed loudly with the first pitch before the instruction regarding the deities;
at the midday pressing, they are performed with the middle pitch.
At the third pressing with the best [cup],
[he takes] the Ukthya with "Thou art taken with a support," and the Dhruva with "The head of heaven."
Until the oblation of this [soma], the one pressing it should not void urine or feces (23). And knowing [the ritual], he should offer to Vaiśvānara (24).
Having made the vessels for the *sthālīpāka* full and the *droṇakalaśa* half-full, the one pressing [the soma] pours everything out (25).
The Adhvaryu, Pratiprasthātṛ, Prastotṛ, Udgātṛ, Pratihartṛ, and the one pressing the Soma go out while holding onto one another.
(26) The Adhvaryu goes first, and the others follow in their respective order.
(27) Or, having offered the oblation, they may hold onto one another. (28)
They offer the oblation of drops with the verse "yaste" (29), or the Adhvaryu does so (30).
The Adhvaryu takes up the grass from the altar; they proceed toward the north, bowing low (31).
He throws one blade of grass into the *cātvāla* pit with the formula, "Of the gods... (32).
He throws the other blade silently in front of the *udgātṛ*s (33).
While they are muttering the mantra, "Soma purifies himself," he hands two blades of grass to the *prastotṛ* as the signal for the commencement of the *pavamāna* chant (34).
In all [cases],
35 either without grass 36 or a handful of *kuśa* grass 1.
They sit down facing west; the sacrificer is to the south in front.
While the hymn is being chanted, the Unnetṛ, having placed the filter over the Ādhavanīya vessel, pours [the Soma] into the Pūtabhṛt.
At the end of the Stotra, he issues the command: "O Agnīdh, spread the fires, strew the sacrificial grass, and prepare the sacrificial cakes! O Pratiprasthātṛ, come with the animal!"
He scatters embers from the Āgnīdhra fire onto the hearths according to where they were previously sown; he strews sacrificial grass along the spine of the altar;
and while [the sacrificer] holds on to him, he draws the cup for the Aśvins with the verse, "O you two... (RV 1.93.1).
He gazes at the cups while reciting the formulas for the spaces as they were drawn: "For my breath," and so on, mantra by mantra (8).
The Upāṃśusavana stone is the second;
the Āśvina cup is the sixth; the Śukra and Manthin cups are together; and the Pūtabhṛt and Ādhavanīya jars are together with the formula, "For all [my vital powers]" (10).
"Who are you? [he asks]. He murmurs "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ" over the Droṇakalaśa vessel.
He should cause those who are knowledgeable, beloved, and learned in the Vedas to sit nearby.

Having appointed the *dhruvagopa*, he performs the rites beginning with the girding [of the sacrificial post]. Having drawn out the front part of the cord, [the animal] for Agni is the *savanīya* animal at the *agniṣṭoma*; at the *ukthya*, the second is for Indra-Agni;
at the *ṣoḍaśin*, the third is a ram for Indra; and at the *atirātra*, the fourth is for Sarasvatī, or a ewe.
This is the stomāyana.

Having performed the selection of the Hotṛs up to the mention of their names, and having called for the *śrauṣaṭ* for each subsequent one, he chooses them according to their respective characteristics:
the two Āśvina priests from the office of the Adhvaryu.
Mitra and Varuṇa from the office of the Praśāstṛ;

Indra from the office of the Brāhmaṇ—thus [he addresses] the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin. 8. The Maruts from the office of the Potṛ; the divine ladies (Gnās) from the office of the Neṣṭṛ; Agni from the office of the Āgnīdhra—"Agni indeed [is the first] of the divine [priests]"—thus [he addresses] the sacrificer. 9.

They offer two oblations as they have proceeded, with the formulas: "May I be pleasing to speech; may I be pleasing to Vācaspati. O Goddess Speech, that which is the sweetest and most pleasing part of your speech—place me therein, Svāhā! To Sarasvatī! (10). With the verse "O purifying one... (pāvakā naḥ), they offer the second oblation (11).

Having performed the rites up to the wiping of the omentum, those associated with the sacrificial fires, together with the sacrificer, worship the hearths with the respective mantras beginning with "Thou art pervasive" (vibhūr asi) (12).

Having performed the *utkarānta* rite, he touches the *sadas* with the formula, "Thou art speech" (*vāg asi*). He consecrates the two door-posts with the formula, "The two doors of Truth" (*ṛtasya dvārau*), using the subsequent [verses].
He addresses the sun with the formula, "Of paths, the lord of paths" (*adhvanām adhvapatir asi*). 13–15.
"Mitrasya tvā... [is recited] by the officiating priests (ṛtvij);
"Agnayaḥ sagarāḥ... [is recited] for the hearth-fires (dhiṣṇya).
This is the ritual movement (sarpaṇa).
The touching of the Sadas and so forth occurs in the two later pressings;
he proceeds with the sacrificial cakes;
there is a single offering.

Having placed [the offerings] in a single vessel—the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) in the middle, fried grains (dhānāḥ) in front, and the other items in the various directions according to their number, moving clockwise—4. At each morning pressing, he causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verses (anuvākyā) for the sacrificial cakes dedicated to Indra. 5. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "O Praśāstṛ, give the command for the oblations (praṣya) of the sacrificial cakes set forth for the morning pressing. 6.

In this manner, according to each libation, he performs the recitation and the *praisha* (direction); and from the *upabhṛt* ladle onwards, he cuts the portions. Having offered both like the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), he places the cakes upon the *hotṛ*-hearth.
He performs the *veḍ* call for those who have descended.

He proceeds with the offerings for the dual deities (*dvidevatya*). He causes the Pratiprasthātṛ to recite the invitatory verse for Vāyu and Indra-Vāyu. Having taken [the draught] from the *droṇakalaśa* with the Āditya vessel, saying, "Thou art taken with a support," he offers the dual-deity libations one after another on the northern half [of the fire].
Even at the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call (13);
and the *āśruta*, *pratyāśruta*, and *praisha* formulas [are performed] because of their equality (14);
not because of immediate sequence (15).
It may be so, because there is no contradiction. 16.

He pours the remainder after remainder into the Āditya vessel with the formula, "To the Ādityas thee! 17. Having poured it all together, he covers it with that [ladle] while reciting, "O Viṣṇu, grant wide space! 18.
He causes them to recite while they are being filled;
he pours [the soma] into nine cups, having placed them behind the northern altar;
[he performs] the under-layering and the sprinkling from the *śukra* cup.
First, they perform the rites with the Hotṛ’s cup; 22. They proceed with the Śukra and Manthin offerings: 1.
the Adhvaryu with the Śukra, and the Pratiprasthātṛ with the Manthin. 2.

Taking two chips from the sacrificial post, one sprinkled with water and one unsprinkled, they perform the covering with the sprinkled ones and the wiping with the unsprinkled ones: the Adhvaryu wipes with "Śaṇḍa has been wiped away," and the Pratiprasthātṛ with "Marka has been wiped away.
They step out with "The gods have accepted you," according to the respective signs.

Placing the two measuring-sticks together behind the Uttaravedi, they lay them down on the two buttocks of the Uttaravedi without releasing their hold: the Adhvaryu on the southern one and the Pratiprasthātṛ on the northern one, with the formula "Thou art unassailable."
With the words "O thou of good heroes," the Adhvaryu goes to the southern spot for the sacrificial post; with "O thou of good offspring," the Pratiprasthātṛ goes to the northern one.
With the verse "Having come together," they join their forearms in front of the post according to the respective gender-markings.
If they are unable [to do so], they do it to the east.
The two un-sprinkled [stalks] he throws out; the Adhvaryu says, "Śaṇḍa is thrown out," and the Pratiprasthātṛ says, "Marka is thrown out.
9. They throw the two sprinkled [stalks] into the Āhavanīya fire; the Adhvaryu says, "The support of the Śukra," and the Pratiprasthātṛ says, "Of the Manthin. 10.

Having muttered, "Of the unsevered," and having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the Soma-pressings set forth for Indra, accompanied by the Śukra and dripping with sweetness, belonging to the morning pressing. 11.
Facing west toward the sacrificial post from both sides, they offer the oblations: (1) the Adhvaryu first with "That is the first," (2) the Pratiprasthātṛ following him,
and (3) the Camasādhvaryus as well.
And he gives the command: "Let the cup of the Hotṛ go forward;

let that of the Brahman go forward; let that of the Udgātṛs go forward; let that of the Sacrificer go forward; let those of the Sadasyas go forward. O Camasādhvaryus of the Hotrakas, come hither; fill up the Śukra vessel! 5.
Having returned, the Pratiprasthātṛ pours the remnant into the Śukra vessel. 6.
They pour those [libations] five times into the Hotṛ’s cup (hotṛcamasa).
Having caused the announcement (āśrāvya) each time, he gives the direction (preṣyati) to the Praśāstṛ and the others, saying, "Sacrifice by mentioning the name; sacrifice! for each.
Having first offered to the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin with "O Brahman, sacrifice! (10), or last, he mutters, "May they be satisfied" (11).
He sits down facing west toward the Hotṛ, saying, "The Āgnīdhra has sacrificed" (12).

One consumes the cups dedicated to two deities; the first [priest] should consume them because he is the one who performs the pressing and the oblation, according to the scriptural statement (śruti): "The first [priest] should consume because of the initial injunction. Or rather, the Hotṛ [should consume], on account of the wording of the mantra-texts.
Not the Adhvaryu, because of the [syntactic] co-occurrence [with the Hotṛ].
Because there is no injunction for the mantras (16),
because the cause is the same (17),
[one recites] "He receives the draught for Indra and Vāyu; may the wealthy one, the possessor of much wealth, come" (18).

The consumption [of the Soma] is like that of the Hotṛ: "May the goddess of speech, being pleased, be satisfied with the Soma together with the vital breath; Svāhā!"—in this manner the consumption of all Somas is performed. (19) Other than what is stated by a specific injunction, (29) [one uses] "Bhakṣe hi me" or according to the indicative mark. (21)

In the same way, he pours the remainder of each [portion] into the Hotṛ’s cup with the respective formulas: "May the Vasu come," "The Vasu-providing one comes," and "The Vasu who bestows wealth. He throws a portion the size of a sacrificial cake into the cup for Indra and Vāyu, curdled milk into the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa, and parched grains into the cup for the Aśvins.
The Pratiprasthātṛ places them on the northern track of the southern *havirdhāna* cart;
he offers the *iḍā*;
and they lift up the cups.
1. Or, after it has been wiped with the horse-hair filter, they proceed [with the offering], because the *sūktavāka* and *śaṃyuvāka* serve a different purpose.
2. Or rather, as previously stated, because there is no such occasion [for them].
3. They consume the Soma from the *hotṛ*-cup.
"Stimulate my limbs, O Lord of the Bay Steeds; as one who is auspicious, take your station upon the seven Ṛṣis. Sit above my navel; do not go below my navel"—with these words they touch their limbs.
(4) With the two verses beginning "Swell up," they touch the cups.
(5) Or they pour Soma [into the cups] with the mantra, because [the cups] cannot [otherwise] come into being. (6)
He places those cups, which do not contain all [the Soma],
behind the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart;
these are the *nārāśaṃsa* cups until the *vaiśvadeva* offering.
Taking a fragment of the *puroḍāśa* cake and saying, "We have been invited," he stands up.
(10) Handing this over to the *acchāvāka*, he says, "O *acchāvāka*, speak what you have to say.
(11) When [the *acchāvāka*] says, "Come to us," he says to the *hotṛ*: "This Brahmin desires an invitation; O *hotṛ*, invite him. (12)
When [the cup] is being filled, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite the invitatory formula (*upahūta*). 13.
He fills the *acchāvāka*’s cup, doing everything as in the case of the *hotṛ*’s cup. 14–15.
Having performed [the rites] up until the placing [of the cups]. 15.
And to the east of the Āgnīdhra fire-altar (16),
the officiating priests of the Haviryajña consume the *iḍā* in the Āgnīdhra shed (17),
as does the wife in another hall (18).

When the Acchāvāka has sat down, they proceed with the Ṛtu-grahas from the Droṇakalaśa, [with the formulas] "Thou art taken with a support; for Madhu thee," and so on, twelve times with a separate mantra for each.
Of these, the first mantra belongs to the Adhvaryu.
Each subsequent [cup] belongs to the Pratiprasthātṛ;
they should take the first two simultaneously and the last two alternately, with the performance of all occurring in the middle.
One goes out while the other enters.
The Pratiprasthātṛ is each time subsequent because it occurs at a later time;
he grasps the Adhvaryu on both sides with the vessel;
[the offerings] are all burnt except for those prior to the last two.
With "By the season," he sends forth six;
with "By the seasons," he turns over four at the mouth of the vessel; the last two are pronounced six times.
When the sacrificer has been prompted, he should say, "O Hotṛ, recite the offering-verse for this! (12).
Both Adhvaryus [should do so] (13).
If he so desires, he should draw the thirteenth cup with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; for Aṃhasaspati, thee! (14).
He offers following the Pratiprasthātṛ.

Having placed the remnants in either one [of the vessels], he draws the draught for Indra and Agni with the formula "For Indra and Agni," and the Pratiprasthātṛ draws [the draught] for Indra and Agni.
He brings the portion for consumption to the Hotṛ, Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, Agnīdh, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and Praśāstṛ.
The vessels of the Hotṛ, Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Acchāvāka are to be exchanged [with those of the Adhvaryu].
(18) It is as stated [in the rule] for the Hotṛ, due to his connection with the sacrificer, like the act of choosing. (19) Or, the Hotṛ’s consumption [of the Soma] is due to a specific cause. (20)

The obstruction [of the offering] is due to non-attainment (21). By reversing [the order], the vessel belongs to the Hotṛ; there is a double consumption (22), or rather, it is so because of the previous [view] that all has been offered (23).
Having taken down the vessel, he sits facing east in front of the Hotṛ.
When the [verse] has been recited, he turns around and responds with "Śauṃsāva" and then with "Othāmo daiva," using the syllable Om at the beginning and at the end.
Or he may simply say "Om."
At the end of the *śastra*, [the word] "nityam" (always) [is used], or the word at the end of the speech comes first;
having taken up the cup for Indra-Agni and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "O reciter of the *uktha*, recite the offering prayer for the Soma! (29).
This is the command for those with weapons;
30 there is shaking of the *nārāśaṃsa* cups while the oblation is being offered;
31 if they have been set down, the offering belongs to the one with the weapon. 32

Having performed [the rites] from the consumption [of the remnants] up to the depositing [of the cups], he takes the Vaiśvadeva cup with the Śukra vessel from the Droṇakalaśa while [the Adhvaryu] is touched by [the sacrificer], with the verse: "O Viśve Devas... (RV 1.3.7). 1–2.
Having poured the *śukra* into the *pūtabhṛt* jar, he joins it with the strainer in the *droṇakalaśa*. 3.
He offers the *savanīya* oblations, beginning with the *paśupuroḍāśa*, excluding the *payasyā*.
4. He introduces the *stotra*, touching the cup with two blades of grass, saying, "Turn back! 5.
Thus, in all cases involving the *dhurya* [carts], (6) the *camasa* cups are for all-consumption; (7) the washing of the vessels takes place at the *mārjālīya* fire-altar. (8)
He draws the Ukthya cup in three portions with the formula, "For all the gods thee! (9); or, if for the Praśāstṛ, with "For Mitra and Varuṇa thee! (10);
the setting down is silent (11).
He begins the hymn of praise (stotra).
"O reciter of the Uktha, sacrifice the Soma-libations"—this is the call (praiṣa) when the Nārāśaṃsa cups have not been offered.
He draws the first cup for him whose portion is divided.
And he pours the remainder of the draught into this [cup];
15. In the same manner, the Pratiprasthātṛ [pours] with the next two [verses];
16. With "O Indra, that which... [he pours] for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; 17.
[The Adhvaryu] says, "For Indra and Agni, thee! for the Acchāvāka.
(18) The bringing down of the Soma occurs before the formal separation of the Acchāvāka.

(19) He pours half of the *vasatīvarī* waters into the *ādhavanīya* jar [with the formula]: "May the Viśve Devas, the Maruts, and Indra not abandon us at this second pressing; may we, long-lived and speaking what is pleasing to them, abide in the good favor of the gods. (20)
And [the fee] is one and a half *dhanas* (21).
When all have performed [the rite], the *praśāstṛ* should say, "May they move forward.
The moving forward of those who have been impelled; the moving forward of those who have been impelled. 23.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Kātīya Śrautasūtra: the midday pressing, beginning with the *sarpaṇa*. 1.
Having placed the *vasatīvarī* waters into the *hotṛ*-cup, he hands it to the sacrificer; he gives the turban to the *grāvastut*. 2.
From the *adrāya* onwards, he performs three rounds of pressing; he measures out what has been taken,
because there is no scriptural injunction regarding the shaking of the *upāṃśusavana* stone.
"ihā3 ihā3"— this is the first round (paryāya). 6.
The second [recitation] is without delay; the third is rapid.
(7) In the highest position of non-delay, [the syllables] "bṛhat bṛhat" [are recited]. (8) Or, it is half [a measure], because there is no specific instruction [to the contrary]. (9)
The drawing of the four cups beginning with the *śukra* is [performed] ten times;
the *āgrayaṇa* is from its own third streams. Prior to the *ukthya*, the *marutvatīya* cup is drawn with the *ṛtu-pātra* using the formula, "O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts."
Some perform the subsequent rites, beginning with the departure while holding onto [the sacrificer], up until the call "O Āgnīdh, the fires! (13).
The introduction of the Pavamāna chant takes place in the Sadas (15).
And in every *ahargaṇa* sacrifice, excluding the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya*, [the rule applies]. 16.
Having drawn back the call "Obeisance to the animal," there is an addition to the *praiṣa* formulas: "Bring curds for the *dadhigharma*; bring the sacrificial fees. 17.
The *dadhigharma* occurs when the *pravargya* rite is performed. 18.
Having sat down in front of the assembly, he takes the portion as prescribed in the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle which contains the *pavitra* strainer.

(19) He says, "O Hotṛ, speak what is to be recited by you. At the end of the recitation, while rising, he says, "The oblation is cooked. (20) He issues the command: "Recite the offering prayer for the *dadhigharma*. (21)
The officiating priests, together with the sacrificer, consume the remains of the oblation (hutaśeṣa) by calling out to one another as prescribed.
Or, those who have not been initiated (adīkṣita) consume it by taking a sip (prāṇabhakṣa).
Having performed the ritual with the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa), he proceeds with the cake-offerings and so forth until the placement of the hearths (dhiṣṇya).
From the time they are being carried forward until the placing of the water for rinsing, he pours out ten [measures] at each stage. He gives the command:
"O Hotṛ, recite the invitatory verse for the Soma juices set forth for Indra—the Soma juices belonging to the Niṣkevalya portion of the midday pressing, which are bright and dripping with sweetness."

Or, at the place of the *madhuścut* [cup] with the formula "O you who possess the churning-stick" (Manthīvataḥ), having partaken of the *iḍā*, he performs the *dākṣiṇa-homa* at the door of the hall; having placed gold tied in a cloth into the *havanī* ladle, he offers four spoonfuls with the verse "Upwards that [sun]" (Ud u tyam);
the second offering is with the verse "The bright [face] of the gods" (Citraṃ devānām).
At the Āgnīdhrīya fire, [he recites] "O Agni, lead us... (RV 1.189.1). If he should give another horse—whether yoked or unyoked—with the words "Come here" (RV 1.35.2), he gives a garment and gold.

The sacrificer, accompanied by gold, standing to the east of the hall, consecrates it with the mantra "By form... (TS 1.7.6). Standing to the south outside the altar, he addresses the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇās*) as they stand to the south with the mantra "By form... (TS 1.7.6). He passes beyond a hundred cows or twelve.
There are also the stirred-rice (*mantha*), boiled rice (*odana*), sesame, and beans.
Between the hall and the *sadas*, by way of the southern *āgnīdhra* passage,
he either sends forth the *subrahmaṇyā* call or follows after the one pressing the Soma from the *āgnīdhra*.
Before the recitation, he goes to the *sadas* with the verse "vi svah" (15);
he looks at the members of the *sadas* with the words "yatasva sadasyaiḥ" (16). (17)
Having approached the Āgnīdhra fire with the verse beginning "O Brahmin, today," he sits down;
he gives him gold with the words, "May we be yours" (asmadrā tā).

And to an Ātreya who has sat down to the east of the Sadas, like the Āgnīdhra, having said three times, "Who is the Ātreya? Who is the Ātreya? he then says once, "The Mahāleya, the Avāleya, the Akauḍeya, the Aśaubhreya, the Avārathya, and the Agaupavana."
He gives sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests; 21.
either separately by hundreds according to the distinction of persons, 22. or rather there is a distribution [of the total] because the action is the primary factor. 23.
According to the commencement [of the recitation], twelve [verses] are for the first [groups], six each for the second, four each for the third, and three each for the others (24).
For the Brahman, Udgātṛ, and Hotṛ (25),
and for the two Adhvaryus seated at the Havirdhāna shed (26).
"O Agni, for you," with these words he receives gold;
"O Rudras, for you," a cow; "O Bṛhaspati, for you," a garment; "O Yama, for you," a horse.
"Who has given?"—this applies to all other [gifts]. 27–29.

If he so desires, he may recite the mantra for the Prastotṛ, Praśāstṛ, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, Acchāvāka, Unnetṛ, Grāvastut, and Subrahmaṇya (31). And [he may do so] for others who have entered [the sacrificial ground], with the exception of the Kaṇvas, the Kaśyapas, and those who are begging (32).
One should not give silver to a kinsman who is not a Śrotriya on the sacrificial grass (barhis), for there is a Vedic revelation stating: "Before a year has passed, they weep in his house.
And the wife also gives [the gift].
Having given to all, he afterwards causes the Pratihartṛ to recite the verses beginning with "indrā yāhi" for Indra accompanied by the Maruts,
and [the verses] beginning with "adānamataḥ."
The drawing of the Marutvatīya cup is performed with the Ṛtupātra vessel [using the formula]: "Thou art taken with a support; thee for the vigor of the Maruts.
(3) He offers following the Adhvaryu.
(4) But when there is a Śastra, it is done according to the sequence of the ritual order. (5)
And because of the third [Vedic] revelation, the Marutvatīya cup is drawn by the Vaśin; [the formula is] "him who possesses the Maruts" (marutvantam).
When the vessel has been removed, the Hotṛ recites the Śastra.
At the verse "janiṣṭhā ugra," the response is "madāmo daiva" once;
this applies in place [of the usual response] during a modification (vikṛti).
Having performed [the rites] up to the placing [of the cup], he draws the Māhendra cup with the formula "māhām̐ indra," as in the case of the Vaiśvadeva.

Having poured the *śukra* into the *pūtabhṛt* vessel and having brought forward the back [of the cart], he gives the command: "Pressers, press! Raise up the mortars! O Āgnīdh, mix the *āśira*! Be mindful of the Soma-offering! 12.
