They press the stalk mixed with the dregs (*ṛjīṣa*), however it may be, even without water. 13. He places it in the *ādhavanīya* vessel. 14.
Or rather, it is [performed] with three turnings because of the instruction for pressing;
because [the act] has already been performed except for the touching of the sun;
and because there is no *śukra* [cup], the purifying [act] begins from the *pūtabhṛt* [vessel].
While the pitcher is being praised, the placing of the *ārjīṣa* [is performed] (18).
The *savanīya* sacrificial cakes are prepared (19).
The *saumya* pap and the one-pot-sherd cake for Varuṇa are additional (20).
Having performed [the rites] up to the washing of the vessels, he draws the Ukthya cup as before with the formula, "O Indra, for thee... for all [the deities].

(21) He pours in the Vasatīvarī waters with the verse: "This is the third pressing of the sages, those who prepared the cup of Ṛta; may those sons of Sudhanvan, having attained heaven, lead our well-offered sacrifice toward greater prosperity. (22) And [he pours in] the remainder of the Ekadhana waters. (23)
The sacrifice comes to its conclusion. 24.
"Come, O sacrificer," he says; the Adhvaryu, the Yajamāna, the Pratiprasthātṛ, the Āgnīdhra, and the Unnetṛ enter the Havirdhāna shed, and the wife follows behind them. 2.

With the door [of the Āditya-vessel] covered, having taken the Āditya-vessel and the residues (saṃsrava) over the *pūtabhṛt* jar, he then draws the Āditya cup from the residues with the verse, "kadā cana.
3. Having set it aside, again with "kadā cana. 4. He mixes it with curds at the western end or in the middle with the verse, "yajño devānām. 5.

He mixes it with the Upāṃśusavana stone, saying, "O Vivasvat Āditya! (6). He hands the Upāṃśusavana stone to the Unnetṛ and says, "Release the pressing-stones! (7). Having placed the pressing-stones in the Ādhavanīya vessel or in a cup containing Soma, he sets them down in their place. (8)

When he is stepping out through the open door, having covered the cup with his hand or with a vessel, [the Adhvaryu], while being touched by [the sacrificer], says, "Recite for the Ādityas. At either the *praisha* or the recitation, he says: "To the dear ones, whose abodes are dear, whose vows are dear, the lords of the great dwelling, the overseers of the wide mid-region.
Having offered, he hands over the two remnants to the Pratiprasthātṛ.
In this context, the gliding of the Āditya cup [takes place] before the third pressing, according to the scriptural injunction;
having taken the Āgrayaṇa vessel, he pours it into the *pavitra* over the *pūtabhṛt* vessel,
and the Pratiprasthātṛ likewise pours the two residues.
From the Ādhavanīya jar, the Unnetṛ draws [the Soma] with a dipping-spoon or a cup;
from there he takes the Āgrayaṇa draught,
and the Ukthya draught with one [verse] for each of the subsequent ones.

He pours the *āśira* mixture into the *pūtabhṛt* vessel with the mantra: "May the *āśira* grant me vigor, good progeny, food, wealth, and splendor; may I, O Indra, conquering lands by force, bring low my rivals. (6) The wife gazes at it with the verse, "Faith in him, O men...
(7) He performs the rites beginning with the exit while they hold onto each other, as at the midday pressing. (8)
In the animal sacrifice, at the place where the call for agreement is normally made, one says, "O Agnīdh, give the call! (paśau saṃvadasva).

From the beginning of the morning pressing until the point of the formal agreement, according to the scriptural injunction, having performed the rites from the instruction of the *śamitṛ* up to the end of the *iḍā*, and from the cake (*puroḍāśa*) onwards until the consumption of the *iḍā*, [the distribution] is done by means of the *camasa* cups alone.

Having taken up the Hotṛ’s cup and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the Somas belonging to the third pressing, accompanied by the Ṛbhus, the Vibhus, the Vājins, Bṛhaspati, and the Viśve Devas—sharp, mixed with milk, and presented for Indra. The term "mixed with milk" (*āśīrvataḥ*) is used in place of "pure" (*śukra*). Before the consumption of the *iḍā*, they pour into their respective cups from the *havirdhāna* cart portions the size of sacrificial cakes, without water; the rites beginning with the offering and ending before the smelling are performed as in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.
Or rather, [the offering is] for the ancestors of the sacrificer, because they have the right to its fruit (15).

Having consumed the *iḍā*, at the appropriate time, he takes the *sāvitra* cup with either one of the two vessels used for the *upāṃśu* and *antaryāma* offerings, saying "The desirable today... (16); with the other vessel, he takes the *pātnīvata* cup;
he causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse for the god Savitṛ (1).
2. While [the cup] has not yet been consumed, the Hotṛ recites the formula for the drawing of the Mahāvaiśvadeva: "Thou art taken with a support; thou art a good refuge. 3.
While the verse beginning with "With one and with ten" is being recited, the Pratiprasthātṛ washes the cups dedicated to two deities and places them on the mound (khara).
4. While the verse beginning with "With one and with ten" is being recited, the Pratiprasthātṛ washes the cups dedicated to two deities and places them on the mound (khara).
In the verses beginning with *pradyāvā yajñaiḥ*, the response is threefold: *madāmo daiva*.
If he desires it, [he recites] the *svāduṣkīlīyā* verses.
Having performed [the rites] up to the washing of the vessels, he proceeds with the Soma offering.
He performs the enclosing oblations on both sides with clarified butter,
or on one side only;
he says, "Sacrifice with ghee," pronouncing the word "ghee" in a low voice (upāṃśu).

He proceeds with the *saumya* offering while saying, "Sacrifice for the *saumya*. (11) This continues as long as prescribed for the *saumya*, because of the repetition of the term "*saumya*" [in the text].

(12) Having poured clarified butter, he hands the *saumya* portion to the Udgātṛ. With four spoonfuls taken by means of the *pracaraṇī* ladle, he offers oblations upon the *dhiṣṇya* hearths according to how they were assigned, kindling the fire-sticks (*śālākā*) and reciting the formulas one by one, beginning with "Thou art the pervasive one" (*vibhūr asi*). (13)
Desiring [to perform] again at the Āgnīdhrīya fire, he proceeds from the west;
the Pratiprasthātṛ draws the Pātnīvata cup with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; of thee, pressed by Bṛhaspati...
He mixes it with the remnant of the *pracaraṇī* ladle with the formula: "This one I [place] beyond..."
"O Agnīdh, recite the offering prayer for the Pātnīvata," he says.
"O Agni, accompanied by the wives," he offers on the northern half [of the altar].

And he sends forth [the command]: "Sit upon the lap of the Neṣṭṛ; O Neṣṭṛ, lead up the wife and have her look at the Udgātṛ; O Unnetṛ, pour out [the Soma] following the Hotṛ’s cup, so that the Soma does not remain in excess.
19. In the Ukthya and subsequent rites, [he says] "Make it manifest. 20. The consumption [of the Soma] takes place in the Āgnīdhra fire-shed by means of the Vaṣaṭ-call and the invitation. 21.
He places the vessel on the lap of the Neṣṭṛ;
or rather, the consumption [of the contents] takes place there, because of the functional requirement of bringing the vessel [to that spot].
Having washed the vessel, the Agnīdh places it upon the mound (khara).

He introduces the Yajñāyajñiya stotra, touching the Hotṛ’s cup. If he chooses, he covers himself as the Udgātṛ does. Having caused the wife to enter the Sadas, he makes her look at the Udgātṛ while she is seated to the west, to the north, with the formula: "Prajāpati, you are the bull."
He sprinkles [the sacrificer] with the *pānnejanī* waters while exposing his right thigh.
He proceeds either after being permitted by the *udgātṛ* or after being looked at by him three times.
While the verse "evā na indro maghava" is being recited, he pours the *dhruva* [draught] into the *hotṛ*'s cup with the formula, "The *dhruva* with the *dhruva*."

If [the cup] has been drawn for the sacrificer, one should say "I take" at the place where one would otherwise say "I pour down"; [this applies] to Vaiśvānara. At the end of the washing of the vessels, the after-offerings (anuyāja) begin with the fuel-stick (samid).

The mention of the Ukthya [cup] applies to the subsequent [rituals]: "To Indra and Varuṇa," "To Indra and Bṛhaspati," and "To Indra and Viṣṇu. If there is a Ṣoḍaśin cup, the Stotra and Śastra are added. At the third pressing, there is the Prasava [permission].

"The lifting of the *sruva* ladle for Agni, for Vanaspati, for Indra accompanied by the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Ṛbhus, the Vibhus, the Vājins, Bṛhaspati, and the Viśvedevas; [the offering] of Soma as the conqueror. "May Agni, Vanaspati, Indra with the Vasus, with the Rudras, with the Ādityas, with the Ṛbhus, with the Vibhus, with the Vājins, with Bṛhaspati, with the Viśvedevas, and Soma as the conqueror, eat it.

(13) [The offering] is for the animal deities and for Vanaspati, or for the others because of the mention of Soma. (14) Or rather, all [are included] because of the presence of the *savanīya* and the *saumya* offerings. (15)
Having set aside the two offering-ladles, he takes the Hāriyojana draught from the Droṇakalaśa with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; thou art the tawny one. 1.
Dhātṛ pours in the parched grains with the formula: "The grains for the two tawny ones. 2.
The Unnetṛ, having placed them on his head, causes [the Hotṛ] to recite: "Recite the invitatory verse for the grains and Soma! 3.
Having caused the announcement to be made, he says, "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the *dhānās* and *soma*s that have been set forth.
If he so desires, he may take a portion;
or, having placed them on the *uttaravedi*, he may distribute them as he pleases.
Having consumed the *prāṇabhakṣa* portion with the verse, "He who is the gatherer of horses," they pour it out upon the *uttaravedi*.
(7) They place the wooden splinters with the respective formulas, "Of that which is made by the gods," and so forth.

(8) To the west of the *cātvāla*, they touch the *camasa* cups and the full vessels, each according to its own [deity], after having placed green *kuśa* grass within them, with the formula, "With luster. (9)
They touch their faces. 10.
At the Āgnīdhra fire, they consume the curds with the verse, "O Dadhikrāvan... 11.
The Patnīsaṃyāja offerings are performed as at the animal sacrifice. 12.
With the nine verses beginning "sam indra naḥ," he offers the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations, one with each mantra (13).
He carries the *audumbarī* post and the *āsandī* seat to the *cātvāla* pit. He also carries that which has been smeared with Soma (14).
He throws the black antelope horn and the girdle into the *cātvāla* pit with the formula, "May I not become a serpent" (15).
The Pratiprasthātṛ [places] the peg and the yoke-thong silently (16).
He causes the sacrificer to recite, "Wide indeed...
(17). He gives the command for the Sāman, saying either, "Sing! or "Recite! (18).
And at the end of the journey and at the edge of the water, all reach their end;
taking what has been brought, they go to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha); among the flowing waters, the stationary ones [prevail]. 19–21.
In the absence of that, [he offers] other [oblations]. 22.
Saying "Obeisance to Varuṇa," he causes [the student] to recite while making him step into the water. 23.
Having thrown a fuel-stick [into the fire], he makes an offering over it with four ladlings [of ghee], [reciting] "The face of Agni... 24.
With another [formula], he offers the prayājas, excluding the barhis; 25.
he offers them into the waters; 26. "They proceed with the offering after having taken portions from the cake on one potsherd," so it is said. 27.
Desiring the *ṛjīṣa*, he should offer the remainder as a complete oblation (*sarvahuta*) to Agni and Varuṇa (28).
And [he should offer] the *ṛjīṣa* once, if [the previous offerings] were performed first (29).
He should perform this [rite] when the *vaśa* [verse] occurs (30).

When the sacrificer has spoken, the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are performed, as well as the *anuyāja*s excluding the *barhis*; having performed either one [of these], he causes the *ṛjīṣa*-jar to float with the verse, "In the ocean, O ye... (samudre ta iti). 1.
Having released [the water] with the words, "O divine waters," he stands near [it].
With the word, "Ablution," he causes [himself] to be immersed.
And ending with the black antelope skin, [he recites]: "O Indra, do not deprive me of my preeminence and excellence! 4.
Having given this to his son, [the ritual] proceeds from the bath onwards up to the placing of the fuel-sticks, just as in the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifice;
he throws in the Soma-residue;
there is no giving in the case of the two preceding sacrifices.

The Unnetṛ, having drawn the water with the verse, "Upwards we two," they proceed while muttering the Āmahīya hymns: "We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal; we have reached the light, we have found the gods. What now can the enemy do to us? What, O Immortal One, can the malice of a mortal? (RV 8.48.3).

The sacrificer stands behind the door of the hall, holding a black antelope skin on his lap. He offers a spoonful with the mantra: "O Indra, may Agni bestow upon me preeminence and excellence, svāhā! (TS 2.6.7.5).
Having set aside the black antelope skin, the Udayanīyā offering is performed as at the Prāyaṇīyā.
The *pathyā-svasti* formula is the fourth [offering]. 11.

From the sprinkling of the vessels up to the placing of the clarified butter (*ājya*), it is like the *savanīya* animal sacrifice; from the girding of the sacrificial post onwards, there is the *vaśā* cow for Mitra and Varuṇa as the *anūbandhyā*. 12.
Or rather, [the ritual] begins with the concealment of the *svaru* because [the previous acts] have already been performed. 13.
In the absence of a barren cow, a bull [is offered]; 14. in the absence of both, curdled milk (payasyā) [is offered]. 15.
Having placed it [on the altar], some [perform the rite] starting from the two butter-portions (ājyabhāga) and ending with the iḍā; 16.

The Udavasānīyā offering consists of a cake on five potsherds for Agni, performed with fire that has been rekindled from the kindling-wood already mounted upon the fire-drills. Gold is the sacrificial fee, or alternatively, a draft-ox. Or else, the oblation is performed according to the ritual procedure for animal sacrifices.
At the end of that [rite], there is the evening oblation (20).
It is a subsidiary part of the Soma sacrifice, because of proximity and because of contradiction [otherwise] (21).
Or rather, the morning oblation is obligatory, because of the Vedic revelation (22).
Therefore, their actions are restricted (23).
This is the first Soma (24). Having been kindled, they enter (25).
In the *Ṣaḍuttara* sacrifice, there are the Agniṣṭoma, Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśī, Vājapeya, Atirātra, and Aptoryāma.
(26) Among these, the Ukthya concludes with the Acchāvāka cup; the others conclude with the Hotṛ cup.
(27) For a Vaiśya or a Rājanya performing the Soma sacrifice, one who desires [to obtain] the portions for consumption should tie on shoots of the Nyagrodha tree. (28)
Beginning from the purchase [of Soma], one proceeds with the Soma ritual; the procedure up to the placing [of the vessels] is the same as before the pressing.
At the time of drawing the cups, having brought [the curds] and stirred them with curds, one should draw that cup following [the others].
While the oblations are being offered, one offers with a young blade of Kuśa grass, saying "I am you," "I am you."
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Kātīya Śrautasūtra; hereafter follows the office of the Brahman priest: (1) he remains silent while the ritual action is being performed. (2)
When the *hiraṇyavatī* has been offered, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) follows [the sacrificer] until the purchase [of the Soma].
Once it has been purchased, having passed to the east and having gone around the cart either by the front or by the rear, it follows [the sacrificer] to the south until the placement [of the Soma].
Or, in the case of the *gharma* vessel, it follows behind the *dakṣiṇāgni*.
He will carry away the *stambayajus*; he sits to the south of the Āhavanīya fire together with the altar (*vedi*).
Thus it is everywhere prior to the leading forward of Agni and Soma; or rather, he follows each respective rite accompanied by the altar.
While the Āhavanīya fire is being carried forward, he recites the twelve verses of the Apratiratha hymn over the fire; according to some teachers, this is done in all cases.
Having approached the strewn altar as required, [he performs the rites].
For the purpose of leading forward Agni and Soma, he sits to the south, having gone around the *dhiṣṇya* hearths by the north and the hall-door by the east.
(12) Once the oblation has been offered, he takes the Soma and follows after the fire;
or the sacrificer himself may carry the Soma. (13–14)
Having given it to another and not having placed it down, he returns by the same way he came and sits to the south (15).
When the oblation has been offered, he takes up the Soma and, passing beyond the Āhavanīya fire (16),
he desires to proceed with the carrying forward of Agni and Soma as in the latter part of the night (17).
Having performed the oblation of the droplets, the Pratihartr should touch the Adīkṣita (the uninitiated). 18.
Addressed by the Prastotr, having said, "O God Savitr, this is for you; [I have] praised; at the impulse of Savitr," he gives the impulse. 19.
[He says] either, "O God Savitr, O Bṛhaspati, go forth! 20.
Or, [he should do so] with each mantra individually, beginning with "With the ray, for truth" (TS 1.4.25). 21.
The crawling [of the horse] takes place in that direction by which it was led in. 22.
Having gone around the sacrificial post from the east, [he should do so] if [the horse was led] from the west. 23.
He sits to the south of the *praśāstṛ*;
the others sit behind the *dhiṣṇya* hearths,
including the *neṣṭṛ*.
The *viṣaṃsthitasacvara* [chanting] proceeds either to the north of the *praśāstṛ*'s seat or to that of the *apavamāna*;
each of the others [proceeds] to their respective [seats]. Thus ends the eleventh chapter of the Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra.
The properties of the Jyotiṣṭoma [apply] to the Ekāha and Dvādaśāha sacrifices because those qualities are observed in them;
[they apply] to the first [of the Ahīnas] because of a scriptural statement regarding the Vrātyastoma, Sadyaskra, and others;
and according to some, also to the Agniṣṭut sacrifices.

The twelve-day rite is both a *sattra* and an *ahīna*. "They sit" (*āsate*) and "they enter upon" (*upayanti*) are the characteristic marks of a *sattra*; "he sacrifices" (*yajate*) is the mark of an *ahīna*.
A *sattra* has an *atirātra* on both sides; an *ahīna* has it only at the end.
All those performing the sacrifice in *satras* [are sacrificers],
because there is no sacrificial fee (*adakṣiṇāni*) due to their connection with the master;
and the householder is [the sacrificer] because he is joined with the act of sacrificing.
And because of being seen (11),
because all [are] conditioned (12),
and because of the statement regarding seeing (13).
The Gṛhapati performs the anvārambha (touching) for all;
for when it is for the sake of others, he does it alone because it has already been performed [by him].
When about to establish the fires, the Gṛhapati, having consigned the fires [into his own], churns them in the middle, while the others do so half by half to the south and north.

17. The casting away of the embers takes place at the Gṛhapati’s Āhavanīya fire. 18. There, the animal sacrifice belongs to Prajāpati. 19. The Patnīsaṃyāja offerings are performed with clarified butter, excluding the Gṛhapati.
On that day, the initiation (dīkṣā) [is performed]; 20.

in case of inability, there is the performance of the prescribed rites; 21. in all cases where [the fire] has been kindled and maintained; 22. at the time of initiation, the churning is performed as before in a fire-wood [structure] facing north.
The throwing [of the grass] takes place here at the Gārhapatya fire (23);
from there, the Āhavanīya fire [is established] (24); therein, the initiation (dīkṣā) [takes place] (25).

From the day of the Upavasatha until the carrying forward of the Agni and Soma, having extinguished them, he piles these [fires] from the *śālādvārya* fire-altar toward the south and north, according to the scriptural injunction regarding the *dhiṣṇya* hearths (27),
or as stated for the *gṛhapati*’s fire (28). When the Āgnīdhrīya fire is lifted, they carry a single ember each from the *śālādvārya* fire for every subsequent piling (1).
The sacrificial cakes for the *savanīya* offerings are placed toward the fire, so that there may be a greater remnant of the oblation at the conclusion, according to the Śruti; 2.
and the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are performed as before; 3.
or, having sat down around the *gṛhapati*, they churn [the fire]. 4.
The householder is the first; he is the first in every respect.
As each [oblation] is produced, the householder throws it into the Gārhapatya fire in both cases.
From the Upavasatha day onwards, the procedure is the same for all.

Regarding the two kindling woods (*araṇi*), they say: "The fire which shall be born from here for the householder—may that be common to us. Whatever we shall win by this sacrifice, whatever by this animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*)—may that be common to us. Common to us be our good deeds; separate be our evil deeds. Whosoever shall do evil, let that belong to him alone. Having said this, the householder first consigns his own fires into them, or the others according to their respective [fires]. At the time of initiation, beginning with the dialogue, [the procedure] is the same as for a sacrificial session (*sattra*) in place of the animal sacrifice.
On the best day, which lasts for one day, there are the *śālā*, the *gārhapatya*, the *puroḍāśa*, and the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.

(11) In the rites involving a single *puroḍāśa*, since the *vratya* offering is impossible, one should offer either a five-portioned mess of boiled rice (*pañcaśarāva odana*) or a *puroḍāśa*, according to the scriptural injunction: "If they prepare it as boiled rice, or if they prepare it as a cake. (12) Some authorities prescribe an offering to Bṛhaspati. (13)

There are the initiation (dīkṣā) and the twelve Upasad days. 14. The Adhvaryu initiates the Gṛhapati; the Pratiprasthātṛ initiates the Brahmā and the others, as well as the Adhvaryu and the others; the Neṣṭṛ initiates the Pratiprasthātṛ and the others; the Unnetṛ initiates the Neṣṭṛ and the others; and the Brahmacārī, the Snātaka, or another Brāhmaṇa who is not yet purified, should initiate [the Unnetṛ], according to the Śruti: "One who is not pure should not purify. 15.
The wives follow in succession, each one after the other. 16.

These very [priests] of the *unnetṛ* shake their black antelope skins at the time of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and go along the southern path, saying: "That which has gone away from me while I was free from disease—that I lead back to you as a fee, O one free from disease. "Here I lead this [person], the son of such-and-such, the grandson of such-and-such, for the sake of desire, as a sacrificial fee.
The first [six-day period] is the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*, the fourth is an *agniṣṭoma*, and the others are *ṣoḍaśin* and *ukthya* sacrifices.
In that regard, the taking of the *atigrāhya* cups occurs on the third day; [one cup] on each successive day for three days (1);
or on the last two days (2); or on both the last two days (3); or on both the first and last days (4).
The *māhendra* *manu-homa* is performed five times.
The consumption [of the remnant] by the sacrificers is done with the formulas: "O Agni, full of splendor," "O Indra, most victorious," and "O Sūrya, most radiant.
At the time of the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra], the moving of the chariot takes place; on the first day, it is to the south of the altar.
In the second [round], the introductory rite is performed with the sound of a drum;
in the third, with fans;
in the fourth, there is churning with the two fire-drills and an oblation on the thigh of the Udgātṛ.
In the fifth [chapter], the disciples [are described].
In the sixth: 11. By one who lives in a common household;
12. Having united the calves with their mothers, they turn them away from the *sadas* to the east.

"Yoke for yourselves today the chariot that comes hitherward, worthy of being approached, drawn by men; perform the unyoking here for both of you, and mix the oblations with honey. For indeed, having come, drink the Soma, O ye who possess abundant wealth.
(14) The response of the Hotṛ is the *pratigara*.
(15) And it is the original form (*prākṛta*), because the others serve a different purpose. (16)

At the end of the six-day period, one should not speak much; one should not question another, nor should one answer another. (17) There is the tasting of honey or of clarified butter. (18) The three Chandomas follow as the latter Ukthyas. (19)

The Attyagniṣṭoma and the Avivākya are the tenth [day]. (20) The days end with the Patnīsaṃyājas, except for the final one. (21) Each [priest], restraining his speech, guards the Soma until the awakening. (1)
Or [the rule] beginning with the setting aside of the *vasatīvarī* waters;
2. the others are dismissed for the sake of Vedic study or for the sake of the sacrificial fuel-sticks; 3. even there, eating [is permitted]. 4.
Or rather, [the fire] is established on the tenth day because of its proximity (sannidhi).

5. After sunset, the placing of fuel-sticks (samid-ādhāna) is performed for all [fires]. 6. On the tenth day, in the afternoon, having touched water, there is the entry into the hall (śālā-praveśana). 7.
While those at the door of the hall hold on [to him], he offers an oblation with the verse, "May there be delight here.

[With the verse] beginning, "Releasing the other [mare]," he moves around by the north, enters behind the two *havirdhāna* carts, and, touching the rear pole of the northern *havirdhāna*, they sing the *sattrasyarddhi* chant: "The prosperity of the *sattra*. Thus [they chant] "The prosperity of the *sattra*. 8–10.
Either at the western corner of the *uttaravedi* or on its northern side, they go out toward the east along the bottom of the southern axle with the verse, "You two [O Aśvins]... (RV 8.73.2).

He draws the cup for Prajāpati; the drawing, the setting down, the commencement of the *stotra*, the *āghāra* oblation, the eating, the bringing back, and the consumption are all performed mentally. The vessel used is that of Vāyu, and the vessel for the earth is used as the means of drawing.

The explanation of the Caturhotṛ formulas belongs to the Hotṛ (14). The Gṛhapati says, "He has known" (15). He responds, "These sacrificers have succeeded; it has become auspicious for these sacrificers" (16).
They recite a theological discourse (brahmodya) [17],
the narrative of Prajāpati’s lack of qualities [18],
or that discussion in the case of a lack of ready wit [19].
Or [they perform] the rite named Āśvamedhika. 20. Before sunset, having taken up a staff made of Udumbara wood, they restrain their speech. 21.
After sunset, having gone out, they sit behind the Uttaravedi; the Pratiprasthātṛ carries around the Vasatīvarī waters. 22.
The release of speech is for one desiring a sacrificial session (sattra);
for those with separate desires, it is "bhūr bhuvaḥ.
The Subrahmaṇyā invocation belongs to the Gṛhapati, or rather, [it is addressed] to whichever one is the Gṛhapati.

"O Indra, the fourth" (24);
"Belonging to Agni" (25).
An oblation of barley cooked in milk for Varuṇa (26);
likewise elsewhere (27);
and an oblation of Gavedhukā grass for Rudra (28).
The *vāhinī* offering to Indra and Dadhyañc (29);
that same sacrificial fee (30);
the *apāmārga* oblation (1).
Having placed *apāmārga* grains into a *sruva* ladle made of *palāśa* or *vikaṅkata* wood,
he offers them three times toward the fire in the directions as in the *tryambaka* rite,
or toward the east.
"O Agni, be victorious!"—with these words he takes up the firebrand (ulmuka).
"In the name of the god..."—with this formula he offers the oblation.

"In the name of the Rakṣases..."—with this formula he throws the offering-spoon (sruva) toward that direction in which he has offered. Saying, "We have struck down the Rakṣas," they return without looking back.

In the Triṣaṃyukta [sacrifices]: 8. the offering to Agni-Viṣṇu, the offering to Indra-Viṣṇu, and the offering to Viṣṇu; a dwarf (vāmana) is the sacrificial fee. 9. In cases where no specific mark is mentioned, a cow is used everywhere. 10.
The [sacrifices] for Agni and Pūṣan, for Indra and Pūṣan, and for Pūṣan; a dark-grey animal is the sacrificial fee. 11.
[The sacrifices] for Agni and Soma, for Indra and Soma, and for Soma; a brown animal is the sacrificial fee. 12.
The first [offering] is on eleven potsherds; the others are oblations of cooked grain (caru). 13.
On the first day, there is either an offering to Viṣṇu on three potsherds,
or on the second day, an offering to Vaiśvānara on twelve potsherds and one to Varuṇa within the same ritual framework; or on the second day, there is only one [offering].
A bull is the sacrificial fee for the first [offering]; a black garment for the second; in its absence, a non-black one. 17.
There are twelve additional Ratna-havīṃṣi (jewel-oblations), one for each house, day after day. 2.
For the fire produced by churning when it has been mounted [on the hearth], there is an offering for Anīkavant Agni;
3. a *caru* for Bṛhaspati is for the domestic priest; 4. one for Indra is for the sacrificer. 5.
For Aditi the queen 6;
for Varuṇa the charioteer 7; for the Maruts the village headman 8.
One for Savitṛ for the Kṣattṛ; one for the Aśvins for the Saṃgrahītṛ; one for Pūṣan for the Bhāgadugha.

The Raudra [offering] is from the axle, the footprints, and the house of the cow-slaughterer of the sacrificer; [it consists of] Gavedhuka seeds. He offers four ladlefuls with the mantra: "May he who enjoys the path of the clarified butter accept it"—this is for the messenger.

The Nairṛta [offering] is for Parivṛtti; [it consists of] black rice grains split by the nails. He performs a Darvihoma with the mantra: "This is for thee, O Nirṛti," or he offers at the utterance of Vaṣaṭ.

The sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) are, respectively: gold, a white-backed bull, a milch-cow, a horse, a speckled white ox, and a black ox born in succession to the one sacrificed for Yama; a black goat is the fee for the offering to Rudra; either a white-armed or white-tailed [animal] for the two [offerings]; a sword; a human skull; and a gambling board with dice bound by a tail-hair rope. 15–17.
For the northern [altar] as well, there is a bow encased in leather (18),
leathern quivers containing arrows (19),
and a red turban (20).

A black heifer is for the one whose best [cattle] have been stolen (21). He prescribes an exchange, saying, "Let her not stay among the cows of another" (22). Thereafter, there is a caru-oblation to Soma and Rudra, prepared in the milk of a white cow that has a white calf (23).
That same [fee] is the sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā).
24 Even one who has studied the Vedas may sacrifice if he is devoid of fame.
25 However, this applies when he is afflicted by the disease of leprosy (kilāsa). 26
There is a *caru* offering for Mitra and Bṛhaspati (maitrābārhaspatya).
Having placed the portion for Bṛhaspati on the fire, he covers it with a vessel made from a branch of the *aśvattha* tree that has broken off by itself toward the east or the north.
Having poured into that same vessel fresh butter produced spontaneously from the cream of curds collected from a chariot, he pours the largest grains of rice for Mitra.
It becomes cooked by heat (ūṣman). 30.
One offering is made in the other [vessel] after [the contents] have been reduced to the smallest amount. 31.
A cow is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 32.
The sacrificial grounds for the Abhiṣecanīya and the Daśapeya are the southern and northern [grounds] respectively;
the southern one belongs to the Abhiṣecanīya.
One undergoes initiation for the Abhiṣecanīya on the full-moon day of the fortnight of Phālguna.
The Bhārgava is the Hotṛ priest.
There are five sections. Having purchased the Soma and tied it in two bundles, having carried them around, he places one in the house of the Brahman priest.
Following the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, he offers the oblations to the Devasū deities with the appropriate *yajus* and *praisha* formulas:
five of the *plāśuka* (quick-growing) grains to Savitṛ, the one of true impulse;
five of the *āśu* (swift) grains to Agni Gṛhapati.
In the northern [quarter] are the cooked offerings: 7.
*śyāmāka* for Soma Vanaspati;
8. *naivāra* for Bṛhaspati Vāc.
To Indra, the lord of the years;
to Rudra, the lord of the cattle;
to Mitra, the true one, by name.

"To Varuṇa, the Lord of Dharma"— having performed [the rite] with this final [verse], he says, "Savitṛ [be] yours," and taking the right arm of the sacrificer, he pronounces his name in the mantra at the appropriate place. He also pronounces the names of the mother and father.
And because the king belongs to whichever [clan] he is born into (16), because of the instability of the country (17),
and because the ritual procedure for the animal-cake offering is primary (18).
Or rather, because of the greater number of the others;
and because of the scriptural mention of the Sviṣṭakṛt;
at the end of the Iḍā, he takes water.
Having gone to the north of the sacrificial post— since there is no possibility of [the other offerings] being occasional—
one performs the Sārasvata oblations separately in vessels made of Udumbara wood.
From a beast or a human who has plunged in and emerged, [the waters] flow forward and backward (26),
streaming forth (27), and moving against the current (28).
The rivers flow toward the lord of rivers (the ocean), like logs suddenly cast up by the current; they are to be settled there.
The stationary plants receive from the flowing waters as they are warmed by the sun; 33.
having received from the atmosphere the rain that falls during sunshine; 34. from the lake, from the well, and from the dew-drops, [they receive] honey, milk, and clarified butter. 35.
He takes up the Sarasvatī waters with the formula, "The waters, O gods... (RV 10.9.1).

He offers oblations with the subsequent verses; with the first four verses beginning with "vṛṣṇa ūrmyā" (VS 10.30–33), each ending in *svāhā*, he takes up the water four times for each respective mantra, and with the following verses he takes it up further.
With the verse, "The self-sovereign waters... (RV 10.9.2), he pours all of them together with his joined palms.
He pours them together into a vessel made of Udumbara wood with the verse, "These [waters] rich in honey...

(RV 1.23.16). He places them in front of the Maitrāvaruṇa’s hearth with the formula, "Sit down, unassailable ones! He also silently places the vessels—the footstools made of Palāśa, Udumbara, Nyagrodha, and Aśvattha wood—for the consecration.
Tomorrow there will be the Ukthya sacrifice.

A hundred thousand is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). At the end of the Marutvatīya offerings, he spreads a tiger skin to the east with the formula, "The splendor of Soma," and places lead at the western edge.
For the sons of Pṛthā, he offers six oblations with the formula "To Agni, svāhā! and so on, one for each mantra.
Having prepared two strainers, he fastens a piece of gold to them; with those two, he purifies the waters with the verse, "By the impulse of Savitṛ...
At the Abhiṣecanīya rites, he pours these [waters] together with the verse, "In the revelry..."
He causes him to put on a garment of fine silk, or one of linen, or one made of three strands.
Some [say] it is raised with ghee. He wears a garment of the form of the sacrifice, white and yellow.
Having fastened an upper garment and wrapped a turban around his head, he wears it either hanging down or encircling the region of the navel.

With the respective mantras, "The silken garment and so forth belong to the Kṣatriya," he discards the garments worn at the consecration because of their incompatibility; or alternatively, he puts them on again during the Mahendra and subsequent offerings after having set these aside.
With the mantra, "Indra’s weapon that slays Vṛtra," he strings the bow.
With the mantra "Of Mitra and Varuṇa," he rubs his two arms;
16 with "By you this [man]," he hands over the bow;
17 having taken up three arrows with the respective mantras beginning with "You are a restrainer," he hands them over with the respective mantras beginning with "Strike him. 18
He makes [the sacrificer] recite, "Manifest to the noble ones" (āvirmaryāḥ). 19.
He strikes with a piece of iron [the sacrificer] who is seated at the edge of the Sadas, saying, "Seized! (aveṣṭāḥ). 20.
Making him step toward the quarters, he makes him recite, "Ascend the eastern quarter," according to the respective indicative marks for each direction. 21.
Having stepped upon it with his foot, he pushes it away, saying, "It is cast out.
(22) He causes [the sacrificer] to mount the tiger skin, saying, "The splendor of Soma. (23) He places a gold disk beneath his foot, saying, "From death. (24)
And on the head, he [touches] the nine apertures or the hundred apertures with the mantra "Thou art vigor" (vāja asi).
25. He raises his arms with the mantra "Of golden form" (hiraṇyarūpāḥ). 26. Or [he raises them] with the mantra "Thou art Mitra, thou art Varuṇa" (mitro 'si varuṇo 'si). 27.

The domestic priest or the *adhvaryu* consecrates him while he stands facing the east. First, with a vessel made of *pālāśa* wood, and afterwards with the others; with the second [vessel] for the *svastr̥*, with the third for a *rājanya*, and with the fourth for a *vaiśya*. At each [verse], he recites the mantra: "With the splendor of Soma...
(VS 10.20), and everywhere adds "I consecrate thee," because the [mantras] are syntactically expectant.
And [he adds]: "Be thou the lord of kṣatriyas among kṣatriyas" (VS 10.21). 28–30.
With the formulas "imam amuṣya" and so forth, he performs the first [offering] as in the *devasū* sacrifice (31).
He offers six oblations with the formula "indrāya svāhā," reciting a separate mantra for each (32). And he issues the command regarding the *Śaunaḥśepa* [story] (1).
At the conclusion of the gambling match, "Oṃ" is the response for the Ṛg-verses, and likewise "Tathā" (so be it) for the Gāthās;
the Hotṛ and Adhvaryu priests sit upon two golden couches spread with woolen rugs.
At the conclusion of the Śaunaḥśepa [section], he gives separately one hundred or a thousand [cows] on the seat.
While scratching himself, he anoints [the boy] with the consecration water with the verse, "Upon the mountain...

(RV 10.73.6). He makes him step three times upon a hide with the mantra, "Of Viṣṇu... (RV 1.22.17), reciting a separate mantra for each step. Having poured the remaining water onto a Palāśa leaf, he gives it to his most beloved son, saying, "May my son continue this work of mine and this heroic power."

He offers at the door of the hall while his son holds on to him from behind; he pronounces the names of the son and the sacrificer with the verse beginning "O Prajāpati," having substituted the word "father" for "son," and subsequently [pronounces them] according to their respective order.
11. He offers the remnants with a Palāśa twig on the Āgnīdhrīya fire in the northern half with the verse "O Rudra, that which is thine...
12. He places a hundred cows or more to the north of his own Āhavanīya fire. 13.
He brings the chariot together with the eastern fire;
having brought it forth like the Vājapeya, he yokes it at the southern corner of the altar with the four verses beginning "For Mitra and Varuṇa," as before.
Having traveled by the southern path, he stops it to the west of the Cātvāla pit.
With the words, "For freedom from distress," the one pressing [the Soma] mounts [the cart].
17 With the words, "Of the Maruts," he drives out the right-hand draft-ox.
18 He stations it in the midst of the cows with the words, "Of waters. 19
The sacrificer touches the cow with the tip of the bowstring, saying, "May I win these [cows] together with my power" (TS 1.7.8.1).
He says, "I shall conquer these; I shall make these submissive.

Having given her back to the owner of the cows for as much or even more than that, he leads her around the sacrificial post by the east and stations her in the *antaḥpātya* region, saying, "May she not [injure] you" (TS 1.7.8.1).

He offers four oblations for unyoking the chariot with the formulas beginning "To Agni Gṛhapati," one with each mantra; he puts on a boar-skin shoe with the formula "Thou art the essence of cattle. He looks at the earth with the formula "O Mother Earth";
he descends [from the chariot] with the verse "The swan dwelling in purity."
Having unyoked the chariot with its driver, he places it on the chariot-stand; this is the action for the cart. To the south of the shed, the driver dismounts.
At the southern end of the chariot-stand, he fastens two hundred-measure coins (*śatamāna*) upon two circular objects.
He embraces an Udumbara branch along the path and touches it with the formula, "Thou art the atmosphere, a hundred measures.
Having given those two [cups] to the Brahman priest, he touches the branch with the formula, "Thou art vigor.
He draws out his two arms with the formula, "Of Indra, you two," while the Payasyā remains situated on the place of the tiger skin.
He gives him a bow with a golden arrow-head (seṣuka).
Having carried away the northern altar (uttaravedi), he proceeds with the curd-mixture (payasyā) prior to the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.
He places a stool made of Khadira wood upon the tiger-skin area with ropes, saying: "Thou art pleasant."
He spreads the upper garment over it with the formula, "The womb of sovereignty.
He makes the one pressing [the Soma] sit upon it with the formula, "Sit upon the pleasant seat.
With the formula, "He has sat down," he touches her breast.

Saying "The Conqueror," he places five dice in his hand; then they strike him gently and silently from behind with staffs of sacrificial wood, either saying, "We drive away your evil," or "I lead you beyond death. Having chosen a boon, he addresses the Brahman five times, saying, "O Brahman!"
He responds with the names in reverse order: "Savitṛ," "Varuṇa," "Indra," and "Rudra," using the formulas beginning with "You are the Brahman" (tvaṃ brahmāsi) and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the last name is included as well.
He calls him by his [actual] name, saying, "O you of such-and-such a name."
The domestic priest or the Adhvaryu hands him a wooden sword (*sphyam*), saying, "O Indra, this is thy thunderbolt.
The king, the king’s brother, either the charioteer or the carpenter, the village headman, and the kinsman—each preceding one [hands it] to the succeeding one.
Having been handed [the sword], the kinsman and the Pratiprasthātṛ, together with the eastern fire, prepare the gambling ground with the *śukrapuroruc* verse.
Having placed gold on the gambling ground at the place of the *manthin* cup, he makes an offering with four ladlings, saying, "Agni Pṛthu. He then pours down the dice, saying, "Consecrated by Svāhā!"
"Play for a cow," he says;
or one may stake [the cow] against those beginning with the Kṛta throw, starting from the Rāta throw;
[one should play] for a member of the same caste at the Kali throw.
Having brought a cow, they slaughter it;
the draft-ox for the eastern fire is the sacrificial fee;
he performs the *payasyā*, the *sviṣṭakṛt*, and the *iḍā* for the Mahendra cup as well.
Having descended, he goes forth, dispatched for the sake of praise (23).
With one [verse], [he performs] the avabhṛtha bath, provided there are garments such as the tārpya (24).
With one [verse], he emerges from the water (25).
And he throws away the garment worn during initiation (26).
He should give these [garments] either at the end of the offering of the omentum of the Anūbandhya victim (27),
or at the Udavasānīyā offering (28).
The *udavasānīyā* sacrifice consists of three oblations: a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Viṣṇu made of rice and barley;
the third [oblation] is of barley placed in the middle;
and there is also the act of placing it upon the fire.

He gives three sets of three sacrificial gifts: gold coins weighing a hundred mānas to the Brahman, cows to the Hotṛ, garments to the Adhvaryu, and a cow to the Agnīdh. (32) This same [offering] is also used for healing and for malevolent magic. (33) He offers ten successive oblations of the *saṃsṛp* sacrifices. (1)
He moves forward one step at a time until he reaches the edge of the sacrificial ground;
the final step is inside the hall.
The oblations for Savitṛ, Sarasvatī, Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, Indra, Bṛhaspati, Varuṇa, Agni, Soma, and Viṣṇu are performed as previously prescribed.
He offers lotuses,
or golden ones;
in the three highest [verses], five [are offered].
He fastens a garland upon them;
that constitutes their initiation (dīkṣā). The two rites share a single ritual procedure because the purchase (kraya) is one.
"Or rather, they are different, because of the scriptural texts concerning the *avabhṛtha* and the *dīkṣā* (11);
but there is one [set], because of the connection with the sequential order (12);
the repetition of the *avabhṛtha* and the *dīkṣā* is due to a specific injunction (13)."

On the seventh day, having brought Soma from the house of Brahmā, he performs the touching of the *āsandi* seat and so forth; he offers the oblations for the deities of the *upasad* rites and concludes the *upasad*s as previously prescribed (14).
Having counted the ten groups of ancestors who drink Soma, the *sarpaṇa* (creeping) takes place (15).
Or, having recited the section beginning with "O Savitṛ" (16).
Ten persons consume each cup one after another; 17.
[They may be] Kṣatriyas belonging to the sacrificer; 18.
Or Brāhmaṇas, according to the Śruti. 19.
They are equal by virtue of their number (20).
He gives to the Brahman priest a sacrificial fee like a sunbeam (21).

A golden garland to the Udgātṛ; a golden plate to the Hotṛ; two golden mirrors to the two Adhvaryus; a horse to the Prastotṛ; a barren cow to the Maitrāvaruṇa; a bull to the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; two garments to the Neṣṭṛ and Potṛ; a single-yoked cart filled with barley to the Acchāvāka; and a cow to the Agnīdh. (22)
At the conclusion of the consecration ceremony, there is a retreat for one year for the purpose of shaving the hair (23),
as well as not standing upon the ground (24);
and this [practice] is to be observed without shoes for as long as one lives (25).

In the northern [part], on the white ground, there are five pits: 1. An oblation of cooked rice (caru) for Agni, Indra, Soma, or Viśvedevas; a dish of curdled milk (payasyā) for Mitra-Varuṇa; and a caru for Bṛhaspati. 2. The placing of the offerings is according to the directions: the one for Agni in the east, the others in a clockwise direction, and the last one in the middle. 3.
Having performed the preliminary rites repeatedly, there is the pouring of the intermediate residue.

4. A golden sacrificial fee belongs to the offering for Agni; he gives it to the Āgnīdhra. For Indra, a bull; for Soma, a brown one; for the Viśvedevas, a spotted one; for the Brahman priest, a cow fit for curdling milk (payasyā); in its absence, a barren cow; for the two Adhvaryus, [the fee] for Bṛhaspati is a white-backed bull, which belongs to the Brahman priest.
5. This same [rite] is also for one who desires food. 6.
There are twelve additional *prayug* verses;

eight months [are to be recited] in between; or, from the Āhavanīya fire, at a distance of a *śamyā*-throw to the east, at each *śamyā*-throw, [the verses] for Agni, Soma, Savitṛ, Bṛhaspati, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Vaiśvānara are recited as previously stated.
For one who has returned in this manner, there are six sacrificial cakes for Sarasvatī, Pūṣan, Mitra, Kṣetrapati, Varuṇa, and Āditya; these six are performed in a single ritual procedure.
For each of these six [sets], two bulls are the sacrificial fee for the first two fires. 10–12.
Like the Aṣṭāpada sacrifice, there are two animal sacrifices for two pregnant cows, with their respective qualities as the sacrificial fee (13).
[An offering] to Śyenī and the Ādityas, or to Aditi (14).
A spotted cow dedicated to the Viśvedevas or to the Maruts (15).
At the end of that [period], there is an Atirātra sacrifice involving the shaving of the hair, with the Soma-pressing on the full moon day (16);
then follow the subsequent months (17),
and finally the Vyuṣṭi-dvirātra (18).
The Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra [sacrifices] constitute the Kṣatraghṛti;
some perform them on both sides with Triṣṭomas and Jyotiṣṭomas.
Either after one year from the Abhiṣecanīya, there is the Keśavapanīya Atirātra, concluding with the Soma sacrifice (22).
In the following bright fortnight, the Sautrāmaṇī takes place (23).
Having tied together rice that has sprouted and rice that has not sprouted in a hempen cloth, he purchases it from a eunuch for lead (24).
Having cooked the rice and ground the sprouted grains into powder, he mixes them together, saying, "Cook for the two Aśvins," and he throws in the hair of a lion, a wolf, and a tiger;
or he does so among the sacrificial animals.
The rules for the *puroḍāśa* cake apply [to the animal sacrifice] because of the commonality of the substance; 28.
those pertaining to the Soma sacrifice apply as far as stated, because they are subordinate elements;
29. the *paśubandha* sacrifice consists of three animals on the fourth day after the full moon. 1.
Or, when [the Soma] has been pressed: 2.
A white goat for Āśvina; 3.
A ewe with pendulous udders for Sarasvatī.
The bull [is for] Indra; [the goat is for] Sutraman; in the absence of those qualities, [the goat is for] Aja. 5. The first [victim] is red; 6.
there are three sacrificial posts because of the indicative mark of the *vaikādaśini* (set of eleven). 7.
The two fires are treated as at the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifice. 8.
There is no altar on the south side. 9.
At the end of the cleansing of the omentum, he purifies the fermented liquor with kuśa grass, [reciting]: "Vāyu is pure. 10.
He throws in the powders of *kuvala*, *karkandhu*, and *badara* fruits; he draws the cup with the verse "kuvidaṅga," or three times for each deity using this same verse;
there is a simultaneous recitation of the *anuvācana* and the call "yajā."
The other two [oblations] follow the first without being offered separately (14).
The *parisrut* oblation is performed in the southern fire (15).

Having brought the portion for consumption and poured the remainder of the *parisrut* into it, he places a perforated jar—like a gold plate—upon a sling; holding it over the southern fire so that it drips, he worships with the three verses addressed to those who have drunk Soma, those seated on the sacrificial grass, and those consumed by the fires (*tṛcaiḥ somavatāṃ barhiṣadām agniṣvāttānām*). (16)
He offers the oblations dedicated to Savitṛ, Varuṇa, and Indra, as prescribed for the purpose of the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa). 17.
A eunuch, or a mare that pulls a chariot, is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 18.
This same [rite] also applies to one who has been over-intoxicated by Soma (somātipūta). 19.

At the end of the *anuyāja* offerings, he performs the ritual for the sake of the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) with the oblation for the Aśvins, prior to the portions being cut off, or alternatively, with the sacrificial materials (*havirbhiḥ*).
However, there is no [offering] for the Aśvins in the case of a deficiency.
The Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice performed by one who has completed the Rājasūya at the conclusion of that ritual,
due to its connection with the sequence of the Traidhātavī—
thus ends the fifteenth chapter of the Kātyāyana-sūtra.
Agni is a subsidiary part of Soma because of the intermingling of their qualities. (1) For one who desires [the fruit], there is a restriction at the Mahāvrata. (2) Not at the first meal. (3)
4. From the time of the placement of the fire on the *uttaravedi*.

5. One desiring to perform [the sacrifice] sacrifices with the full-moon offering (*paurṇamāsa*) in the later month of Phālguna and immolates five animals without giving a sacrificial fee (*adakṣiṇa*).
6. Or he may give them to the Brahman priest.
Some [perform this] on the new moon day.
(7) For the Agnis and for Kāma, [he sacrifices] a man, a horse, a goat, and a sheep.
(8) The man has the longest halter; the others follow in order of size. (9)

Or they are equal for all [the fires]. 10. Between the *samidhyamānavatī* and *samiddhavatī* verses, he places nine [verses] beginning with "O Agni, you are the same" (*samāstvāgne*). 11. There are twelve *āprī* verses, beginning with "His [flames] rise upward" (*ūrdhvā asya*). 12.
At the end of the eleventh [chapter], he performs the *śāsa-praiṣa* and other rites. 13. The immolation of the man takes place in an enclosed space. 14.
He cleanses the goat because it is employed for the performance of the ritual. 15.
Or rather, it applies to all without distinction (sūtra 16);
[it may be] a Vaiśya man or a Rājanya (sūtra 17); they take up the heads after placing a blade of grass between their necks (sūtra 18).
19. The casting away of the body into the four [elements], water being first; 20. Then [the casting away] for the sake of earth, bricks, and stones; 21. He proceeds with a goat.
When he has passed away, there is the disposal of the remnants by all together (22);
or by one alone (23), according to the Vedic text: "What would it matter even if one person were to collect them? (24).
The animal-cake offering is dedicated to Vaiśvānara; the deity of the animal sacrifice is [Agni] Upāṃśu;
and the invitatory and offering verses (yājyā-anuvākyā) are addressed to Agni and contain the word "kāma."

He should abstain from sexual intercourse until the full moon day (Paurṇamāsī). (28) If he so desires, he may sit upon a seat made of meat. (29) He places heads smeared with ghee, from which the skin and brain have been removed, [upon the altar]. (30)
Whether they be all [thirty-one],
or others [thirty-two],
whether made of gold or made of clay— one should not touch these.
Or, one belonging to Prajāpati should be a dark-spotted animal;
he should offer six [oblations];
the *sruva*-ladle offering is made with the verse beginning "hiraṇyagarbhaḥ."
Or rather, the first [offering] is due to the commonality of the deity (39),
while the latter two are due to both commonality and explicit instruction (40).
Or one should offer two white, water-dripping [cows] to Vāyu Niyutvat (41).

The animal-cake for Prajāpati is on twelve potsherds; for both [the Prajāpati and Vāyu offerings], the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses contain the word *kad*, or those containing the word *śukra* for the Vāyu offering, or they may be for the omentum (*vapā*). 43–45.
Everything else is the same for all [the fires].
46 On the eighth day, he prepares the fire-pan (ukhā).
To the east of the Āhavanīya fire, in a square pit dug by hand, he places a lump of clay level with the ground. 2.
At another point along the path, he places a lump of earth into a hollow in an anthill.

To the south of the Āhavanīya fire, three horses, a donkey, and a goat stand facing east, bound together with a triple-strand of *muñja* grass having five joints; the donkey is in the middle, preceded by the horse.

To the north of the Āhavanīya, at a distance of one cubit (*aratni*), there is a bamboo spade (*abhri*) that is perforated and sharp on both ends; in the absence of a spotted one, it may be unspotted, measuring either a span (*prādeśa*) or a cubit.
Some [say] it is made of gold. 6.
He offers eight portions, continuously drawing up [the butter] with the verse, "He who yokes... 7.
Having taken the spade with the formula, "Thee for the god," he consecrates it by placing it in his hand with the formula, "Having placed thee in my hand... 8.
And [he addresses] the horse and the others verse by verse with the mantras "Pratūrtam," "Yujāthām," and "Yoge-yoge. 9.
Touching them, he makes them step forward toward the east, verse by verse, with the mantra "Pratūrvan urv antarikṣam pṛthivyāḥ sadhasthāt. 10.
While the fires are blazing, they go to the funeral mound with the mantra "Agniṃ purīṣyam. 11.
And from the south, he gazes simultaneously at the animals and the false man (anaddhāpuruṣa), [reciting]: "The gods, the ancestors, and men [look upon] Agni Purīṣya for no purpose" (12-13).
Having taken a mound of earth from an anthill, he gazes at the funeral cake through the hole [in it], [reciting]: "Agni has followed" (14).
Having seen it, he places it down;
with the words "having come," he consecrates the horse;
with the words "having stepped upon," he causes the horse to step upon the cake.
Saying "Dyaus te," he places his hand upon the back [of the horse] without touching it (18);
saying "Ut-krama," he makes it step out (19); saying "Udakramīt," he consecrates it with the mantra (20).
He establishes [the clay] like the Āhavanīya fire.

Having sat down, he makes an offering over the lump of clay with two interlinked verses beginning "I sprinkle thee" (RV 10.175.1–2), using the dipping-spoon (sruva) for the offering at the horse's footprint.
With a spade (abhri), he traces around the lump three times, each time further out, with the successive verses beginning "The lord of booty" (RV 10.175.3–5).
With the formula, "By the spade he digs the clod," [he digs] with the words, "Of the god thee.
(24) Having spread a black antelope skin to the north, (25) upon it he places a lotus leaf with the words, "The back of the waters. (26)
He wipes it with the formula, "May he wipe this from heaven" (27);
he touches both [the earth and the clod] with, "You two are a refuge" (28);
and [he takes] the clod with, "You are the filler of the soil" (29).

He takes hold of it with his right and left hands; having held it all at once with the six verses beginning "O Agni, thou who art with the waters" (*dakṣiṇaḥ sābhristvām agne*), he places it upon a lotus leaf.
He pours water into the pit with the verse "The divine waters" (*apaḥ devīḥ*).
With the verse "United with thee" (*saṃ ta*), he throws away the wind-leaf.
He strews [the grass] with his ring finger from the front, the back, the south, and the north (4).
He lifts up the ends of the two layers [of grass] with the verse, "Well-born" (5).
He binds them together with a triple-stranded girdle of Muñja grass with the verse, "A garment for Agni" (6).
He stands up, taking the rice-ball, saying, "O thou who standest in the waters" (RV 10.9.1).
With his arms raised, he holds it forward, reciting, "Upward, indeed, for us" (RV 1.36.13).
Having brought it down and holding it above the navel, he consecrates the horse and the other animals with the mantra, "Once born, be firm; be auspicious" (RV 10.121.2).
Without touching the sacrificial cake, he holds it over these [animals] with the verse, "May the vigorous stallion, Agni... for the horse and the donkey (10).
Having brought [the goat] from the donkey with the verse, "O Agni, come hither," he proceeds with the goat up until its placement with the formula, "Right is truth" (11).
Having turned the animals back, they enter; the goat is in front, and the ram is in the middle (12).
He gazes at the man who is not a true man (anaddhāpuruṣa) as before, [saying], "The fire for the soil" (agnim purīṣyam). 13.

To the north of the Āhavanīya fire, on ground that has been dug up, sprinkled with water, strewn with sand, and enclosed with an enclosure having its door to the east, he places a lump [of earth] with the words, "O plants! (oṣadhayaḥ). 14.
With the words, "For the sake of the nest" (nipājase), he releases it; then, taking goat-hair, he lets the animals loose toward the northeast. 15.
With the verse "āpo hi ṣṭhā," he pours water boiled with a decoction of *parṇa* leaves onto the lump (16);
then, having silently added froth (17),
he mixes it with goat's hair while reciting "mitraṃ saṃsṛjya" (18).
"Let the Rudras mix [the clay] with sugar, iron filings, and stone powder," [he says]; 19. "It has been mixed," [he says as he] kneads it together;
20. He fashions the *aṣāḍhā* brick; the first wife who has conceived is called by that name. 21.
The sacrificer makes the fire-pan (ukhā) out of clay, measuring one foot in length, marked with three lines, and one span in width and height. He does so while reciting, "The head of Makha.
He spreads it out to five *prādeśas* or the measure of an arrow in width for an animal sacrifice; [he does so] with the formula, "May the Vasus [spread] thee" (VS 5.25).
Having raised the edges on all sides, he first applies the layer with the formula, "May the Rudras [place] thee" (VS 5.27).

Having smeared it and made it smooth, he levels it with the formula, "May the Ādityas [protect] thee" (28) and "May the Viśvedevas [protect] thee" (29). On the northern third, he makes a channel all around with the formula, "The girth-rope for Aditi" (30).
The upper [vartīs] are silent; four others reach the directions, and two reach the sides. He raises them at the tips like breasts—some say there are two breasts, some say eight.

He takes the *bilva* fruit with the formula, "Aditi has stood," and having performed [the rite], he deposits it with the formula, "For this purpose. According to some teachers, there are three [fruits].
There are three *viśvajyotis* bricks, each with distinct characteristics, which are drawn separately. (6) He places the clay for the *upaśaya* brick down.
(7) He fumigates the fire-pan (*ukhā*) with seven horse-droppings, kindled from the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*), using one at a time with the formulas beginning, "O Vasus, thee... (8).
With the formula, "Aditi has dug this," he digs a square pit with a spade.
Having spread out the cooking-fire, he places the fire-pot upon it as prepared. With the formula, "For the gods thee," he turns the fire-pot upside down.
Having covered it with the cooking vessel, he kindles it with fire from the Dakṣiṇāgni while reciting, "May Dhiṣaṇā favor thee.
Or, the fumigation and cooking may be done with fire produced by friction.
Looking at it, he mutters, "May Varūtrī favor thee."
"He behaves toward a friend" (15);
"as long as he should so behave" (16); "only during the day, when burning [the fire-pan], it should be lifted out" (17).
He pours out the cooking vessel;
with "The god [has] thee," he [pours] the fire-pan;
with "Unwavering," he makes it face upward.
He raises it with the verse, "He rises up" (RV 10.31.11).
Having taken hold of it, he places it in the vessel with the formula, "O Mitra, this for thee" (RV 10.31.5).
He sprinkles it with goat's milk, reciting the formulas beginning with "The Vasus thee" (VS 1.22) for each mantra.
Therefore, the preparation of the bricks for those [bricks] that are drawn [on the ground] is as described; 24.
either an unlimited number or none at all are drawn on the two northern [altars]; 25.
the fire is used for cooking as previously [stated]. 26.
On the new-moon day, having performed the new-moon sacrifice,
[there follow] the offerings to Agni-Viṣṇu and Vaiśvānara (27–28), and a pap of ghee for the Ādityas (29).

Having offered the ordinary *audgrabhaṇa* oblations and the seven *agnika* oblations with the respective mantras beginning with "ā-kūtim," and having performed the rites up to the raising of the staff (*daṇḍocchrayaṇa*), either the Adhvaryu or the Sacrificer places the fire-pan (*ukhā*) upon the Āhavanīya fire; it is spread with a nest of *muñja* grass and a nest of *śaṇa* grass, and while standing facing north-east, he places it with the mantra, "O *śaṇa*, do not break me.
This applies also during the fastening of the gold plate (*rukmapratimocana*), the Viṣṇu-strides (*viṣṇukrama*), and the Vātsapra rite.

When the fire has been ascended [into the pit], he places thirteen fuel-sticks, each a span (prādeśa) long, into it. According to some, he does so without having ascended, after throwing in the embers.
He offers them with the verse: "O butter-fed one, like an archer, flow forth."
"One made of *vaikaṅkata* wood with [the verse] 'of the highest' (RV 10.97.20)" (36);
"one made of *udumbara* wood with [the verse] 'of the furthest' (RV 10.97.21)" (37);
"one not cut by an axe with [the verse] 'O Agni, when' (RV 10.97.22)" (38).
"If he eats what lies below" (39);
"daily, verse by verse, [he recites] those beginning with *pālāśīḥ*" (40);
"for a Kṣatriya who desires [victory], [he recites] the penultimate [verse]" (41).
The first [verse] belongs to the domestic priest;
both [verses] belong to another.
The utterance of "svāhā" occurs in all [verses] containing the word "ukhā."
Some [teachers] say that here [the ritual] begins with the Audgrabhaṇa and ends with the Daṇḍa-offering.

At this point, the sacrificer puts on a gold ornament (rukma) around his neck; it is circular, consisting of twenty-one beads, strung through the hair of a black antelope skin at its white and black spots, and tied with a triple-stranded hempen cord above the navel, with the beads facing outward. He does so with the mantra: "Shining like gold... (RV 10.88.1).
For the poles, the sling-ropes, and the throne, there are triple-stranded ropes made of Muñja grass, smeared with clay.
With the two rounded handles he grasps the mouth [of the ladle] with the verse, "Night and Dawn" (RV 1.93.1–2).
He carries it forward with the verse, "Heaven and Earth" (RV 1.159.1–2).
He places it on a square-legged stand provided with a looped sling, to the east of the Āhavanīya fire, like the seat of the Udgātṛ priest, with the verse, "The gods [placed] Agni" (RV 10.87.1–2).
He fastens the sling-loop with the verse, "The six-fold elevation, all forms.
He draws it forward together with the sling-loop, like a ball, with the formula, "Thou art a well-winged bird.
And there is the supporting [of the sling].

Having consecrated it with this modification, some pile another altar: one piled with a wooden trough (*droṇacit*), one piled with a chariot wheel (*rathacakracit*), one piled with a heron’s head (*kaṅkacit*), one piled with a *prauga* (front part of a chariot), one piled with a *prauga* on both sides, and one piled with a *samūhya* (heaped) layer of earth (*purīṣa*).
In the case of the *samūhya-purīṣa*, there is gold for each direction.
He takes the strides of Viṣṇu, reciting the formula "Of Viṣṇu... with each respective mantra.
And the lifting of the fire takes place at each respective [step]; in the fourth [step], there is no such sequence; he gazes toward the quarters with the mantra, "Step forth following the quarters."
He takes it up toward the northeast like a lump [of earth] with the verse, "Agni has cried out" (RV 10.88.1).
He carries it away with the verse, "O Agni, you who turn back" (RV 10.88.2).
Holding it above the navel, he consecrates it with the mantra, "I have brought you hither" (RV 10.88.3).
Having released the nooses with the mantra "ud uttamaṃ" (18),
he takes hold of the eastern and southern [ends] like a *piṇḍa* with "agre bṛhan" (19),
and he lowers it with "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat" (20).
He performs the rite with the stool, saying "The Great" (bṛhat);
he pays homage with the verse "Sit thou down" (sīda tvam);
and with the Vātsapra hymn, beginning with "From the sky" (divas pari), consisting of eleven verses.
Some [perform the rite] with each Anuvāka; 24.
"This one is initiated" [is said here]; 25. from this point on, there is a repetition for a year. 26.

The removal of the ashes from the *ukhā* [fire-pan] takes place at sunset; having released his speech into the vessel, he performs the placing of fuel with the verse, "Night after night, without failing...
(RV 8.43.9). In the same manner, the removal of the ashes and subsequent rites are performed at sunrise.

The establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) is performed day by day; likewise, the *viṣṇukrama* and *vātsapra* rites are performed with the reversal of the days. Having offered a fuel-stick (*samidh*) at sunrise, the rites beginning with the unfastening of the gold plate (*rukmapratimocana*) up to the *vātsapra* are performed, followed by the *viṣṇukrama* steps.
Or [the rite may be performed] without conflict with the Soma sacrifice, because of its predominance.
Having set aside the fuel-stick when the vow has been undertaken, the installation [of the fires] takes place with the mantra "O Lord of Food" (annapate) for each undertaking.
This applies both to one who has maintained the fires for a year and to one who has not.
One year for those about to give birth; ten years for one who has maintained the sacred fires; and likewise for one who has been born.
The final [observance] lasts for six months (13). Or, for another person, it lasts for a year (14).
Having placed the fire to the east, the placing of fuel-sticks on the north side of the Ukhyā fire is performed with the verse, "With fuel, Agni... (15).
Lifting up the cart together with its seat, he places it on the southern side of the cart with the mantra "ud u tyam.
He places the Gārhapatya vessel in the cooking pot behind [the cart].
Having yoked the two oxen, he drives them eastward with the mantra "pra id agne," proceeding according to his purpose.
He may either climb up or go along the side (19).
While the axle creaks, he mutters, "The fire has cried out" (20).
When he brings it down into the dwelling, having raised and sprinkled the ground, the taking of the fuel-sticks occurs from the north with the verse, "He goes forward" (21).
This carrying back and forth [of the ashes] may be performed during the consecrations (dīkṣās) whenever one so desires. 22.
The scattering of the ashes into water may be done at the time of the purchase of the Soma and other such occasions. 23.
One may do it elsewhere as well, if one so desires. 24.
After the carrying of the firewood upwards by means of the sequential method,
[he offers] water with one verse, "O divine waters" (RV 10.9.1),
and then with two verses.
Or, first, with the two initial [verses] (28);
he takes up the flour with his ring finger, saying "Be gracious" (29);
having thrown it into the pan, he stands over it, saying "Be mindful of me" (30).
Having offered fuel-sticks for the expiation, he offers clarified butter with the verse, "To Viśvakarman" (VS 8.45).
Having stood up, he places a fuel-stick on the fire with the verse, "May it be thine again" (VS 2.28).
If the *gārhapatya* fire goes out, one should produce it by friction; during the *sutyā* days, having carried it from the *āhavanīya* by means of the *sāṅkāśina* vessel,
one places it to the north of the *āgnīdhrīya* and the *sadas*.
One should perform the *āvṛt* for the *ukhya* fire and the expiation (*prāyaścitti*) for the *adhvara*; in all cases, one should perform each preceding rite at its proper time.
If the *ukhā* is broken, one places the *ukhā*-lid into a new vessel (*navasthālī*) that serves as a great *ukhā* and pours [the contents] into it.

Having ground the clay for the *ukhā* and the *upaśaya* together with earth, he fashions the *ukhā* according to the prescribed ritual procedure (9). When it is baked, he places the potsherd [upon it] (10).
Having ground the clay for the *ukhā* and the *upaśaya* together, he mixes them and sets them aside (11).

Having sat down for the internal piling (abhyātma-cayana), having placed the left arm between [the knees], [he piles] with bricks possessing the characteristics of the north; in the case of the permanent [piling], after the placing of the Sādana and Sūdadohas formulas, he recites "With that deity" and "Those [bricks] of his" for those [subsequent layers].
Because the instruction is without distinction (15);

because there is no prohibition of what has not been prescribed (16); and because, in the case of single injunctions that pertain to only one part, [the rule applies] by way of a common framework (tantra) (17).
The *yajuṣmatī* bricks are placed upon the self;
there are ten *lokampṛṇā* bricks in each of the ten directions, with the mantra "Fill the world" (*lokaṃ pṛṇa*),
and their settling is likewise performed.
Placing two [bricks] at each subsequent layer (praticiti), 21;
in the middle of the odd-numbered series (ayugmagana), on the spine (anūka), 22; and one more, 23.
On both sides, there are pairs [of bricks]; the groups face north in the eastern and western [sections],
and face east in the southern and northern [sections].
27. There is no piling together of the broken and the black [bricks]. 28. On the final day of the consecrations, the measurement of the altar and the fire-altar [is performed].
29. In the place of the *ukhya* fire, he traces around the *gārhapatya* fire with a cord measuring half the span (*vyāma*).
Or the stepping out from the mandala belongs to the *antaḥpātya* [space] (30);
afterwards, that of the *citya* [altar] is at a distance of one foot from the sacrificial post-hole (31);
while the sacrificer stands with arms raised, heels lifted, or standing upright (32).
Having measured a cord of two *puruṣas* with loops at both ends, [make] a mark in the middle (1),
and marks on both sides at the half-*puruṣas* (2), and at the fifth *puruṣa* from the middle (3).
Having stretched the cord along the spine by half [a puruṣa], he fixes two stakes in the two loops;
having released the loops from between the two half-puruṣas and having fastened them to the two half-puruṣa markers, he stretches it southward and makes a mark at the middle.
Having released one loop and having fastened it to the middle peg, and having drawn the cord taut to the south, a peg is fixed at the middle [point].

(8) Having fastened the loop to that peg and having drawn the cord taut to the south, a peg is fixed at the middle [point]. (9) And [another peg is fixed] at a distance of half a man's height behind. (10)
Having unfastened [the cord] from the eastern end and fastened it at the western end, having stretched it toward the south, a peg is driven into the middle;
then two more are driven on either side at a distance of half a man's length.
In this same manner, the northern end is established.

On the southern side, having stretched [the cord] as before, a peg (śaṅku) is fixed at the fifth part [of the span]; having fastened the loop to that, and having joined it with the eastern half-puruṣa-mark and the fifth-part-of-an-half-puruṣa-mark, a peg is fixed there—[making] 15 [units]. In the same way at the back—[making] 18 [units].
Thus is the northern side (19).
Having measured in that manner (20), desiring [the correct proportions], one draws in and draws out four finger-breadths at each of the junctions of the wings and the tail (21).

A man is five *aratnis* tall; a foot (*pada*) is ten [of his] feet, and a pace (*prakrama*) consists of three such feet. Having measured around [the site] with a cord divided into equal parts, one erects the enclosing stones (*pariśrit*) at the sixty-first hundred [of the divisions], or at the ninety-fourth, or at the third [hundred]. 22–25.
The pebbles in the excavation are upright (26). To the north, according to the measurement of one hundred and one layers of men (27),
the size of the bricks for the fire-altar and the sacrificial altars is determined (28).
Desiring [to place them] between the Antaḥpātya and the Gārhapatya fires,
he erects the enclosing stones (pariśrita) in the western corner of the northern wing, measuring a knee-high, a navel-high, and a mouth-high stone— [repeating] "mouth-high"—
thus ends the sixteenth chapter of the Kātyāyana Śulba Sūtra.
Having performed the rites beginning with the consumption of food on the following day and ending with the expiation (prāyaścitti), there is the combined performance of the Viṣṇukrama and Vātsapra.
If one intends to perform the Upasthāna after performing the Vātsapra,
he sweeps around the Gārhapatya fire with a Palāśa branch, verse by verse, in each direction, starting first in the east with the words "Go away, depart" (apeta vīta).
Having cast aside a northern branch, he scatters the saline soil with the formula, "For recognition" (VS 12.53).
He covers the circle [of the altar] with sand,
as in the case of the saline soil, with the formula, "The ash of Agni" (VS 12.54).
He encloses [the altar] with the *pariśrit* bricks as before, using twenty-one, with the formula, "O you who are piled...
(VS 15.63). In the middle, he lays down four *ardhabṛhatī* bricks, facing east, two to the south and two to the north, verse by verse, with the formulas, "This one is Agni" (VS 15.64) and so forth.
In the permanent [altar], it is done once.
Then, together with the *sahita* bricks, there are two measuring one foot on the west and two transversely on the east;

having circumambulated from the west, he places them at the back with the formula "O Agni, [thou art] the *iḍā*" for each mantra, and on the north side; with the formula "Thou art the layer" (*cidasī*), he places them at the front on the south side, for each mantra.
In the permanent [fire-altar],
there is one brick for each of the thirteen transverse corners; in the southeast corner, there are half-bricks measuring one foot.
In the remainder, there are sixteen crooked ones (vakrāḥ); the mantra is in three *lokampṛṇā*s and ten [bricks] (17),
or in two, ten, and one (18).
From the site of the *cātvāla* pit, he scatters the loose earth with the verse, "Indra [with] all... (RV 8.69.1).
Having made it level with the rim, he deposits the *ukhyāgni* fire-pan with the verse, "United...
(RV 10.85.47). He must not look at the empty *ukhā*.

Having made a pit level with the sand, having released [the vessel] from the sling like a mother [releasing] her son, and having placed it down as if with a hoe, he silently pours milk into the middle. 22.
Some [teachers] say it should have three layers. 23.

Having placed three black *nairṛta* grains—cooked with husks, unmarked, and a foot in length—in a place for the oblation of spilled offerings, from south to north, facing south and without touching them, he offers them verse by verse with the [hymn] beginning "He who does not press [Soma]," reciting them in their natural order. 24.
Some [place it] toward the interior;
there is the constant absence [of the cord];
he throws away beyond [the altar] the looped cord, the golden ornament, the sling, and the stool with the formula, "That which... and so forth.
Having sprinkled the water from the pitcher, they rise with the inner self as the brick, saying, "Homage to prosperity.
Having gone away without looking back, he performs the worship at the door of the hall, [reciting] "The dwelling.
At the end of the *prāyaṇīya* offering and the call to the preparer of the oblation, he performs the rites beginning with the wooden sword (*sphya*) up to the wiping of the Mahāvedi.
At the conclusion of the Prāyaṇīya offering, he yokes a plough made of Udumbara wood with a triple-stranded rope made of Muñja grass;
he yokes six, twelve, or twenty-four oxen, placing the northern shoulder of the team toward the east.
Standing to the west of the southern buttock of the fire-altar, he consecrates the plough being yoked with the verse, "They yoke the ploughs" (RV 10.101.4).
He ploughs upon his own body, following the outline of the altar, verse by verse with the hymn, "The good ploughshares" (RV 10.101.5–12),
