starting from the south and moving eastward.
The others [the other wives] circumambulate to the right; 13.
silently, three times each, to the right; 14. across the rear of the fire. 15.
Diagonally across the two hips and shoulders (16);
along the spine (17);
diagonally across the two hips and shoulders (18).
Or, when long-employed, men plow [the field];
having repeatedly released the oxen with the words, "Be released," he dismisses them like cattle and gives [the field] to the Adhvaryu at the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having placed a ploughshare upon the heap of earth, he lays down a bunch of *kuśa* grass in the middle silently;
then, lifting it up with fivefold-drawn ghee, he makes an offering over it with the verse, "In harmony with the year... (RV 10.87.22).
In each of the four furrows, he pours out three water-scoops with a four-cornered ladle made of Udumbara wood:
three in the furrows that have been ploughed and those that have not,
or [he may pour] only in the furrows that have been ploughed.

Into that [fire-pan] he pours all the medicinal herbs, omitting only one; then, from its breath, he pours [the remaining herb] with the three verses beginning "The plants which... (RV X.97.1–3), as is done with the water-pitcher.

Having performed the pouring of Soma and the rites up to the preparation of the guest-offering (*ātithya-havis*), he consecrates the enclosing stones of the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra "Thou art piled" (*cita stha*).

Having taken seven or nine *lokeṣṭakā* bricks with the wooden sword (*sphya*) from outside the altar, he places them while standing at the ends of the spines (*anūka*), verse by verse and in each direction, the first one in the east. He places the last one behind the north-western corner.
He wipes away the sand from the northern side with the verse, "I abandon this...
(12). Having poured sand upon the northern altar (uttaravedi), he covers himself with it (14).
He touches the sand with the two verses beginning with "Swell up" (āpyāyasva) (15).

Having performed the Upasad rites with the remnants of the Ātithyā offering and so forth, he prepares the bricks for the first layer on a red bull's hide spread inside the *antaḥpātya* space, positioned in front [of the fire-altar];
for the other layers, the bricks are self-perforated (*svayamātṛṇṇā*), and they may also be prepared according to one's own intention.

Having poured ghee upon the tips of the *kuśa* grass, he sprinkles them silently while a white horse stands in front; in the absence of a white horse, [he does so] with a non-white horse, and in the absence of a horse, with an ox.

(19) He causes [the Hotṛ] to recite the invitatory verse for the fires as they are being carried forward. (20) When the verse has been recited three times, having carried the pile forward preceded by the horse, he places it to the south of the tail. (21)

He makes the horse mount by way of the *tīrtha*, behind the western wing; according to some, in front and behind. He leads the ploughed earth around with a sacrificial formula, first toward the north.
Having caused the animal to smell the fire that has come toward him and having led it around, he releases it like an animal.

Having performed the rites from the sprinkling of the *uttaravedi* up to the pouring down of the *sambhāra* materials, the sacrificer stands behind the *uttaravedi* and mutters, "I take [the breath] within me.
He sings the *satyasāman*.
He places a lotus leaf upon the grass-bunch as before;
on that, he places a gold disk with its convex side down, with the verse "The Brahman was born first" (RV 10.121.1).
Upon that, he places a golden man facing east with the palm upward, with the verse "Hiraṇyagarbha" (RV 10.121.1).
He sings the Sāman on the variegated man. Having circumambulated from left to right, the sacrificer stands nearby, saying, "Homage be [to you]."
Having sat down, he offers the five-fold portion, moving around in each direction verse by verse with the hymn beginning "puruṣe kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ" (1.25).
Having returned, [he offers] from the south; the first and last offerings are behind.

Having covered the man from the chest, he draws a line without touching him with his arms, ending at the [shoulder] joints. 10. Therein, he places the offering-ladle (*sruk*) on the two eastern [lines]. 11.

To the south, he places one made of *kārṣmarya* wood, with a bowl the size of a hand, a handle the size of an arm, or the size of a foot, as required; it is filled with clarified butter, [reciting] "Having sacrificed to Agni... 12.
In this manner, he places an udumbara branch filled with curds to the north with the formula, "For Indra thee. According to some, two horizontal [branches] are used.
He places a pebble perforated by a hole upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick in the center of the man, with the formula, "Thou art firm."
He sings the Sāman on this [syllable] "bhūḥ" (16),
and also on other vyāhṛtis (17).
On a dūrvā grass-blade possessing both root and tip, he places it so that its tip reaches the ground, [reciting] the verse beginning with "kāṇḍāt kāṇḍāt" (18).
Each preceding [verse] is followed by the subsequent ones;

"yāsta" constitutes the second [section] consisting of two *yajus* formulas; the mortar [is placed] at the level of the *retaḥsic* (the ring-stone), as it is heard in the text to be one *aratni* in measure.
With the mantras "Virāj" and "Svarāj," he places the two *retaḥsic* bricks, one for each mantra (22).
With the mantra "Prajāpati," he places the *viśvajyotis* brick (23).
With the mantra "Madhu and Mādhava," he places the two seasonal (*ṛtavya*) bricks (24).
"Thou art the invincible," [he says] regarding the *aṣāḍhā* brick.
(25) He makes marks on the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, the *retaḥsic*, the *viśvajyotis*, the *ṛtavyā*s, and the *aṣāḍhā*s with a cord for the purpose of defining their boundaries.
(26) He anoints a tortoise with curds, honey, and ghee, [reciting]: "The winds carry honey... (27)
At a distance of one *aratni* to the south, he places the *aṣāḍhā* stone; above it, he places a man facing [the fire].
With the three verses beginning with "apāṃ gambhan," he strikes [it] with the middle one. 28. 1. 2.

To the north of the mortar and pestle, at a distance of one *aratni*, there should be two posts made of *udumbara* wood, each a span (*prādeśa*) long and four-cornered. The mortar should be narrow in the middle, with its top rounded, and the pestle should be placed to the south of the mortar. With the verse "The deeds of Viṣṇu...

(RV 1.22.19), he places the mortar in the mortar. Having fashioned a fire-pan (*ukhā*) in the mortar, having ground the clay for it, and having poured it out, he places the pan in front with the verse "Thou art firm" (VS 11.60).
With the verses beginning "O Agni, yoke thy steeds" (VS 11.61–63), he offers oblations from the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) into the fire-pan, verse by verse.
Or, for one who has not performed the *samvatsara-bhūti* sacrifice, there is the *upasthāna*.
He places seven pieces of gold on the mouth at each head, saying, "They flow together. On the northern [side], he places two at each.
"Ṛce tvā" for the two nostrils;
"bhāse tvā" for the two eyes;
"abhūd idam" for the two ears.
Some [place] all [the heads] facing west in a single cauldron;
having lifted up the head of the man with the words "O giver of a thousand," they place it in the middle.
To the north of the horse and the sheep, [he places] the eastern and western [bricks];
to the south of the cow and the goat, [he places them] with each mantra, "The sun is the embryo" (ādityaṃ garbham). 15–17.
With the verse "The manifold [glory] of the gods," he offers two spoonfuls of oblations at the midpoint, half-verse by half-verse (18).
Standing outside the sacrificial altar facing north, he worships with the *utsarga* formulas, "Do not harm this one," reciting each mantra separately (19).
Some teachers say that he should circumambulate the fire-pot (20).
Or, placing them one by one according to their respective gender;
some [place] all the mantras upon this [fire], while others [place] them individually;
changing the placement-mantras, he places [the fuel-sticks] on the thumb, the little finger, and the head.
Having approached with the verse, "And you, O youngest one," he performs the worship of the altar (*cityopasthāna*).

Having approached behind the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone, he places five *āpasyā* bricks at each of the five joints with the respective formulas, "Thou art the essence of the waters" (*apāṃ tvemam*), for each mantra.

Like the sprinkling of ghee (*vyāghāraṇa*), he places ten *prāṇabhṛt* bricks together with the *karṇa* bricks, ten for each person, at the boundary of the *retaḥsic* bricks on all sides as appropriate, with the respective formulas, "This [is] the stronghold" (*ayaṃ puraḥ*).

The second [brick] with the formula "this one behind" (dvitīyamayaṃ paścāt) is placed from the middle of the southern shoulder toward the end of the spine, moving clockwise to the eastern [shoulder]. Having returned, he places the remainder.
The wings and tail [are laid down] from the *parāñc* bricks up to the *apyayas*;
thus everywhere.
In the middle, he scatters loose earth (*purīṣa*) as previously described.
First, he covers the front half; then, moving clockwise, he covers himself, as well as the wings and the tail.
In this manner, in every case,
he worships the *citi* containing the loose earth (*purīṣavatī*) with seven verses beginning with "For the slaying of Vṛtra" (*vārtrahatyāya*);
some [do so] with eight.
Or, with ten [verses],
during the morning and afternoon sessions and in the interval between them, at the time of the piling of the altar and the pouring of the loose soil;
having led the horse around three times, he releases it like an animal until sunset and returns by the same way he went.
The marriage ceremony [is performed] up to the placing of the fire (6).

There are two [oblations] at the Upasad of the sacrificial post; three in the first [layer], five in the middle [layer] (7), and those beginning with the five-fold ladled butter in the last [layer] (8).
And in the nine Uttarās,
there are six with *purīṣa*, one for each;
in the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) with eleven *upasads*, the *citi*s and *purīṣa*s alternate.
On the eleventh day, beginning with the Vikarṇī;
on the twelfth day, for those performing the four-month session; on the thirtieth day, for those performing the thirty-six-day session; and on the thirtieth day, in the year-long session.
In the month of Tāpaścita, [he offers] the Catuṣṭoma on the days of the Citipurīṣa;
on the fifth day, the Asapatnā Virāj; on the first day, the Stomabhāgās every day.
For one month, [he performs] the *purīṣa* silently (18);
for one month, beginning with the *nākasad* [bricks] (19);
and the *purīṣa* as well (20).
In the two highest Ahīnas, the Vikarṇī and so forth are as before;
the first [set] consists of two thousand [bricks], and the Lokampṛṇās are fifty less than that; and so too are the subsequent ones.
The highest [altar] consists of three thousand [bricks]; for those not drawn in curved lines, there are two thousand four hundred in the south and north, and the others in the middle;
or else, the third [type] consists of thirty-six hundred, and the others consist of eighteen hundred.
The *lokampṛṇā* bricks for the *gārhapatya* fire-altar are placed on the first layer; the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths are on the last layer; or there may be an unlimited number of bricks.

In the first and last [circles], one should divide the lines into ten groups each and, having increased them by thirty units— each being a quarter-measure more than the others— one should construct the *utkara*. In the second [circle], at the boundary of the *retaḥsic* [altar] in every direction, one should place the *āśvinī* [lines].
With the northern [side], he places the eastern [brick] on the second layer;
with the eastern [side], the southern;
with the southern [side], the western.
The *uttarā* [verses] follow next; the fifth is the *dakṣiṇā* following the *uttarā*;
[these are] the *vaiśvadevī* verses.
The eastern [side] with the south (8); the southern with the west (9);
the western with the north (10).
The northern one to the east of the former; 11.
thus from the Vaiśvadevīs come the Prāṇabhṛts; 12.
from the Prāṇabhṛts come the Apasyās; 13.
As before, there are five [verses] for all [the bricks]; 14.
"Āśvinī, Dhruvā, Kṣiti... with each mantra; 15.
"Śukraśca Śuciśca" are the two Ṛtavyā bricks placed above the first two; 16.
And the following seventeen [verses] addressed to the Viśvedevas, with the mantra "In harmony with the seasons," for each verse; and the following [verse].
"May the breath of the breath-bearers be mine," [he says] for the Prāṇabhṛt bricks (20).
"Make the waters swell," [he says] for the Apasyā bricks (21).
For the Vayasyā bricks, five each at the ends of the sections, with the formulas beginning "The head, strength... (22).
Four [bricks] in the east;
twenty-three in the south, in the north, and in the west;
the *lokampṛṇā* bricks on the southern buttock as before.
On the third day, [he places] "Indra and Agni" in the middle of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks;
on the spine [bricks], five regional bricks as in the *vaiśvadevī* rite, beginning with "The royal one";
and with "Viśvakarman," he places the *viśvajyotis* brick above the eastern one.
And in the last month of the two summer months, Nabhas and Nabhasya;
[the bricks] are Avakās, shaped like tortoises;
others say they are Iṣa and Ūrja.

In the first half, he places the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks with the formula "ten are the life-span" for each mantra (7). He places twelve *chandasyā* bricks at each of the corners with the formula "O *Chandas*, do not harm me" for each mantra (8).
Having left a space behind, he places the *bālakhilyā* bricks (9).
The seven Bālakhilyas are before [the breaths], or those after the Prāṇabhṛts are twelve,
and those after the latter are twelve.
With each mantra, "Thou art the head, the ruler," he places [the bricks]; knowing them as *yajuṣmatī*s,
he places the *lokampṛṇā*s from above the northern hip as before.
On the fourth [day], two [lines] each are drawn to the south and north at the ends of the anūkas; 1.
fourteen more are drawn behind the first two; 2.
six are drawn behind those; 3.
Some say it is in the intermediate direction between the east and the south; others say it is north or south;
others say it is north of the two eastern [fires], being swift and threefold.
"In the southern of the two western [stomas], there is the Dharuṇa, the twenty-onefold," [he says].

7. "In the southern of the two southern [stomas], there is the Bhānta, the fifteenfold," [he says]. 8. "In the southern of the two northern [stomas], there is the Vyoma, the seventeenfold," [he says]. 9.
"Fourteen for each mantra, eighteen for the *pratūrti*," [is the rule];
"the southern [quarter] is the portion of Agni for the two eastern [fires]," [and] "the northern [quarter] is the portion of Mitra for the two western [fires]."
"The northern one of the two southern ones is the portion of the Man-viewers," [he says]; 13.
"The northern one of the two northern ones is the portion of Indra," [he says]; 14.
"Six for each mantra are the portion of the Vasus," [he says]. 15.
The two seasonal bricks are *Ṛtavyā*, namely *Saha* and *Sahasya*.
At the time of the *Retassig* brick, seventeen [bricks] are placed on all sides; nine to the south of the spine (*anūka*), with each mantra beginning, "With one they sang praise.
From above the northern shoulder, the *Lokampṛṇā* bricks are placed as before.

On the fifth [day], at the end [of the rites], there are the *asapatnā* formulas like those for Aśvinī; 1. the space between the two elbows [is measured] to the south; 2. with the mantra "O Agni, those born" (*agne jātān*) for each respective formula; 3.
The second [section] is at the west;
there are ten [bricks] for each direction. "First, the *gāyatrī* is the metre" (VS 14.23)—this is recited with each mantra.
(Sūtra 4–5) There can be no *gāyatrī* among the groups of rival metres, because of its impossibility therein. (Sūtra 6)

Having placed the *ardhapadī* bricks after the *uṣṇih* ones—[namely] the *asapatnā*, the *aspṛśaḥ*, and the *anyatontarāḥ* on one side, and the *sarvatontarāḥ* and *aṣāḍhā* at the boundary—the *stomabhāga* bricks are placed with each respective mantra: "With the ray, O true one... and so forth.
Fifteen [bricks] along the spine on the right side.
"Veṣaśrīḥ, quicken the kṣatra for the kṣatra"—some recite this as the thirtieth.
He scatters loose earth with a mantra, or silently, because it is so heard in the case of Tāpaścita.
The *nākasad* bricks are placed on the *anūka*, excluding the first one, at the time of the *ṛtavyā* bricks, with the formula "O Āśvinī, you are the most wise," recited for each mantra.
(1) Having scattered the loose earth (*purīṣa*), he places five *cūḍā* bricks on top, one for each mantra, saying "This city... and so forth.
(2) They are placed in each direction according to its respective characteristic mark. (3)
The four [verses] beginning with *paścimottamā*;
three each of the *chandasyā* verses at the ends of the sections; the *gāyatrī* verses beginning with *agnirmūrdhā* at the beginning, verse by verse; and the subsequent [verses].
Before the *triṣṭubh* verses, at the time of the seed-sower, [he recites] "Bhuvo yajñasya" (7). And behind [the *triṣṭubhs*], [he recites] "Ayam iha" (8), which are *jagatī* verses.
Following those, [he recites] the *anuṣṭubh* verses: "Sakhāyaḥ saṃ vaḥ" (9).

Before the time of the Aṣāḍhā full moon, [he should recite] "bṛhatīrenā va" (10) and "bhadro na" (11), which are Kakubh verses; from these, according to the sequence of the mantras, he should extract the Bṛhatī verses by means of the intermediate hearing (antaraśruti).
If he so desires, he may transpose them. 12.
Another [set] consists of *gāyatrīs* and *uṣṇih*s beginning with "O Agni, for the sake of booty" (RV 6.47.1).
At the end of the *anuvāka*, on the right side, there are *paṅkti*s beginning with "That Agni" (RV 8.44.24).
On the left side, there are *padapaṅkti*s beginning with "That Agni today" (RV 8.44.27).

In the *purīṣavatī* [layer], the first [verse] is in the *aticchandas* metre; the two eastern [verses] are accompanied by *purīṣa*: "The auspicious gift at the slaying of Vṛtra," "Unwavering," and "Agni the Hotṛ. (16) At the end of the *anuvāka*, there are two more verses in the *dvipadā* metre. (17) The *gārhapatya* hearth consists of eight bricks placed in the center. (18)
Furthermore, one should likewise pile up the *citi* above with the verses beginning "yena ṛṣayaḥ," verse by verse (19). Some [place it] at the joint of the tail (20),
or having placed the *gārhapatya* fire at the front half, they place it at the joint of the tail (22).
The two seasonal bricks are *Tapaḥ* and *Tapasyaḥ*.
(23) The *Viśvajyotis* brick is laid with the formula, "Parameṣṭhī tvā.
(24) From the southern shoulder, at a distance of one cubit toward the west, the *Lokampṛṇā* bricks are placed as before. (25)

Having covered the *vikarṇī* and the *svayamātṛṇṇā* with soil, and having touched the two pebbles at the openings, he recites over the northern *vikarṇī*, "prothad aśvaḥ," and over the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, "āyoṣṭha.

(26) This is done once for each [opening] as a rule. (27) Standing, he sprinkles the fire as in the *puruṣāhuti* rite; he scatters two hundred gold chips each time, reciting "of the thousand" with each mantra, "of the thousand" with each mantra. (28)

For the Śatarudriya oblation, in the western corner of the northern enclosure wall, using a vessel made of *arka* leaves and a fuel-stick of *arka* wood, while standing and facing north, he offers a continuous stream of *gavedhuka* groats mixed with wild sesame (*jartila*), or according to some, mixed with goat's milk, reciting the chapter beginning with "Obeisance to you" (*namas te*).

At the end of the first three sections (anuvākas), there is a *svāhā* utterance when the fire reaches the height of the knee; at the end of the fifth section, there is one when it reaches the height of the navel.
Before the descents, he offers [the oblations] into the mouth alone;
for the descents, he offers them in reverse order, with the formula "Homage be [to you]" for each mantra, according to the measures.
He throws [the remnants] into the *cātvāla* pit during the offering.
The Agnīdh priest sprinkles the citya-water, having placed the pressing-stone in his right armpit; [he pours] upon the stone with the mantra, "In the stone, vigor" (RV 10.53.6).
Having placed the water-jar on the stone with "Hunger for thee in the stone" (RV 10.53.7), he takes it up with "In me, thy vigor" (RV 10.53.8).
He does this twice more in the same manner.
He goes around it in the opposite direction.
Having placed a stone on the pitcher, standing facing east at the southern corner of the altar, he pours out [the grain] while saying, "Him whom we hate.
He should say, "It must be broken," regarding the unbroken [grain].
The breaking [of the vessel] occurs in the *kumbha* by implication (7);
or rather, in the *aśman* (stone) because of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) (8),
and because it is so stated (9).
Having approached without looking back, standing facing north or east, he mutters "These [are mine]" (*imā me*) while reaching over himself until the end.
Having tied frogs, oyster shells, and branches of the *vetasa* reed to a bamboo pole, he pulls them down verse by verse with the mantra "Thee, of the ocean... (*samudrasya tvā*).
And he pulls the wings and tail toward himself with the mantra "O purifying Agni, with thy light... (*agne pāvaka rociṣā*).
The last [verse] is the response (13).
Having placed the bamboo pole on the heap of grass and standing while touching the funeral pile,
he utters the *hiṃ* sound and sings the *Sāman*, first the *Gāyatra*.
On the right wing is the Rathantara (3),
on the left is the Bṛhat (4), and in the center is the Vāmadevya (5).
He recites the Yajñāyajñīya on the tail;
the Prajāpatihṛdaya on the right armpit.
"Recite the Agnyukthya," he says.
On the day of the Upavasatha, having released his speech, he throws five lumps of gold into the *pañcagṛhīta* (fivefold-drawn) clarified butter.

Having poured together curds, honey, and ghee into a vessel, or into a large-mouthed pot, and having taken a handful of *kuśa* grass over both, he ascends the altar with the mantra, "Homage to thee... (TS 4.2.5.1).
He offers the *pañcagṛhīta* into the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick with the formula, "To the one who sits among men, veḍ! (TS 4.2.5.1), for each mantra, and the appearance of gold is like that of a navel.
He sprinkles the water that has been poured out with the *kuśa* grasses over the enclosure and outside it with the verse, "Those gods who... (VS 11.59).
With the words, "The givers of breath," (VS 11.60) he descends.
Thus [is] the ascending and descending from here.
At the conclusion of the *upasad* rites, the removal (*utsādana*) of the *pravargya* vessel is performed as previously prescribed, either in the fire or in the flowing water (19).

First, he offers an oblation upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone, touching it; he offers five portions (*pañcagṛhīta*) with the verse, "Agni with his sharp [weapon]... (16). He offers half of sixteen portions with the remainder of the section (17).
With another *anuvāka*, "The father of the eye," [he places] three fire-sticks of *udumbara* wood, soaked in ghee, with the verse beginning "Upward him" (*udenam*), one for each verse.
He leads forward the fire. 18–20.
He sends [the assistant] forth; he takes up the fuel; having taken up the implements for the fire-laying, [he says]:
"Recite for the fire as it is being carried forward! O Agnīdh, follow with the single wooden sword (ekasphya)! O Brahman, mutter the Apratiratha hymn!
When [the verse] has been recited three times, having lifted [the fire], [he says]: "Upwards, O Agni! (udu tvā). 21–23.
"Fifteen go to the city" (24).
From the location of the Āgnīdhra fire, he places the *pṛśnyaśman* stone to the south, together with the *pṛṣṭhyā* cord, [with the verse] "The measurer" (25).
It is not [performed] at the permanent [fire-altar] (26).
Having set him down, they step across while reciting, "All [the gods] [follow] Indra.
27. With the verse, "Step forward with Agni," they ascend the altar-site (*citya*).

Holding the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick over the middle of the fire-altar, he makes an offering of milk from a cow with a white calf. While pouring the milk from a black cow onto the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, he recites, "Anointed are Dawn and Night. 2.

On that [altar], some place a fire made of Pītudāru wood and other woods with the formula "Thou art a well-winged bird," accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ* call; and this is done on the two permanent altars as well.

The placing of the fuel-sticks consists of those made of *śamī*, *vikaṅkata*, and *udumbara* wood; he offers them verse by verse with the mantra "Of Savitṛ... (RV 3.8.10), the last stick being provided with its ear. 6.
In the absence of an ear, it is smeared with drops of curd. 7.
He offers two oblations with the *sruva*-ladle, verse by verse with the mantra "O Agni, him today... (RV 4.1.4). 8.
And the full oblation with the verse "sapta ta" (9).
In all cases, one stands when offering the fuel-sticks (samidh) in the middle (10),
but sits when offering the oblations at the ends (11).
In this context, there is the worship with the seven-verse hymn using the fifth [verse] because it serves as a foundation for all;
or rather, having consecrated the *dhiṣṇya* hearths, because of its connection with the subsequent [rite];
he should touch them, reciting, "Thou art the year."
Thus,
as prescribed, he offers the Vaiśvānara and the Māruta oblations;
having placed the Vaiśvānara over the fire, he places the two Māruta offerings to the south and north.
And afterwards, [the two verses] are more closely joined (18);
likewise the other two (19);
afterwards, it should be recited in the forest (20).
21. Having spread out *kuśa* grass to the west of the *puccha* (tail) for both the oblations and the placing of the vessels, or having placed them there together with the *Āhavanīya* fire; 22.

having performed the rite for Vaiśvānara with an offering made in its entirety (*sarvahuta*), he sits down and offers the *Māruta* oblations with his hand, or [offers] to Vaiśvānara while making Vaiśvānara broad, with each mantra beginning "O you of bright light" (*śukrajyotiḥ*). 23.
The *vimukha* [mantra] is to be recited in the forest (24).
He mutters "indraṃ daivīḥ" (25),
or he causes [the student] to recite "imaṃ stanam" (26).

He offers the Vasordhārā with five portions of ghee taken from an Udumbara branch, continuously, while the sacrificer recites the eight Anuvākas beginning with "vājaśca me" at the Araṇye'nūcya fire when it has been reached;
having offered, he discards the *sruk* ladle.
He performs six offerings for the earth (*pārthāni*) with the formula "agnaye svāhā."
Having collected the *vājaprasavīya* materials like those for the *vapā*, he pours the *vājapeya* portions with the *sruva*-ladle using the formula "Of the strength (*vāja*) this... (4).
Then the *āgnika* portions with "Now of the strength...
(5). Having thrown the *sruva* ladle [into the fire], having spread the black antelope skin upon the enclosing stones, and having poured water upon the remainder to the north of the tail (6).

By virtue of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), [the sacrificer] is consecrated there with milk and water, according to the Śruti text: "Or [the waters] of the Vājapeya"; while being touched by the one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), he is consecrated with the mantra, "Of the god thee... (*devasya tvā*).
Standing, one who desires to thrive; seated, one who has become [prosperous]; on a goat-skin, one who desires nourishment.
If both desire it, both [should do so]. 13.
Some say [it should be done] on the south side of the *citī* or within the *citī*. 14.
Having thrown the cup [into the fire], he offers six oblations with the formula "To Indra, svāhā! and so forth, one for each mantra. 15.

He offers twelve portions of clarified butter in separate ladlings with the formulas beginning "Ṛtāṣāṭ," ending each with *svāhā*. These are the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* (sustainers of the kingdom) offerings; the first mantra ends with the sound *vāṭ*.
While the chariot-head is being held over the Āhavanīya fire, he offers five portions of clarified butter five times with the mantra beginning "sa naḥ bhuvanasya.
He then circumambulates the interior of the chariot-seat from left to right.

Or like the oblation of a man (puruṣāhuti). 19. Facing the front of the chariot, 20. the Adhvaryu, having taken up [the materials] with his joined palms, offers the Vāta-homas: in front, outside the altar, below the southern yoke-pole; then to the north of the northern yoke-pole; then to the south of the southern yoke-pole; and to the south of the right-side horse—each with a separate mantra beginning, "Thou art the ocean. 1.

And the removal of the girdle is performed everywhere; (2) the Adhvaryu's taking of his dwelling is done after he has been formally addressed; (3) at the time of the sacrificial fees, he gives [the fee] to the Adhvaryu. (4)
He offers nine oblations of horse-flesh with the mantra "yās te" for each verse; or, if he knows them, he may offer those prescribed by the Brāhmaṇa.

Having performed the rites from the washing of the *havirdhāna* shed up to the touching of the *āgnīdhra* shed, he builds the *dhiṣṇya* hearths. He piles eight bricks with *lokapṛṇā* formulas on each side, making them four-cornered; having laid them down one by one, [he places] the *pṛśnyaśman* stone on the *āgnīdhrīya* hearth.
The mantra is recited only once.
In the Hotrīya [fire-altar], there are three sets of twenty-one;
in the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsī [fire-altar], two sets of eleven; in the Mārjālīya, six; and the remaining eight are bricks.

Having laid down the enclosing stones as far as desired, he silently pours the loose earth (purīṣa) [upon them]. From the subsequent portion onwards, the rites up to the Sviṣṭakṛt offering of the sacrificial cake are performed like those of the Abhiṣecanīya sacrifice.

When about to commence the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*) with the yoking of the fires, he should touch the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and, as before, recite verse by verse: "I yoke Agni... (17). Prior to the *agnimāruta* stotra, he performs the unyoking at the junctions of the enclosing sticks, reciting verse by verse: "The head of heaven... (18). Some say that after yoking at the introductory night-sacrifice (*prāyaṇīyātirātra*), one should perform the unyoking at the concluding sacrifice (*udayanīya*). (19)
Others [say] that at the end of the *sam̐iṣṭayajus* of the *adhvara*, one should recite "The sacrifice has been offered" for each verse (20).
Following the *paśupuroḍāśa*, he offers the oblations for the *anūbandhya* animal sacrifice and the *devikā* offerings, including the *yajñapraiṣa* formulas (21).
There are rice-pap offerings (*caru*) for Anumati, Rākā, Sinīvālī, and Kuhū; and a cake on twelve potsherds for Dhātṛ, which is to be offered entirely (22).

At the end of the heart-rite (hṛdayaśūla), he offers eight oblations with the dipping-spoon (sruva) verse by verse, beginning with "yadākūtāt" (TS 3.3.11). Having given the name "Citras" (the Bright One) to the fire-pile, he worships it with the verse "ye 'gnayaḥ" (TS 3.4.6.1).

At the conclusion of the rite, there is a curd-offering (payasyā) for Mitra and Varuṇa, a hornless goat (tūpara) as a pair serves as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and the concluding offering (udavasānīyā) takes place at the end.
26. He rains down [semen] without sexual intercourse;
27. he eats the food of birds;
28. he approaches a woman of his own caste.
In the second [case], she herself;
in the third, none at all;
the vows [apply] for as long as one lives, because there is no distinction.

Or for one year, because time is not fixed [for the performance] (Sūtra 32), and because of the scriptural injunction regarding that vow (Sūtra 33). Furthermore, in the case of inability to construct the fire-altar, at the subsequent Soma sacrifice, one of the following should be used: the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, the *viśvajyotis*, or the *ṛtavyā* bricks (Sūtra 34).
Furthermore,
the *punaściti* (re-piling) or the *acitya* (non-piling) results in the attainment of the *āhavanīya* fire;
this is a sacrifice for Brahmins intended for one desiring prosperity through the *sautrāmaṇī*.
[The rites] for one who has built the fire-altar, for a Soma-sacrificer, for one purified by Soma, for one who has vomited Soma,
for a king who has been deposed,
for one who is not fit for cattle, and for one who is without cattle.
The *āditya* oblation is a *caru*;
it is at the end [of the sacrifice],
or else it is prior to the *āmikṣā*.
A cow is the sacrificial fee (8);
a calf is in the east (9); a mother [cow] is in the north (10).
Saying "I place [the fuel]," he places three pieces of fuel on the Āhavanīya fire, verse by verse. 11.
He is a speaker of truth. 12.
He eats the remnants of the oblation. 13.
For four nights he offers the Agnihotra;
there is an animal sacrifice for Indra.
Some [prescribe] the reversal of the cow and the sheep.

(17) At the place within the enclosure, on the hide, [the purchase is made]: with lead for the seller of *surā* and *soma*, with young grass for the purchase of *tokmān*, with wool for parched grain (*lājān*), and with threads for the seller of *surā* and *soma*. Having addressed him repeatedly, "O seller of *surā* and *soma*, these are the *surā* and *soma* to be purchased," [the purchase is made]. (18) Some [prescribe this] for eunuchs and the like. (19)

Having carried [the materials] with his right hand and having made them into a powder, he pours separate rinsings of rice and *śyāmāka* grain into them, mixes them with the powder, and sets it aside; that is the *māsara*.
Having mixed the two types of cooked rice with the powder and the *māsara* while reciting "Thee, the sweet one, with the *aśu*," he sets it aside for three nights.

He sprinkles around [the fire] with the milk of one [cow], mixed with curds, using the verse, "Sprinkle all around" (RV 10.9.6). He also scatters powdered grass-blades. In the morning, he performs the same for two [cows] with the milk of Sarasvatī.
And parched grain flour (26);
with the *aindra* [sūkta], the best of the three [is offered] (27);
and parched rice flour (28).
He measures out the two altars as in the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifice. 1.
He measures the northern altar by turning back one-third of a prakrama, as in the Soma sacrifice. 2.
Behind those two, he prepares two mounds (khara). 3.

On the following day, he performs the rites beginning with the *praṇayana* and the *ādāna*, up to the placing of the clarified butter (*ājyāsādana*). He takes up the wooden sword (*sphya*) and other implements on the southern side, as in the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifice. On this [southern] side, there is a mound for Sūrya. Having dug a pit and placed a donkey’s skin to the west of it, and having poured the *parisrut* (fermented liquor) over it, he places a filter (*kārotara*) upon it. Or, from the filter onto the skin—because of the indicative mark of the mantra, "They pour out, they sprinkle all around"—he takes up the purified liquid.
"He purifies with the hair of a cow and a horse; he purifies your *parisrut*," [he says] for the *pūta*. "Purified by Vāyu," [he says] for the *atipūta* Soma.
"Eastward," [he says] for one who vomits it.
In the northern direction, [he takes] milk with a strainer made of reeds and the wool of a goat and a sheep, [reciting] "The Brahman and the Kṣatra... (10).
[He recites] "O Adhvaryu, with the stones... (11) as the consecration by the Brahman. He draws the milk-libations [with the verse] "O, indeed... (12).
13. [The offering] has separate origins for the two diseases;
14. the settling of the two donkeys;
15. [the offering] for the Aśvins with a leaf of the Aśvattha tree.
He pours in the flour of wheat and water-lily with the formula, "Thou art splendor" (16);
[he offers] the *sārasvata* oblation with a vessel of udumbara wood (17);
and he pours in the flour of upavāka and jujube with the formula, "Thou art vigor" (18).
With a fruit of the *nyagrodha* tree, [he offers] to Indra (19);
with the flour of barley and jujube fruits, [he offers] to Bala (20);
with earthen cooking-pots, [he offers] to Sūrya; and with various foods, [he offers] to the two [Aśvins], alternating [the order] (21).
First,

he purifies either the cups for the *payas* (milk) or the cups for the *surā* (spirituous liquor) with the mantra "Ojas asi" (*Ojas asi*), using hair from a wolf, a tiger, and a lion mixed together, respectively, for each mantra.
According to some teachers, this is done according to the respective order.
He worships the cups simultaneously with the section beginning "Somo rājā" (25),
or alternatively, with four [verses] for the milk-cups and the remainder for the Soma-cups (26).
He purifies [the sacrificer] like one initiated within the *antaḥpātya* enclosure with two eagle-feather fans, [reciting] "yā vyāghram" (27).
He causes [the sacrificer] to look at the fire with the verse, "When he crushed... (RV 10.16.7). 28.
The touching of the milk-cups is performed with the verses, "O ye who are united... (RV 10.191.2) and "O ye who are separated... (RV 10.191.3);
these belong to the Sauras. 1.
He performs the rites with the spade and other implements;
2. the goat of the Aśvins is smoke-colored; 3. the ram of Sarasvatī. 4.
The *ṛṣabha* for Indra [is placed] in the middle as the sacrificial post (6);
those for Indra-Vāyu and the Aśvins are to the south and north [of it] (7).
At the end of the wiping of the omentum, having taken up the cups as before, the announcement is made: "Recite for the Surā and Soma! (8).
But [this] includes the formal command (9), and also [the formula] "It has been set forth" (10).
Everything [is performed] for the Tripaśu sacrifice (11).
He offers with the verse "surāvantam" (12).
[The offering] is made with Palāśa wood; it is not earthen, because of the Vedic revelation: "He who desires the measure of an oblation" (13).

The Adhvaryu, the Pratiprasthātṛ, and the Āgnīdhra consume the portion for the Aśvins with the formula "O Aśvins," repeating it twice each time. (14) The Hotṛ, the Brahman, and the Maitrāvaruṇa consume the portion for Sarasvatī in the same manner as the Aśvins.
(15) He pours the remainder of each into the northern vessel of the preceding one. (16)
The sacrificer [partakes] of the portion for Indra (aindra). 17.
When they consume the portions for Sūrya here, they do so according to their consumption, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītinaḥ), toward the south. 18.
Some [consume] by means of a breath-sip (prāṇabhakṣa). 19.
Or else, one who has been hired from either a Vaiśya or a Rājanya [serves as the assistant].

20. He offers oblations on the coals outside the enclosing stones: to the Aśvins in the northern [space], to Sarasvatī in the middle, and to Indra in the southern [space], with a separate formula for each, saying "To the Pitṛs. 21.
With the mantra "The Pitṛs have eaten," he sprinkles water upon them using the rinsing water. 22.
He mutters, "O Fathers, be purified.

(23) Having suspended the pitcher and having placed within it a hundred-fold perforated vessel like a jar, along with a hair-strainer and gold, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite the nine verses beginning with "May they purify me.
(24) [This applies to] those belonging to Soma, those seated on the sacrificial grass (Barhiṣads), and those consumed by fire (Agniṣvāttas). (25)
If one has been excessively intoxicated by Soma, it is as before;
the sacrificer offers with the verse "Those who are equal" (RV 10.191.2),
and with the subsequent verse while wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder.
While they maintain contact, he offers milk with the verse, "Two paths there are" (RV 1.164.33).

29. The sacrificer consumes the remnant with the formula, "This is the oblation. They perform the purificatory sprinkling at the *cātvāla* pit together with their wives, having placed gold between [themselves and the water].
30. He prepares the animal-cake offerings: one for Indra, one for Savitṛ, and one for Varuṇa on ten potsherds. 1.
Having placed the single-potherd cake for the *avabhṛtha* rite,
he performs the two *ājyabhāga* offerings; here, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and *vanaspati* offerings follow because their *praiṣa* (directions) are observed [in the texts],
or rather, as previously stated, because there is no specific injunction for the mantras.
He gives thirty-three sacrificial gifts, including a cow with her calf and a barren cow. 5. The rules for the set of eleven victims apply to the groups of animals. 6.

Having performed the rites from the instruction of the *śamitr* up to the end of the *vanaspati* offering, he places a throne-seat (*āsandi*) between the two altars—its legs being knee-high—just as one does for the Soma-throne, saying, "The womb of the Kṣatra. 7.
He spreads a black antelope skin upon it with the verse, "May it not [harm] thee.
(8) The sacrificer sits down upon it with the verse, "Sit down.
(9) He places two gold ornaments on his feet—a silver one on the left—with the words, "From death... (10)
Some say that one should place a golden [image] on the head; thus [it is said].

(11) He offers thirty-two oblations of marrow with the hooves, verse by verse, using the [mantra] beginning with "With lead" (*sīsena*). (12) Having offered two at a time, he places the remaining [hooves] into a vessel. (13)

He sprinkles [the horse] with the remainder of all fragrant substances, letting them flow down from the mouth and in every direction, with each mantra: "Of Savitṛ," "of the Aśvins," "of Sarasvatī," and "of Indra" (one mantra for each).
With all [these mantras together], he performs the fourth [sprinkling].
According to some, [he does so] with the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
Or with the *uttama* [verse] (17).
At the consecration, some perform the rubbing down with the *avanīya* [fire] (18).
He touches the sacrificer [with the formula], "Who are you? (19).
The Adhvaryu calls out "Suśloka" when the victim has been seized;

he seizes the limbs according to their respective characteristics with the formulas beginning "My head," reciting one mantra for each limb. They lift him up in the same manner as prescribed for the Śatarudriya rite.
As he descends onto the black antelope skin, [he recites] "In every kingdom... (VS 23).
He draws the thirty-third fat-offering with [the verse] "He who of beings... (VS 24).
Some [draw] the butter-offering with a twig of the *aśvattha* tree. (VS 25)
He sends forth the *sāman*;
he sings on a *bṛhatī* verse addressed to Indra.
They all conclude with the *nidhana*: "For hearing, for wide-hearing, for true-hearing, for fame."
"For conquest, for victory, for truthful conquest, for conquest"—this is for the Kṣatriya.
"For prosperity, for abundant prosperity, for truthful prosperity, for prosperity"—this is for the Vaiśya.
Or rather, all [mantras] may be used according to the traditional recitation.
He sits down, intending to consume [the remains].
At the conclusion of the recitation, he offers with the verse, "The three gods... (TS 3.2.5.6).
The remaining priests consume the remainder by the *prāṇabhakṣa* method, saying, "O protector of the breaths... (TS 3.2.5.6).
The sacrificer consumes [the portions] directly; "the hairs are the exertion" [is the formula].

Having performed the rites from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering up to the *barhis* oblation, he takes the vessels smeared with the milk-foam (*parisrut*) and proceeds as in the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) ritual.
Having performed the rites from the consecration of the spit (*āśūla*) up to the *udakādhiṣṭhāna*, he proceeds up to the *avabhṛtha* sacrifice.
He floats a vessel of meat with the verse, "O gods...

(RV 10.97.13). 13. The immersion is as before. 14. Having taken water in his joined palms with the verse, "May they be friendly to us... (RV 10.97.16), he sprinkles it around his enemy with the verse, "May those be unfriendly to us... (RV 10.97.17), having stepped two strides toward the north. 15.
Having bathed like the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), he discards his garment with the verse beginning "drupadādiva" (16).
His departure and return are like those of the Soma sacrifice (17).
He pays homage to the Āhavanīya fire with the verse "apo adya" (18).

Having taken a fuel-stick with the formula, "Thou art fuel," he places it on the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "Thou art kindling. He offers an oblation with the verse, "He who turns back together.
Having moved away from the sacrificial ground, there is a curd-mixture for Mitra and Varuṇa.
At the end of that [offering], there is an animal sacrifice for Indra Vayodhas (22).
In the Sautrāmaṇī, the iṣṭi and animal sacrifices have separate ritual procedures (*tantra*) because of the difference in time.
There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses. 2.

The two *ājyabhāga* offerings are [respectively] the *vārtraghna* and the *vṛdhanvat*; or alternatively, they are the *vṛdhanvat* in animal sacrifices because of their being modifications of the *sānnāyya*;
and also in the case of the *āmikṣā*.

In the sacrifices to deities with whispered formulas (upāṃśu), the two Virāj verses are the invitatory and offering verses (saṃyājye), because they are taught without qualification. For the Vasiṣṭhas and Śunakas, there is the Nārāśaṃsa cup.
And according to some, among the Atris,
the first and last *prayāja* and *anuyāja* calls (*praiṣas*) are in the natural form;
the first belongs to Indra, while for some, the last belongs to Vāyodhas.

"Samiddha indra" and so forth are the *āprī* verses for the first [offering], serving as both the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* for the omentum (*vapā*), the cake (*puroḍāśa*), and the animal victim. "Āyātu indra" [is the *anuvākyā*] for the omentum.
"Hotā yakṣat samidhāgnim" and so forth are the *prayāja-praiṣas* for the three animals.

"Āpriyaśca samiddho'gniraśvinā" (The Āpriya verses and "samiddho'gniraśvinā")—these are the invitatory and offering verses for the omentum-offerings, three in number, beginning with "aśvinā haviḥ. Having recited the first [verse], the second is the offering verse; having recited the second, the third is the offering verse; having recited the third, the first is the offering verse.
For the *puroḍāśa* cakes, [the offering formula] is "O Indra... as before (18);
for the oblations, it is "O Aśvins, with cows... (19); and for the cups, it is "You two [drank] the *surāma*... like a son" (20).
For the animal sacrifice (paśu) sviṣṭakṛt offering, [the verse] is "yasminnaśvāsaḥ" and "ahāvyagne". 21.
For the omenta (vapā), there are three invitatory verses beginning with "hotā yakṣadaśvinā", according to their respective marks (liṅga). 22.
The fourth [verse] is for the cups (graha). 23.
The [recitations] for the oblations follow in the order of their characteristics (yathāliṅga). 24. The last two belong to Vanaspati and Sviṣṭakṛt. 25.
When the Adhvaryu has sat down, intending to respond, he calls out, "O Śaṃsin! and recites the section beginning with "O Aśvins, with splendor. 26.

The first and the last [verses] are recited three times (27). Having called out at the beginning of the *tṛca* verses (28), and having left the final verse aside, up to the ninth or the tenth [verse], there are three deities; the *nivit* consists of seventeen [syllables], with the *avasāna* at the end of each verse and the *oṃ* at the end of the *ṛc* (29).
In the final syllable, beginning with the vowel, there is elision in the *praṇava*;
according to some, the *praṇava* itself is elided at that point.
"O Aśvins, with splendor; O Aśvins, drink"—these are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for the [offering] accompanied by a *śastra*.
The directions for the recitation and the directions for the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) are combined; [the formulas] "O divine sacrificial grass" (*devaṃ barhiḥ*) and the *yājyā* verses [are used];
and the direction for the *sūktavāka* is "Agni today" (*agnim adya*).
The ordinary [form] applies from the *sūktavāka* onwards until the *avabhṛtha* offering;
likewise for what has not been specifically stated.
The verse "imaṃ me varuṇa" is for the single-pot-sherd (*ekakapāla*) offering.
For the oblation to Agni and Varuṇa, [he recites] "tvannaḥ" and "sa tvam"; 8.
for the oblation to Āditya, "sutrāmāṇam" and "mahīm u ṣu mātaram"; 9.
for the curd-mixture (payasyā), "ā naḥ" and "pra bāhavaḥ. 10.
"Of the steed, may there be auspiciousness for us in every prize"—this is the *yājyā* to be recited without pausing.
"Vāyodhasa," "the dear ones," "Agni is kindled," and "with fuel"—these are the *āprī* verses. 13.

The invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā-anuvākyā*) for the omentum, the sacrificial cake, and the animal sacrifice are [to be recited] with the formula "by the spring season. The Horse Sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), a royal sacrifice for one desiring all objects of desire,
takes place on the eighth or ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna.
In the summer, some cook the *brahmaudana* rice; [he cooks] four vessels and a handful for each.
Having anointed it, he hands it over to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

To them he gives four thousand [cows] and as many *śatamāna* weights of gold. Having anointed the rope with the remainder of the clarified butter, he sets it aside, measuring twelve or thirteen *aratnis*.
Or, at the time of taking it up, he applies collyrium to it.
While putting on the gold ornament, he causes [the student] to recite: "Thou art brilliance" (9).
"Restrain thy speech" (10). There is restraint of speech until the granting of the boons (11).
And the wives come adorned, wearing golden neck-ornaments: the chief queen, the favorite, the discarded wife, and the daughter-in-law of the Pālāgala, each with her attendants by the hundreds.
There are one hundred daughters of kings for the first [wife], and one hundred daughters of nobles for the second.
The charioteers and village headmen [receive] on the third day; the warriors and charioteers [receive] on the fourth day.

Having entered as at the *agnyādheya* (establishment of the sacred fires), when the *agnihotra* has been offered, he lies down to the west of the *gārhapatya* fire with his head toward the north, while the *avāvātā* wife lies between his thighs as a student (*brahmacārī*).
The others follow in sequence.

(18) When the morning oblation has been offered, at the conclusion of the full-oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the granting of boons is made to the Brahman priest and to the Adhvaryu priest; [as a reward] a gold necklace (niṣka) is bestowed upon each. (19–20)
A sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is for Agni Pathikṛt;
the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is one hundred mānas of gold.
This applies to the measurement of gold elsewhere as well.
He offers a *caru* oblation to Pūṣan; a hundred garments are the sacrificial fee.
Having taken the halter with the formula, "Thee for the God," he says, "O Brahman, I shall tether the horse.
Being permitted by the Brahman with the words, "Tether it," he ties the three-colored horse with the formula, "Thou art the fetter."
Or it may take any form at all; it is swift and equal to the strength of a draft-ox.
The *sāhasra* [is the thirty-first],
the *lalāma* [the thirty-second], or the *kṛttikāñji* [the thirty-third].
The front part of the body is black and the other part is white (33),
or it is black-spotted (34).
Having gone to the stagnant waters, he sprinkles the horse with each mantra, saying, "For Prajāpati, thee" (35).
He says to the Āyogava, "Strike the four-eyed dog! (36). Some say [he strikes] a male *calūma*.
(37) He strikes it with a *sidhraka* pestle. (38)
He causes [the sacrificer] to recite, "So'arvantam" (VS 24.20).
He causes the horse to wade through water from below by means of a reed-mat while [the sacrificer] recites, "Paro marta" (VS 24.21).
Having brought it near the fire, he offers oblations with each mantra of the Anuvāka, beginning with "Agnaye svāhā" (VS 24.22).
Or he performs a thousand repetitions,
or until the ceasing of the sound of the horse's neighing;
he offers twelve potsherds, with distinct ritual procedures and a *śatamāna* coin as the sacrificial fee for the central one, dedicated to Savitṛ Prasavitṛ, Savitṛ Āsavitṛ, and Savitṛ Satyaprasava.

During the *prayāja* offerings, to the south, a Brāhmaṇa sings three self-composed *gāthās* for the sacrificer concerning his sacrificial gifts, in the *uttaramandrā* melody (7). A Rājanya sings [three] *gāthās* concerning steadfastness and victory in battle during the *dhṛti* verses (8).
The Adhvaryu and the sacrificer mutter the formula "Vibhūr mātā" at the right ear of the horse (9).

The release [of the horse] is like that of cattle; when one hundred horses have been lost, he assigns guardians for it with the formula, "O gods, protectors of the quarters," appointing as many attendants of various kinds—equipped respectively with armor, quivers, sword-belts, and staffs—as there are [horses].
He prevents mares from approaching [the stallions].
From water used for ritual bathing (prasneya), 13;
a Brāhmaṇa ignorant [of the rules] at the Aśvamedha sacrifice, his livelihood is yours (to take); 14;
and cooked food [is forbidden] in all [such cases]. 15.

And those who have lived in the house of the chariot-maker shall attain the status of consecrated kings; thus he says regarding the princes. To the south of the altar, they sit upon seats made of gold.
The Adhvaryu and the Sacrificer [sit] on two bundles of grass (kūrca), or on two wooden boards;
the Hotṛ, the Brahman, and the Udgātṛ [sit] on cushions (kaśipu).
"O Hotṛ, recount the beings; cause this sacrificer to dwell within these beings," thus he gives the direction for the *pāriplava* recitation.
"O Hotṛ! he responds.
At the end of that, he gives the direction: "Let those who play the lute and the drum sing together with the royal seers for the sacrificer."

He offers oblations in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire with the formulas "To the Hiṅkāra, svāhā! and so forth, taking three steps; then, after sunset, he offers four Dhṛti-oblations in the Āhavanīya fire with the verses beginning "May there be delight here.
For one year, he performs the Vāvātā, Samveśana, Sāvitrī, Uttara, Mandrā, Gāna, Pāriplava, and Dhṛti rites.
Some [teachers] say that [he gives gifts] for half a month, a month, three months, or six months (Sūtra 6).
He gives one hundred [cows] each to two lute-players and singers (Sūtra 7).
The singing in accompaniment with the royal seers continues until the Dīkṣaṇīyā offering (Sūtra 8).
At the end of the initiation (dīkṣā), [the sacrifice] was performed by the gods starting from the day of preparation (aupavasathya);
at the beginning of the animal sacrifice (paśu) and others, it was performed by Prajāpati; and at the Soma-pressings (sutyā), as well as at the conclusion, [it was performed by the same].
The sacrifice for wild beasts is performed with *caru* offerings dedicated to Savitṛ;
[an offering] to Pūṣan when there is a fracture;
and one to Sūrya when there is an eye disease.
If it dies in water, [the cake] belongs to Varuṇa (15);
if it dies in fire, [the cake] belongs to Bhūmikapāla Vaiśvānara for the sake of safety (16);
according to Jātūkarṇya, [there should be] a cake on potsherds made of clods of earth because of the breaking [of the original vessel] (17).
In the case of destruction, [the oblations are] for Heaven and Earth, milk, for Vāyu, and for Sūrya (18).
Also elsewhere (19),
when [an animal] has been born, [there is an offering] for Vāyu (20).
1. He performs the taking of the girdle and other rites for another [victim] instead of one that is dead or not seen, which is improper for a horse.
2. Having performed the animal sacrifice (paśvālambhana) and so forth for the initiation of the *ādhvara*, he offers four *udgrabhaṇa* oblations belonging to the *ādhvara*.
3. And he offers three *āśvamedhika* oblations with the formula "To Kāya svāhā! and so forth.

4. From here on follows the initiation with the black antelope skin (kṛṣṇājina). 5. There are four [formulas] for the initiation of the Adhvara sacrifice, and three each for those belonging to the Aśvamedha. 6.
The daily rite ends with the black antelope skin, because the original vow has not been performed.
And on the seventh day, he offers the oblation for Agni;
he performs the rites beginning with the anointing;
there are six offerings for Agni in four locations.

The tenth [verse] is "viśvo devasya" (RV 5.50.1). Having performed the rites from the spreading of the black antelope skin up to the placing of the fuel-stick, he mutters "ā brahman" (RV 10.72.6–8). According to some, this occurs at the time of the formal renunciation (utsarga).

There is initiation and twelve *upasads*. (13) The sacrificial ground for the gods must always have water in front of it. (14) The first fire-altar is either double, triple, or twenty-one-fold in size. (15)
There are twenty-one sacrificial posts, as in the case of the Ekādaśinī;
the central one is made of Rājjudāla wood,
and on both sides are two made of Pītudāru wood.
There are six [stakes] each made of Bilva, Khadira, and Palāśa wood;
three on each side; and for each sacrificial post, there are Agniṣomīya animals.
In the morning, there is the Agniṣṭoma; 22. there are two sets of eleven Savanīya animals; 23. in the midday [pressing], there are two for Agni. 24.
And of the two northern [groups],
there are many-colored cows in the highest [group] (26).
From the middle of the Vijaya [group], the eastern direction belongs to the Hotṛ, the southern to the Brahman, the western to the Adhvaryu, and the northern to the Udgātṛ (27).
Day after day, he gives away the third [portion] each time, with the exception of the property of the king’s men and Brāhmaṇas.
(28) Having drawn the Ukthya cup for the third pressing, he divides it into three parts at the time of the Āgnimāruta Shastra. (29) The oblation and the consumption follow those cups. (30)
Having taken up the *vasatīvarī* waters and having poured them out in each direction, he carries them around.

(31) He offers one oblation each of clarified butter, barley meal, parched grain, and fried grains, with the formula "Svāhā to Prāṇa! and so on for each mantra, revolving throughout the entire night. (32) With the formula "To the Dawn," he offers when the dawn has broken. (33)
When "for heaven" has been uttered (at the morning pressing), the Ukthya sacrifice begins;
he draws the two Mahiman cups: the first with a golden vessel with [the verse] "Hiraṇyagarbha," and the second with a silver vessel with [the verse] "Yaḥ prāṇata."
Having touched the horse for the *bahis-pavamāna* procession,
he shows a mare; she neighs while that *stotra* is being chanted,
or they may chant it.
He gives a śatamāna [of gold]. 6. They cause the horse to step upon the āstava. 7. Having dedicated the animals of the eleven-fold set, beginning with the horse. 8.
"O Hotṛ, praise the horse!"—thus he gives the command.
(9) He yokes it with the verse, "They yoke the ruddy one. (10) And they yoke the others with the verse, "They yoke his [steeds]. (11)
Horses adorned with golden ornaments (12),
and a chariot (13);
having gone to the water and entered it, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite the verse beginning with "yad vāta" (14).

Having brought the horse that has been released, the chief queen, the favorite wife, and the discarded wife anoint its forequarters, midquarters, and hindquarters with clarified butter according to their respective positions, with the formulas "The Vasus for thee," etc., recited for each mantra (15).
They fasten one hundred gold beads each onto the manes and tails while the horse is not being let loose, with the Great Utterances "Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ," recited for each (16).
According to some teachers, the attendants do this silently (17).
He gives the remnants of the night-oblation to the horse with the words, "O you who eat parched grain and eat curds.
(18) He causes it to be thrown into the water while it is still eating.
(19) The Brahman asks the Hotṛ, regarding the sacrificial post: "Who indeed is the one alone? (20)
He says, "The Sun. 21. [The Hotṛ asks] the Brahman, "What was there? 22.
He replies, "The Sky. 23.

1. He performs the churning of the fire and other rites. 2. He binds the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal to the post standing near the fire. 3. He assigns the deities to the horse and the others as previously prescribed.
On the two horses harnessed to the side-poles, there are fifteen [animals] each; on the others, fifteen each, beginning with the *rohita* and ending with the *saura*.
Between the sacrificial posts, there are thirteen each, beginning with the *kapiñjala* and ending with the *pṛṣata*.
The sprinkling of the horse is performed with the formulas "adbhyas tvā" and "vāyuṣ ṭvā.
He supports it [the horse] with the formula "apām perur agniḥ paśuḥ.
They release the kapiñjala birds and others from the fire that has been carried around them.
The horse is slaughtered upon cloths spread over golden coverings (10).
Having offered the *paripaśavya* oblation, he offers three further oblations with the formula, "To Prāṇa, svāhā! (11).
Leading the wives away, he causes them to recite, "Homage to you, O Mother" (12).
They walk around the horse three times each, as if it were among the ancestors, with the words: "Of the dear hosts, of the treasures.
(13) When they have been washed, the chief queen lies down beside the horse, saying: "May I not be born [again].
(14) She covers him with an upper garment, saying: "In the heavenly world. (15)
"The stallion, the vigorous one, places his member in her lap," [with these words] 16;
"With uplifted thighs... 17—with this verse, the sacrificer addresses the horse.

The Adhvaryu, Brahman, Udgātṛ, Hotṛ, and Kṣattṛ converse with the young girls who are the wives [of the priests], using two verses at a time from the ten-verse hymn beginning with "Which of us here... 18; having called out, "O you, O you, so-and-so! they address each other.
The attendants respond; 19.
according to some, the female attendants [respond]; 20. having raised the chief queen, the men recite, "O Dadhikrāvan... 21.
Three wives prepare the sword-paths for the horse with needles made of iron, silver, and gold, numbering as many as the gems—namely, the *gāyatrī*, the *triṣṭubh*, and so on;
or alternatively, with silver, gold, and lead, because of the recitation of the mantra;
the horse has a golden sword.
The iron [implements] belong to those animals tied to the sacrificial bed; the others are made of bronze.
He dissects the horse with the Anuvāka beginning, "Who has pierced you? (VS 23.17).
They extract the fat for the sake of the omentum,
and they cook its blood;
the cooking and the offering of the omentum and the oblation take place to the north of those belonging to Prajāpati.

Before the offering of the omentum, the Hotṛ and the Adhvaryu converse in the Sadas with four verses beginning, "Who indeed is alone? as before (10). The Brahman and the Udgātṛ [converse] with the verse, "I ask thee" (11).
Again, as before, behind the Uttaravedi, they converse with the verse, "What was it that was? (12).
"And who are the two northern ones of Katya?
(13) "I, the sacrificer, am asking you, O Adhvaryu," (14) "This is the altar," says the Adhvaryu. (15)
He proceeds with the greatness of the *sarvahuta* offering; he offers with the verse, "That which you [did] today" (RV 10.88.19).
16. Or rather, there is the taking up [of the oblation] here. 17. He proceeds with the omenta (*vapā*). 18.
Goats, kids, and rams are designated as "animals" according to their respective genders (Sūtra 19). Because the word used in the injunction is a quality-denoting term (Sūtra 20),
and because there is no mention [of such animals] in the archetype (prakṛti) (Sūtra 21).
Some [perform] twenty-one offerings for the deities of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, excluding the Pitṛs and the Traiyambaka offerings (22).
Some [perform] the Aindrāgna, Vaiśvadeva, and Kāya offerings (23).
However, according to the system of the deities, [the sacrifice is performed] as a single unit (24).
Not because of a difference in time;
at the end of the omentum-offering, he offers with the second [oblation] as before, saying, "He who [sacrificed] at night";
the cooking of the horse's remains takes place on the spit.
Having performed [the rites] from the crawling forward until the offering of the final breath,
he cuts off the blood into a copper vessel from the throat of the *gomṛga* and from a horse's hoof;
and [he cuts off] the portions for the *prājāpatya* offerings upon branches of the *vetasa* reed.

Or, having offered a spit-roasted portion of the horse between the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *vanaspati* offerings, he makes oblations from the limbs of the horse to the deities, saying "Svāhā to such-and-such," for each deity individually, beginning with the hoof and ending with the skin,
and also for those parts beyond the muzzle.
With the two sections beginning with "mā no mitra," he recites verse by verse; the final verse belongs to Dyāvāpṛthivī.
At the end of the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, he offers the blood according to the rule with the formula: "To the Agnis Sviṣṭakṛts, svāhā! (6–8).
Or [he offers] with a horse-hoof at the end of the after-offerings (anuyāja) (9);
or with an iron [implement] at the end of the offerings to the wives (patnīsaṃyāja) (10);
and the two-footed verses beginning with "imā nu kam" (11).
The Atirātra is the last [sacrifice].
(12) It consists of all the Stomas, or it may be the Jyotis, Gaur, Āyus, Abhijit, Viśvajit, Mahāvrata, or Aptoryāma.
(13) In the Aptoryāma, the final night-round (rātriparyāya) follows the Tiro’hnīya chants. (14)
There are two offerings to Prajāpati at the Agniṣṭha.
At the conclusion of the Avabhṛtha sacrifice, while submerged in the waters, he offers an oblation upon the head of a man who is tawny, bald, perspiring, and white-haired, saying: "To Jumbaka, svāhā!
When the sacrificer has emerged from the water, those who have committed evil deeds enter [the water] without having performed their vows.
They are known as purified by the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha),
or else there are various purificatory baths (avabhṛtha);
for the first two [cases], it extends up to the killing of the jar-like [victim].
In the remaining case, because of the absence of the initiation vow (dīkṣā-vrata), [the rule applies]; or rather, everything [applies] because of the Vedic revelation;
there are twenty-one *anūbandhya* animals.
At the conclusion of the Udavasānīyā offering, the wife gives [the cows] according to the agreement, along with their attendants (24).
She gives the maiden and the Pālāgalī cow to the Adhvaryu (25);
or rather, she gives the attendants, because the others are intended for the fruit [of the sacrifice] (26).
And because it is not specifically prescribed [as a substitute],
during the twelve-day sacrifice, there should be either a cake for Agni (āgneya-puroḍāśa) or the Brahma-rice porridge (brahmaudana).

At each season, he immolates six animals: six for spring and so forth—those dedicated to Agni, Indra, Parjanya, the Maruts, Mitra-Varuṇa, Indra-Viṣṇu, Indra, and Indra-Bṛhaspati. (30) The Puruṣamedha sacrifice involves twenty-three days of initiation for one who desires preeminence;
it is for both Brāhmaṇas and Rājanyas. (1–2)
Between the Agniṣṭoma and the Atirātra, there is the Ukthya section;
there is a set of eleven sacrificial posts (yūpaikādaśinī);
there are as many Agniṣomīya animals.
When about to dedicate the sacrificial animals at the Atirātra, he offers three oblations, verse by verse, with the mantra "O God Savitṛ...

(RV 3.62.10–12). Having dedicated the animals of the set of eleven (aikādaśina) as well as the Brāhmaṇa and the others, at the time of the formal assignment (niyoga), he assigns the first forty-eight [animals] to the Agniṣṭha post.
In the other eleven [cups], there are eleven [verses] each (9).
When the second has been raised, Brahmā praises the remaining appointed [cups] with the *anuvāka* beginning "Thousand-headed" (*sahasraśīrṣā*), just as the Hotṛ does (10–11).
They release the Brāhmaṇas and others, as in the case of the *kapiñjala* birds and so forth (12).
Between the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *vanaspati* offerings, he makes oblations to the deities of the persons (13).
Including the persons, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is like that of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) (14).
The entire property belongs to the Brāhmaṇa priest. 15.
For each deity, there are three *anūbandhya* animals; five are for the last one. 16.

At the end of the *traidhātavī* sacrifice, having consigned the two fires into himself and having performed the worship of Sūrya, he should go to the forest with the anuvāka beginning "From the waters you were gathered," and without looking back, he shall not return. 17.
One who desires to dwell in a village or in the forest [should perform] the Sarvamedha for one who desires all things; it consists of ten nights. 18, 1–2.
Agni is the highest (3).
There are three Agniṣṭut Ukthyas: the Indra-stut, the Sūrya-stut, and the Vaiśvadeva-stut. The Vrata, the Vājapeya, and the Aptoryāma—everything he offers in this sacrifice (4).
He offers the skins of the Avapāka plants (5).
He offers every kind of food at the end of the omentum-offering, including the cutting of herbs and forest trees;
and also at the third pressing, once the oblations have been offered.
The Āśvamedhika [stoma] is the middle one in the place of the vow (9);
the Pauruṣamedhika belongs to the Vājapeya (10); the Triṇava and Trayastriṃśa are two Ukthya sacrifices (11).
The Atirātra Viśvajit [is performed];
the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is as in the Puruṣamedha, including the land;
the Pitṛmedha [is performed] when the year is not remembered.
Or on odd-numbered days, or under a single lunar mansion, or on the new moon day.
In the months of Nidāgha, Śarad, and Māgha,

they take as many jars as there would be [bodies] to be carried out, along with an unlimited number of umbrellas; having brought the bodies near the village, they place them upon a bed in a jar, cover them with a new cloth, and while iron vessels are being struck and a lute is being played, the ministers walk around three times, fanning them with upper garments or fans.
Or women; (8) during the first, middle, and last watches of the night; (9) and this [is] food that has been carried away by crows. (10)
And it is like dancing, singing, and instrumental music.
(11) Some bring food to him.
(12) At dawn, the sacrificial gifts go forth with his body. (13)
As if the sun were to rise upon one who is performing [the rite],
on a slope that heats up,
on saline soil, or on ground sloping toward the north or level ground.
Some [say it should be] sloping toward the south (17);
[it should be] out of sight from the village (18);
[and] far from the path (19).
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after *nyagrodha*, *aśvattha*, *tilvaka*, *haridru*, *sphūrjaka*, *bibhītaka*, and words having the sense of "sin"; 20.
and as in the case of *citi*; 21.
[the suffix *cha* is applied] after *śamvat* and *kamvat*; 22.
To the west, a variegated [color]; 23. in its absence, water to the north; 24.
[the pit] should be filled with *vīraṇa* grass. 25.

Having erected a splinter of wood at the edge of the village, one should not set it down within the houses; rather, one should raise it. (26) One measures a man's length toward the corners of the quarters. (27) It is broader on the north side and at the rear. (28)
Having dwelt [there], he drives stakes into the corners:
a palāśa stake in the east, and śamī, vāraṇa, and deha stakes in the others;
the deha stake is the vṛtra stake.
Having cast away the rope with which it was encircled by means of a *palāśa* branch, saying, "May those who have departed go away," he sweeps [the site] with the branch.
(32) Having thrown out the southern branch, he encloses [the altar] with enclosing-stones (*pariśrit*), as before, using an unlimited number.
(33) When the ploughs made of *udumbara* wood are being yoked to the six-bull team from the north, having given the command, "Yoke [them]," he mutters the verse, "Savitṛ [has yoked] thee. (34)
Along each furrow, he plows four furrows with the mantra "May Vāyu purify," reciting a separate mantra for each.
The first furrow is from the north toward the west;
in the middle, there are an unlimited number of furrows, performed silently.
Having unyoked the oxen with the formula, "May they be released," he throws away the plough towards the south with the verse, "In the Ashvattha tree... He sows all kinds of herbs.
With the verse, "Savitṛ [has impelled] thee," he pours down the bones in the middle.
Another person silently sprinkles a water-pot after having run through [the field] without pausing towards the south.
When the breath has returned, he mutters the verse, "May death go far away" (RV 10.18.2.7).
Having arranged [the bricks] according to their respective parts with the verse, "May the wind be auspicious" (RV 10.183.1), he places an unmarked brick silently in the center.
At the ends of each direction, he places three bricks each, facing outward, unmarked, and measuring one foot.
Having taken earth from a fissure or having scraped it from all sides except the east,
there are pebbles not piled with fire;
the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa has an upward measurement.
The chest of a Kṣatriya (13),
or with arms raised (14);
the thighs of a Vaiśya (15).
The lap for a woman; the knee for a Śūdra;
or for all [castes], below the knee.

Having covered it with *avakā* plants and *kuśa* grass (19), if the ground has been ploughed, one should sow barley (20). Having dug crooked trenches to the south, they fill them with milk and water; seven [trenches] to the north are filled with water, facing east (21).
They throw three stones each with the verse "The stone-bearing... (RV 10.53.8). They step upon the stones with the verse "The stone-bearing... (RV 10.53.9).
They wipe away evil with *Apāmārga* plants with the formula "Away the evil... (VS 3.47).

Having bathed with the verse "May we be dear to the gods" (*sumitriyā naḥ*) and wearing unwashed garments, they follow behind the tail of a bull while holding onto it, reciting "The bull" (*anaḍvāham*) and "Upwards we two" (*ud vayam*).
They proceed until they reach a clod of earth at the boundary between the village and the cemetery, where he places it with the verse "This [clod] for the living" (*imaṃ jīvebhyaḥ*).

Having applied collyrium and ointment, having strewn grass around the *aupāsana* fire, and having placed enclosing sticks made of *vāraṇa* wood, he offers one oblation with a *vāraṇa* ladle, saying: "O Agni, the lives; may I be long-lived, O Agni" (*agna āyūṃṣy āyuṣmān agne*).
Then he recites their entrustment: "These have led the cow around" (28).
He throws out [the fire] toward the *aupāsana* fire by a way other than the door, saying: "The flesh-eater" (29).
He mutters: "Right here is this one" (30).
A throne with a cushion is the sacrificial fee; likewise, a draft-ox and barley—everything that is old. If there is more, he may choose it. 31. Now, the one-day sacrifices (ekāha): 1.
In the absence of a specific statement, the Agniṣṭoma [is the model]. 2.
The earth is the sacrificial fee for the *dhenu*; light is [the fee] for the two *ukthya* rites, *go* and *āyus*. 3–5.
The Abhijit and Viśvajit sacrifices;
(in the Abhijit) a thousand [cows] are the sacrificial fee for the Abhijit,
or alternatively, one hundred horses.
The thousand [cows] consisting of all one's possessions belong to the Viśvajit sacrifice.
(9) Having excluded the eldest son from the inheritance, [the gift belongs] to all [sons] because of the specific nature of the yoga, with the exception of land and Śūdras.
(10) Or rather, there is a gift to a Śūdra, because it is seen [in scripture] and because it does not contradict [the rules]. (11)
Because there is no substance [for it], its end is [determined] by that;
or rather, its completion is enjoined by the scriptural mention of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath);
and because of the instruction regarding the *dīkṣā*s (initiatory rites).
Not so, because of equality (15); nor in [the case of] magnitude, because everything would be without distinction (16);
or rather, it is greater, because of the favoring of the primary cause (17).
Not so, because of impermanence (18),
and because of the word "action" (19).
Having emerged from the *avabhṛtha* bath, they put on two reddish-brown garments with their fringes and tails intact (20).
He dwells for twelve nights carrying a hoe like an *ukhā* (fire-pan),
or one made of *udumbara* wood,
and also a turban.
Three sets of three [verses] (24);
subsisting on roots and fruits by an udumbara tree (25); among the Niṣādas (26).
The *jana* is the twenty-seventh; the *jana* is the Vaiśya, and the *rājanya* is the *samānajana*, according to the Śruti. (28–29)
The Niṣādas shall eat village food and drink from earthenware vessels (30).
They shall not beg for alms for one year (31),
nor shall they refuse what is being given to them (32).
Or one may sacrifice with the two Yamas,
either in the eastern and western [sacrificial grounds] simultaneously, or in the southern and northern sacrificial grounds.
To the south of the Abhijit [hall] (36); the Patnīśāla [hall] is to the north (37);
there are no officiating priests (ṛtvij) [in this case] (38).
Or rather, because they are abundant,
these very [verses] are equal to those outside the Vedic [collection],
while the others are not.
In the *Karmasannipāta*, each preceding [sacrifice] is the *Abhijit*. 42.
For each [of these], the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is one thousand [cows]. 43.
The *Sarvajit* is characterized by a great vow (*mahāvrata*), involves initiation for a year, a pressing of Soma for seven days, and three or six *upasads*. 44.
The initiations are like fire (45).
He gives a chariot drawn by a hundred horses to the Adhvaryu while the fire-altar is being built (1);
to the Udgātṛ at the time of the vow (2).
At the time of the *śastra* for the *hotṛ*, three; then for the *brahman*, four; at the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), one thousand for all.
There are four thousand [cows], with a thousand as the sacrificial fee (sahasradakṣiṇā). 6.
The third is the Ukthya sacrifice. 7.
It consists of the Jyotis, Viśvajyotis, and Sarvajyotis [stomas], and is equal to a three-night (trirātra) rite. 8.
There are six Sadyaskras. The first [is for those] desiring heaven, desiring cattle, or having rivals.
A white horse with a golden ornament on its forehead is the sacrificial fee.
In the absence of a horse, a cow [is substituted]; 12. He gives that to the Udgātṛ; 13.
There is no cessation of the original [gift], because of its connection with the Udgātṛ. 14.
Cessation [of the ritual] occurs due to the connection with the sacrifice;
[this applies] to one person because of a scriptural statement;
for those desiring freedom from long illness, stability, and food, there is a second [alternative].

The sacrificial fee consists of twenty-one horses, or a single horse; 18. For one who has fewer [horses], there is a substitute; 19. The sacrificial fee consists of a hundred [cows] together with a horse, or a single horse; 20.
The Viśvajit sacrifice is for a craftsman (21). One should perform it in a country possessing the requisite materials and give to them according to their capacity (22).
To those of noble birth, one should give horses (23).
