In the eastern regions, there are twenty-four elephants;
in the northern regions, there are mule-drawn chariots; or else, there is a substitute consisting of one's entire property.
A cow, a bull, a furrow, grain, a pair of slaves, a kitchen, a ladder, a pavilion, and a bed; 27.
For one practicing exorcism, a hawk [is the sacrificial fee]; that place where plants do not grow is the site for the sacrifice to the gods. 2.
Or it may be burning; or it may be cut from the trunk of a tree; or it may be stripped of its bark.
It should slope toward the south;
the sacrificial post (yūpa) is without a wooden ring (acaṣāla) and has a wooden sword (sphya) at its top; it is made of *tailva* wood or *bādhaka* wood.
The fuel-stick is made of Vibhītaka wood; the sacrificial grass is made of Śara reeds;
the two pressing-boards are made of Śyena wood.
The two chariots are the two *havirdhāna* sheds; the animal to be sacrificed for Agni Rudravat is red;
the officiating priests proceed wearing red garments and red turbans.
Wearing the sacred thread around the neck (nivīta), with unstrung bows, and carrying quivers.

He gives nine new sacrificial fees for each of the liṅgas—consisting of one-eyed, lame, hump-backed, mutilated, and emasculated men—or for nine men, because of the entitlement to give; or there is the leading away of the ordinary [victim] separately. 18–20.
At the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), they should pierce this [cow] with thorns. 21.
For those who have not been tormented, there is clarified butter for those who have been tormented. 22.
It follows the ritual rules of the Sādyaska sacrifice, provided she wears a golden garland. 23.
In the Ekatrika sacrifice, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is one hundred and sixty-six [cows]. 24.
The rules for the Sādyaskra sacrifice are as follows: 25.
Beginning with the initiation (dīkṣā), everything is performed on the same day. 26.
He immolates the sacrificial animals together. 27.
Or rather, there is a cake-offering (puroḍāśa) in the place of the one for Agni-Soma. 28.
At the end of the omentum-offerings, there is the cessation of the Subrahmaṇyā litany. 29.
The officiating priests dwell in every direction; the Hotṛ priest is one *yojana* to the east,
while the others are at intervals of one *krośa* each.
The Udgātṛ [stands] to the north (33),
the Adhvaryu behind, and the Brahman to the south (34).
They bring them forward with four horse-chariots and water-skins filled with milk (35).
As many times as the horse [is struck], 36;
then fresh butter for the clarified butter, 37;
a three-year-old bull with testicles for the purchase of Soma, 38.
The sacrificial altar is the fertile field; 39. one settles upon the cooked rice or barley grains; 40. the threshing floor is the northern altar (uttaravedi). 41.
A threshing floor for grain [is used] because of the indicative mark (pratyaya) [at ŚB 3.5.1.26].
42. Those [deposits] which are around the altar (vedi), they place in the region of the Uttaravedi, because of the indicative mark [at ŚB 3.5.1.27].
43. Or rather, a threshing floor for dust [is used], because there is no specific indicative mark [to the contrary] and because it favors the original model (prakṛti). 44.
The threshing-post serves as the sacrificial post; the plough-pole serves as the *caṣāla* (top-ring) for the sake of the *kalāpī*;
and because of the mention of "completed" [forms], there is the cessation of the archetypal [details].
There is no cessation from possession [of a defect] due to [the performance of a rite].
48. Or rather, it is like the case of *urvarā* and so forth, because of the proximity of a second [instance].
49. There are four *vrātyastoma* sacrifices. 1.
The second [rite] is the Ukthya. 2.
Those of the Vrātya-gaṇa who are accomplished should sacrifice with the first; 3.
those who are censured and cruel, with the second. 4.
By the third [term], the youngest (kaniṣṭhāḥ) [are indicated];
by the fourth, the eldest (jyeṣṭhāḥ); and by that [fifth term], those who have passed their procreative age, the elders (sthavirāḥ), are designated.
Among them, whichever one is the most cruel, or the wealthiest, or the most learned in the Vedas—of him they should undergo initiation at the *gārhapatya* fire.
They should remain sitting, partaking of his sacrificial food (*bhakṣa*).
These are the possessions of the *vrātya*.

The horse's hoof is the *tiryaṅnaddha* (transverse-fastened) *uṣṇīṣa*; the whip is the *pratoda*. 11. The bowstring is the *jyā*; that which is unfit for use is called the *dhanus* (bow). 12. The garment is the *kṛṣṇaśaṃ* (black-spotted) *kadru*. 13.
It should be non-black or black-fringed, and be called by that name; 14. A *vipatha* is one covered with wooden planks; 15.
Some say it should be yoked to two horses or mules that are trembling. 16.
A silver coin (niṣka), 17;
on a skin with its flanks attached, black and white, made of wool, 18;
that belongs to the householder, 19.

In the same way, the others [wear] skins (ajināni). 20. [They wear] garments made of wool with fringes, having two tufts at the ends; these are called by their respective names, being either with red borders or black borders. 21. There are two cords (dāmanī), each consisting of two [strands]. 22.
And some say that the two sandals should be black and have straps.
At the time of the sacrificial fee, they should give the wealth of the *vrātyas* to a pseudo-Brahmin from the Magadha country;
or rather, to those who do not cease from the conduct of *vrātyas*.
"For they go cleansing themselves in those very [fires]," so says the Śruti.
(26) They should give thirty-three sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) each. (27) According to some, the householder [should give] double. (28)

Having sacrificed with the Vrātyastoma, they should desist from the state of being Vrātyas; they become fit for social intercourse. The Agniṣṭut is for those who desire spiritual luster, vigor, food, and stability, and for one who might consider himself as if unpurified.
And [the rule applies] to one whose sacrifice has failed (yajñavibhraṣṭa) 32;
or from which they might fail (vibhraṃśeran) 33;
there is a specific rule in the Chāndogya according to one's desire 1.
The Subrahmaṇyā belongs to Agni; likewise according to the specific praise; some say everything [belongs to Agni].
One should give according to one's enthusiasm: (5) bulls, gold, horses, goats, and sheep belonging to the Āgneyas;
(6) four [cows] for the Trivṛt [stoma]. (7)
The first sacrifice desired is one with an unexpressed morning pressing (aniruktaprātaḥsavana);
it is for one desiring a village, or [for any sacrificer].
The sacrificial fee is a chariot drawn by four horses, one of which is a dark-grey horse.
The Bṛhaspatisava is for one who desires splendor, sacred luster, and the office of domestic priest.
He offers the oblations to the gods.
He draws the cup as if accompanied by the *atigrāhya* libations, with the verse: "O Bṛhaspati, that which surpasses the enemy... (RV 2.23.15).
The Bārhaspatya [cup] is to be offered as a reproachful oblation (upālambhya). 14.
When the Nārāśaṃsa goblets have been set down at the morning pressing, without removing them, he assigns eleven sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇā). 15.
At the midday pressing, there are twelve including a horse. 16.

He removes both sets [of sacrificial utensils]. (17) There are eleven [verses] at the third pressing. (18) The removal takes place at the end of the offering of the omentum of the Anūbandhya animal. (19)
And the exceeding of all [these] may be eleven hundred, or eleven thousand.
At the midday pressing, however,
there is additionally a horse; it is consecrated with clarified butter like the Vājapeya sacrifice upon a black antelope skin,
or with the remnants of the Śukra and Manthin cups.
But from others he should receive a salutation (26).
He should not descend [from his status] (27).
They should call him "sthapati" (architect/chief) (28).

That king whom the Brahmins should place at their head shall sacrifice with this [rite]. (29) The arrow should fly like a hawk. (30) For one who desires death, there is the *sarvasvāra* sacrifice. (1)
The sacrificial fee consists of prepared food; 2.
at the initiation and other rites, one merely smells the portions to be consumed; 3. for those [soma-less sacrifices], there is the disposal of the remnants into water. 4.
While the Ārbhava Pavamāna is being chanted, he lies down to the south of the Udumbara post on a black antelope skin, with his head toward the south and covered.
(5) He dies right there. (6) If he should live, they should perform the Dairghaśravasa rite for him in his own *yajñāyajñiya* stotra. (7)
If [the sacrificer] dies, [the ritual] ends with that, because the purpose [of the sacrifice] has ceased to exist (8).
Having thrown the sacrificer’s vessels, the *ṛjīṣa*, and the sacrificial offerings into the *āhavanīya* fire, they may go as they please (9).
Or rather, there is completion [of the ritual], because of the injunction for both (10).
At the conclusion of the *samiṣṭayajus* offering, the bringing of the wood [is performed] with the verse, "They have impelled you together" (*saṃ tvā hinvanti*).

(11) The carving [is performed] with the verse, "They have fashioned you together" (*saṃ tvā tatakṣuḥ*). (12) The washing [is performed] with the verse, "They have moistened you together" (*saṃ tvā riṇanti*). (13)
"May they groom you together"—with this [verse], as if with a stool, he brings him to the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath).

Having brought him to the *avabhṛtha* by means of a stool, having sprinkled him, and having covered him with the Soma-wool-wrapper, at the end of the offering of the omentum of the *anūbandhya* animal, he has all his hair, beard, and body-hair shaved on the southern corner of the altar. This is also the procedure for one who has maintained the sacred fires until death.

At the conclusion of the *anūbandhyā* sacrifice, having brought the fires from the middle of the altar to the southern part of the *āgnīdhra*, the *udgātṛ* sings three times with the *yāma* chant over the fire deposited on the altar facing southward with its head toward the north, using the verse beginning "In the sky, the eagle... (RV 10.149.1).

When the smoke reaches [the fire], he recites: "Your smoke, O brilliant one, spreads forth... (RV 10.149.2). When the fire is reached, [he recites]: "O Agni, be gracious, O great one... (RV 10.149.3).
Or [the sacrifice may be completed] by one of the two ways mentioned in verse 19; or at the end of the *udavasānīyā* offering, because the whole is finished (verse 20);
if he should live, it is by this very undertaking; if he should wish to die, [it is likewise]. (Verse 21)
Or one may desire to live [longer] (22). Three [priests] are to be excluded from the office of the *ṛtvij* (23).
It is the *sarvastoma* sacrifice (24).
Having separated the two final days of the Chandomas,
there are four Vācastomas (25);
there is a specific rule regarding these in the Chāndogya (26–27).

The *pṛṣṭhya-stomas* are the *trivṛt*, *pañcadaśa*, *saptadaśa*, *ekaviṃśa*, *triṇava*, and *trayastriṃśa*. According to the Śruti, "In the three seasonal festival positions (*parvasthāna*), the *pārṣṭhika-pṛṣṭhas* are distributed. Thus, at the position of the Vaiśvadeva, the first [is performed]. 28. The *Cāturmāsya* Soma sacrifices [are performed] at the three festival positions; the *pārṣṭhika-pṛṣṭhas* are distributed, as stated in the Śruti.
At the position of the Vaiśvadeva, the first [is performed]. 2.
3. The cake offering; 4. the preparation of the high altar;
5. the tethering of the animal to the enclosing stick.
In the second [period], there is the two-day rite called Dvirdiva;
some say the Agniṣṭoma is first.
In the third [period], there is the three-day rite, with the Atirātra as the last.
Some [say] the Agniṣṭoma is first;
[it is] the Jyotiṣṭoma in the place of the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice.
There are five Savanīya offerings: those dedicated to the Viśvedevas, Varuṇa, the Maruts, Agni, and Indra-Agni.
In the sixth [day], there are eleven [animals] for each; in the seventh, eleven for Vāyu;
every day he gives fifty and fifty; in the last [day], one hundred and twelve.
Or there are fifty calves born according to the seasons; 15. there is a purificatory bath at every ritual juncture; 16. during the intervals between the junctures, he wears unwashed (new) cloth. 17.
He avoids sexual intercourse (18), he does not eat meat (19),
and there are the Anubandhyā cows dedicated to Bṛhaspati, Mitra-Varuṇa, Sūrya, and Aśvin, according to the procedure for the Avabhṛtha bath (20).
The *pratikarma-soma* sacrifices are twenty-one:
the *agnyādheya*, *punarādheya*, *agnihotra*, *darśapūrṇamāsa*, *dākṣāyaṇa-āgrayaṇa*, the *ukthya*, and some include the *paśubandha*. (21–23)
He offers the oblations following the morning pressing (prātaḥsavanīya). 1.
There are two milk-offerings for the two Agnihotra rites. 2.
The final deity is the Anūbandhyā cow; first come the Savanīya offerings. 3.
In sacrifices dedicated to a single deity, both [the *sāmidhenī* verses and the *anuvākyā*] are used; likewise, some say this applies to the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices.
There are five sets of seventeen [verses].
The Upahavya sacrifice, which is undefined, is for one desiring a village,
or for one who is being falsely accused;
a dark-grey horse is the sacrificial fee, and he gives it to the Brahman priest.
For one desiring heaven, there is the Ṛtapeya sacrifice;
there are twelve initiation days and twelve Upasad days; [or] three Upasad days.
Or there are six in each case; or rather, there are twelve because of their being qualities;
he consumes clarified butter as his vow-food.
On the first Upasad day, the *camasa* vessel is filled and measured on all sides by the first joint of the little finger;
on the second day, by the second joint;
and on the third day, by the third joint.
Those intending to consume [the Soma] should speak the truth (19); or those intending to cook it in the sacrificial hall (20);
a Soma-cup made of Udumbara wood is to be given as a sacrificial fee to the Brahman priest who is of the same lineage (21).
Because the *pūtabhṛt* vessel serves all purposes;
(22) some [hold] the *aṃśu* cup, because of the scriptural statement, "With that he should sacrifice"; (23) it is like the horse. (24)
And because of the censure of cattle [in the case of the *paśubandha* sacrifice], [the sacrificer] has two names, possesses much gold, and is difficult to overcome.
At the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering, he gives twelve *māna* measures of gold. 1.25–26.1.
And in the subsequent [sacrifices], each preceding one is doubled. At the Prāyaṇīyā, Ātithyā, and Upasad rites,

at the end of the animal offerings, at each pressing when the Savanamukhīya oblations have been placed, at the Udayanīyā, the Anūbandhyā, and the Udavasānīyā, [the sacrificial fee] consists of a garland for the Udgātṛ and a gold plate for the Hotṛ.
A hundred oxen for all [the priests] at the appropriate time;
5. The Vaiśyastoma is for one who desires cattle or the status of a Vaiśya; 6. The pressings (savana) contain blessings (āśis). 7.
At the morning pressing, the mixing is with fresh milk; at the midday pressing, with boiled milk;
at the third pressing, with curds. The sacrificial gifts are heifers, five years old, speckled.

And there are heifers one year old, two-year-old cows that have not yet calved, five-year-old cows with spotted bellies, those with speckled bellies, those that are ruddy, those that are tawny, and those that are brindled. 11.
For both [the sacrificer and the wife], there are either a thousand or one hundred and twelve [cows]. 12.
For one who has been over-indulged in Soma, the Ukthya sacrifice is performed with strong Soma. 13.
For one who has been deposed from his royal status,
or for those desiring long life, a village, offspring, or cattle,
the Soma sacrifices are as described previously.
They milk a hundred cows for the *āśira* mixture;
that itself is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*);
and there is the consumption [of the soma] during the recitations of the *acchāvāka*.
Among the others, there is smelling [of the soma];
for them alone there is the drawing up [of the cups], according to the Śruti text: "They draw up the Somas one after another.
Both the Adhvaryus and all the Camasādhvaryus respond for the Acchāvāka.
The first of the pairs is for a Kshatriya who desires sovereignty;
he should give twenty-one groups according to his capacity.
The bull belongs to Indra; it is the concluding sacrifice.
For one desiring food, [the sacrifice is] the Virāj;
he should give ten groups according to his ability; the animal sacrifice is dedicated to Agni and is a secondary rite.
For one desiring offspring, there are *upaśads*;
the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is one hundred and twenty-four;
the animal sacrifice for Viśve Devās is the concluding rite of the sacrifice.
For one who, having accepted much [wealth], should think of it as if it were poison, there is the *punastoma* sacrifice, which is an *ukthya*.

(16) The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of twelve pairs for those who have returned [to the vow], according to their ability. (17) There are two animal-sacrifices (*paśukāma-yajña*), both of which are *catuṣṭoma*. (18)
The sixteenth [chapter] follows. 19.
In the former [case], one should give single-hoofed animals according to one's ability; 20. In the latter, both kinds. 21.
And he offers the two oblations, Udbhid and Balabhid, conjoined with the preceding one;
having sacrificed with the former, he must necessarily sacrifice with the latter.
Between these two, there is an arrow-like offering, namely a cake (puroḍāśa) for Agni.
The sacrificial grass-bundle is spread out;
the enclosing sticks are provided with arrows;
[this is performed] for half a month, a month, or a year.
The Gāyatrī [meter] with twenty-four feet is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), according to one's ability; 28.
For one desiring honor, there is the *apaciti* [sacrifice]; 29. Some say these two are sacrifices for kings (*rājayajña*). 30.
A sacrificial gift consisting of a horse-chariot with four yokes on both sides (31),
a bronze armor (32),
and horses worthy of a hundred (33).
The two Agnistomas with the piling of the fire-altar have initiation rites for all-conquering [victory];
the former is the Pakṣya and the latter is the Jyotis.
There are four Dhānyācita offerings, and four [cows] each as the sacrificial fee.
For the former [rite], there are six oxen; for the latter, four oxen. (2) The Ṛṣabha and Gosava [rites] are both for the king. (4)
The sacrificial fee consists of a thousand bulls, or twelve hundred;
this Ukthya sacrifice, the Gosava, has ten thousand as its fee.
Some say it is the sacrifice of a Vaiśya.
He whom the people together with the king place at their head should perform this sacrifice.
He is consecrated upon a leveled mound (sthaṇḍila) to the south of the Āhavanīya fire using the *pratiduh* vessel.
They should address him as "the builder" (*sthapati*).
The Marutstoma, characterized by the sacrificial fee of the Vaiśyastoma, is a group-sacrifice (gaṇayajña) for brothers or friends.
(11) The Aindrāgnakulāya is for those desiring offspring or cattle.
(12) The Dviyajña, characterized by the sacrificial fee of a family, is for two brothers or two friends. (13)
The *Indrastoma* is a royal sacrifice with a thousand as the sacrificial fee (14).
The *Ukthya* (15).
For one desiring the office of domestic priest, there is the *Indrāgnistoma* (16).
Or [the sacrifice may be performed] by the king and the royal priest together as sacrificers (17),
or separately (18);
the sacrificial fee for the Brāhmaṇa consists of a cow corresponding to the Gāyatrī (19).
The two *jagatī* verses for a king; [the two] *vighana* verses for one desiring cattle or for one practicing sorcery.

Those consisting of *bṛhatī*s are for one desiring cattle; those well-known [as such] are for one practicing exorcism; those shaped like tongs and like a thunderbolt are for one practicing malevolent magic.
The *ṣoḍaśin* is a *vajra* [stotra]; 26.
The *lohakarṇī* cow of *śuṇṭhādhī* is the purchase-price cow (*somakrayaṇī*) for the *ṣoḍaśin*; 27.
Because there is no distinction even in the case of a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*). 28.
And the Viśvajit and the Parivāsa [should be performed];
or rather not, because of their connection with their own [original] context;
one should perform the Ekarāja sacrifice alone as a counter-rite against the former.
One should employ the *vajra* [verse] for the countryside; 32.
one should apply it to Vena in reverse order;
33. having pacified or having strewn [the ground], one should sacrifice with the *pratiṣṭhāman* for the sake of peace, for the sake of peace. 34.
1. The twelve Upasads constitute the Ahīna sacrifices, concluding with the month.
2. The consecrations (dīkṣās) are determined by the remainder of the Soma-pressings and the Upasads.
3. They range from two days up to twelve days.
In that regard, some [include] the Atirātras because they are not mentioned [therein];
[they include] the days of the ten-night sacrifice (*dāśarātrika*) by adding one day at a time to the two-day periods and so forth, because the qualities of those [days] are observed;
[and they include] those with a thousand-fold sacrificial fees (*sahasradakṣiṇā*).
In sacrifices lasting four nights and more, [the fee] is either increased [by one thousand each day],
or the standard [one thousand] is given every day;
in the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, ten thousand [gold pieces].
He gives them equally divided every day; on the final day, there are thirteen additional *atirātra* rites,
and four initial *aṣoḍaśika* rites.
The *navasaptadaśa* [stoma] is for one desiring offspring;
the *viṣuvant* is for the eldest son of the eldest wife;
the *gaura* [sāman] is for one who has rivals.
For one desiring heaven, [the sacrifice lasts] seventeen [days];
or for one who is ill.
For those desiring prosperity, cattle, Vedic luster, vigor, food, and stability, respectively, there are the Jyotiṣṭoma, Viśvajit, Trivṛt, Pañcadaśa, Saptadaśa, and Ekaviṃśa [sacrifices].
The Aptoryāma [is for one] from whom cattle might indeed fall away; the Abhijit [is for one] who has rivals;
the Sarvastoma [is for one] desiring prosperity.
In this [sacrifice], there is a set of eleven sacrificial posts (yūpaikādaśinī); three two-day rites (dvyaha) follow;
and in the latter two [days], there are Atirātras without the Ṣoḍaśin cup.
The Āṅgirasa, Caitraratha, and Kāpivana [are the stomas];
some say that the second Ukthya comes first.
One who has been deprived of his prosperity, as it were, should sacrifice with the first [stoma].
With the second [offering], one desiring offspring;
with the third, one desiring heaven or cattle. There are three sets of five.
The Garga, Baida, Chandoma, Antarvasu, and Parāka [sacrifices]—the second set of three Trivṛt Atirātras are all for one desiring sovereignty;
the Antarvasu is for one desiring cattle. 9–11.
The Parāka penance is for one desiring heaven;
there are four [types] of four-day [penances];
Atri, Caturvīra, Jāmadagna, Vasiṣṭha, Saṃsarpi, and Viśvāmitra.
The son of Jamadagni is consecrated for twenty days for one desiring prosperity; there are fifteen *upasads* involving sacrificial cakes;
he offers the *anūpasad* oblations.
The properties of clarified butter [apply] due to the displacement of the locus (18); or the properties of the medicinal herbs [apply] due to the commonality of the substance (19);
and the sacrificial cakes are subordinate to the oblations (20).

By means of the addition of the *pratyupasada* oblations, there are the potsherds for those [sacrifices] beginning with the single-potsherd offering: namely, those dedicated to Agni, Aśvin, Viṣṇu, Soma, Savitṛ, Dhātṛ, the Maruts, Bṛhaspati, Mitra-Varuṇa, Indra, and the Viśvedevas.
(21) Their oblation: "O Agni, perform the office of the Hotṛ; perform the sacrifice! Bring hither Vaiśvānara Pitṛ for protection! O Indra, offer the oblation to the gods! Svāhā! (2)

There is an Agniṣṭut, an Indrastut, a Sūryastut, and a Vaiśvadevastut, each performed with a single [stotra].
Or [the Soma sacrifice may be performed] with the Trikadruka cups for the Ahīnas and Ekāhas, except for the Aptoryāma and the Rājasūya, using one cup at a time;
or alternatively, by means of the Go and Āyus sacrifices.
In the event that repetition is not possible, the Jyotiṣṭoma serves as the filler.

Having performed the praise (stotra), the stotriya, the luster (varcas), or the Sāman, the Yajus, the day (ahan), or any other [component] as previously described, one should sacrifice. (19) This is done by way of transposition at the end. (20) There is no end to these. (21)

The *ayanam* for those who perform the *utsarga* consists of variations of the *gavāmayana*. (22) Having performed five *ukthya* days and three *abhiplava* periods, they proceed to the fourth [period] consisting of four *ukthya* days. (23) Or, there may be the abandonment of the *stoma* on a single day. (24)
Or else, there is the performance of the sacrificial procedure for the animal; or rather, there is non-commencement [of the sacrifice];
or it is an option regarding the *tāpaścita* [rite]. 25–27.
This very Prāyaṇīya Atirātra should constitute the entire Sattra, with the Pṛṣṭhas as previously specified. 28. Now another [option]: 29.
Four Jyotiṣṭomas and the Abhijit [constitute] six months. 30.
The *vrata* sacrifice at the *viṣuvat* stage (31);
the four *Viśvajit-jyotiṣṭoma*s by which one attains the highest (32).
This is the supreme [attainment] of the Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa; this is the supreme [attainment] of the Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa (33).
When a transgression occurs during the performance of a rite, the expiation is to be performed at that very time;
or rather, it may be enjoined for another time because of the word [indicating] "time"; or rather, it is to be performed at that time because of the specific cognition [of the occasion].
In the absence of a specific instruction, the offering of the Mahāvyāhṛtis is performed by the Hotṛ priest; with "Bhūḥ" at the Gārhapatya fire,
and with "Bhuvaḥ" at the Dakṣiṇāgni fire by the Adhvaryu priest.
In the Āgnīdhrīya fire during the Soma sacrifice, [the word] "Svar" is used for the Audgātra; in the Āhavanīya fire,
these [oblations] are always taken four times.
And for every expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*), [one offers] with the five [verses] verse by verse;

with the two verses beginning "tvanno agne" (10); and with "yāścāgne 'sy anabhiśastipāśca," "satyam it tvam ayā asi," "ayā no yajñam vaha," "ayā no dhehi bheṣajam svāhā," "ye te śataṃ varuṇa ye sahasram," "ye yajñiyāḥ pāśā vitatā mahāntaḥ," "tebhir no adya savitota viṣṇur viśve muñcantu marutaḥ svarkāḥ svāhā," and "ud uttamam" (11).
In the case of an unknown [defect], one offers the Great Vyāhṛtis (*mahāvyāhṛti*) each separately, all together as the fourth, and the *sarvaprāyaścitta*. (12)

If the Agnihotrin cow should sit down, one should make her rise with the *yajus* formula: "The divine Aditi has risen; she has bestowed long life upon the lord of the sacrifice, preparing a portion for Indra, Mitra, and Varuṇa.
(13) Having milked her, he should give her to a Brāhmaṇa whom he does not intend to visit again.
(14) Or, having struck her with a staff or made her rise by force, he should perform the milking. (15)
"And [the verse] beginning with 'adānam' (16), and [the verse] 'aduhānāyām anyām' (17):

if she should low, one should let her eat by pulling up grass, [reciting]: 'O blessed one, may you have good pasture; and may we too be blessed. Eat the grass, O inviolable one, at all times; drink pure water as you move along. (18)
He offers with her milk.
Having enclosed the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire for a red milking, having said, "Step across," and having offered to Rudra in hot ashes, the gift is as before.
The sacrificial substance is what is in the cow that belongs to Rudra.
When it has been approached, it belongs to Vāyu;
while being milked, it belongs to the Aśvins; when milked, it belongs to Soma.
When it has been placed on the fire, it belongs to Varuṇa; when it has risen to the brim, it belongs to Pūṣan;
when it is overflowing, it belongs to the Maruts.
The Bindumat Sārasvata (10), the Śānta Maitra (11), and the Udvāsyamāna of Savitṛ (12).
The portion set aside for Aditi (13),
that which is being lifted for the Viśvedevas (14),
and that which has been lifted for Bṛhaspati (15).
That which is being struck is for Dhātṛ (16);
that which has been struck is for Viśvakarman (17); that which is between the two fires is for Vaiśvānara (18).
The first oblation belongs to Heaven and Earth;
the second to Indra and Agni;
the third to Prajāpati.
The offering to Indra is [performed] twenty-two times.
When [an offering] falls out of its proper time, having offered that which belongs to its respective deity, or having extended that [procedure] by analogy, one should offer with another [substance].
If it should spill, one should touch it with the mantra "It has not spilled; it has been placed within," and then offer with the remainder.

If [the fire] should break out or go out, one should touch it with the expiation for spilled [oblation], pour water over it with the *vyāhṛtis*, and then perform the scattering of ashes over the potsherds with the formula, "O lords of the earth...
(for a *havis*-sacrifice);
"The gods have gone to heaven" (for a *soma*-sacrifice). 25–27.
One should sprinkle water with the mantra "yayorojasā" (VS 34.11).
(28) In the event of the lifting of all [the portions], the spilling of the ladle, or the breaking of the ladle, the sitting remains in that very place.
(29) Having lifted another [portion], one should offer it to him; by means of that, the oblation is performed. (30)
If the Āhavanīya fire goes out after the first oblation has been offered, then what has been stated [in the Śrauta-sūtra] applies:
one should offer a piece of wood or gold, according to the scriptural injunction.

If the Āhavanīya fire should go out after it has been drawn out three times, then, having smeared the places where the water was kept and having churned [a new fire], some say that the evening and morning homas should be performed in that fire once it has been drawn out.
If the Gārhapatya fire goes out, one should rub the two kindling woods together after touching them with the ashes;
or, if the Āhavanīya fire has gone out, one should take it out from that very same [Gārhapatya] fire;
or, having brought [the fire] from elsewhere.
Or [the fire] brought from Upala-rājya (7), or produced by friction (8),
or having been rekindled or not rekindled, having first extinguished it, the oblation is performed as before (9).

If the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire, having been brought three times, should go out, some say that its non-rekindling on that day [constitutes a fault]. (10) If one should rekindle the *āhavanīya* fire while it is still burning, that has already been explained. (11) Having placed it behind or in front, some say that the oblation (*homa*) should be performed in both cases. (12)

At the Abhinidhāna rite, there is a cake for Agni Agnimat; or the worship is performed with the two verses beginning "samitam" (VS 27.29–30); and if the fire is carried away while being taken up, one brings it back with the verse "anv agniḥ" (VS 27.31).
In the absence of a specific instruction, the *puroḍāśa* offering is prescribed everywhere (16).
If the sun sets while the fires have not yet been carried forth, an Ārṣeya Brāhmaṇa should carry forward the fire from the fuel-wood placed behind two pieces of gold tied with *kuśa* grass (17).
There is an oblation to Viṣṇu (18).
And [an offering] to Agni accompanied by Sūrya (19);
at the rising of the moon, the wearing of silver [is prescribed] beforehand (20);
[and finally] the Vaiśvadeva oblation (21).
And [an offering] for the luminous Sūrya; 22.
the extraction [of the oblation] is the same; 23.
or at both [offerings], there are rice-cakes for the Viśvedevas; 24. [the cake is] without a base.
If both [fires] go out, there is either a re-establishment of the fires (punarādheya) or [the establishment] separately,
because they are not prescribed to be established together.
If [the fire] does not arise while being churned, one should fetch Yama from afar and offer oblations into it;
or [offer them] into the hand of a Brāhmaṇa; and there is also the removal of the garments.
Or on the right ear of a goat; 4. fasting for him; 5.
or on a clump of *kuśa* grass; 6.
There is no fixed seat for him; or he may stay in water, according to the Vedic revelation: "One should not feel aversion toward water."
If the sun has risen before the oblation is offered, one should wait until it has set;
having offered the oblation, there is the consecration with "bhūḥ" and the granting of a boon.
In the event of the total loss of the oblations or a defect in them, it has been stated:
(13) or, having calculated [the deficiency], the sacrifice to the deities may be performed with clarified butter; (14) and there is a repetition of the rite. (15)
In the case of a division [of the fire], it is due to either a ritual transformation or a transgression; 16.
when moving between [fires], no heed is paid [to the usual rule]; 17.
in the case of dogs, pigs, and boars, [the offering is made] with the stream of water, facing east, with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇur... 18.
Or with ashes; 19. for Agni Cakrīvān Pathikṛt; 20.
and also upon the failure of a recognized sacrifice (prajñātēṣṭi).
Because of the scriptural teaching that transgression is certain [in these cases]:
(22) when there is confusion regarding the *stotra* and the *śastra*,
and (24) at the death of a person.
Because of the capacity for rebirth, [one should offer] to Svajana;
when tears are shed due to the affliction of one who maintains the sacred fires, [an offering] to Agni Vratapati;
and one should not heed social contact.
If [the fire] has been mixed with the village fire, an oblation is offered to Anukrośa Agni; if it has been mixed with [another] fire, an oblation is offered to Saṃsarga Agni (30).
If [the fires] have become mixed with one another, an oblation is offered to Vivica Agni (31).
If [the fire] has been mixed with a forest fire, an oblation is offered to Saṃvarga Agni (32).
If [the fire] comes from lightning, one should offer to Agni Apsumat; 33. if it comes from an impure place, one should offer to Agni Śuci; 34.
if [a horse] is born among the cattle of his wife, he should offer a cake on thirteen potsherds to the Maruts. 35.

In the event of a house fire, there is a cake offering to Agni Kṣāmavat. (36) If the moon rises while the new-moon sacrifice is already commenced, he should observe the vow prescribed for that [offering] beforehand. (37) He should set aside curd as the means for mixing the sacrificial oblation. (38)

Having mixed the calves with their mothers, they are to be separated again. (39) Or, if the prepared oblation is insufficient for the vow, one should divide the rice grains into three parts: the medium-sized grains for Agni Dātṛ, the largest for Indra Pradātṛ, and the smallest for Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa; [one prepares] a pap in curds and a pap in boiled milk. (40) The Sānnāyya offering is characterized by its preparation. (41)
42. Or rather, [the removal occurs] at another time due to the connection with the sacrifice.
43. The removal of the rice-grains for him [occurs] because of the scriptural statement.
44. [The order] is according to the original model (prakṛti), as before.

Or, if everything is seen subsequently due to an omen, having performed the New Moon sacrifice on that very day or on the following day, one should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt, Indra Vṛtrahan, and Vaiśvānara;
a bow with three arrows is the sacrificial fee.
Or a staff [is the fee];
48 if they are commoners, [the fee is] according to their desire; 49 even for one who has not previously performed [the rite] but desires cattle, [this applies]. 50

If a potsherd should be lost while being removed [from the fire], one should offer an oblation to the Aśvins. At both the evening and morning milkings, if there is a mishap, one should offer a five-śarāva measure of cooked rice or a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) to Indra; for even by breaking [the vessel], a transgression has occurred.
A substitute for that [is prescribed] (4);
or rather, there is expiation because of the mention of the deity (5);
when the *sānnāyya* is unavailable, there is a *caru* offering (6).
7. Or, in the place for milking in the evening, there is a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa). 8. Or, it is like the Sānnāyya offering.
9. A defiled oblation is to be cast away into the water.
10. Or [food] in hot ashes;
11. that which is forbidden as food for the learned is defiled;
12. it is said that [the same applies] to what is disliked by a single person.
Or, if they are due to a combination of all three humors (sānnipātika),
he should, if he so desires, offer the remainder with clarified butter (ājya).
Having remembered [the error] between the two oblations, before the principal sacrifice, he should perform the subsequent offering (anvāhāra).
Either before the *samiṣṭayajus* offering or upon hearing the word "conclusion" (*saṃsthā*), [the rite is completed].
(16) If it has already been offered, one should conclude that very rite and then perform the oblation again.
(17) In the event of a transposition of deities, having given a *puṣkala* gift, one should perform the rite according to the proper sequence. (18)
And in the case of the *avadāna*, the *yājyā*, and the *anuvākyā* [verses], 19.
if the ladle (*sruk*) is damaged, there is a re-taking [of the portion], 20.
or rather from the *dhruvā* [ladle], because of the Vedic revelation: "From that, the sacrifice originates. 21.
Some say that [the butter] should be brought from what is not defective;
22. [there is no bringing] from the *upabhṛt* into the *dhruvā*;
24. if there is a defect in the *ājyasthālī*, another [vessel] should be used.

Or rather, there is no fault, for according to the Śruti: "The gods do not feel revulsion toward anything whatsoever. (25) Having ascertained that [the deity] further, one should sacrifice. (26) Or rather, it is not so, because it is not enjoined by a scriptural statement. (27)

"May King Varuṇa come with the wealthy [waters]; may he stand in this place rejoicing. May our heroes be unharmed; let not my milk be spilled"—with these words, one should touch the *praṇītā* waters if they have been spilled.
(28) "Earth has gone to earth; mother has gone to mother. May we increase through sons and cattle; may he who hates us be shattered"—with these words, one should touch a broken earthen vessel.

(29) "He who, even without a bandage, before the breaking of the collar-bones, is the restorer of the joint, the bountiful Maghavan, the lord of many riches—the healer shall mend the fracture again"—with these words, one should touch the *gharmya* [vessel]. (30)
He offers thirty-four oblations beginning with *parameṣṭhin*.
(1) Having milked the Gharma, [he offers] in the morning before milking and in the evening after milking, using a northern cow.
(2) At the place of milking, he uses another cow. (3)
Or, having offered [an oblation] in front of the shed toward the east,
or on the southern bone-joint from the tail-end, he should have [the cow] milked;
some say this should also be done when the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) has been spilled.

And in the event of the death of a Soma-sacrificer, having offered one oblation at each [proper] time, he causes [the patron] to recite, "The milking of the sacrifice. At the *sutyā* rites, on the *āgnīdhrīya* fire, there is the *udgātṛ*-oblation with the verse, "Flow forth, O you who possess gold. 7. If a crow alights upon the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), he should offer an oblation with the verse, "Spreading out the fragments, generating them;

for he is the glowing one, a wide path for the boon. He, the ruddy one, has risen up at the forefront of the destroyers, when he impelled his own body into his own body, Svāhā! 9. If the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) spills, he should offer an oblation with that same verse.

If the cow that provides the warm milk has been killed by a tiger, one should offer the *spṛt* oblations, saying: "To thee, O Moon, I restore the mind, svāhā! To thee, O Sun, I restore the eye, svāhā! To thee, O Wind, I restore the breaths, svāhā! From the quarters I restore thy hearing, svāhā! From the waters I restore thy blood, svāhā! To the earth I restore thy body, svāhā!
Having offered these, he should say, "Offer another oblation.
If he is unable to perform the oblation himself, he should remain in attendance.
If one is unable to approach [the fire], there is lying down below (13).

If, after the evening oblation has been offered, one should become weak, then the morning oblation is to be performed at that very time, because of the scriptural injunction regarding the completion (*saṃsthā*) of the Agnihotra (1).
If he should live, then again at the proper time (2).
Or rather, it is not so, because [the rite] has already been performed;
like the Agnihotra, the New Moon sacrifice [is completed] at the end of the Full Moon sacrifice.
If death occurs while the sacrificial oblations are being brought forward, one should cremate them on the Dakṣiṇāgni fire.
Or rather, it is not so, because it is illogical:
[the acts] beginning with the drawing [of the cup] take place at the Gārhapatya fire until the placing [of the offering],
and from the placing onwards, they take place at the Āhavanīya fire.
It ends with death;
or it is to be established because it has been so ordained;
and the *homa* offering is like that of the *havir* oblation.
He places the cooking-pots upon the fires in the Sandīpanavatī [hall]. 12. Taking the fires produced by heating, they go southward with the sacrificial body. 13.
[They go] with a cart. 14.
Having prepared a canopy over a level area abounding in grass, he piles the altar between the two fires (15).
Having dug up [the earth] with a milky plant, he places [there] those [plants] called *puruṣāhvā* (16),
as well as *viśākha*, *śara*, *aśmagandhā*, *pṛśniparṇī*, and *adhyāṇḍā* (17).
Having trimmed the hair, beard, nails, and body hair, and having removed the feces, he buries the hair and other parts,
anoints [the body] with clarified butter, and places it upon the funeral pyre; having spread out a black antelope skin with the head toward the east,
he throws seven pieces of gold into the seven openings of the vital breaths, the first one into the mouth.
In his right hand, he places the *juhū* ladle filled with clarified butter (21), as well as the wooden sword (*sphya*) (22); in his left hand, he places the *upabhṛt* ladle (23).
The *dhruvā* ladle on the chest (24), the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle on the mouth (25), and the two *sruva* spoons on the two nostrils (26).

The *prāśitraharaṇa* vessels on the two ears, the *camasa* cup on the head, and the *praṇītāpraṇayana* vessel [on the head]; some also [place] the *kapāla* potsherds [on the head]; the two winnowing baskets on the two sides. 27–29.
In the belly [of the sacrificial animal], one places the *pātrī* vessel containing the *samavattas*, the *dhānās*, and the *pṛṣadājya*; in the penis, the *śamyā* and the two *araṇis*;
between the thighs, the other sacrificial vessels;
and the disposal in water of those made of clay and stone.
Or he may give iron [implements] to the Brahmin. 33.
If it is a sacrificial cow (anustaraṇī), having cut off the right ear, [he places] the kidneys in the hands; 34.
"The limbs upon the limbs," says Jātūkarṇya. 35.
Or rather, [the cremation is performed] from the bones and the cloth-wrapping (sandeha).
Having covered the face with the omentum (vapā), they set it on fire with fires.
The son, the brother, or another Brāhmaṇa offers an oblation, saying: "From this you were born; may he be born again from you for the sake of the heavenly world, svāhā! (36–38)
Having approached without looking back, they touch water (39).

On the fourth day, having fed an odd number of Brāhmaṇas, he turns the bones over with a Palāśa stalk; taking them up again and again with his thumb and little finger, he places them in a Palāśa leaf-cup (1).
[He also places] Śamyā-wood, Avakā plants, and mud in the cremation ground (2).

Having anointed the bones with all kinds of fragrant substances, having dug a trench extending toward the southeast, and having strewn *kuśa* grass within it, he pours [the bones] into this [trench], either with the formula "O garment" (*vastra*) or with turmeric (*hāridra*), saying "Speech" (*vāk*).
This is the Vājasaneyaka version;
or alternatively, by means of this [other rite].

"I deposit you, O [Name], with an unafflicted mind, with speech, with the sacred word (*brahman*), with the threefold knowledge, upon the earth, upon the fly, in the essence of the waters. Thus he says.
(6) For one desiring to construct a burial mound, the collection of the bones is done in a jar. (7) And the deposition is performed silently. (8)

If he should die while away from home, [the performer], wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), having milked a cow that has recently calved, places the vessel on the fire to the south and removes it from the fire;
the carrying of the remains proceeds from that very spot, holding a fuel-stick beneath [the vessel].
Having placed the *kuśa* grass with the tips pointing upward and then toward the south,
having scattered [the offerings] once as for the ancestors,

having brought the bodies and performed the procedure for a male upon a black antelope skin, having covered them with wool and sprinkled them with clarified butter, the cremation is performed as previously described.

Upon the destruction of the body, three hundred and sixty palāśa stalks [are to be offered] on a black antelope skin as before. 15. One should not eat of the new grain until one has performed the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice; nor should one eat after having accepted a gift from an outcast, or having officiated at a sacrifice for two who hate each other, or having accepted a ewe, or having accepted a gift from both [father and mother], or whose fires one might have used to officiate for another, or who might have sacrificed for another. One should offer an oblation to Vaiśvānara. 16. A black garment is the sacrificial fee. 17.
If a portion of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is burnt, one should complete the remaining part and then offer that very same [remainder] again;
for even if only a single part is burnt, [the rite continues] because of the connection [of the whole], and because it is so seen [in scripture]. (Sūtras 18–20)
Not so, because of its permanence (21).
The ritual act is for the sake of the vision (22).
If the animal, having been brought forward, flees, one should dedicate another animal of the same color and the same age to Vāyu and immolate it (1).
If he should die after being assigned [as a victim] for Vāyu—
whether due to an accident or through negligence— before the *prayāja* offerings, one should immolate another.
One should offer the omentum of the first animal in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire.

If it is Soma, [one offers] in the Mārjālīya fire with the formula: "The Pitṛs who have sacrificed, the Pitāmahas who have not sacrificed, those who are worthy of sacrifice and drinkers of Soma—for them this animal has been immolated; to Agni Svāhā! To Yama, well-offered among the gods!
Or rather, there is no removal [of the offering], because there is no defect.
If the omentum is lost, one should not pay heed to it;
however, some say that if the heart is destroyed, one should sacrifice another animal, because of the Vedic revelation: "The heart is the animal.
Alternatively, one may sacrifice clarified butter in place of all the organs.

The statement regarding the animal is merely an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda). If, while being slaughtered, the animal should bleat, one should offer an oblation with the verse: "If the animal has made a sound, or if it strikes itself with its feet on the chest—may Agni release me from that sin and from all distress. And [one should offer] with the two verses beginning with "This for me, O Varuṇa," reciting them verse by verse.

If the vessel for the *sānnāyya* or the *ukhā* should leak, he addresses that [vessel] with the mantra: "We have come to the leaking *ukhā*, which is unbound; Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāyu, Earth, and the intermediate space—whatever has flowed out, whatever has been offered into the fire, let that be ours; may Nirṛti not reach it from beyond.
(14) In the case of the sprouting of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), once the internal ritual procedure (*tantra*) has been completed on that day, he should offer a multi-colored animal to Tvaṣṭṛ.
(1) Having extracted the omentum of the *anūbandhyā* cow, he should cause her to touch the embryo, saying: "Let him seek to obtain [the embryo]. (2)

At the time of the viewing, he should instruct that a cooking pot and a turban be prepared. At the end of the omentum-offering, the Adhvaryu issues the command without looking back: "Draw out this embryo! Having split open the hips, he should instruct that it be drawn out facing westward. He consecrates the embryo as it is being drawn out with the mantra, "Let the ten-month-old stir," and the cutting of portions for the embryo is performed like that of an animal victim.
Having cut off the throat into the pot, he places it over the fire to drain the fat, together with the portions to be offered (*avadāna*).
He sets the embryo, wrapped in a turban, down at his side. Having taken the un-anointed portion like the other offerings, he places the fat on the south side.
At the time of offering the portions of the barren cow, the Pratiprasthātṛ cuts off the fat into the *pracaraṇī* ladle.
He offers the Avadāna portions following with the verses beginning "yasyai te" (9).
With the verses beginning "aṅgānyahrutā yasya" and "yasyāḥ," he follows according to the gender (10).
In the case of an unknown gender, he uses the masculine form (11).
Having returned between the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *vanaspati* offerings, the Pratiprasthātṛ cuts off all the fat (*medha*) into the *pracaraṇī* ladle.
He offers the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation following [the main offering] with the verse, "O Purudasma...
At the conclusion of the *sviṣṭakṛt*, there is either the binding of the turban-wrapped [victim] to a tree, its casting into the water, or its scattering upon the mound of earth for the burrows.

However, regarding these [cases], there is fear of being cursed; at the end of the *samiṣṭayajus* offering, one should offer into the *śāmitra* fire while standing with the mantra "O Maruts," without uttering *svāhā*. With the mantra "The great heaven," he covers [the fire] with embers.

16 While the verse "May Brahmanaspati go forth" is being recited, he mutters the names of the winds, beginning with "Thee for the ocean," as he goes toward the Āhavanīya fire. 17
He pours from the *upayamanī* ladle [into the *gharma*] with the words, "Svāhā to the Gharma!
(1). Having murmured, "Svāhā! The Gharma for the fathers," he steps across, calls for the *śrauṣaṭ*, and says, "Recite the offering-verse for the Gharma! (2).
When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the oblation with the verse, "All the quarters... (3).
"Place me in heaven!"—with these words he shakes [the vessel] three times.
4. "Svāhā to Agni!"—at the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call, [he offers]. 5. "O Aśvins, the Gharma!"—with these words the Brahman priest pronounces the consecration formula. 6.
"Drink!"—thus the sacrificer [says]. 7.
"Swell for nourishment!"—with these words he addresses the [milk] as it swells. 8.
"Thou art the Gharma"—saying this, he steps out toward the northeast quarter. 9.
He places [the vessel] on the mound with the formula, "Amen to us.

He offers oblations with chips of *vikaṅkata* wood, dipping them repeatedly into the *gharma* with each mantra: "Svāhā to Pūṣan, to Śaras! Having offered each oblation, he leans it against the first enclosing-stick (*paridhi*).
Looking toward the north, he hides the fourth oblation on the sacrificial grass to the south; 13.

and looking toward the south, he gives the seventh oblation, smeared with all the remnants, to the Pratiprasthātṛ; 14. he (the Pratiprasthātṛ) throws it out toward the north from the north side of the hall. 15.
With the mantra "Svāhā saṃ jyotiṣā," he pours the gharma-mixture into the *upayamanī* ladle; 16.
he offers the *rauhiṇa* oblation; 17. and he throws away the remnants of the clarified butter. 18.
Having offered according to the procedure of the Agnihotra, they consume [the remains] like the *vājina*, saying, "The honey has been offered.

19. Having washed [the vessels] in the mound for the remnants (*ucchiṣṭakhara*), he sets down the *upayamanī* [ladle]. Or, at this point, the throwing-in of the fire-sticks (*upaśritapraharaṇa*) takes place; he causes [the sacrificer] to recite after [the verses] as they are being set down. 20. Some say [he causes him to recite] after [the verses] as they are being set down. 21.
When the verse "sūyavasādbhagavatī" is being recited, some give grass and water to the cow; 22.
he places everything upon the seat; 23.
[he addresses] the mahāvīra with the verse "abhīmam. 24.
The placing and sprinkling [of the implements] are performed once for the mortar, the post, the pegs, the black antelope skin, the spade, the side-lying board, and the stool;
or rather, they are repeated because they belong to the time of the principal rite.
At the conclusion of the Upasads, the Pravargya equipment is removed.

Having placed it in the *parigharmya* vessel within the enclosure, having carried it out by the south, and having kindled three fire-sticks over the *ucchiṣṭakhara*, the *Āgnīdhra* holds them while they are being kindled, reciting the *Śatarudriya* formula in reverse order over the measuring-boards. He makes an offering with four ladlings of clarified butter, reciting for each verse: "O Gharma, that divine heat of thine... Having thrown in the third [stick], he sits down.
With the formula "For the power of the Kṣatriya," he steps out, having placed the wife in front and screened from view; he causes the Sāman to be chanted with the *avabhṛtha* as its place,
and likewise the *nidhana*.
They go to the place of the *utsādana* (removal) unclothed to the *uttaravedi*.
Having sprinkled [the fire] three times with the mantra "He has cried out" (*acikradat*), either according to the sequence of the ritual or according to the sequence of the mantras.
He places the *pravṛñjanīyā* brick so that it does not touch the navel, with the formula "four hymns" (RV 10.184).
The other two [bricks] are oriented eastward. And he silently places the *upaśayā* brick.
The two *parīśās* are on both sides; the two *rauhiṇa-havani* ladles are placed outside and drawn away;

the *abhri* is to the north, the throne-seat (*āsandī*) to the south, the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) to the north, and the fans (*dhavitra*), the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), the cord for binding, and the sacrificial grass-bundle (*veda*) are placed behind, having set down the supporting ladle (*upayamanī*).
Behind [the *ukhā*] are the two *piñjūlī* grass-bundles on both sides of the staff; behind [them] is the pillar with its cross-beams,
and also the two *rauhiṇa* potsherds.
In the middle is another [pit]; the *khara* for the vowels is to the north. To the south, outside the altar, is the site of the *mārjālīya*, the *khara* for the remnants;
he fills these with milk so that they may hold liquid, saying: "O Gharma, this is for you."
He gives the remainder, mixed with the fast-food, to the initiated one (24).
If it has been given as pure [fast-food] alone (25),
the sprinkling around takes place here (26).

"Sing the two Vārṣāhara Sāmans at the Iṣṭāhotṛya," he commands. They perform the purificatory sprinkling (mārjana) at the Cātvāla pit with the formula, "O friends, may we... together with their wives. With the verse, "Upwards, we...", he steps out and goes toward the north-eastern part without looking back. Taking a fuel-stick with the formula, "Thou art fuel," he places it on the Āhavanīya fire; the wife likewise places one with the formula, "Thou art kindling-stick," on the Gārhapatya fire. He gives two hundred-measure gold pieces for the Pravṛñjanīya rite to the Brahman priest. He gives the Gharma-milking cow to the Adhvaryu, the sacrificer’s vow-milking cow to the Hotṛ, and a she-goat to the Udgātṛ and the Agnīdh.
Regarding the breaking of the *gharma* vessel, it is said:
"30. One should make another [vessel] like the *ukhā*; 31. one should proceed with an unbroken [vessel]."

"svāhā to the vital breaths together with their presiding deities"—with this [formula], he performs the first and the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) while reciting "the desire and intention of the mind"; 33.
and "Prajāpati being gathered together," at the appropriate times; 34. and "Savitṛ on the first day," every day. 35.
One should prepare the *pravṛñjana* for Avakāśya (36).
Not at the first sacrifice (37).
With the verse "As great as are heaven and earth" (*yāvatī dyāvāpṛthivī*), there is the taking of the *dadhigharma* cup; with "In me that" (*mayi tyat*), there is the consumption (38).
The wiping [of the face] with the mantra "tviṣaḥ saṃvṛk" occurs at the *cātvāla* pit during the Mahāvrata rite (sūtra 39).
The performance of the *śāntikaraṇa* (rite for pacification) takes place at the beginning and the end, because it is observed in the *svādhyāya* (Vedic study) texts (sūtras 41–42).
Thus ends the Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra.
